blocks.question: What makes an input policy useful?
blocks.text: It preserves necessary communication while reducing prompts that do not serve a chosen purpose.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Leave room for recovery and wandering
lessons.name: 06.08 Leave room for recovery and wandering

blocks.text: Does my attention plan include periods when I am not forcing output?
Core idea

Sustained concentration is not the only useful mental mode. Rest, ordinary movement, and unstructured reflection can change how you return to a problem. Do not prescribe a universal schedule from a successful person's routine. Observe your own demands and constraints, and distinguish restorative breaks from activities that leave you more fragmented. Protect adequate rest rather than treating early rising as inherently superior.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Deep focus, stillness, and creative incubation describe complementary practices. They become a conflict when constant intensity is treated as the sole measure of seriousness.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After a demanding draft, you step away and later notice a simpler structure. The break supports the work without needing to guarantee an insight.

steps.label: Recover
steps.text: Allow a suitable change of pace.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify a type of break after which you usually return more steadily.
Course note: Include it in a demanding day and record its effect without expecting a miracle.
Reflection
Course note: Am I resting or merely changing the source of stimulation?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why include recovery in an attention plan?
blocks.text: Attention is used across a whole day, and sustainable work requires more than repeatedly demanding maximum concentration.
Course note: Focus and recovery: [[06.05 Design a focused work session]] · [[08.07 Treat recovery as part of training]] · [[23.03 Build a repeatable work ritual]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Close the day with a next action
lessons.name: 06.09 Close the day with a next action

blocks.text: What can I leave clear enough that tomorrow does not begin with rediscovery?
Core idea

End a work period by recording what is complete, what remains uncertain, and the next concrete action. Capture loose obligations in a trusted place and review the immediate schedule. This reduces the need to reconstruct context later. A shutdown routine should be brief and adaptable; it is not proof that all work is finished or that your mind must become silent.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Capturing commitments connects time management to habit cues and honest promises. Closure is a practical transition, not a demand for perfect emotional closure.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You leave a note saying which argument needs evidence and where the relevant document is, instead of a vague reminder to continue research.

steps.label: Transition
steps.text: Leave work with a usable return point.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: End one work period with a three-line status and next-action note.
Course note: Use the note at the next session and revise anything that was too vague.
Reflection
Course note: What do I repeatedly have to rediscover because I never record it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in a useful closing note?
blocks.text: Completed work, unresolved questions, and a specific next action with enough context to resume.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Review time through evidence
lessons.name: 06.10 Review time through evidence

blocks.text: What did the week reveal about my plan's assumptions?
Core idea

Compare intended and actual time without treating either as a moral score. Look for inaccurate estimates, recurring interruptions, neglected obligations, and genuinely useful deviations. Choose one adjustment rather than redesigning your entire life every week. Preserve what worked. A good review improves the next plan and makes trade-offs visible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This closes the loop between values, habits, and attention. The next module applies the same evidence-oriented approach to learning itself.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Your plan assumed five uninterrupted evenings; only two were realistic. You protect those two and redesign the remaining sessions instead of repeatedly promising an impossible week.
Practice
Course note: Compare one week's planned activities with what actually happened.
Course note: Change one estimate, agreement, or priority for the following week.
Reflection
Course note: Which assumption keeps surviving despite repeated contrary evidence?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a weekly time review produce?
blocks.text: A concrete adjustment based on observed patterns, while preserving effective parts of the plan.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make a daily list fit the actual day
lessons.name: 06.11 Make a daily list fit the actual day

blocks.text: How can a task list help without pretending the day has unlimited capacity?
Core idea

A list records obligations, but it is not a schedule. Estimate the time and preparation each task needs, then compare the total with available time after fixed duties, breaks, and likely interruptions. Identify one or two outcomes that matter most. Move or renegotiate the rest explicitly. This prevents a long list from making every day look like a failure. It also exposes a structural overload that cannot be solved by writing smaller boxes.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[04 Agency, responsibility, and boundaries]] supports renegotiating commitments. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] supplies opportunity cost: choosing one task means giving time from another. Use the list to make that trade-off visible.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You have six hours free and list eleven hours of work. The useful action is to schedule the two essential tasks, tell one person their request will be late, and move the remaining work rather than silently expecting a miracle.
Practice
Course note: Estimate time for tomorrow's tasks and compare it with time truly available.
Course note: Select two priority outcomes, then explicitly defer, delegate, or renegotiate at least one other item.
Reflection
Course note: Was the problem my pace, the list, or the amount of work promised?
Recall check

blocks.question: What turns a task list into a realistic plan?
blocks.text: Comparing estimated effort with available time and making explicit choices about what will not fit.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Recognize busywork as avoidance of uncertainty
lessons.name: 06.12 Recognize busywork as avoidance of uncertainty

blocks.text: Am I doing easy visible tasks to postpone a harder important one?
Core idea

Small tasks can be necessary, but they also offer quick completion and a feeling of control. Notice when you repeatedly choose them before a task whose next step is unclear, whose result will be judged, or whose consequences matter. Ask what uncertainty you are avoiding. Define the smallest useful step in the important work and give it a short protected window. The purpose is not to despise administration; it is to prevent administration from occupying every hour in which thinking could happen.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] describes resistance during uncertain work. [[03 Emotions, acceptance, and a steadier response]] helps you stay with discomfort long enough to start. A time log can distinguish a real operational duty from an avoidance pattern.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You keep reorganizing project folders while a proposal remains unwritten. The first useful step may be listing the audience, decision, and three missing facts. That is less polished than a new folder system but moves the proposal.

steps.label: Clarify
steps.text: Name the uncertainty and first step.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify an important task repeatedly displaced by small tasks. Write the specific uncertainty you face.
Course note: Work on a ten-minute first step before opening routine messages. Record what became clearer.
Reflection
Course note: Which small task was necessary, and which protected me from an uncertain one?
Recall check

blocks.question: How can busywork differ from useful administration?
blocks.text: It may create visible activity while repeatedly displacing a more important task whose uncertainty has not been addressed.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Give interruptions an agreed route
lessons.name: 06.13 Give interruptions an agreed route

blocks.text: How can I protect focus while remaining reachable for real needs?
Core idea

An interruption policy works only when other people know how to reach you for genuinely urgent matters. Choose a focus period, a channel for exceptions, and a time when ordinary requests will be handled. Invite colleagues or family to help define what counts as urgent. If your role requires immediate responses, design shorter focus windows rather than pretending the demand does not exist. The goal is a shared arrangement, not disappearing without explanation.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] helps negotiate the arrangement. [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] shows how an individual schedule depends on team expectations. Attention is partly a coordination problem.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A teammate needs quick answers during a release. You agree that production failures go by phone, routine questions go in a shared queue, and the queue is checked at two set times. Both responsiveness and concentrated work have a route.
Practice
Course note: List the three most common sources of interruption and which truly need immediate attention.
Course note: Propose one focus window and one urgent channel to the relevant people. Revise it from their feedback.
Reflection
Course note: Which interruptions came from unclear expectations rather than unavoidable events?
Recall check

blocks.question: What must an interruption policy include?
blocks.text: A focus period, a route for genuine urgency, a time for ordinary requests, and agreement with affected people.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Leave a buffer for work that does not announce itself
lessons.name: 06.14 Leave a buffer for work that does not announce itself

blocks.text: Why does a tightly filled calendar fail even when my estimates look reasonable?
Core idea

Estimates often describe the visible task and omit setup, travel, recovery, clarifying questions, and unexpected changes. A calendar filled to its edges assumes none of these will occur. Look at recent days to estimate ordinary variability, then leave space for it. A buffer is not wasted time; it is capacity for the work as it actually happens. If every buffer is immediately claimed by new commitments, the plan has not gained resilience.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] calls this attention to uncertainty and slack. [[27 Physical training, recovery, and nutrition literacy]] makes a similar distinction between useful load and capacity to recover. A schedule is a model, not a command to reality.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Four meetings are planned back to back. Each needs five minutes of preparation and one follow-up. A buffer between two meetings protects those tasks and reduces errors more than pretending the meetings are the only work.

steps.label: Adjust
steps.text: Use actual days to revise estimates.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Review three recent days and identify time omitted from the original plan.
Course note: Add one evidence-based buffer to tomorrow's schedule and record whether it was used.
Reflection
Course note: Did I treat necessary transition time as a personal failure?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a buffer represent?
blocks.text: Capacity for ordinary uncertainty, transitions, and follow-up that a task-only estimate leaves out.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Limit inputs to fit the work in front of you
lessons.name: 06.15 Limit inputs to fit the work in front of you

blocks.text: Which incoming information is useful for this task, and which only creates activity?
Core idea

More input can improve a decision until it overwhelms the attention needed to use it. Before a focused session, name the question and the sources or messages required now. Keep a place to capture other items for later review. An input limit is a temporary design for the task, not a rule to ignore responsibilities or people. Afterward, check whether the limit helped the work and whether anything important was missed.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] asks for relevant evidence. [[04 Agency, responsibility, and boundaries]] helps agree on availability where others depend on you.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A writer drafts a proposal with the brief and two reference documents open, while placing unrelated messages in a scheduled review window.
Practice
Course note: For one work block, list the inputs needed and two common inputs to defer.
Course note: Set a clear route for urgent matters that genuinely cannot wait.
Reflection
Course note: Which source felt productive merely because it arrived during the session?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a task-specific input limit?
blocks.text: A temporary choice to admit information needed for the current question while routing other inputs to a later review.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Count the cost of switching tasks
lessons.name: 06.16 Count the cost of switching tasks

blocks.text: What happens when I repeatedly leave a difficult task and return?
Core idea

Switching can be necessary, but every restart may require recovering context, remembering a decision, and resisting the next interruption. Track a short period before declaring yourself incapable of focus. Group related tasks where possible, write a restart cue before leaving, and agree on an interruption route with people who need you. The point is to reduce avoidable switching while preserving responsiveness to real needs.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07 Learning, memory, and understanding]] uses retrieval cues. [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] makes handoffs and interruptions visible.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An analyst writes the next calculation and open question before pausing for a meeting; the note cuts the time needed to resume.
Practice
Course note: Count task switches in one ordinary work period and note what triggered each.
Course note: Write a one-line restart cue before the next planned interruption.
Reflection
Course note: Which switch was unavoidable, and which did I use to escape uncertainty?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why record a restart cue before switching?
blocks.text: It preserves the next step and unresolved context so returning requires less reconstruction.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Begin with a question you can answer
lessons.name: 07.01 Begin with a question you can answer

blocks.text: What exactly am I trying to learn from this material?
Core idea

A learning goal should identify a performance, not merely a topic. Understand economics is too broad to guide a study session. Explain opportunity cost using a real choice can be practiced and checked. Start by naming the question, what you already know, and what evidence would show improvement. Revise the question as the subject becomes clearer.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Reflective inquiry and deliberate practice meet when a question becomes a testable skill. The study plan should change when you discover that your first question was too vague.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You want to improve presentations. Instead of collecting tips, you choose to check whether a listener can state your main point after a two-minute talk.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite one broad study intention as a specific question and performance.
Course note: Attempt a small example before reading; note what you cannot yet explain.
Reflection
Course note: What would count as evidence that I learned something?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a learning goal testable?
blocks.text: It specifies a performance or explanation that can be attempted and checked.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Explain before rereading
lessons.name: 07.02 Explain before rereading

blocks.text: Can I reconstruct the idea without seeing the page?
Core idea

Rereading can feel fluent because the words are familiar. Close the source and try to explain the central claim, evidence, and limits from memory. Then reopen it to find omissions or distortions. Difficulty during retrieval is information about what still needs work. Keep the explanation short enough to compare with the original material.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Recall cards are useful for discrete distinctions, while longer explanations reveal whether you can connect steps in an argument. Use both when the topic demands them.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After reading about a causal claim, you write what the proposed cause changes and what other factor might explain the association. The source reveals that you forgot the comparison group.
Practice
Course note: Study one short passage, close it, and explain its main idea in your own words.
Course note: Reopen the passage and mark three errors or missing details, then retry later.
Reflection
Course note: Which idea felt familiar but was difficult to produce?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why test recall before rereading?
blocks.text: Retrieval exposes gaps that familiarity with the page can conceal.
Course note: Memory and understanding: [[07.05 Use a memory palace with clear limits]] · [[07.07 Compare examples that almost fit]] · [[07.12 Design retrieval cues that survive forgetting]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish facts, principles, and procedures
lessons.name: 07.03 Distinguish facts, principles, and procedures

blocks.text: What kind of knowledge is this, and how should I practice it?
Core idea

A fact can often be retrieved directly; a principle should explain several cases; a procedure requires performance under conditions. Do not study all three only as definitions. Practice a principle by applying it to a new example and testing its limits. Practice a procedure through appropriate, safe performance and feedback. Some specialized procedures require qualified instruction rather than reading alone.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The collection ranges from philosophy to sport to engineering. One study method will not fit all its forms of knowledge.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Knowing that a balance sheet has assets and liabilities is different from explaining how a transaction changes both, which differs again from keeping accurate records over time.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Check performance in a new case.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Classify one chapter's main content as facts, principles, procedures, or a mix.
Course note: Design a matching check for each kind of knowledge you identified.
Reflection
Course note: Am I memorizing words for a skill that requires application?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why classify the knowledge type?
blocks.text: Different kinds of knowledge require different practice and evidence of understanding.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build associations that help retrieval
lessons.name: 07.04 Build associations that help retrieval

blocks.text: What cue will help me reconstruct this idea later?
Core idea

Memory improves when information connects to an existing structure. Create a cue that points to the meaning, not just an arbitrary sound. A vivid image can help recall a list, but recall of the list does not guarantee understanding of its use. Use associations for material worth retaining, then test them after a delay and replace cues that fail.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Mnemonic systems and explanation-based learning have different strengths. A cue retrieves a point; reasoning tells you whether and when the point applies.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You remember the three parts of a strategy by picturing a map with a problem marked, a route chosen, and coordinated travelers. You still test whether your real plan contains each part.

steps.label: Link
steps.text: Attach new material to a cue.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Create one image or association for a short useful list.
Course note: Retrieve the list later and explain what each item does in a real example.
Reflection
Course note: Does the cue help me use the idea or only repeat its label?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a memory cue for?
blocks.text: It aids retrieval; understanding and appropriate use still need separate checks.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use a memory palace with clear limits
lessons.name: 07.05 Use a memory palace with clear limits

blocks.text: How can spatial cues help me remember ordered information?
Core idea

Choose a familiar route with distinct locations. Place one memorable image at each location and mentally walk the route to retrieve the sequence. Keep the mapping stable and check whether each image uniquely points to its intended item. This can help ordered recall, especially for a speech or list. It does not create photographic memory or make an argument true.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The memory palace described in several collection texts works best when paired with explanation and spaced retrieval rather than treated as an all-purpose replacement for learning.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You place three distinct images along a familiar room route to recall the opening, comparison, and conclusion of a short talk.
Practice
Course note: Choose five familiar locations and assign one non-sensitive idea to each.
Course note: Recall the sequence later without looking, then explain the ideas without relying on the images.
Reflection
Course note: Which image was ambiguous or easily confused with another?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a memory palace provide?
blocks.text: Spatial retrieval cues for ordered information, not automatic understanding or proof.
Course note: Memory and understanding: [[07.02 Explain before rereading]] · [[07.07 Compare examples that almost fit]] · [[07.12 Design retrieval cues that survive forgetting]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Space practice and revisit errors
lessons.name: 07.06 Space practice and revisit errors

blocks.text: When should I return to material after first learning it?
Core idea

Revisit ideas after enough time that recall requires effort, then adjust the interval according to performance. If you cannot retrieve something, correct it and return sooner; if it is stable, spend more time on harder items. Space must not mean abandoning a confusing concept between sessions. Use short checks, then apply the idea in new settings.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Habit design helps make reviews repeatable. Feedback ensures the repeated work targets real gaps rather than the easiest familiar material.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You review a reasoning distinction the next day, a few days later, and again after using it in an argument. The precise schedule changes when you miss it.

steps.label: Adjust
steps.text: Use errors to set the next review.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Create a modest return schedule for three concepts you want to keep.
Course note: Track misses and move the hardest concept into an earlier review.
Reflection
Course note: Am I revisiting a concept because it is easy or because it needs attention?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of spaced retrieval?
blocks.text: To check and strengthen recall over time while directing more practice to unstable knowledge.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare examples that almost fit
lessons.name: 07.07 Compare examples that almost fit

blocks.text: Where does this concept apply, and where does it fail?
Core idea

A single vivid example can make a concept feel clearer than it is. Compare a case that fits, a case that does not, and a boundary case. Explain the decisive feature in each. This prevents learning only the surface appearance. When people disagree about a concept, look at the cases where their definitions produce different judgments.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Logic, science, and skill coaching all use discriminating examples to reveal the real rule. This also improves the quality of flashcards: ask for a distinction, not only a term.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You study sunk costs by comparing a past payment that cannot be recovered with a future expense that can still be avoided. Treating both as sunk would lead to a poor decision.
Practice
Course note: Create one fitting, one nonfitting, and one uncertain example for a current idea.
Course note: Explain the feature that changes the classification in each case.
Reflection
Course note: Which example exposed a limit in my first definition?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why use near misses in learning?
blocks.text: They reveal which features actually distinguish a concept from similar cases.
Course note: Memory and understanding: [[07.02 Explain before rereading]] · [[07.05 Use a memory palace with clear limits]] · [[07.12 Design retrieval cues that survive forgetting]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask for feedback that identifies an error
lessons.name: 07.08 Ask for feedback that identifies an error

blocks.text: What kind of feedback would tell me what to change?
Core idea

General praise or disappointment gives little direction. Request feedback on a specific attempt against a known standard. Ask where the explanation breaks, which step is missing, or what alternative was overlooked. Evaluate feedback carefully: an observer may see the result but not the underlying conditions. Use the response to design the next attempt.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Self-study and instruction both become more effective when feedback is timely, specific, and tied to a skill. A score alone cannot explain the gap.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Instead of asking whether an essay is good, you ask whether each paragraph supports the stated claim and where the evidence is insufficient.
Practice
Course note: Choose one work sample and write a specific feedback question.
Course note: Ask a knowledgeable reader or compare it with a reliable worked example.
Reflection
Course note: Which comment identified a change I can actually test?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes feedback actionable?
blocks.text: It identifies a specific feature of performance against a standard that can guide another attempt.
Course note: Repetition and improvement: [[05.09 Distinguish repetition from deliberate improvement]] · [[08.03 Build a feedback loop]] · [[38.06 Practice one technical component at a time]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Transfer an idea without stretching it beyond evidence
lessons.name: 07.09 Transfer an idea without stretching it beyond evidence

blocks.text: What part of this lesson can be used in a different setting?
Core idea

Transfer means recognizing a shared structure across different situations. Name the structure, the differences, and the conditions required for the idea to work. A metaphor is a starting point, not proof. Sport, business, and personal decisions can all involve planning, but their stakes, feedback, and ethical limits differ. Transfer carefully enough that the new setting can challenge the original idea.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: An integrated course depends on transfer. It becomes superficial when every domain is treated as interchangeable.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: In a practice drill, you identify several approaches before choosing. In a work decision, you similarly list alternatives, but you also ask affected colleagues and consider costs that the drill does not contain.
Practice
Course note: Apply one idea to a second domain and list two relevant differences.
Course note: State one condition under which the transfer would fail.
Reflection
Course note: Am I learning a structure or forcing an appealing analogy?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes transfer responsible?
blocks.text: It identifies a shared mechanism while checking differences, limits, and consequences in the new setting.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep a living knowledge map
lessons.name: 07.10 Keep a living knowledge map

blocks.text: How can my notes show relationships instead of becoming a pile of excerpts?
Core idea

Record each important idea as a question, an explanation, and a link to a related or conflicting idea. Keep the link meaningful: say whether the ideas support, narrow, or challenge each other. Revisit the map as your understanding changes. A graph full of connections is visually pleasing but educationally weak if its edges have no reason.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course knowledge map makes real lesson links visible. Your own map should add evidence from your attempts, not merely copy the site's structure.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You link habit cues to digital prompts, then note that a cue can serve a chosen practice or a product's engagement target.

steps.label: Revise
steps.text: Use evidence to update the map.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Create three linked notes with one sentence explaining each relationship.
Course note: Add a counterexample or limit to one connection after a real application.
Reflection
Course note: Which important tension is missing from my notes because I prefer a tidy story?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a knowledge link useful?
blocks.text: An explicit relationship that can be explained, applied, and revised.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Turn a chapter into answerable questions
lessons.name: 07.11 Turn a chapter into answerable questions

blocks.text: How do I find out whether I understood a reading rather than merely recognized it?
Core idea

Before or after reading a section, write questions it should help you answer. Include at least one question about a claim, one about how it works, and one about its limits. Close the book and answer in your own words. Check what you missed, especially distinctions you blurred. Recognition while looking at a page can feel like mastery, but retrieval shows what you can use without the page present.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[10 Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement]] helps ask about support and assumptions. [[08 Practice, performance, and adaptation]] turns retrieval errors into the next practice target. Not every chapter contains an answer to every question; that absence is also useful information.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After reading about opportunity cost, you ask what choice is being compared, what the next-best option is, and whether the example includes non-money costs. Your answer reveals that you remembered the slogan but omitted the alternative.

steps.label: Ask
steps.text: Write claim, mechanism, and limit questions.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Correct gaps and improve the questions.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a short chapter and write three answerable questions before rereading it.
Course note: Answer without the text, check each response, and revise one question that was too vague.
Reflection
Course note: Which idea felt familiar but was difficult to explain from memory?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why use self-written questions during reading?
blocks.text: They make the intended understanding explicit and create a retrieval test beyond recognition.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Design retrieval cues that survive forgetting
lessons.name: 07.12 Design retrieval cues that survive forgetting

blocks.text: What will help me find an idea again after its original context is gone?
Core idea

A cue should point clearly to the information you need, yet not contain the whole answer. A location in a memory palace, a distinctive image, a question, or a well-chosen example can make retrieval easier. Test the cue after a delay. If it retrieves several competing items or nothing at all, revise it. Memorized material still needs understanding and external verification when accuracy matters. A vivid cue is a route to an idea, not proof that the idea is true.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[31 Mind, behavior, and consciousness]] reminds us that memory is reconstructive. [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] distinguishes a tool for recall from evidence for a claim. Use cues especially where exact recall serves a real task.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: To remember three stages of a process, you place distinct images at three familiar locations. The next day, the second image recalls only a vague feeling. You replace it with a more specific image and test again.
Practice
Course note: Build three cues for three ideas you need next week. Write the intended answer beside each cue.
Course note: Test after twenty-four hours and note which cue was ambiguous. Revise that cue rather than rereading everything.
Reflection
Course note: Did the cue help me retrieve an understood idea or only a label?
Recall check

blocks.question: How do you know a memory cue works?
blocks.text: It reliably retrieves the intended information after a delay without confusing it with similar items.
Course note: Memory and understanding: [[07.02 Explain before rereading]] · [[07.05 Use a memory palace with clear limits]] · [[07.07 Compare examples that almost fit]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Troubleshoot a memory palace
lessons.name: 07.13 Troubleshoot a memory palace

blocks.text: What should I change when a memory journey stops working?
Core idea

A memory palace is a route through familiar locations with items placed at distinct points. Failures can come from crowded locations, an unclear order, similar images, or trying to store material you do not understand. Rewalk the route and identify where retrieval breaks. Repair that point: make the image more distinctive, move it, split a crowded location, or learn the concept before encoding it. Keep a separate record for high-stakes facts, because the method can fail like any other memory aid.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07.12 Design retrieval cues that survive forgetting]] focuses on individual cues. [[07.06 Space practice and revisit errors]] adds delayed checks. The useful question is not whether the method is powerful in theory but whether this route works for this material and learner.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You remember a list of ten concepts but confuse items four and five because both were placed near the same doorway. Giving each a separate landmark and testing the route backward clarifies the sequence.
Practice
Course note: Build a five-location route with five familiar items. Test it forward after a delay and mark the first failure.
Course note: Change only the failed location or cue, then test again the next day.
Reflection
Course note: Was the problem the route, the cue, or my understanding of the item?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should be diagnosed when a memory palace fails?
blocks.text: The order and distinctness of locations and images, plus whether the underlying material is understood.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Teach back a procedure without skipping decisions
lessons.name: 07.14 Teach back a procedure without skipping decisions

blocks.text: Can I explain when to use each step, not only repeat its name?
Core idea

A procedure includes choices about when to begin, what to check, what to do next, and when to stop or seek help. Teach it to an imagined beginner using a normal case and one exception. If you cannot explain why a step occurs or what changes in the exception, return to the source and identify the missing distinction. Teaching back is a test of understanding, not a license to instruct someone in a high-risk task from memory alone.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] emphasizes scope and assumptions. [[37 Health literacy and responsible care]] shows why a textbook procedure and qualified supervision are different. The method is most useful for ordinary study and safe practice.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You teach someone how to reconcile a small expense record. You can name the entries but cannot explain what to do when a receipt is missing. That exception shows what you need to learn next.
Practice
Course note: Select a low-risk procedure you are studying. Explain its start condition, steps, checks, and stop condition aloud.
Course note: Add one realistic exception and explain how the procedure changes. Mark any step you cannot justify.
Reflection
Course note: Which decision point did I omit when I first explained the procedure?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does teaching back reveal about a procedure?
blocks.text: Whether you understand its conditions and decision points rather than only remembering step names.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Take field notes that separate seeing from guessing
lessons.name: 07.15 Take field notes that separate seeing from guessing

blocks.text: What could I record now that memory might later rearrange?
Core idea

A field note preserves concrete details, timing, and uncertainty before a later story forms. Record what was seen or heard, then mark interpretations as interpretations. Keep the note short enough to make during real life and protect other people's privacy. When reviewing, look for omitted context and what changed your understanding. This is especially useful when a decision depends on a sequence of events, not on one dramatic impression.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] begins with description. [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] uses records to locate when a result changes.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team notes when requests arrive, when they are assigned, and when they are completed before guessing which person causes delays.
Practice
Course note: Write a brief hypothetical field note with time, observed detail, and a separately labeled inference.
Course note: Add one missing context question you would check later.
Reflection
Course note: What detail would I likely have filled in from expectation if I had waited a week?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a field note useful?
blocks.text: It preserves dated observations and uncertainty separately from later interpretation.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Test a remembered lesson against the page
lessons.name: 07.16 Test a remembered lesson against the page

blocks.text: Did I learn the author's claim, or a simpler version I made up?
Core idea

Retrieval practice is valuable, but a remembered answer can be confidently wrong or strip away qualifications. Explain the idea from memory first, then compare with the passage or worked example and mark differences. Note what the text actually supports and where your own application begins. This prevents both passive rereading and false certainty from an easy flashcard. If an original source is contested, accurate recall still does not make its claim true.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] separates a source's claim from its support. [[33 Philosophy, knowledge, and the good life]] asks for fair representation before criticism.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A learner recalls a chapter as saying intuition always fails; the text's narrower point concerns specific conditions for intuitive judgment.
Practice
Course note: Recall a source idea in three sentences without looking, then compare it with the original passage.
Course note: Write one qualification or counterexample your first recall omitted.
Reflection
Course note: Which simplification made the lesson easier to remember but less accurate?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why compare retrieval with the source?
blocks.text: Recall can expose learning and also reveal missing qualifications or mistaken claims.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define the skill you are practicing
lessons.name: 08.01 Define the skill you are practicing

blocks.text: What component of performance needs attention today?
Core idea

A broad performance goal can hide the exact skill limiting progress. Break the activity into components without forgetting how they work together. Choose a component that matters to the whole task and describe what a successful attempt would look like. A skill map should guide practice, not become a long inventory that delays it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Coaching, writing, and deliberate practice share the need to isolate a weakness and return it to full performance.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Instead of improving public speaking in general, you practice opening with a clear claim and one supporting example before adding delivery details.

steps.label: Reintegrate
steps.text: Use the skill in the whole task.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: List the component skills in one activity and select one limiting component.
Course note: Define a visible success criterion for three attempts.
Reflection
Course note: Is this component actually limiting the whole activity?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why isolate a component?
blocks.text: It makes practice and feedback specific enough to change performance.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Work at a useful level of challenge
lessons.name: 08.02 Work at a useful level of challenge

blocks.text: Is the task difficult enough to teach me and manageable enough to attempt?
Core idea

Practice should expose an error you can notice and correct. Tasks far below current ability maintain fluency; tasks far beyond it can produce confusion without useful feedback. Adjust speed, complexity, support, or stakes to find a workable challenge. The right level changes as you improve and may differ across days.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Flow discussions and sport progressions both concern challenge, but enjoyment is not guaranteed and safety matters in physical practice.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A football player practices one passing pattern before a varied game situation. A writer revises one argument paragraph before a full manuscript.
Practice
Course note: Rate a current practice task as maintenance, useful challenge, or overwhelming, and explain why.
Course note: Change one difficulty variable and compare the quality of your attempts.
Reflection
Course note: Am I hiding in easy repetition or jumping past the prerequisite?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes challenge useful?
blocks.text: It reveals a correctable limitation while remaining feasible and appropriately safe.

Course note: Physical challenge and care: [[27.02 Understand load, adaptation, and progression]] · [[28.02 Progress from isolated technique to live decisions]] · [[37.04 Distinguish wellness practice from clinical care]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a feedback loop
lessons.name: 08.03 Build a feedback loop

blocks.text: What signal will tell me whether my attempt improved?
Core idea

A feedback loop connects an attempt, an observation, an explanation, and a changed attempt. Choose a signal close to the skill, not merely a distant outcome. External results may be affected by luck, opponents, or conditions. Seek feedback from a reliable observer or an objective record where possible, while checking what each signal cannot show.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Decision quality and performance quality differ. A better method can have a disappointing single result, so compare repeated attempts and process evidence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A football player tracks whether they looked up before receiving, not only whether the team won. Video and coach feedback can reveal the choice process.
Practice
Course note: Identify one process signal and one outcome signal for a skill.
Course note: Use both after a short practice set and note where they disagree.
Reflection
Course note: Which signal have I been treating as the whole story?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in a feedback loop?
blocks.text: Attempt, observation, explanation, and a targeted change for the next attempt.

Course note: Repetition and improvement: [[05.09 Distinguish repetition from deliberate improvement]] · [[07.08 Ask for feedback that identifies an error]] · [[38.06 Practice one technical component at a time]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use mental rehearsal as preparation
lessons.name: 08.04 Use mental rehearsal as preparation

blocks.text: What can rehearsal clarify before the real attempt?
Core idea

Imagery can help you rehearse sequence, attention, and a response to a likely difficulty. Make it specific to the task and combine it with physical or written practice when appropriate. Imagining success does not guarantee performance, remove the need for feedback, or substitute for safety training. Rehearse how you will recover from a mistake as well as how you hope the ideal attempt unfolds.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Sports psychology and motivational visualization sometimes make very different claims. Keep the practical preparation function separate from claims that thought alone produces an external outcome.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before a presentation, you mentally walk through the opening and how you will answer an unclear question by asking for clarification.
Practice
Course note: Rehearse one short sequence and one likely interruption.
Course note: Perform the real or simulated task and compare what imagery prepared you for with what actually happened.
Reflection
Course note: Did rehearsal improve preparation or create an illusion of having practiced?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can mental rehearsal reasonably support?
blocks.text: Preparation of attention and sequence when paired with real practice and feedback.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Train under varied conditions
lessons.name: 08.05 Train under varied conditions

blocks.text: Will this skill still work outside the exact conditions in which I learned it?
Core idea

Repeating the same drill improves that drill. Varying context can reveal whether the underlying skill transfers. Add variation gradually: different examples, timing, partners, or constraints appropriate to the domain. Keep safety and prerequisites in view. Variation should test a capability, not create random difficulty for its own sake.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Sport drills, writing revisions, and conversation practice all benefit from moving between isolated exercises and realistic situations.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After practicing a clear explanation alone, you try it with someone who asks questions and then refine the part they found unclear.
Practice
Course note: Name one condition that is constant in your current practice but variable in real use.
Course note: Safely vary that condition and observe what breaks down.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of my ability exists only in a familiar setup?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why vary practice conditions?
blocks.text: To test whether a skill transfers beyond the exact drill or example used to learn it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Respond to pressure with a process cue
lessons.name: 08.06 Respond to pressure with a process cue

blocks.text: What should I attend to when the stakes feel high?
Core idea

Pressure can pull attention toward imagined judgment or consequences. Choose a small task-relevant cue that helps you return to the present action. The cue should be observable and rehearsed under lower stakes. It cannot remove all anxiety and should not become a superstition. Review afterward whether it improved the process rather than only whether the outcome was favorable.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Present-focus advice and performance planning work together when a cue points to a practiced behavior.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before answering a difficult question, you pause, restate what was asked, and then give the main point. The cue is the pause and restatement, not a command to feel confident.
Practice
Course note: Choose one short process cue for a recurring pressure moment.
Course note: Practice it in a low-stakes version before using it in a real attempt.
Reflection
Course note: Did the cue direct attention to an action or to how I looked to others?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a process cue useful?
blocks.text: It directs attention to a task-relevant action that has been practiced.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Treat recovery as part of training
lessons.name: 08.07 Treat recovery as part of training

blocks.text: What allows repeated practice without accumulating avoidable harm?
Core idea

Learning and physical training require periods in which the system can adapt. Plan sleep, suitable rest, and changes in workload according to the activity and individual condition. More intensity is not automatically more progress. If pain, illness, or persistent distress changes the situation, use appropriate qualified guidance rather than interpreting endurance stories as instructions to continue.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: High-intensity narratives and sport-science progression differ on how to read limits. The useful synthesis is disciplined effort with feedback and recovery, not a universal rule to push harder.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A runner facing persistent pain changes the training plan and seeks a qualified assessment rather than treating the pain as a test of character.
Practice
Course note: Record practice load, rest, and the quality of two consecutive attempts.
Course note: Adjust one recovery condition and observe whether performance and wellbeing improve.
Reflection
Course note: Am I calling depletion dedication because I have not defined a training plan?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is recovery part of practice?
blocks.text: Repeated learning and performance depend on conditions that allow adaptation and reduce avoidable harm.

Course note: Effort and limits: [[02.02 Choose the difficulty attached to the ambition]] · [[03.11 Separate discomfort, danger, and the need for support]] · [[27.05 Plan recovery as part of the session]].
Course note: Focus and recovery: [[06.05 Design a focused work session]] · [[06.08 Leave room for recovery and wandering]] · [[23.03 Build a repeatable work ritual]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Study failure without worshipping it
lessons.name: 08.08 Study failure without worshipping it

blocks.text: What did the unsuccessful attempt actually teach?
Core idea

Failure can reveal information, but the lesson is not automatic. Describe the objective, the action taken, the outcome, and the uncertainty. Separate an error in preparation from an unlucky result, and separate an ambitious attempt from a preventable risk. Some failures impose serious costs; do not romanticize them. Use the evidence to choose a narrower next test.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Resilience books emphasize returning after setbacks; decision science adds the discipline of analyzing process and uncertainty.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A proposal is rejected. You ask which requirements were unmet, identify one missing comparison, and improve the next proposal rather than declaring either permanent defeat or inevitable success.
Practice
Course note: Review one unsuccessful attempt with action, outcome, possible causes, and missing evidence.
Course note: Design a next attempt that tests one specific change.
Reflection
Course note: What am I claiming to have learned without actually checking it?
Recall check

blocks.question: Does failure automatically produce growth?
blocks.text: No. Learning requires examining causes, limits, and a testable change.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a practice cycle
lessons.name: 08.09 Build a practice cycle

blocks.text: What will I repeatedly do, inspect, and change?
Core idea

Combine a target skill, a suitable challenge, a feedback signal, a recovery plan, and a review date. Keep the cycle small enough to repeat. After each review, either continue, raise the challenge, change the method, or reconsider whether the goal is still worthwhile. The practice cycle should improve both capability and judgment about where to direct effort.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This closes the foundation phase: values select the skill, habits make practice regular, attention protects it, and learning methods reveal what you know. The next phase improves observation and reasoning.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: For three weeks, you practice a short explanation twice weekly, ask a listener to identify unclear steps, and revise one step at a time.
Practice
Course note: Write a one-page practice cycle with target, schedule, challenge, feedback, recovery, and review.
Course note: Run one full cycle and decide what changes in the next one.
Reflection
Course note: What evidence would make me continue, change, or stop this practice?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a practice cycle adaptive?
blocks.text: Specific attempts, relevant feedback, recovery, and a planned decision about the next cycle.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate practice from performance
lessons.name: 08.10 Separate practice from performance

blocks.text: Why should training look different from the moment I must deliver?
Core idea

During practice, you can pause, repeat, isolate errors, and accept a temporarily awkward method. During performance, you must often act with the skill available now and keep attention on the task. Trying to repair every detail in the middle of performance can interfere with it; never reviewing errors afterward prevents improvement. Plan both modes. Use practice to change a specific component and performance to test how the whole skill holds together.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] makes the distinction visible: a pilot can be paused and revised, while a live service must work with its current design. [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] makes room for drafting before release. The modes support one another when you review the transfer.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A speaker rehearses pauses and transitions slowly. During the talk, they focus on the audience and the next idea. Afterward, they review the recording and choose one component for the next rehearsal.

steps.label: Perform
steps.text: Use the whole skill in context.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify one skill and write what practice permits that performance does not.
Course note: Schedule one isolated drill and one whole-task attempt, then compare what transferred.
Reflection
Course note: Was I trying to learn during performance or only to look good during practice?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the practical difference between practice and performance?
blocks.text: Practice can isolate and repair components; performance uses the current skill in a whole task under real constraints.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use a brief pre-performance routine
lessons.name: 08.11 Use a brief pre-performance routine

blocks.text: How can I prepare for a demanding attempt without making preparation an endless ritual?
Core idea

A pre-performance routine can reduce last-minute decisions by checking equipment, reviewing the task, and choosing one process cue. Keep it short, repeatable, and tied to what the performance actually demands. A routine cannot guarantee calm or success. It should help you begin with usable attention, even if nerves remain. If preparation expands until it delays the attempt, it has become another problem to examine.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[06 Attention, time, and a workable day]] supplies a bounded preparation window. [[03 Emotions, acceptance, and a steadier response]] helps you act without demanding that anxiety disappear first. The cue should point to an action, not a mood.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before a difficult call, you check the agenda, write the first question, take a pause, and dial. You do not spend another hour trying to feel perfectly confident.
Practice
Course note: Design a three-step routine for one upcoming performance: necessary check, process cue, and start signal.
Course note: Use it twice and note whether each step helped the task or merely postponed it.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of preparation put my attention on the work?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a useful pre-performance routine?
blocks.text: It is brief, repeatable, and directs attention to the task without requiring a particular feeling or guaranteeing an outcome.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Train the weak link without making it your identity
lessons.name: 08.12 Train the weak link without making it your identity

blocks.text: How do I improve a limiting component of a skill?
Core idea

A whole performance may fail because of one component: reading the situation, preparing, executing, or recovering. Identify the limiting step from evidence, then design a drill that targets it. Keep the drill close enough to the real task that improvement can transfer. Retest in a whole attempt. Do not turn a current weakness into a permanent self-description; the point of isolating it is to make change possible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] uses the idea of a decisive constraint. [[27 Physical training, recovery, and nutrition literacy]] adds that increasing load without capacity can cause harm. A weak link is a training hypothesis, not a reason to ignore rest or context.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A player can pass accurately in a stationary drill but loses the ball after receiving under pressure. More stationary passes may not solve the limiting step; a supervised drill with scanning and movement may be needed.

steps.label: Retest
steps.text: Check transfer in a whole attempt.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Review a recent whole-task attempt and name the earliest step where performance broke down.
Course note: Design one safe, short drill for that component and one whole-task retest.
Reflection
Course note: Did improving the component change the whole performance, or was another constraint more important?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why retest a weak-link drill in the whole task?
blocks.text: Improvement in an isolated component matters only if it transfers to performance in context.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Set a challenge limit before motivation takes over
lessons.name: 08.13 Set a challenge limit before motivation takes over

blocks.text: What conditions would make continuing practice unwise today?
Core idea

A difficult goal can invite meaningful effort and also make a person ignore signals that need attention. Before a demanding session, define the intended challenge, support available, and reasons to stop or modify it. A memoir of extraordinary endurance can motivate questions about persistence, but it is not a training prescription for a different body or situation. Review performance over time, including recovery and ordinary functioning.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[27 Physical training, recovery, and nutrition literacy]] examines bodily warning signs. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] warns against copying an exceptional story as a general rule.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A runner sets an effort goal and also agrees to stop for worsening unusual pain, rather than treating every stop as weakness.
Practice
Course note: Write a challenge goal and two conditions for modifying a hypothetical practice session.
Course note: Identify who could give competent feedback if those conditions appear.
Reflection
Course note: Was I using ambition to make a safety question feel shameful?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why set a challenge limit in advance?
blocks.text: It preserves judgment about safety and recovery when effort and identity make stopping harder to consider.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Select feedback near the decision it should improve
lessons.name: 08.14 Select feedback near the decision it should improve

blocks.text: When and from whom will feedback be specific enough to use?
Core idea

Feedback is more actionable when it follows a visible attempt and addresses a decision or movement that can be changed. Ask a qualified observer for what they noticed, what effect it had, and one next adjustment. Immediate correction can help a simple skill; reflection after the attempt may serve a complex performance better. Avoid accumulating so many comments that none can be practiced. Check whether the change improves performance in the real setting.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07 Learning, memory, and understanding]] uses feedback to locate an error. [[28 Sport, movement, and supervised skill]] tests transfer beyond a drill.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A speaker asks a colleague to note where listeners became confused in a practice talk, then revises one transition before the next attempt.
Practice
Course note: For one skill, define the next attempt, observer, and one feedback question.
Course note: Choose a single change to test and a sign it helped.
Reflection
Course note: Was I seeking a judgment of my ability or information about the next attempt?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes performance feedback actionable?
blocks.text: It describes a specific attempt and a change that can be tested in the relevant setting.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Describe before interpreting
lessons.name: 09.01 Describe before interpreting

blocks.text: What did I actually see or hear?
Core idea

Observation records a detail that could, in principle, be checked. Interpretation gives it a meaning. The distinction matters especially when emotion or urgency makes the first story feel certain. Record timing, setting, and exact behavior when possible. Do not pretend observation is free of attention or memory limits; the point is to make the inference visible and open to correction.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Careful inquiry in science and in relationships begins with the same move, though the standards of evidence differ by setting.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A teammate spoke twice while you were presenting is more precise than the teammate tried to humiliate me. The first statement can anchor a conversation.
Practice
Course note: Write five observations from a recent event without motive words.
Course note: Add your interpretations in a separate column, each with an alternative.
Reflection
Course note: Which adjective was doing the work of evidence?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why separate observation from interpretation?
blocks.text: It makes the inference visible, testable, and open to other explanations.
Course note: Observation and interpretation: [[01.02 Separate facts, interpretations, and judgments]] · [[09.06 Interpret body language with humility]] · [[11.01 Ask what a claim would predict]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Establish a baseline before calling something unusual
lessons.name: 09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual

blocks.text: Compared with what is this behavior unusual?
Core idea

An anomaly is a difference from a relevant baseline, not merely something that catches your attention. Observe the person's or situation's ordinary pattern when appropriate and consider setting, role, and culture. Avoid profiling or treating a single movement as a reliable sign of deception or danger. If safety is at issue, use concrete behavior and appropriate support rather than speculative character reading.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Situational awareness can be useful; popular body-language claims often exaggerate how much a gesture reveals. Context matters more than a universal gesture dictionary.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A normally quiet meeting participant speaking more may reflect preparation, an urgent concern, or a changed meeting format. It does not identify a motive by itself.
Practice
Course note: Pick one noticed difference and describe the relevant baseline and context.
Course note: List at least two ordinary explanations before acting on the anomaly.
Reflection
Course note: Am I comparing this event with reality or with a stereotype?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is needed to interpret an anomaly?
blocks.text: A relevant baseline, context, and more evidence than a single ambiguous cue.
Course note: Intuition and evidence: [[09.08 Separate intuition from expertise]] · [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes]] · [[21.03 Separate symptoms from candidate causes]].
Course note: Safety and autonomy: [[18.08 Build a defensive pause]] · [[29.01 Define safety by the situation]] · [[29.03 Use distance and help before confrontation]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Notice selection and survivorship
lessons.name: 09.03 Notice selection and survivorship

blocks.text: Who or what is missing from the examples I can see?
Core idea

Visible successes are often selected from a larger set of attempts. If unsuccessful cases are absent, the qualities shared by winners may not explain success. Ask how cases entered the sample and what comparable failures looked like. This is especially important in advice drawn from famous people, spectacular companies, or elite athletes.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Motivational stories can supply possibilities and questions, but they are weak evidence for a guaranteed method when the denominator is unknown.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Ten successful founders wake early. Without examining unsuccessful early risers and successful late workers, wake time is not established as the cause.
Practice
Course note: Choose a success story and identify the missing comparison group.
Course note: Find one plausible alternative factor that could explain the result.
Reflection
Course note: Which inspiring example have I treated as a complete sample?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is survivorship bias?
blocks.text: A distorted conclusion caused by examining visible survivors while missing relevant failures or excluded cases.

Course note: Anecdote and selection: [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence]] · [[13.06 Tell an example without claiming it proves everything]] · [[36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use base rates before vivid details
lessons.name: 09.04 Use base rates before vivid details

blocks.text: How common is this outcome before I consider the special story?
Core idea

A vivid description can draw attention away from how often an event occurs in the relevant group. Begin with a reasonable base rate, then ask how much the new evidence should change it. Do not invent a precise probability from thin information. The aim is calibrated judgment: neither ignoring a distinctive clue nor letting it completely replace the background frequency.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Bayesian reasoning and everyday decision-making both rely on combining prior frequency with case-specific evidence. The quality of each input matters.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A rare condition does not become likely simply because one symptom sounds familiar. The appropriate next step may be professional assessment, not self-diagnosis from a memorable anecdote.
Practice
Course note: For one claim, identify the relevant group and approximate frequency information you would need.
Course note: State what new evidence would materially change the initial estimate.
Reflection
Course note: Did a vivid detail make me forget the broader comparison?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why consider base rates?
blocks.text: They provide a starting context for interpreting case-specific clues rather than letting vividness set the whole estimate.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Look for confirmation and disconfirmation
lessons.name: 09.05 Look for confirmation and disconfirmation

blocks.text: What evidence would challenge my preferred explanation?
Core idea

When a hypothesis feels right, it is easy to collect examples that support it and ignore failures. State the hypothesis in a form that predicts something observable, then look for evidence that could distinguish it from alternatives. A disconfirming case may reveal a boundary rather than destroy the whole idea. Do not manufacture symmetry where the evidence is genuinely one-sided.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Personal narratives, scientific inquiry, and evaluating advice all improve when a claim risks being corrected by observation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You believe you only focus at night. A carefully planned morning session succeeds, suggesting that quiet and preparation may matter more than the hour.
Practice
Course note: Write one favored explanation and one prediction that could fail.
Course note: Seek a counterexample or an alternative explanation in the next week.
Reflection
Course note: What observation would I be tempted to explain away?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a hypothesis useful?
blocks.text: It leads to observations that could distinguish it from other explanations.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Interpret body language with humility
lessons.name: 09.06 Interpret body language with humility

blocks.text: What can a nonverbal cue tell me, and what remains uncertain?
Core idea

Posture, expression, timing, and tone can help you notice that something may need clarification. They rarely reveal a hidden thought uniquely. People differ, situations vary, and the same movement can have many causes. Prefer respectful questions, patterns over time, and the person's own report. Avoid using a cue to diagnose deception, consent, attraction, or intent.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Observation books and fast-impression books can be read as prompts to notice more, while their strongest inference claims need critical evaluation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A listener looks away repeatedly. You ask whether the explanation is clear or whether a break would help instead of deciding they are dishonest.
Practice
Course note: Describe one nonverbal cue and list three plausible meanings.
Course note: Ask a neutral clarifying question if the situation warrants it.
Reflection
Course note: Have I turned an ambiguous signal into a verdict because certainty feels useful?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a responsible use of nonverbal cues?
blocks.text: As context-sensitive prompts for clarification, not as unique proof of a hidden mental state.
Course note: Observation and interpretation: [[01.02 Separate facts, interpretations, and judgments]] · [[09.01 Describe before interpreting]] · [[11.01 Ask what a claim would predict]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Recognize framing and anchoring
lessons.name: 09.07 Recognize framing and anchoring

blocks.text: How is the presentation of a choice influencing my judgment?
Core idea

A first number, label, or comparison can shape later estimates even when it is arbitrary. The same outcome can look different when framed as a gain, loss, risk, or missed opportunity. Write the underlying quantities and alternatives separately from the pitch. Ask whether the conclusion changes under a neutral description. A frame may be informative, but it should not be the only view available.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Marketing and behavioral finance use framing descriptively and strategically. Personal judgment needs the ability to examine its effects.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A plan is called 80 percent successful. Before choosing it, you also consider the 20 percent failure rate, the severity of failure, and the available alternatives.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite one persuasive offer using neutral quantities and all relevant options.
Course note: Compare your reaction to gain and loss descriptions of the same outcome.
Reflection
Course note: Which starting number or word narrowed my attention?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is anchoring?
blocks.text: An initial reference point influences later judgment, sometimes beyond its evidential value.

Course note: Money, framing, and risk: [[25.05 Compare borrowing by full cost and purpose]] · [[25.06 Treat investing as risk management, not a prediction contest]] · [[25.07 Notice behavioral traps around money]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate intuition from expertise
lessons.name: 09.08 Separate intuition from expertise

blocks.text: When is a fast judgment likely to be informative?
Core idea

Quick recognition can improve with repeated exposure to a stable environment and timely, accurate feedback. It is less trustworthy when the situation is novel, cues are weak, or feedback has been sparse or misleading. Notice confidence, but do not use it as the test of accuracy. Slow down when stakes are high or when the first impression rests on stereotypes or a single feature.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Accounts praising intuition and accounts cataloging bias are in tension. The practical question is what the environment and learning history permit the intuition to know.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An experienced editor notices an awkward transition in familiar prose. The same confidence does not establish a stranger's motives after one meeting.
Practice
Course note: Recall a fast judgment and identify the feedback history behind it.
Course note: Choose one high-stakes judgment to check with independent evidence.
Reflection
Course note: Where have I mistaken familiarity with a story for expertise in a domain?
Recall check

blocks.question: What conditions strengthen intuition?
blocks.text: Repeated experience in a sufficiently regular environment with useful feedback.
Course note: Intuition and evidence: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual]] · [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes]] · [[21.03 Separate symptoms from candidate causes]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep uncertainty visible
lessons.name: 09.09 Keep uncertainty visible

blocks.text: How sure am I, and why?
Core idea

Use ordinary calibrated language: observed, plausible, likely, unknown, or disputed. Identify the evidence and the remaining alternatives. Do not add numerical precision that the material cannot support. Confidence should change when relevant evidence changes. A judgment can still be actionable under uncertainty if its stakes, reversibility, and possible harms are considered.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This course contains claims of very different kinds. Calibrated language prevents a personal anecdote, philosophical argument, and controlled finding from sounding equally established.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You say a colleague may have misunderstood the deadline, supported by one message, rather than declaring their intention to sabotage the work.
Practice
Course note: Rate three recent claims by confidence and list the reason for each rating.
Course note: Revise one claim after finding new information.
Reflection
Course note: Which word makes me sound more certain than the evidence permits?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does calibrated judgment require?
blocks.text: Stating evidence, alternatives, and confidence at a level the evidence can support.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Run an observation audit
lessons.name: 09.10 Run an observation audit

blocks.text: Which of my judgments deserves another look?
Core idea

Select one recurring judgment and trace its path: observation, interpretation, prior expectation, missing comparison, and action. Identify where a bias could enter without assuming every judgment is biased. Then ask what low-cost check would improve the decision. Preserve the ability to act when perfect information is impossible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This module prepares the next three: logic checks argument form, science checks evidence, and systems thinking checks interactions over time.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You think a routine always works because you remember dramatic successes. A simple record reveals modest results and several unremembered failures.
Practice
Course note: Audit one judgment using the five-part path.
Course note: Perform one fair check and update the judgment, even if the update is small.
Reflection
Course note: What did I learn about how I form this kind of conclusion?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is an observation audit for?
blocks.text: To inspect how a conclusion arose and choose a check that could improve it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Stop sunk costs from making the next choice
lessons.name: 09.11 Stop sunk costs from making the next choice

blocks.text: What should I do when I have already spent time or money on a poor route?
Core idea

A past cost can explain why a choice matters emotionally, but it cannot be recovered by repeating a bad choice. Compare the future benefits and costs of continuing with those of changing course. Include switching costs, obligations, and learning already gained; do not pretend they are zero. The key distinction is whether a consideration changes what happens next or only makes you want to justify what happened before.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
