blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] provides a decision frame. [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] adds a limit: finishing a difficult project may still have future value. Sunk-cost reasoning is a warning to assess that value honestly, not a command to quit.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You paid for a course that teaches the wrong skill. Completing it might still provide a useful credential, or it may consume six weeks needed for a better route. The fee is gone either way; the coming six weeks are the decision.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Evaluate future options and switching costs.

steps.label: Choose
steps.text: Act on the better forward path.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose one commitment you hesitate to revise because of what you already invested. Separate past costs from future consequences.
Course note: Compare continuing and changing using only what each option can still produce.
Reflection
Course note: Which past investment was I trying to make feel worthwhile?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the sunk-cost mistake?
blocks.text: Allowing an irrecoverable past investment to decide a future choice when it does not change the options' future value.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Check availability before judging frequency
lessons.name: 09.12 Check availability before judging frequency

blocks.text: Am I treating a memorable example as a common event?
Core idea

Stories that are vivid, recent, frightening, or easy to recall can feel frequent. That feeling may be useful as a signal to investigate, but it is not a count. Ask what population and time period the claim concerns, how cases were selected, and whether a base rate is available. Sometimes reliable statistics are unavailable; in that case, say what you do not know rather than replacing data with a single memorable case.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] explains how to judge a sample. [[29 Safety, awareness, and de-escalation]] reminds you that a low-frequency event may still merit preparation when its cost is high. Frequency and consequence are different dimensions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After seeing a dramatic report about a travel incident, you consider cancelling every trip. You check how often comparable incidents occurred on the route and what practical precautions are relevant. The story remains real without becoming the whole risk estimate.

steps.label: Count
steps.text: Seek a relevant base rate or sample.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify a judgment influenced by one vivid example. State the population and time frame you would need to estimate frequency.
Course note: Find a reliable count if available; otherwise write an explicit uncertainty statement and a proportionate precaution.
Reflection
Course note: What made the example memorable, and did that change its frequency?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is recall ease a weak frequency measure?
blocks.text: Vividness and recency affect memory, while frequency requires information about the wider set of cases.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep hindsight from rewriting the decision
lessons.name: 09.13 Keep hindsight from rewriting the decision

blocks.text: How can I judge an earlier choice after I know how it turned out?
Core idea

Once an outcome is known, the path toward it can appear more obvious than it was. Preserve the information available at the decision time: options, forecasts, warnings, and reasons. Then review the decision against that record, not against facts learned later. A lucky outcome can hide a weak process, and an unlucky outcome can follow a sound one. Hindsight is most useful when it identifies a warning you realistically could have noticed.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12.03 Separate decision quality from outcome quality]] makes the core distinction. [[40 Integration and the life-practice capstone]] uses dated decision records so later learning does not become a fictional memory of certainty.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A project failed after a supplier closed unexpectedly. If the supplier's financial instability was visible beforehand, the plan may have missed a risk. If not, the better lesson may be to build a backup option rather than to claim you should have predicted that closure.

steps.label: Learn
steps.text: Change only what could improve a future choice.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Review one past decision. Reconstruct what you knew before the result without using later information.
Course note: Identify one warning that was genuinely available and one fact that only became known afterward.
Reflection
Course note: Did the outcome make my past confidence look more justified or less justified than it was?
Recall check

blocks.question: How does a decision record limit hindsight bias?
blocks.text: It preserves the information and reasons available before the outcome was known.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Calibrate confidence with a track record
lessons.name: 09.14 Calibrate confidence with a track record

blocks.text: How can I know whether my certainty is earned?
Core idea

Confidence is a feeling about a judgment; calibration asks how often similar judgments prove correct. For repeatable, low-stakes predictions, record your estimate before the result and compare over time. Exact percentages are unnecessary if you lack enough cases; broad bands such as unlikely, uncertain, and likely can still expose a pattern. Look for topics where you are too certain and topics where you underrate yourself. The point is to improve decisions, not to perform permanent doubt.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07 Learning, memory, and understanding]] uses feedback to correct errors. [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] supplies the statistical caution: a few outcomes do not establish a stable rate. Use calibration for recurring predictions, not a single unrepeatable life event.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You regularly predict that a work task will take one hour. A month of estimates and actual durations shows it usually takes two. Revising the estimate gives better plans without changing your worth.

steps.label: Forecast
steps.text: Record an estimate before the result.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Record five low-stakes predictions with a confidence band and a result date.
Course note: When results arrive, compare what happened with your bands and identify one domain to estimate differently.
Reflection
Course note: Where did confidence track experience, and where did it track desire?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is calibration?
blocks.text: The match between expressed confidence and how often comparable judgments prove correct over time.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Notice regression after an extreme result
lessons.name: 09.15 Notice regression after an extreme result

blocks.text: Did my intervention cause a return to normal, or might the extreme result have changed anyway?
Core idea

When a measure varies, unusually high or low results are often followed by more ordinary ones even without a new intervention. This is regression toward the mean. It does not prove an intervention failed or succeeded; it warns against giving it automatic credit for improvement after an extreme event. Compare repeated observations and, when possible, a relevant comparison group. Look for a plausible mechanism and timing.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] explains why a before-and-after story may be weak evidence. [[27 Physical training, recovery, and nutrition literacy]] is a common setting: one exceptional workout or bad week need not define a trend.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team changes its meeting format after its worst month and sees better results next month. The change may have helped, but the previous month was unusually poor; the team needs more data before assigning full credit.
Practice
Course note: Find a recent extreme result followed by a more ordinary one. List possible causes besides the action taken in between.
Course note: Choose two additional measures or comparison points that would strengthen the explanation.
Reflection
Course note: Did I give the most visible intervention more credit than the evidence allowed?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is regression toward the mean?
blocks.text: Extreme observations in a variable process tend to be followed by less extreme observations, which can mislead simple before-and-after judgments.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Notice the evidence that is missing
lessons.name: 09.16 Notice the evidence that is missing

blocks.text: If my explanation were right, what else would I expect to see?
Core idea

Observation includes absences, but an absence matters only when there was a clear reason to expect something. State the prediction before treating missing evidence as a clue. Check whether the setting would have made the evidence visible and whether another explanation predicts the same absence. This keeps 'what is not there' from becoming a license for imaginative suspicion. A useful missing clue narrows a question; it rarely settles a person's motive by itself.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] asks what a hypothesis predicts. [[29 Safety, awareness, and de-escalation]] favors concrete behavior over speculative threat reading.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A delivery report is absent from a shared folder. The team checks whether it was due, whether the folder was used, and whether email was an alternative route before inferring neglect.
Practice
Course note: Write one hypothesis and one observation you would expect if it were true.
Course note: Describe how you would know whether the expected evidence could have been seen.
Reflection
Course note: Did I treat an absence as proof without defining an expectation?
Recall check

blocks.question: When is missing evidence informative?
blocks.text: When a hypothesis predicts observable evidence that should have appeared under the actual conditions.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Audit a first impression with a short record
lessons.name: 09.17 Audit a first impression with a short record

blocks.text: How accurate are my quick judgments when I can check them later?
Core idea

An impression may be useful or misleading depending on training, feedback, and context. Write the impression, the specific cues, and a confidence estimate before learning the outcome. Later, compare it with what actually happened and note what remained unknowable. Do this for appropriate low-stakes situations, not as a method of judging strangers' character. The purpose is calibration: learning when to trust a cue and when to ask another question.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[31 Mind, behavior, and consciousness]] distinguishes behavior from an explanation. [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] offers direct conversation when an impression concerns another person.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A project lead predicts that a new handoff will confuse users because two labels overlap. A short user test confirms or challenges that impression.

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.text: Adjust future trust in the cue.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Record three low-stakes predictions with cue, confidence, and later outcome.
Course note: Find one case where an omitted fact changed your interpretation.
Reflection
Course note: Which kind of cue has earned confidence, and which only feels vivid?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of an impression audit?
blocks.text: To compare recorded predictions with outcomes and calibrate which cues are reliable in which settings.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Find the claim and its support
lessons.name: 10.01 Find the claim and its support

blocks.text: What is this person asking me to believe, and why?
Core idea

An argument contains a conclusion and reasons offered for it. In conversation, both may be implicit. State the conclusion in a fair form and identify the strongest available support before evaluating it. A vivid example, an instruction, and an insult are not automatically reasons for the conclusion. Avoid attacking a weaker version because it is easier to defeat.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Socratic questioning and formal logic begin with accurate reconstruction. Fairness makes disagreement more informative, not less rigorous.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A colleague proposes changing the meeting time because late sessions exclude caregivers. The claim concerns scheduling, and the reason concerns participation; it is not simply a dislike of meetings.
Practice
Course note: Take one disputed statement and write its conclusion and supporting reasons separately.
Course note: Ask the speaker whether your reconstruction is fair.
Reflection
Course note: Did I answer the claim they made or an easier one I supplied?
Recall check

blocks.question: What must happen before evaluating an argument?
blocks.text: Its conclusion and supporting reasons should be reconstructed fairly.
Course note: Claim and proof: [[10.02 Distinguish validity from truth]] · [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality]] · [[35.07 Examine formal proof and its assumptions]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish validity from truth
lessons.name: 10.02 Distinguish validity from truth

blocks.text: Would the conclusion follow if the premises were true?
Core idea

Validity concerns the relationship between premises and conclusion. Truth concerns whether the premises accurately describe the world. A valid argument can begin from a false premise; a true conclusion can arise from a poor argument. Test the structure by asking whether you can imagine the premises true and the conclusion false. Then check the premises separately.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Logical rigor and evidence review solve different parts of the problem. Neither can substitute for the other.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: All birds can fly; penguins are birds; therefore penguins can fly has a valid form but a false first premise.
Practice
Course note: Separate the structure and factual premises of one short argument.
Course note: Construct a counterexample if you think the conclusion does not follow.
Reflection
Course note: Have I accepted a conclusion only because it happens to be true?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does validity test?
blocks.text: Whether the conclusion follows from the premises if those premises are assumed true.
Course note: Claim and proof: [[10.01 Find the claim and its support]] · [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality]] · [[35.07 Examine formal proof and its assumptions]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Work carefully with if and only if
lessons.name: 10.03 Work carefully with if and only if

blocks.text: Does this condition guarantee the result, or is it merely required?
Core idea

If A then B says A is sufficient for B, not that B proves A. A necessary condition is something the result cannot occur without. Everyday speech blurs these relationships. Write the direction explicitly and test the reversed claim with an example. This prevents inferring a single cause from an observed result.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Clear conditionals support causal reasoning, eligibility decisions, and honest promises.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: If the alarm is triggered, the light turns on. Seeing the light does not prove the alarm was triggered; a manual switch might also turn it on.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite a real rule as an if-then statement.
Course note: Test its converse and identify another route to the same result.
Reflection
Course note: Which result have I treated as proof of one particular cause?
Recall check

blocks.question: Does “if A then B” imply “if B then A”?
blocks.text: No. B may have other sufficient causes.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Interpret and, or, not, and all
lessons.name: 10.04 Interpret and, or, not, and all

blocks.text: What exactly does the statement include or exclude?
Core idea

Small logical words can change a claim greatly. And requires both parts. Or can allow one or both unless the context specifies an exclusive choice. Not changes the scope of what follows. All claims cover every member of a specified group, while some claims require at least one. Translate a vague sentence into examples before arguing over it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Grammar and logic work together: an ambiguous sentence can produce an apparent disagreement even when people mean the same thing.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “Not every proposal failed” means at least one did not fail; it does not mean every proposal succeeded.
Practice
Course note: Choose three ambiguous statements and rewrite their exact logical meaning.
Course note: Find a case that would make each statement false.
Reflection
Course note: Which small word changed the dispute?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does “not all” mean?
blocks.text: At least one member of the group does not have the stated property.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Test an argument with a counterexample
lessons.name: 10.05 Test an argument with a counterexample

blocks.text: Can the reasons be true while the conclusion fails?
Core idea

A counterexample challenges an inference by showing a possible case in which the stated reasons hold and the conclusion does not. It does not automatically prove the opposite conclusion. Choose a counterexample that respects the opponent's actual terms rather than changing the subject. A strong response may narrow a claim rather than abandon it entirely.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Counterexamples serve logic, personal self-stories, and ethical arguments. They are tools for improving precision.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “Every productive person rises at dawn” is challenged by a productive night worker. The result is a narrower question about what schedule supports particular work.
Practice
Course note: Write a universal claim you encounter and a relevant possible counterexample.
Course note: Revise the original claim to survive the test without becoming empty.
Reflection
Course note: Did the counterexample expose the rule or just an irrelevant exception?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a counterexample show?
blocks.text: That a universal claim or inference needs revision when a relevant case satisfies its conditions but defeats its conclusion.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Identify a reasoning error without name-calling
lessons.name: 10.06 Identify a reasoning error without name-calling

blocks.text: What step of the reasoning fails?
Core idea

Fallacy labels can save time when used precisely, but the label alone does not explain the defect. Identify the missing link: an irrelevant attack, a distorted opponent's claim, an unsupported causal leap, or a limited set of options presented as exhaustive. State why the move matters to the conclusion. A genuine personal conflict may coexist with a valid argument, so do not use a fallacy label to dismiss everything a person says.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Guides to dishonest argument can teach recognition, but fair reasoning also requires checking your own side.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A speaker says a policy is wrong because its proponent is unpopular. You ask whether there is an independent problem with the policy itself.
Practice
Course note: Find one argument you dislike and describe its exact weak inference before using any label.
Course note: Apply the same test to an argument you agree with.
Reflection
Course note: Am I using a label to investigate or to end the conversation?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a fallacy diagnosis useful?
blocks.text: It identifies the exact inferential problem and explains how it affects the conclusion.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask questions that open the reasoning
lessons.name: 10.07 Ask questions that open the reasoning

blocks.text: Which question would clarify an assumption or reveal a consequence?
Core idea

Ask for definitions, evidence, alternatives, and implications in a tone suited to genuine inquiry. A question can be used as a disguised accusation; its form alone does not make it fair. Choose the question that addresses the current uncertainty rather than launching an interrogation. Be willing to answer the same question yourself.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Socratic questioning and active listening meet when questions are precise and reciprocal.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “What would count as a successful trial?” advances a proposal discussion more than “How can you possibly believe that?”
Practice
Course note: Write one clarification, one evidence, and one implication question for a live issue.
Course note: Use only the most relevant question in conversation and listen to the answer.
Reflection
Course note: What answer would I actually be willing to learn from?
Recall check

blocks.question: What distinguishes inquiry from rhetorical questioning?
blocks.text: A genuine question allows the answer to affect the conversation and is applied fairly to both sides.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Disagree with the strongest version
lessons.name: 10.08 Disagree with the strongest version

blocks.text: What would make the opposing view reasonable to someone informed?
Core idea

Before objecting, reconstruct the strongest relevant reasons for another view. Acknowledge what those reasons explain well, then identify the point where evidence or values lead you elsewhere. This does not require saying all views are equal. It makes the real disagreement visible and reduces wasted effort on caricatures.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ethical and political texts in the collection disagree deeply. Studying them together requires preserving tensions rather than declaring a single winner by tone.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: One person prioritizes efficiency in a process; another worries about exclusion. A fair discussion asks whether a design can meet both or which cost should be accepted.
Practice
Course note: Write the best case for a view you oppose, using reasons its advocate would recognize.
Course note: State your disagreement as one specific contested premise or value.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of the opposing case did I initially omit?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why steelman an opposing view?
blocks.text: It directs disagreement toward the strongest real reasons instead of an easily defeated substitute.
Course note: Empathy and disagreement: [[14.02 Reflect back without performing agreement]] · [[17.05 Use empathy without pretending to agree]] · [[32.03 Use reciprocity without erasing differences]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use logic in an everyday decision
lessons.name: 10.09 Use logic in an everyday decision

blocks.text: What conclusion am I drawing, and what would make it warranted?
Core idea

Bring a real decision into a short argument: list premises, note what follows, test alternatives, and separate factual uncertainty from value disagreement. Logic will not decide every trade-off; it clarifies where judgment is required. A valid conditional can still rely on uncertain data or an aim you later reject.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The next module examines empirical evidence, and the one after it examines interacting systems. Logic makes their claims legible without pretending form alone settles the world.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You consider changing jobs. Your reasons include pay, learning, health, and obligation. Writing them separately shows that a pay increase alone does not entail an overall improvement.
Practice
Course note: Write a five-line argument for one upcoming decision.
Course note: Ask what evidence or changed value would reverse your conclusion.
Reflection
Course note: Where did a hidden assumption enter the argument?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can logic contribute to a decision?
blocks.text: It clarifies implications and assumptions while leaving factual and value judgments visible.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep the scope of a negative clear
lessons.name: 10.10 Keep the scope of a negative clear

blocks.text: What exactly is being denied in this statement?
Core idea

A negative can apply to an entire claim, one term, or one part of a condition. Those meanings can lead to different conclusions. Rewrite a complicated sentence in plain alternatives, then test each with a concrete case. In ordinary conversation, ask the speaker which meaning they intend rather than winning an argument against an ambiguity. Clear negation matters in instructions, contracts, reports, and personal expectations.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] addresses wording. [[17 Influence, persuasion, and negotiation]] shows why ambiguous terms can hide an apparent agreement. Logic is useful when it makes the real choice visible.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: 'You do not have to attend both sessions' might mean neither is required, or only that one session is enough. Asking whether at least one is required prevents a mistaken plan.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Use a case to distinguish them.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Find a sentence with 'not', 'unless', or 'either' that could be read two ways. Write both readings.
Course note: Test each reading with a concrete scenario and ask which is intended.
Reflection
Course note: Which disagreement was partly about the position of a negative?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the scope of a negative?
blocks.text: The part of a statement that the negative applies to, which can change the statement's meaning.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Test all, some, and none with small cases
lessons.name: 10.11 Test all, some, and none with small cases

blocks.text: How do quantity words change what follows from a claim?
Core idea

'All' says every member of a defined group has a property; 'some' says at least one does; 'none' says no member does. The group and the property must be clear. A claim that all members of one group belong to another does not automatically reverse. One counterexample can disprove a universal claim, while one supporting example cannot prove it. In ordinary language, 'some' may suggest 'not all', but in basic logic it need not.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] helps find representative evidence. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] reminds you that a logically valid form can still rest on a harmful or false premise about people.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: 'All registered volunteers completed training' does not imply 'All people who completed training are registered volunteers.' A small diagram or list of names makes the missing step visible.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Use a small case or counterexample.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Rewrite one broad claim using an explicit group, property, and quantity word.
Course note: Draw a three-person case that supports it, and another that disproves it if possible.
Reflection
Course note: Did I reverse a one-way claim or treat one example as universal proof?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why does one example not prove an 'all' claim?
blocks.text: A universal claim covers every member of the group; one example checks only one member.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Map premises before debating a conclusion
lessons.name: 10.12 Map premises before debating a conclusion

blocks.text: Which reasons are doing the work in this argument?
Core idea

A conclusion can be supported by several reasons, and each reason may depend on another claim. Draw the structure before deciding whether you agree: what is the main conclusion, which premises support it, and which premises are assumed? Mark whether reasons work independently or only together. This can reveal a missing bridge, a useful point of agreement, or a factual question that could settle part of the dispute.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] helps state each claim fairly. [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] helps assess premises that concern the world. A neat argument map does not make its premises true; it makes their role inspectable.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A proposal says the team should change software because the current tool is slow and the new tool is cheaper. The cost claim may be independent of the speed claim, but the conclusion also assumes migration will not disrupt essential work.
Practice
Course note: Map one real argument with a conclusion, two stated premises, and one plausible unstated assumption.
Course note: Ask which premise needs evidence and what evidence would matter.
Reflection
Course note: Did mapping expose a shared concern hidden by disagreement over the conclusion?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of an argument map?
blocks.text: To show how premises and assumptions support a conclusion so each part can be tested fairly.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use contradiction as a test, not a trick
lessons.name: 10.13 Use contradiction as a test, not a trick

blocks.text: How can an impossible consequence show that an assumption needs revision?
Core idea

Sometimes you can test an assumption by following it carefully until it conflicts with a known fact or with another consequence of the same assumption. The contradiction shows that at least one premise in the chain cannot stand as stated. It does not automatically reveal which premise is wrong if several were used. Trace each step and check whether a term changed meaning along the way.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] distinguishes formal proof from empirical investigation. A contradiction in a model may expose its assumptions; a surprising observation in life also requires checking the observation and context.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You assume a meeting can finish in thirty minutes, but its required agenda contains four ten-minute reports and a discussion. The assumption conflicts with the stated minimum time. Either the agenda, timing, or meeting goal must change.

steps.label: Revise
steps.text: Locate a premise or step to change.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose one plan with an apparently impossible combination of commitments. Write the assumptions that create the conflict.
Course note: Change one assumption and show whether the revised plan becomes feasible.
Reflection
Course note: Which premise had I treated as fixed without examining it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a contradiction establish?
blocks.text: That the set of premises and steps cannot all be correct as stated, not necessarily which single premise failed.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate a confident speaker from a supported claim
lessons.name: 10.14 Separate a confident speaker from a supported claim

blocks.text: What reasons remain if I set aside the speaker's status and delivery?
Core idea

Expertise can be relevant, but a title, fluent voice, or admired history does not make every claim sound. Identify the exact conclusion and evidence, then ask whether the person's expertise covers this question and whether the evidence can be checked. Do not reject a claim merely because an authority stated it; use authority as a clue about where to look, not a replacement for the argument.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[18 Manipulation, propaganda, and independent judgment]] examines authority cues. [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] respects specialist knowledge while checking scope and method.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A successful entrepreneur gives nutrition advice. Their business record may be genuine but does not establish expertise on that health claim.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite a persuasive statement as a claim plus its offered reasons, leaving out status words.
Course note: Name what expertise and evidence would be relevant to evaluating it.
Reflection
Course note: Did the speaker's confidence change my standard of proof?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should authority affect an argument?
blocks.text: It can guide where to investigate, but the claim still needs relevant scope and support.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask whether a reason reaches the conclusion
lessons.name: 10.15 Ask whether a reason reaches the conclusion

blocks.text: Even if this fact is true, does it support the proposed action?
Core idea

An argument may use true details that are emotionally vivid but irrelevant to the decision. Write the conclusion, then explain the bridge from each reason to it. If the bridge depends on an unstated value or causal assumption, name it. A good counterquestion tests that bridge without attacking the person. This is especially useful when a story is moving but supports several different responses.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] makes value premises visible. [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] uses a precise question to reopen reasoning.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A speaker describes one bad customer experience and concludes that a service should close. The story may justify repair, staffing change, or further investigation; closure needs more support.
Practice
Course note: Find the missing bridge in a hypothetical argument from a true event to a broad recommendation.
Course note: Ask one neutral question that would test the bridge.
Reflection
Course note: Which detail was relevant to emotion but not yet decisive for the conclusion?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a relevance check?
blocks.text: Testing whether a stated reason actually supports the conclusion through a defensible premise or mechanism.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask what a claim would predict
lessons.name: 11.01 Ask what a claim would predict

blocks.text: If this explanation is useful, what should we expect to observe?
Core idea

A scientific claim gains force when it helps explain observations and exposes itself to possible correction. Specify what the claim predicts, under what conditions, and what observation would trouble it. Some ideas are valuable as meanings or stories without making testable empirical claims. Keep those roles distinct. An explanation that can accommodate every possible result without revision offers little empirical guidance.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Philosophy of science examines how theories, models, and evidence relate. Everyday inquiry can borrow this discipline without requiring a laboratory for every decision.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “This new schedule improves focus” predicts a measurable difference in completed work under comparable conditions, not just a stronger feeling of intention.
Practice
Course note: Choose one claim and write a possible observation it predicts.
Course note: Identify a result that would make you revise the claim.
Reflection
Course note: Have I protected this explanation from every possible test?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes an empirical claim examinable?
blocks.text: It specifies observable implications and conditions under which evidence could require revision.
Course note: Observation and interpretation: [[01.02 Separate facts, interpretations, and judgments]] · [[09.01 Describe before interpreting]] · [[09.06 Interpret body language with humility]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish correlation from intervention
lessons.name: 11.02 Distinguish correlation from intervention

blocks.text: Would changing this factor change the outcome?
Core idea

Two things can vary together because one affects the other, a third factor affects both, or the pattern is coincidental or distorted by selection. A causal question asks what would happen if one factor were changed while relevant alternatives were addressed. Observing an association is a starting clue, not a completed causal argument.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The ladder from observation to intervention helps organize personal experiments, scientific studies, and policy debate. The relevant design depends on stakes and feasibility.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: People who keep journals report better clarity. They may journal because they are already motivated, or journaling may help, or both. A careful trial would compare what changes when the practice is introduced.

steps.label: Intervention
steps.text: Ask what changing one factor would do.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Draw three possible causal diagrams for one observed association.
Course note: Identify a feasible comparison that would distinguish at least two diagrams.
Reflection
Course note: Which direction of cause did I assume without checking?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why does association alone not establish causation?
blocks.text: Several causal structures and selection effects can produce the same observed pattern.
Course note: Cause and system: [[11.03 Look for confounding variables]] · [[12.05 Use feedback loops to see change over time]] · [[26.03 Understand incentives without reducing people to them]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Look for confounding variables
lessons.name: 11.03 Look for confounding variables

blocks.text: What third factor might influence both the presumed cause and result?
Core idea

A confounder can create or distort an observed relationship. Before recommending an intervention, ask what else differs between groups. Not every variable should be controlled mechanically: some lie on the causal path you want to study. Draw the proposed relationships and explain why a comparison is fair. This is more informative than simply listing every factor you can imagine.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Causal diagrams make hidden assumptions explicit. They also reveal why a statistically sophisticated analysis can still answer the wrong question if the causal structure is mistaken.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A program's graduates earn more than nonparticipants. Prior experience may affect both admission and earnings, so the raw difference may overstate the program's effect.
Practice
Course note: For one causal claim, name one plausible common cause and how it affects both sides.
Course note: Sketch a simple diagram and describe the comparison you would need.
Reflection
Course note: Am I controlling for a relevant cause or adding variables without a theory?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a confounder?
blocks.text: A factor that affects both the proposed cause and outcome, distorting the observed association.

Course note: Cause and system: [[11.02 Distinguish correlation from intervention]] · [[12.05 Use feedback loops to see change over time]] · [[26.03 Understand incentives without reducing people to them]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand comparison groups and selection
lessons.name: 11.04 Understand comparison groups and selection

blocks.text: Who was included, excluded, or assigned differently?
Core idea

A result depends on the group studied and the process that put people into conditions. Random assignment can reduce some biases, but it may be impossible, unethical, or unrepresentative. Observational comparisons need careful attention to baseline differences. Check sample size, follow-up, missing results, and whether the studied group resembles the people to whom the claim is applied.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Survivorship bias and causal inference meet at selection. A precise average can still mislead if it describes the wrong group.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A training method looks effective among volunteers who complete it. People who left may have found it unhelpful or impractical; their outcomes matter too.

steps.label: Transfer
steps.text: Who else is the result meant to describe?

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Find a study summary and identify its groups, selection process, and missing cases.
Course note: State one population to which the result may not transfer easily.
Reflection
Course note: Which excluded outcome would most change my conclusion?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why inspect selection?
blocks.text: Who enters and remains in a comparison can change the apparent effect and its applicability.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate model, mechanism, and reality
lessons.name: 11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality

blocks.text: What does this model illuminate, and what does it leave out?
Core idea

A model simplifies a complex situation to explain or predict selected features. A proposed mechanism describes how a change might produce an effect. Neither is the thing itself. Compare the model's assumptions with the setting in which you use it, and examine whether its predictions hold. A useful model can be incomplete; a memorable metaphor can be misleading when treated as a literal mechanism.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Economic, psychological, biological, and spiritual frameworks in the collection vary greatly in evidence and purpose. Calling each a model does not make them equally tested.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A habit loop helps locate prompts and rewards. It does not by itself explain every effect of poverty, illness, workplace rules, or relationships on behavior.
Practice
Course note: Choose one model and list what it represents and omits.
Course note: Find one case where it offers a useful question and one where it offers little guidance.
Reflection
Course note: Have I confused a simple diagram with a complete account?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a model's proper role?
blocks.text: To simplify selected features for explanation or prediction while keeping assumptions and omissions visible.
Course note: Claim and proof: [[10.01 Find the claim and its support]] · [[10.02 Distinguish validity from truth]] · [[35.07 Examine formal proof and its assumptions]].
Course note: Model and reality: [[33.03 Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing]] · [[35.02 Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration]] · [[35.06 Understand specialist reference books]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence
lessons.name: 11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence

blocks.text: What can one vivid story establish?
Core idea

A personal account can show that an experience is possible, convey meaning, and generate a hypothesis. It rarely tells you how common the outcome is or whether one factor caused it. Systematic evidence can answer broader questions but may miss important individual context. Use each for the question it can actually address, and look for independent checks when a claim is consequential.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The collection contains memoirs, testimonials, experimental discussions, and professional references. Their evidential roles differ even when the prose is equally compelling.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: One person reports recovery after a routine. The account matters, but it does not establish that the routine caused recovery for others.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Seek evidence suited to the broader question.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify the exact claim supported by one anecdote you encountered.
Course note: Write the stronger claim the anecdote does not yet establish and the evidence it would require.
Reflection
Course note: Am I treating emotional force as a substitute for comparison?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can an anecdote establish most directly?
blocks.text: That a reported experience occurred for someone, while broader frequency and causal claims need further evidence.

Course note: Anecdote and selection: [[09.03 Notice selection and survivorship]] · [[13.06 Tell an example without claiming it proves everything]] · [[36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history]].

Course note: Spiritual meaning and empirical claims: [[31.06 Compare competing accounts of consciousness]] · [[34.01 Ask what kind of religious claim is being made]] · [[34.05 Study religious experience with interpretive humility]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Consider replication, uncertainty, and revision
lessons.name: 11.07 Consider replication, uncertainty, and revision

blocks.text: Has a result held up under repeated and independent checks?
Core idea

A single finding can be affected by chance, measurement choices, or a special context. Replication, transparent methods, and converging evidence increase confidence, though they do not create absolute certainty. When a claim is revised, ask what changed and whether the new account explains the evidence better. Do not interpret revision as proof that all methods are equally unreliable.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Scientific humility means confidence can increase or decrease for reasons. It differs from reflexive skepticism that refuses to learn from any evidence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A small initial study suggests a strong effect, while later broader work finds a modest one. The updated conclusion may still support a limited use without the original promise.
Practice
Course note: For one claim, look for independent tests and note differences in population and method.
Course note: State your current confidence and the evidence that would change it.
Reflection
Course note: Am I preserving my first impression after the evidential picture changed?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why does independent replication matter?
blocks.text: It checks whether a result survives new samples, methods, and investigators.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Match evidence to the stakes
lessons.name: 11.08 Match evidence to the stakes

blocks.text: How much confidence does this decision require?
Core idea

The amount of evidence needed depends on potential harm, reversibility, cost, and the availability of alternatives. A low-cost personal experiment may begin with modest evidence; medical treatment, large investments, or public policy require stronger scrutiny and qualified input. Acting under uncertainty can be responsible when the decision process reflects its stakes. Do not let a dramatic claim bypass that assessment.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This connects epistemology to agency: the point of evaluating evidence is to make better choices, not to collect doubt indefinitely.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Trying a new note-taking layout is easy to reverse. Replacing prescribed care on the basis of a testimonial is a very different decision.

steps.label: Action
steps.text: Choose a reversible or qualified path when needed.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Rank three decisions by harm, reversibility, and required confidence.
Course note: Choose a proportionate next step for each, such as a small trial, more information, or qualified advice.
Reflection
Course note: Where have I demanded certainty for a trivial change or accepted little evidence for a consequential one?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should set the evidence threshold?
blocks.text: The decision's stakes, reversibility, alternatives, and potential harms.
Course note: Intuition and evidence: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual]] · [[09.08 Separate intuition from expertise]] · [[21.03 Separate symptoms from candidate causes]].

Course note: Health decisions under uncertainty: [[27.07 Understand food claims through adequacy and context]] · [[37.02 Evaluate a treatment promise]] · [[37.07 Ask about benefits, harms, and alternatives together]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish observation, intervention, and counterfactual
lessons.name: 11.09 Distinguish observation, intervention, and counterfactual

blocks.text: What kind of causal question am I asking?
Core idea

Seeing that two things occur together asks about observation. Changing one thing to see what follows asks about intervention. Asking what would have happened to the same case under a different choice asks a counterfactual question that cannot usually be observed directly. These are related but not interchangeable. State which question you need before choosing evidence. A pattern in observational data may help prediction while leaving the effect of an intervention unresolved.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] needs intervention questions when choosing action. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] helps describe patterns without promoting them to causes. The distinction prevents a predictive model from being mistaken for a treatment plan.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: People who sleep more may perform better on a test. That pattern does not by itself tell you what would happen if every participant slept an extra hour, because other conditions may differ.
Practice
Course note: Take one causal claim and write an observation question, an intervention question, and a counterfactual question about it.
Course note: Name the kind of evidence each question would require and what remains unobservable.
Reflection
Course note: Which question did the evidence actually answer?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is observing an association different from intervening?
blocks.text: The groups may differ in other ways, so changing a factor may not reproduce the observed association.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Draw a causal path before adjusting for variables
lessons.name: 11.10 Draw a causal path before adjusting for variables

blocks.text: Which variables might explain a relationship, and which might lie on the path I want to study?
Core idea

A simple causal diagram can make assumptions visible. Put possible causes and effects in boxes and draw arrows for the directions you think matter. A confounder may influence both the proposed cause and outcome; a mediator may be part of the route by which the cause affects the outcome. Adjusting for variables indiscriminately can obscure the very effect you want to understand. The diagram is a hypothesis that needs domain knowledge, not a picture that proves causation.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] uses diagrams to expose assumptions about change. [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] asks where a model's boundaries are. A disputed arrow should remain visibly disputed.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You study whether training improves job performance. Prior experience may influence both who receives training and performance; improved skill may be a mediator of training's effect. They play different roles in the question.
Practice
Course note: Draw a four-box diagram for a low-stakes causal claim. Label one possible confounder and one possible mediator.
Course note: Write one arrow you are uncertain about and what evidence or expertise might clarify it.
Reflection
Course note: Did the diagram reveal an assumption I had hidden in prose?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the role of a causal diagram?
blocks.text: It makes assumed relationships and variable roles visible for testing; it does not prove that the arrows are correct.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate prediction from explanation
lessons.name: 11.11 Separate prediction from explanation

blocks.text: Can a model be useful for forecasting while still giving a poor account of why something happens?
Core idea

A model may predict an outcome from a pattern without identifying the mechanism behind it. Conversely, a plausible mechanism may not forecast accurately in a changing setting. Ask whether the task is to anticipate, to explain, or to choose an intervention. Evaluate the model against that task. When a predictive pattern changes, the explanation may need revision; when an explanation is elegant, it still needs contact with observed results.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] examines what a model represents. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] helps avoid overconfidence when a pattern has only been seen in one sample. The value of a model depends on its purpose and domain.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A shop predicts busy days from previous traffic patterns. The prediction helps staffing, but it does not show whether an advertisement caused the demand. A separate comparison would be needed for that question.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Evaluate the model for that question.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Find one model or rule you use. State whether its main purpose is prediction, explanation, or intervention.
Course note: Identify one result that would show it is failing at that purpose.
Reflection
Course note: Have I asked a prediction tool to justify an action it was not built to evaluate?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why can prediction and explanation diverge?
blocks.text: A pattern can forecast outcomes without revealing the causal mechanism, and a plausible mechanism may still predict poorly.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Treat surprising data as a question for the model
lessons.name: 11.12 Treat surprising data as a question for the model

blocks.text: What should I do when evidence conflicts with my preferred explanation?
Core idea

First check the observation: its measurement, timing, selection, and possible error. Then inspect the explanation's assumptions. A single anomaly need not overthrow a well-supported account, but repeatedly dismissing anomalies protects the account from learning. Write down what each plausible explanation would predict next. A good revision may narrow the model's scope rather than replace every part of it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[10 Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement]] helps state the competing explanations. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] warns against confirmation bias. Science improves through disciplined correction, not reflexive loyalty to or rejection of a theory.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A routine study method works for factual recall but fails on transfer problems. Instead of calling the result noise, you check whether transfer requires comparison and application that the routine never practiced.
Practice
Course note: Find an observation that does not fit one of your working explanations. Check how the observation was produced.
Course note: Write two possible revisions and one future observation that would distinguish them.
Reflection
Course note: Did I investigate the surprising result as carefully as a confirming one?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should an anomaly be handled?
blocks.text: Check the observation, examine assumptions, and derive tests that could refine the explanation.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Check whether a measure is only a proxy
lessons.name: 11.13 Check whether a measure is only a proxy

blocks.text: What real outcome am I hoping this number represents?
Core idea

A proxy is a measurable stand-in for a harder-to-observe outcome. It can help track change, but it can also improve while the real purpose does not. State the relationship you assume between the proxy and the outcome, then look for cases where it breaks. Pair the number with a direct observation where feasible. If people are rewarded for the proxy, watch how their behavior changes and whether the measure becomes less informative.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] uses goals without letting them replace judgment. [[26 Economics, incentives, and public choices]] studies incentives around measures.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: More course logins may signal engagement, but learners may still be unable to use what they read. A short application task tests the deeper aim.
Practice
Course note: Choose one common metric and name the outcome it is meant to represent.
Course note: Give a case where the metric improves while that outcome worsens.
Reflection
Course note: Which number had I treated as the goal rather than an imperfect sign of it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the main risk of a proxy measure?
blocks.text: The proxy can improve while the underlying outcome stays the same or gets worse.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Treat a null result as information
lessons.name: 11.14 Treat a null result as information

blocks.text: What did a test rule out, and what remains possible when it shows little change?
Core idea

A test that finds no clear effect is not automatically useless. First check whether the intervention happened, the measure was sensitive enough, and the period was long enough. Then ask which explanations remain. Do not turn a small or noisy trial into proof that an effect is impossible. Report the result plainly and decide whether a better test, a different intervention, or stopping is justified by the stakes.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] reviews implementation and outcome separately. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] keeps confidence matched to the evidence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A reminder email does not change attendance in a two-week trial. The team checks whether people received it and whether scheduling, not forgetting, was the main barrier.
Practice
Course note: Write three interpretations of a hypothetical null result, including one about the test design.
Course note: Choose the least costly next observation that would distinguish them.
Reflection
Course note: Was I tempted to call the idea proven wrong or secretly successful without checking the trial?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is a null result not a final verdict?
blocks.text: Its meaning depends on whether the change occurred, the measure and duration could detect an effect, and alternative explanations.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define the decision before using a model
lessons.name: 12.01 Define the decision before using a model

blocks.text: What choice is actually before me?
Core idea

Decision models are useful only after the options, timing, and stakes are clear. Name the decision owner and what is still negotiable. Some apparent decisions are information gaps or conflicts over aims. A framework should help compare options, not become a way to delay an uncomfortable commitment.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Reflective questioning opens possibilities; structured decision tools narrow them. Both need a clearly stated problem.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “Should I change careers?” becomes “Should I apply for this training program this year, given cost and current obligations?”
Practice
Course note: Rewrite one broad dilemma as a decision with options and a date.
Course note: Identify missing information that could change the choice.
Reflection
Course note: Am I avoiding the actual decision by debating a much larger one?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should be clear before choosing a decision model?
blocks.text: The actual choice, available options, stakes, owner, and timing.
Course note: Context before action: [[20.04 Use position and timing]] · [[21.01 Describe the gap before naming a solution]] · [[22.01 Define the deliverable in the recipient's terms]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use opportunity cost and reversibility
lessons.name: 12.02 Use opportunity cost and reversibility

blocks.text: What do I give up by choosing this option, and can I change course?
Core idea

Every allocation of time, money, or attention excludes another use. Compare the best realistic alternative, not an imaginary perfect path. Reversibility matters: a small trial can generate information without locking in the full cost, while an irreversible commitment deserves more scrutiny. Include opportunity costs borne by others when they are affected.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Economics clarifies trade-offs; practical experimentation reduces the cost of learning about them.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before paying for a long program, you try a short introductory project and compare it with the alternative use of that time and money.
Practice
Course note: Name the best realistic alternative to one preferred choice.
Course note: Design a smaller reversible step that would produce useful information.
Reflection
Course note: Which excluded commitment have I treated as if it costs nothing?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is opportunity cost?
blocks.text: The value of the best realistic alternative forgone when a choice uses a limited resource.
Course note: Values and the calendar: [[02.01 Turn a value into a way of acting]] · [[02.10 Make a values agreement with your future self]] · [[06.03 Schedule values, not just incoming demands]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate decision quality from outcome quality
lessons.name: 12.03 Separate decision quality from outcome quality

blocks.text: Was the process sound given what was known at the time?
Core idea

A good process can lead to a poor outcome because uncertainty remains. A poor process can be rewarded by luck. Review the information available, alternatives considered, values applied, and risk accepted before judging only by the result. Then use the outcome to update future decisions without rewriting what you could have known earlier.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This distinction connects behavioral bias, project review, business decisions, and personal learning.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You prepared carefully for an interview and did not receive an offer. The result matters, but it does not prove that every preparation choice was wrong.
Practice
Course note: Review a past decision using the information actually available then.
Course note: Record one process strength, one process weakness, and one piece of new information from the outcome.
Reflection
Course note: Am I granting luck too much credit or too much blame?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why separate decision quality from outcome?
blocks.text: Uncertainty can produce success from a poor process or failure from a sound one.

Course note: Good decision, mixed outcome: [[21.08 Decide whether to continue, change, or stop]] · [[25.07 Notice behavioral traps around money]] · [[40.06 Review outcome and decision quality separately]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a strategy kernel
lessons.name: 12.04 Build a strategy kernel

blocks.text: What obstacle does my plan address, and how do its actions fit together?
Core idea

A useful strategy identifies the central challenge, chooses an overall approach, and coordinates actions that implement it. A goal alone says what you want; it does not diagnose the obstacle or specify how to overcome it. Avoid adding many initiatives that compete for the same resources. Check whether each action supports the chosen approach.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This structure applies across work and personal projects, though the ethics and stakes change by domain.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A course completion problem is diagnosed as unclear practice time, not low ambition. The approach is to protect two sessions weekly, supported by calendar agreements and smaller lesson batches.
Practice
Course note: Write diagnosis, guiding approach, and three coherent actions for one project.
Course note: Remove an action that does not serve the approach or conflicts with another.
Reflection
Course note: Have I called a wish a strategy?
Recall check

blocks.question: What are the three parts of a strategy kernel?
blocks.text: A diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding approach, and coordinated actions that implement it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use feedback loops to see change over time
lessons.name: 12.05 Use feedback loops to see change over time

blocks.text: What effect might this action create that later feeds back into the situation?
Core idea

A system contains interacting parts, delays, and feedback. A reinforcing loop amplifies a pattern; a balancing loop resists change. Map a few important relationships instead of drawing every possible arrow. Check timing: an intervention may appear ineffective before its effect becomes visible, or appear successful while creating a later cost.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Habit loops describe local repetition; systems thinking expands the view to relationships, organizations, and resource constraints.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Faster replies create an expectation of immediate availability, increasing interruptions and reducing time for substantive work. A new response agreement changes the loop.

steps.label: Intervene
steps.text: Choose a leverage point and review it.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Draw a small loop for one recurring organizational or personal problem.
Course note: Identify one delay and one unintended response your intervention might trigger.
Reflection
Course note: What pattern is being maintained by the current arrangement?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why include feedback and delays?
blocks.text: Actions can change later conditions and responses, so immediate effects may not represent the full result.
Course note: Cause and system: [[11.02 Distinguish correlation from intervention]] · [[11.03 Look for confounding variables]] · [[26.03 Understand incentives without reducing people to them]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Beware local optimization
lessons.name: 12.06 Beware local optimization

blocks.text: Could improving one measure make the whole situation worse?
Core idea

A department, habit, or metric can improve while the larger purpose suffers. State the overall aim and the dependencies among parts. Ask who bears the cost of the local improvement and what information the measure omits. Do not treat more of a good thing as always better; beyond a point, it may consume resources needed elsewhere.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Systems thinking and ethics meet when a narrow performance measure hides transferred costs.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team reduces average response time by sending brief answers, but users need follow-up clarifications. The local speed metric rises while total service worsens.
Practice
Course note: Choose one metric and list two outcomes it fails to capture.
Course note: Add a balancing measure or qualitative check to the review.
Reflection
Course note: Who pays for the improvement I am celebrating?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is local optimization?
blocks.text: Improving a part or metric in a way that may worsen the wider system or purpose.

Course note: Metrics and local optimization: [[19.05 Set goals without letting metrics replace judgment]] · [[24.08 Review the business by value and harm]] · [[26.07 Interpret averages, risk, and distribution]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use scenarios rather than one confident forecast
lessons.name: 12.07 Use scenarios rather than one confident forecast

blocks.text: What would I do if different plausible futures occur?
Core idea

A forecast is uncertain, especially when several systems interact. Build a few plausible scenarios around the variables that matter most, then identify robust actions and early signals. Scenarios are not predictions that each future will happen. They help expose assumptions and prepare responses without claiming control over events.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Strategic surprise literature and personal decision-making both benefit from considering more than one path while avoiding endless speculation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You plan for stable income, a temporary reduction, and a major disruption. The scenarios point to different spending choices and a common need for clear records.
Practice
Course note: Write three plausible scenarios for one consequential plan.
Course note: Identify one action useful across scenarios and one signal that would trigger revision.
Reflection
Course note: Which future have I silently treated as guaranteed?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of scenario planning?
blocks.text: To expose assumptions and prepare adaptable choices across plausible futures.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make a decision reviewable
lessons.name: 12.08 Make a decision reviewable

blocks.text: How will I know whether to continue, adjust, or stop?
Core idea

Before acting, state the rationale, expected signals, review date, and conditions for changing course. This prevents hindsight from rewriting your reasons and protects against sunk-cost thinking. A review should allow for learning, including the possibility that the initial aim no longer matters. Do not use a single number as a verdict when qualitative consequences are important.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The complete decision cycle joins values, evidence, strategy, and systems. Later modules apply it to relationships, work, money, and safety.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You commit to a three-month learning project with a monthly review of skill demonstrations, time cost, and its effect on other commitments.
Practice
Course note: Write a decision record for one upcoming choice.
Course note: Set a review date and two signals that would justify a change.
Reflection
Course note: What evidence would I be reluctant to see after committing?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a decision reviewable?
blocks.text: A recorded rationale, relevant signals, a review point, and conditions for revising the choice.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: See stocks, flows, and delays in a changing system
lessons.name: 12.09 See stocks, flows, and delays in a changing system

blocks.text: Why can a sensible action take time to change the result I care about?
Core idea

A stock is something accumulated, such as savings, inventory, or practiced skill. Flows add to or subtract from it. Delays mean an action today may affect the stock or its visible measure later. If you react to every short-term fluctuation without allowing for the delay, you can overcorrect. Draw the stock, the inflows and outflows, and the observation you use to judge progress. The diagram is a simplification; check it against real records.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[05 Habits and behavior design]] applies this to repeated actions. [[25 Money, records, and financial judgment]] applies it to cash reserves. The same language links personal and organizational decisions without claiming their details are identical.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A shop reduces purchasing but inventory remains high for a month because existing orders still arrive. Increasing the reduction again without noting that delay could create a shortage later.

steps.label: Wait
steps.text: Review at a time scale that fits the system.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose one changing quantity in your life or work. Draw its main inflows, outflows, and likely delays.
Course note: Identify one observation you might misread because it responds slowly to an action.
Reflection
Course note: Did I expect a flow change to transform the stock immediately?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the difference between a stock and a flow?
blocks.text: A stock is an accumulated quantity; flows are the rates or events that add to or remove from it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Find a proximate objective
lessons.name: 12.10 Find a proximate objective

blocks.text: What useful target can I reach when the final ambition is still distant?
Core idea

A distant goal may be too broad to guide this week's work. A proximate objective is challenging but close enough that you can specify actions, constraints, and evidence of completion. It should solve a real part of the larger problem rather than create a ceremonial milestone. Choose it after diagnosing the current obstacle. Reaching it may change what the next objective should be, so leave room to revise.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[20 Strategy, competition, and cooperation]] asks where effort has leverage. [[08 Practice, performance, and adaptation]] translates that into a specific training target. A proximate objective connects ambition to capability.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: 'Build a successful business' gives little direction. 'Interview ten potential customers and test whether three will pay for a small pilot' is a nearer objective that can change the plan.

steps.label: Learn
steps.text: Use the result to choose the next step.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: State one distant goal and the obstacle closest to your current capability.
Course note: Define a four-week objective with a result you can verify and a reason it matters to the larger goal.
Reflection
Course note: Will completing this objective teach me something or merely let me tick a box?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes an objective proximate?
blocks.text: It is close enough to act on and verify while resolving a meaningful part of the larger challenge.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Check for a chain-link bottleneck
lessons.name: 12.11 Check for a chain-link bottleneck

blocks.text: Does the whole result depend on several parts working together?
Core idea

Some systems behave like a chain: improving one part produces little benefit while another part remains below the necessary standard. Map the components and the minimum each must provide. Then look for the constraint that prevents the whole path from working. This differs from improving the part that is easiest to measure or most visible. Be careful with human systems: people are not interchangeable links, and a bottleneck may be created by poor coordination or unrealistic demands.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] examines responsibility for the system. [[24 Business, customers, and useful value]] applies the idea to delivery. Changing one metric without the connected process may waste effort.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A clinic improves appointment booking but lacks enough staff to follow up results. More bookings alone cannot deliver better care. The connected service must be examined as a whole.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Improve the whole path, not only one score.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Map one work process from request to result. Mark three components that must all function.
Course note: Identify the present constraint and one way to test whether relieving it improves the whole result.
Reflection
Course note: Was I optimizing a visible part while another part limited the outcome?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a chain-link system?
blocks.text: A system whose overall performance depends on several complementary parts, so a weak part can limit the value of improvements elsewhere.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use a decision threshold before results arrive
lessons.name: 12.12 Use a decision threshold before results arrive

blocks.text: What evidence would make me continue, revise, or stop a plan?
Core idea

A decision threshold names the result at which an action changes. Set it before you see the outcome when possible, because disappointment or excitement can move the standard afterward. The threshold should include measurement quality, costs, and stakes. A number alone may be misleading; combine it with qualitative warning signs and a review date. If new information reveals the threshold was badly chosen, revise it openly and record why.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09.13 Keep hindsight from rewriting the decision]] preserves the earlier standard. [[40 Integration and the life-practice capstone]] uses this method to make an experiment reviewable. Precommitment improves learning when it remains open to justified revision.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You pilot a paid workshop. You decide in advance what enrollment, participant feedback, and delivery cost would justify another session. Afterward, you can discuss a surprising result without quietly changing the definition of success.

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Run the trial and record results.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: Apply or openly revise the standard.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: For one upcoming low-stakes trial, write continue, revise, and stop conditions before it begins.
Course note: Add a review date and one reason that could justify changing the threshold after new evidence.
Reflection
Course note: Which result would I have been tempted to explain away without a prior standard?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why set a decision threshold in advance?
blocks.text: It makes the response to evidence less vulnerable to wishful revision after the result is known.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Plan for a surprise without pretending to predict it
lessons.name: 12.13 Plan for a surprise without pretending to predict it

blocks.text: What would I do if an important assumption changed suddenly?
Core idea

A scenario plan is useful when it identifies a trigger and a response, not when it dramatizes every imaginable catastrophe. Choose two plausible changes that would alter the decision, such as a lost resource or a new opportunity. Define an early signal, options you could preserve now, and whom you would need to inform. Revisit the plan as facts change. Preparedness should reduce fragility without consuming the resources needed for ordinary life.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[29 Safety, awareness, and de-escalation]] uses proportionate preparation. [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] turns a contingency into roles and communication.

blocks.title: A worked example
