Strategy includes response, but people are not fixed pieces. Consider several plausible reactions, their incentives, and the information they have. Avoid treating one imagined reaction as certain or designing plans around stereotypes. Where cooperation is possible, ask directly instead of inferring everything through a competitive lens.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Game theory and negotiation offer structured alternatives to a single forecast, while listening supplies information those models may miss.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A price change may lead customers to leave, accept it, or change usage. A pilot and interviews are more informative than choosing one assumed response.
Practice
Course note: List three plausible responses to one proposed action and what would motivate each.
Course note: Identify a low-cost way to learn which response is more likely.
Reflection
Course note: Have I turned an uncertain human response into a fact in my plan?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should strategic anticipation include?
blocks.text: Several plausible responses, incentives, uncertainty, and opportunities to gather information.
Course note: Competition and cooperation: [[17.06 Generate options before dividing a fixed pie]] · [[20.06 Know when competition is the wrong frame]] · [[28.04 Understand spacing and support]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Know when competition is the wrong frame
lessons.name: 20.06 Know when competition is the wrong frame

blocks.text: Are we facing a rival, a shared problem, or both?
Core idea

Competitive framing can clarify scarce resources and conflicting interests. It can also invent an enemy where coordination would help. Identify whether gains truly require another person's loss. Look for shared aims, repeat interactions, and external costs. Preserve legitimate boundaries even when seeking cooperation; collaboration is not the same as surrender.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: War metaphors appear across business and self-help texts. Their transfer to relationships or civic life can mislead when it erases mutual benefit or human dignity.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two departments compete for a budget, but both lose from duplicated data collection. A shared system may free resources before the budget decision.
Practice
Course note: Reframe one rivalry as a shared problem and note what conflict still remains.
Course note: Propose one cooperative option without concealing the genuine trade-off.
Reflection
Course note: Who benefits from my treating this situation as a zero-sum contest?
Recall check

blocks.question: When is a competitive frame incomplete?
blocks.text: When shared interests, repeat relationships, or joint value are ignored.

Course note: Competition and cooperation: [[17.06 Generate options before dividing a fixed pie]] · [[20.05 Anticipate responses without pretending to predict people]] · [[28.04 Understand spacing and support]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare strategic traditions in context
lessons.name: 20.07 Compare strategic traditions in context

blocks.text: What does this framework assume about people and the setting?
Core idea

Different traditions emphasize deception, virtue, flexibility, duty, decisive action, or institutional legitimacy. Read each within its original context before applying it. A tactic for armed conflict is not automatically a guide to friendship or leadership. Compare the problem each tradition addresses and its moral costs. Preserve a disagreement if the texts rest on different values.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Integrating Sun Tzu, Clausewitz, samurai writing, and modern business requires explicit limits, not a blended list of slogans.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “Win without fighting” can inspire conflict avoidance, but it does not settle what a fair negotiation requires when the other party is vulnerable.
Practice
Course note: Compare two strategic ideas by context, aim, and acceptable costs.
Course note: Identify one domain where each idea should not be transferred without major revision.
Reflection
Course note: Which metaphor is doing more work than the evidence allows?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why study strategic traditions in context?
blocks.text: Their aims, assumptions, and moral limits differ, so transfer needs justification.

Course note: Classical rules and exceptions: [[21.05 Compare fixes against the same criteria]] · [[22.07 Handle a change request without losing the plan]] · [[33.05 Study a philosophical tradition in context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Write a strategic brief
lessons.name: 20.08 Write a strategic brief

blocks.text: How will I turn this analysis into coherent action?
Core idea

State the situation, objective, decisive constraint, guiding approach, coordinated actions, likely responses, ethical limits, and review signals. Keep the brief short enough to use. A brief is a working theory, not a guarantee. If evidence changes the diagnosis, change the strategy rather than defending its wording.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This prepares the problem-solving and delivery modules, where choices can be tested against real constraints and their consequences for other people.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community project identifies low return attendance as the constraint, tests a clearer welcome process, and reviews both attendance and participant experience.
Practice
Course note: Write a one-page strategic brief for a real, non-harmful project.
Course note: Ask someone affected which assumption is least credible.
Reflection
Course note: What observation would cause me to abandon the current approach?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a strategic brief useful?
blocks.text: It links diagnosis, coordinated action, ethical limits, and evidence that can revise the plan.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Choose a setting that suits the real goal
lessons.name: 20.09 Choose a setting that suits the real goal

blocks.text: Can I change where and when I act instead of only increasing effort?
Core idea

A plan can improve by changing the setting: audience, channel, timing, partnership, or scope. Before assuming you must work harder against the strongest obstacle, ask whether another route can reach the legitimate goal at lower cost. Avoid importing military language literally into ordinary relationships. In cooperative settings, the better move may be a shared design rather than an opponent's weakness.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] identifies constraints. [[24 Business, customers, and useful value]] asks where a service genuinely fits. Context is a strategic variable, not a moral judgment about people.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community workshop struggles at a weekday location. Moving it to a library near public transport may do more for attendance than more advertising to the same audience.

steps.label: Choose
steps.text: Select the route with justified fit.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Name one goal and three settings in which it could be pursued.
Course note: Compare access, cost, risk, and who benefits in each setting before choosing one.
Reflection
Course note: Was I treating the current setting as fixed because I had already invested in it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can changing the setting do for a strategy?
blocks.text: It can alter constraints and opportunities so a legitimate goal becomes more reachable without merely increasing effort.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use information without pretending it is complete
lessons.name: 20.10 Use information without pretending it is complete

blocks.text: What must I know before acting, and what will remain uncertain?
Core idea

Strategy needs information about objectives, constraints, other participants, and the environment. More information can help, but waiting for perfect knowledge can delay a reversible opportunity. Identify the unknowns that could change the choice, how they might be checked, and the cost of checking. Distinguish a trustworthy signal from a rumor designed to provoke action. Privacy, consent, and lawful conduct still limit how information may be gathered.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] helps weigh uncertain observations. [[30 Digital security and privacy]] defines boundaries for information gathering. A good information plan is targeted and ethical.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before opening a pop-up service, you need to know foot traffic, permission requirements, and basic costs. You do not need to predict every customer's preference; a small pilot can answer some questions more cheaply.

steps.label: Act
steps.text: Use what is known while preserving revision.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: For a current plan, list three unknowns and rank them by how much they could change the decision.
Course note: Choose one low-cost, lawful way to learn about the highest-ranked unknown.
Reflection
Course note: Which fact did I seek because it mattered, and which because certainty felt comforting?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes information gathering strategic?
blocks.text: It targets unknowns that could change the action and weighs the cost and ethics of obtaining them.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish a strategic analogy from a recipe
lessons.name: 20.11 Distinguish a strategic analogy from a recipe

blocks.text: What can a historical or business case teach without dictating my behavior?
Core idea

Analogies reveal a structure: scarce resources, timing, cooperation, or a bottleneck. They also conceal differences in stakes, rules, consent, and what counts as success. State the feature you are borrowing and the features that do not transfer. A successful tactic in one domain is evidence that it worked there, not proof it belongs in another. Human relationships especially require care that a competitive analogy may miss.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] asks whether a borrowed idea survives a real test. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] asks whether a transferred method respects people outside the original case. A good analogy helps formulate a question.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A business turnaround may show the value of choosing a decisive constraint. In a family disagreement, treating another person as a constraint to overcome would be harmful; the useful transfer is to notice what limits the conversation before choosing a response.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Use the analogy to ask a better question.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Take one strategy analogy you like. List two structural similarities and three important differences from your real situation.
Course note: Rewrite its lesson as a question you can investigate rather than a rule to copy.
Reflection
Course note: Which difference between domains most changed the advice?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the safe use of a strategic analogy?
blocks.text: Borrow a specific structural insight while naming differences in rules, stakes, and ethics before applying it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask when a clever tactic damages the relationship
lessons.name: 20.12 Ask when a clever tactic damages the relationship

blocks.text: Could this short-term win make later cooperation harder?
Core idea

A tactic can achieve an immediate goal and still weaken trust, reputation, or the conditions for future exchange. Name the people whose cooperation you may need again and what they will infer from the tactic. Compare the gain with the longer relationship, and consider whether a direct, fairer approach can reach the same aim. Competitive language should not make ordinary partners into enemies. Some conflicts are real, but even then the method matters.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[17 Influence, persuasion, and negotiation]] examines implementable agreements. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] tests whether a win respects others' choice and dignity.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A supplier could exploit an unclear term to save money once, but a transparent discussion may protect a long working relationship.

steps.label: Choose
steps.text: Use the method that fits the whole aim.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a hypothetical clever tactic and list its immediate gain and likely later effects.
Course note: Design a direct alternative and compare both against the real goal.
Reflection
Course note: Was I impressed by the tactic because it was smart, or because it served the whole strategy?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a tactic be judged against?
blocks.text: The full goal, including future cooperation, trust, costs, and ethical limits.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use a warning signal without becoming alarmist
lessons.name: 20.13 Use a warning signal without becoming alarmist

blocks.text: Which early change would justify revising the plan?
Core idea

Strategic surprise is easier to manage when a team has named a small set of signals connected to its major assumptions. A signal is a prompt to investigate, not proof that a forecast has come true. Define the threshold for review and the options available at that point. Avoid collecting every possible warning into an overwhelming dashboard. The aim is timely adjustment with a clear record of why the plan changed.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] uses scenarios and decision thresholds. [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] separates a measured change from its possible causes.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A service expansion depends on stable staffing. A sustained rise in unfilled shifts triggers a capacity review before new bookings are promised.

steps.label: Assume
steps.text: State what the plan relies on.

steps.label: Review
steps.text: Investigate when the threshold is met.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Name one strategic assumption, one early signal, and a review threshold.
Course note: Write two alternative explanations for the signal before deciding what it means.
Reflection
Course note: Did I treat a signal as a cue to learn or as a certainty about the future?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a strategic warning signal for?
blocks.text: To prompt timely review of a consequential assumption, not to prove a prediction automatically.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Describe the gap before naming a solution
lessons.name: 21.01 Describe the gap before naming a solution

blocks.text: What result differs from what is needed, and for whom?
Core idea

A proposed fix can arrive before the problem is clear. Describe the current condition, the desired condition, who is affected, and when the gap appears. Include what still works. Avoid a definition that already smuggles in your preferred solution. A specific problem statement helps you choose evidence and prevents a tool, meeting, purchase, or rule from becoming the goal by default.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[01 Self-knowledge and your starting point]] uses a baseline for personal change. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] uses a diagnosis for strategy. The same discipline applies to a team problem with more stakeholders.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: 'We need a new app' is a solution. 'Volunteers miss changes to the rota because updates arrive through three channels' describes a gap that might have several fixes.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite one proposed solution as a statement of current result, needed result, affected people, and context.
Course note: Ask one affected person whether your statement captures their experience and what it misses.
Reflection
Course note: Which solution had I treated as if it were the problem itself?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in a useful problem statement?
blocks.text: The current and desired conditions, affected people, context, and evidence of the gap, without assuming one fix.
Course note: Context before action: [[12.01 Define the decision before using a model]] · [[20.04 Use position and timing]] · [[22.01 Define the deliverable in the recipient's terms]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Set the boundary of the problem
lessons.name: 21.02 Set the boundary of the problem

blocks.text: Which connected factors belong in this attempt, and which must be noted but handled elsewhere?
Core idea

A problem can expand until it includes an entire life or institution. Draw a boundary around the process you can study and change now. Record inputs, outputs, people affected, and links to larger systems. A narrow boundary can make an experiment feasible, but a boundary that excludes crucial effects will mislead. State what you are leaving outside and why; revisit it if the intervention causes effects there.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] treats system boundaries as choices. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] asks whether the boundary hides costs borne by someone else.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A school studies late homework submissions. It can examine its assignment process while noting that home access to devices and care obligations also affect students. A school-only fix should not pretend those conditions vanish.

steps.label: Revisit
steps.text: Expand the view if results demand it.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Draw a simple boundary around a recurring problem, with three factors inside and two connected factors outside.
Course note: Ask who might bear a cost if the outside factors are ignored.
Reflection
Course note: Did the boundary make action possible while still keeping important consequences visible?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why make a problem boundary explicit?
blocks.text: It defines a feasible investigation while exposing connected factors and costs that the chosen scope may omit.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate symptoms from candidate causes
lessons.name: 21.03 Separate symptoms from candidate causes

blocks.text: What might produce the visible problem, and what evidence would distinguish explanations?
Core idea

A symptom is what you observe; a cause is an explanation of why it occurs. Generate at least two plausible explanations before selecting one. Look for timing, exceptions, and points in the process where the outcome changes. Avoid blaming the nearest visible person when the system may set them up to fail. A causal hypothesis should imply a testable difference: if it is true, what else would you expect to see?

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] clarifies confounding and intervention. [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] reminds you that incentives and role design can produce repeated individual errors.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Orders arrive late. One explanation is slow packing; another is late information from sales. Timestamps at each handoff can distinguish where delay accumulates.
Practice
Course note: For one problem, list two candidate causes and one observation each would predict.
Course note: Find a case where the symptom did not occur and compare its conditions with a typical case.
Reflection
Course note: Which explanation felt satisfying before I had checked it?
Recall check

blocks.question: How is a cause hypothesis different from a symptom description?
blocks.text: It proposes a mechanism that should predict additional observations or responses to change.
Course note: Intuition and evidence: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual]] · [[09.08 Separate intuition from expertise]] · [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Break a complex problem into linked parts
lessons.name: 21.04 Break a complex problem into linked parts

blocks.text: Which smaller questions must be answered before the whole problem can improve?
Core idea

Decomposition makes a complex challenge workable, but dividing it badly can hide the connections that matter. Separate stages, decisions, resources, and failure points, then draw how they affect one another. Choose a part that can be tested while keeping a measure of the whole outcome. If improving the part does not improve the whole, the original division or assumed link may be wrong.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12.06 Beware local optimization]] warns about optimizing one part at the system's expense. [[20 Strategy, competition, and cooperation]] asks which constraint is decisive rather than merely easy to see.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community event has low attendance. Possible parts include awareness, location, timing, cost, and relevance. Posting more advertisements tests only awareness; the overall attendance measure shows whether that part mattered.

steps.label: Link
steps.text: Show how they affect the outcome.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Watch both the part and the whole.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Split one problem into three to five linked components and mark a plausible bottleneck.
Course note: Select one component to test and one whole-outcome measure to protect.
Reflection
Course note: Did my chosen part have a credible route to the result I cared about?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the risk of decomposition?
blocks.text: A part can improve while the whole problem remains or worsens if important connections are ignored.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare fixes against the same criteria
lessons.name: 21.05 Compare fixes against the same criteria

blocks.text: How can I compare attractive solutions fairly?
Core idea

Generate several feasible options before committing to one. Judge each against criteria chosen from the problem: likely effect, cost, reversibility, time, people affected, and uncertainty. Do not let a precise score disguise weak evidence. A small pilot may be better than a full commitment when the leading options are uncertain. Record why you chose one route so later review can improve your judgment.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] offers opportunity cost and reversibility. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] adds distribution and consent. A solution is not good simply because it is clever.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A group can hire an administrator, simplify a form, or reduce the number of approvals. The best first test may be the simpler form if evidence suggests the form causes most delays and the change is easy to reverse.

steps.label: Choose
steps.text: Record the reason and review point.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: List three feasible responses to one problem and five criteria tied to the real outcome.
Course note: Compare options in plain words, including what you do not know and who bears each cost.
Reflection
Course note: Which criterion did my favorite solution encourage me to overlook?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why choose criteria before comparing fixes?
blocks.text: It reduces the chance of changing the standard to favor the first solution you liked.

Course note: Classical rules and exceptions: [[20.07 Compare strategic traditions in context]] · [[22.07 Handle a change request without losing the plan]] · [[33.05 Study a philosophical tradition in context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Design a small test that could fail informatively
lessons.name: 21.06 Design a small test that could fail informatively

blocks.text: What can I try that will teach me something even if it does not work?
Core idea

A useful pilot has a clear change, a relevant measure, a time boundary, and a plausible comparison. State what result would support the idea and what would weaken it. Keep the test proportionate to risk and avoid experimenting on people without appropriate consent or oversight. A pilot is not proof from one success; it is a way to learn before committing more resources.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] explains why comparison matters. [[40 Integration and the life-practice capstone]] applies the same design to a bounded personal project.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A library tests a new reminder message for one month and compares return rates with a similar period, while noting seasonal differences. The result may justify a longer trial rather than a sweeping conclusion.

steps.label: Learn
steps.text: Use both success and failure to revise.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write a one-page pilot brief: change, group or setting, measure, duration, and stop condition.
Course note: State one result that would make you revise the explanation rather than simply try harder.
Reflection
Course note: Would the test teach me something if the outcome disappointed me?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a pilot informative?
blocks.text: A defined change, relevant observation, comparison where possible, time boundary, and result that could challenge the hypothesis.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Watch for side effects and displaced costs
lessons.name: 21.07 Watch for side effects and displaced costs

blocks.text: Did the fix improve the target while moving the burden somewhere else?
Core idea

A change can make a visible metric better by shifting work, risk, or delay to another person or stage. Before and after a pilot, identify who does more work, who waits longer, and which errors become less visible. Ask affected people about consequences the original measure cannot capture. Side effects do not always make the change unacceptable, but they belong in the decision.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] makes hidden labor part of accountability. [[26 Economics, incentives, and public choices]] asks about external costs and distribution. A good local result is not the whole result.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team reduces call time by asking customers to complete a longer form first. Staff workload falls, but customers with limited access may abandon the service. Both effects belong in the review.
Practice
Course note: For one proposed fix, list three people or stages that might receive displaced work or risk.
Course note: Add one side-effect measure and one question for affected people to your review.
Reflection
Course note: Whose experience was missing from my original success criterion?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a displaced cost?
blocks.text: A burden moved to another person, stage, or time while the chosen measure appears to improve.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Decide whether to continue, change, or stop
lessons.name: 21.08 Decide whether to continue, change, or stop

blocks.text: What should the result of a trial cause me to do next?
Core idea

Review the pilot against the problem statement and criteria, not only against enthusiasm for the team that ran it. Separate implementation failure from a weak idea: did the change actually happen as intended, and did it affect the outcome? Decide to continue, revise, or stop with a reason and next review date. If evidence is too thin, say so and design the next test. A stopped idea can still be a useful result when it prevents a larger mistake.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] guards against hindsight and sunk costs. [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] carries the lesson into revision and release.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A new intake process saves staff time but confuses users. The team can revise the instructions and run a second pilot rather than declaring total success or abandoning the entire approach.
Practice
Course note: Make a three-column review for one trial: intended change, observed implementation, and observed outcome.
Course note: Choose continue, revise, or stop, and state the evidence that would change that decision later.
Reflection
Course note: Did I learn from the trial or defend the effort already spent?
Recall check

blocks.question: What two questions belong in a pilot review?
blocks.text: Whether the change was implemented as intended and whether it improved the relevant outcome without unacceptable side effects.

Course note: Good decision, mixed outcome: [[12.03 Separate decision quality from outcome quality]] · [[25.07 Notice behavioral traps around money]] · [[40.06 Review outcome and decision quality separately]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define evidence before a proposed change
lessons.name: 21.09 Define evidence before a proposed change

blocks.text: What would count as improvement before I know which option wins?
Core idea

When the measure is chosen after a trial, almost any result can be called a success. State the outcome, a baseline, and the observation window before acting. Include an experience measure from the people affected when a numerical target could hide inconvenience or exclusion. Decide what change would be meaningful, and mark any evidence that would make you stop. A measure should help judgment, not become a substitute for it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] separates a measure from the thing measured. [[12.06 Beware local optimization]] shows why a single improved number can mislead.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before changing a sign-up process, a volunteer group records completed sign-ups, the time applicants spend, and reasons for abandonment.

steps.label: Define
steps.text: Set measures and a review date.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Judge the result against both benefit and burden.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write one outcome measure, one experience measure, and a time window for a small change.
Course note: State a result that would count against your favored fix.
Reflection
Course note: Would I have been tempted to choose the measure after seeing the result?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why define evidence before a change?
blocks.text: It makes the comparison clearer and reduces the temptation to redefine success after seeing the outcome.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Choose a reversible first step
lessons.name: 21.10 Choose a reversible first step

blocks.text: How can I learn while limiting the cost of being wrong?
Core idea

Not every solution requires a complete rollout. When uncertainty is high, look for a bounded step that produces information while preserving an exit. Reversibility depends on more than money: trust, privacy, and disruption may be hard to restore. Tell affected people what is being tried and what would trigger revision. Where even a small trial carries substantial harm, seek appropriate expertise and oversight before acting.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] compares options by consequences and reversibility. [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] turns a chosen trial into a coordinated plan.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team tries new meeting notes for two weeks with an agreed review, instead of permanently changing every reporting process at once.
Practice
Course note: Break one large proposed change into a limited first step with an exit condition.
Course note: List what would be easy and hard to undo after that step.
Reflection
Course note: Did I call a choice reversible because it was convenient for me, while someone else bore a lasting cost?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a first step truly reversible?
blocks.text: Its likely costs, including trust and disruption, can be contained or repaired if the idea fails.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask whether a fix works beyond the pilot
lessons.name: 21.11 Ask whether a fix works beyond the pilot

blocks.text: Would the same approach work under normal demand and ordinary constraints?
Core idea

A pilot often receives unusual attention, motivated participants, or spare capacity. A good result in that setting may not survive routine use. Identify which conditions made the trial possible and whether they exist at a larger scale. Watch for bottlenecks that move when volume rises. Scale in stages and keep a way to notice decline in quality. A failed transfer can reveal a capacity limit rather than an error in the original observation.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12.05 Use feedback loops to see change over time]] asks where the constraint moves. [[24 Business, customers, and useful value]] asks whether value can be delivered consistently.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A helpful personal reply works for ten customers a week; at two hundred, the team needs a different process or more capacity.
Practice
Course note: List three conditions that made a successful small test work.
Course note: Imagine demand doubling and identify the first likely bottleneck.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of the pilot depended on special attention that cannot continue?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why can a successful pilot fail at scale?
blocks.text: Its conditions, attention, or capacity may change when the approach becomes routine.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep a decision record others can challenge
lessons.name: 21.12 Keep a decision record others can challenge

blocks.text: Can another person see why this fix was chosen and what would change my mind?
Core idea

A short decision record captures the problem, options, evidence, uncertainties, affected people, chosen action, and review date. It is a tool for later learning and accountability, not a defense brief written to prove you were right. Name the strongest alternative and an observation that would favor it. Invite someone affected to correct the record. When outcomes arrive, add them without rewriting the earlier reasoning to fit hindsight.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] shows how hindsight distorts memory. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] shows why decisions that affect others need records that can be examined.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team records why it changed office hours, whose access may be affected, and which attendance and complaint patterns will prompt review.

steps.label: Review
steps.text: Compare outcomes without changing the old record.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write a six-line decision record for a real low-stakes choice.
Course note: Ask one person to identify a missing option or affected group.
Reflection
Course note: What did an outside reader see that my original explanation hid?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a decision record useful for learning?
blocks.text: It preserves the original reasons, alternatives, uncertainties, and review conditions for later comparison.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define the deliverable in the recipient's terms
lessons.name: 22.01 Define the deliverable in the recipient's terms

blocks.text: What must exist at the end, and how will the intended recipient use it?
Core idea

A plan becomes clearer when it names the output, the person who needs it, and the conditions under which it will be useful. 'Finish the project' is too vague if nobody can tell whether the result is ready. Describe a deliverable and an acceptance check that reflects its purpose. Avoid promising a perfect product before you have learned what is needed. The person receiving the work should have a chance to clarify the result.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] helps test whether the proposed output addresses the problem. [[24 Business, customers, and useful value]] asks whether delivery creates value rather than only activity.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A neighborhood group needs a sign-up form. The deliverable is a form people can complete on a phone, with responses reaching the organizer securely; a visually polished mockup alone would not meet the need.
Practice
Course note: State one project deliverable in one sentence naming recipient, use, and acceptance check.
Course note: Ask an intended recipient what would make it useful and what would make it fail.
Reflection
Course note: Was I planning to complete work or to deliver something another person could use?
Recall check

blocks.question: What defines a useful deliverable?
blocks.text: A concrete output tied to a recipient's use and an acceptance check based on that purpose.
Course note: Context before action: [[12.01 Define the decision before using a model]] · [[20.04 Use position and timing]] · [[21.01 Describe the gap before naming a solution]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Map dependencies before assigning dates
lessons.name: 22.02 Map dependencies before assigning dates

blocks.text: Which tasks cannot begin until another result exists?
Core idea

A list of tasks does not show their order. Draw the dependencies: which decision, resource, approval, or component must arrive before another task can proceed. Estimate dates only after the path is visible and include ordinary delays. Identify work that can happen in parallel and work that is truly sequential. An early missed dependency deserves attention even if many easy tasks are on schedule.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[06 Attention, time, and a workable day]] helps make individual capacity realistic. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] shows how a chain of connected tasks can limit the whole result.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A public event needs a venue before invitations can give a confirmed location. Designing the invitation can begin earlier, but sending it depends on the booking.

steps.label: Schedule
steps.text: Assign dates with capacity and uncertainty.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Draw five to eight tasks for a current project and connect the true dependencies.
Course note: Identify one dependency with high uncertainty and a backup route if it is late.
Reflection
Course note: Which deadline did I set without checking the work it depends on?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why draw dependencies before dates?
blocks.text: Dates are only credible when the order of required work and likely delays are visible.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Limit work in progress
lessons.name: 22.03 Limit work in progress

blocks.text: How does starting too many tasks slow the work that matters?
Core idea

Each open task consumes attention, coordination, and unfinished follow-up. A team can look busy while every deliverable waits. Choose a small number of active tasks, make blocked work visible, and finish or deliberately pause one item before adding another. The right limit depends on role and urgency; it is a way to expose overload, not a rule that every person must do only one thing.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[06 Attention, time, and a workable day]] addresses the individual's day. [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] addresses the team's system. A work-in-progress limit is useful when it improves flow and honest prioritization.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Three people each start five improvements and none is ready for users. They agree to finish two shared priorities first and park the others with named review dates.

steps.label: Finish
steps.text: Complete or pause before starting more.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Count active tasks in one project and identify which have no realistic next step this week.
Course note: Set a temporary limit for a week and track completions, delays, and urgent exceptions.
Reflection
Course note: Did starting a new task feel easier than finishing a difficult one?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a work-in-progress limit help reveal?
blocks.text: Whether too many simultaneous commitments are slowing completion or hiding blocked work.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Give each handoff a clear owner
lessons.name: 22.04 Give each handoff a clear owner

blocks.text: Who knows when a task is ready for the next person?
Core idea

Handoffs fail when the sender assumes work is done and the receiver discovers missing information later. Name the owner of the current step, the recipient, the format, and what must be checked before transfer. Keep the handoff light enough to use. Do not make one person responsible for an outcome they cannot control; give them a route to report a blocked dependency.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] links authority with accountability. [[17 Influence, persuasion, and negotiation]] helps agree on terms rather than relying on unspoken expectations.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A writer sends a draft to a designer. The handoff includes the approved text, image rights, required dimensions, and a contact for unresolved questions. Without those details, the designer cannot safely finish.

steps.label: Confirm
steps.text: Verify the next step can begin.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify one recurring handoff and list what the receiver needs to start confidently.
Course note: Agree on a short handoff check with the next person and test it once.
Reflection
Course note: Which missing detail repeatedly returned work to the previous stage?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a handoff complete?
blocks.text: A named owner and recipient, usable materials, an acceptance check, and a route for unresolved issues.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Communicate progress by exceptions and decisions
lessons.name: 22.05 Communicate progress by exceptions and decisions

blocks.text: What does a teammate need to know to act, rather than to admire an update?
Core idea

A useful status update tells others what changed, what is blocked, what decision is needed, who owns it, and when the next update will arrive. It need not narrate every hour of work. Be especially clear when a forecast changes; early notice protects options for everyone else. A status ritual should fit the project's pace and avoid consuming more time than the information is worth.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] makes the message concise. [[04 Agency, responsibility, and boundaries]] supports raising a limit before a promise silently fails.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: 'The prototype is mostly done' is hard to use. 'The form works on desktop; mobile validation is blocked by missing test accounts; Priya will provide access Tuesday; the release date may move one day' supports action.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite one vague project update as progress, blocker, decision, owner, and next date.
Course note: Ask a teammate which part of the update helped them act and which part was unnecessary.
Reflection
Course note: Was I reporting reality or trying to sound on schedule?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in an actionable progress update?
blocks.text: Relevant change, blocker, needed decision, owner, and next check point.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Protect quality with an acceptance check
lessons.name: 22.06 Protect quality with an acceptance check

blocks.text: How do I know a deliverable is ready for its actual use?
Core idea

Quality is not only absence of obvious defects. It includes whether the work serves the user, meets agreed constraints, and can be corrected if something was missed. Turn the deliverable's purpose into a short check that someone other than the maker can perform. Include important accessibility, privacy, safety, or accuracy requirements where relevant. A check should not become so elaborate that it prevents a small reversible pilot.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] distinguishes release from endless polishing. [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] asks whether the test matches the claim being made. Quality is contextual and observable.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A weekly report is ready when its numbers reconcile, its conclusion matches them, and the recipient can locate the action needed. Decorative formatting alone is insufficient.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: Have another person try the use.

steps.label: Correct
steps.text: Fix failures before or after a bounded release.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write three acceptance checks for one deliverable, including one from the recipient's perspective.
Course note: Ask someone unfamiliar with the work to attempt the intended use and note where they struggle.
Reflection
Course note: Which check protected the purpose, and which only protected my preference?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should an acceptance check test?
blocks.text: Whether the deliverable serves its intended use and meets the important agreed constraints.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Handle a change request without losing the plan
lessons.name: 22.07 Handle a change request without losing the plan

blocks.text: What should happen when the goal or constraints change during delivery?
Core idea

Change is normal, but unexamined additions can overload a project. Describe the requested change, the reason for it, its effect on time, cost, quality, and other commitments, and who may decide. Consider what would be removed or delayed to make room. A necessary change should be welcomed and planned, not hidden under the old deadline. Record the decision so the team shares the new target.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] uses opportunity cost. [[17 Influence, persuasion, and negotiation]] helps discuss terms with the requester. A project plan is a living agreement, not an excuse to ignore evidence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A client adds a second language to a brochure. The team can accept with a revised date and translation review, or schedule it for a later release. Pretending the original timeline still applies makes errors more likely.
Practice
Course note: Take one change request and write what it adds, what it displaces, and who must agree.
Course note: Present two honest options with different time or scope consequences.
Reflection
Course note: Did I treat a request as free because I wanted to appear helpful?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should accompany a project change?
blocks.text: A clear description of its effects on scope, time, cost, quality, and commitments, plus an authorized decision.

Course note: Classical rules and exceptions: [[20.07 Compare strategic traditions in context]] · [[21.05 Compare fixes against the same criteria]] · [[33.05 Study a philosophical tradition in context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Close the work and keep the learning
lessons.name: 22.08 Close the work and keep the learning

blocks.text: When is a project finished, and what should be learned before the team moves on?
Core idea

Closing a project includes confirming delivery, handing over maintenance or support, settling open commitments, and recording what was learned. Review the original problem, decisions, surprises, and effects on users. Ask what to repeat and what to change in the next cycle. Do not use a retrospective to assign easy blame after the outcome is known; look at conditions and information available at the time.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] supplies the test record. [[40 Integration and the life-practice capstone]] turns review into a continuing practice. A completed artifact and a completed learning cycle are related but distinct.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After launching a community guide, the team confirms who updates it, gathers first-use feedback, closes unpaid invoices, and records that review started too late for one important translation issue.
Practice
Course note: Write a closeout list for one project: deliverable accepted, remaining owner, obligations, results, and lessons.
Course note: Ask one participant what they would keep and one thing they would change next time.
Reflection
Course note: Did I leave a usable result and a clear owner for what follows?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is included in responsible project closeout?
blocks.text: Confirmed delivery, handover of remaining duties, settled commitments, and a review that improves the next cycle.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Plan capacity with uncertainty in view
lessons.name: 22.09 Plan capacity with uncertainty in view

blocks.text: Can the people and resources assigned actually carry the plan?
Core idea

A schedule is only credible when work fits available capacity. Estimate effort as a range, include recurring duties, and ask where specialized attention is required. Do not fill every hour with ideal work and then call interruptions a failure of discipline. A reserve is useful when uncertainty is real; its size should follow the stakes and the cost of delay. Revisit the plan when new information arrives instead of hiding slippage.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[06 Attention, time, and a workable day]] treats available time as constrained. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] distinguishes a plan from a wish.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A small nonprofit plans a launch around two volunteers' actual weekly availability and leaves room for approvals rather than assigning five full days of work to each.

steps.label: Revise
steps.text: Update the plan when facts change.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Estimate a current deliverable as a range and list the people or resources it depends on.
Course note: Remove or defer work until the plan fits realistic capacity.
Reflection
Course note: Where had optimism been written into the schedule as certainty?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a delivery schedule credible?
blocks.text: Its work, dependencies, and uncertainty fit the capacity actually available.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make feedback useful before the finish
lessons.name: 22.10 Make feedback useful before the finish

blocks.text: When can feedback still change the outcome?
Core idea

Feedback delivered after a project is finished can explain a disappointment, but it cannot cheaply improve the current version. Set review points when work is still changeable. Show an artifact or observed result rather than asking whether an abstract plan sounds good. Ask reviewers what they tried to do, where they became unsure, and what mattered to them. Record a decision about each significant finding, including why a change is declined.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] uses revision to improve the artifact. [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] helps hear feedback without treating it as a verdict on identity.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A service team asks three intended users to try a form while there is still time to change its wording and flow.

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Ask how it works for recipients.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose one project review point before final delivery and name the artifact to show.
Course note: Write three questions that ask about use and difficulty rather than praise.
Reflection
Course note: Was I seeking feedback early enough to act on it?
Recall check

blocks.question: When is project feedback most valuable?
blocks.text: When a concrete result can be reviewed while the relevant choices are still changeable.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Recover from a missed commitment openly
lessons.name: 22.11 Recover from a missed commitment openly

blocks.text: What should happen when a promised step will not be delivered on time?
Core idea

An overdue task is information about the plan and its dependencies. Tell affected people promptly what is known, what is uncertain, and what options remain. Separate the impact from excuses or blame. Replan the next useful step, assign an owner, and confirm the new expectation. Repeated delay may signal a structural issue such as overloaded capacity or unclear approval, not simply a need for more reminders.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] links accountability with system design. [[17 Influence, persuasion, and negotiation]] helps renegotiate a term without pretending the old promise was met.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A report cannot be finished because a data review is delayed. The owner alerts the recipient, shares the completed sections, and agrees on a revised date after checking the dependency.
Practice
Course note: Draft a four-sentence update for a hypothetical missed milestone.
Course note: Name one underlying condition to investigate if the same delay repeats.
Reflection
Course note: Did I communicate early enough for others to adjust their plans?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does responsible recovery from delay include?
blocks.text: Early notice, the actual impact, workable options, a new owner or date, and a check on recurring causes.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Deliver a handover someone else can use
lessons.name: 22.12 Deliver a handover someone else can use

blocks.text: What must the next person know to maintain the result?
Core idea

Delivery includes the information needed to use, maintain, and correct what was produced. A handover should identify the final artifact, owner, location, known limits, routine checks, and how to raise a problem. Keep it short enough to be used. If the recipient cannot perform the next ordinary action without the original maker present, the work may be finished for the maker but unfinished for its user.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[24 Business, customers, and useful value]] judges value by use. [[38 Craft, perception, and material practice]] judges workmanship partly by whether an object serves its setting over time.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A volunteer rota tool is handed over with access permissions, a two-minute update guide, and a contact for errors, not merely a link to the finished screen.
Practice
Course note: Make a one-page handover checklist for a current or past deliverable.
Course note: Ask a recipient to complete one routine action using only the handover.
Reflection
Course note: What knowledge existed only in my head?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a handover complete?
blocks.text: The recipient can locate, use, maintain, and report problems with the delivered result.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Choose a project small enough to finish
lessons.name: 23.01 Choose a project small enough to finish

blocks.text: What result could I complete and learn from?
Core idea

A project is easier to begin when its output, audience, and end condition are clear. Choose a scope that fits present time and skill while still requiring real work. An enormous ambition may be worth keeping, but it needs a first finished unit. Finishing exposes your assumptions to feedback and creates material for the next version.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Resistance writing emphasizes showing up; strategy adds a diagnosis of what must be produced and what can be postponed.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Instead of “write a book,” you create a short essay that argues one point for a specific reader.
Practice
Course note: State output, audience, length or size, and completion condition for one project.
Course note: Remove one feature that does not serve the first finished version.
Reflection
Course note: Which expansion is helping the work, and which is protecting me from evaluation?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why reduce initial scope?
blocks.text: A finished, reviewable unit generates learning that an indefinitely expanding plan cannot.
Course note: Output and customer value: [[23.07 Finish and release at the right standard]] · [[24.02 Define an offer with honest terms]] · [[38.07 Judge workmanship by use and context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate generating from evaluating
lessons.name: 23.02 Separate generating from evaluating

blocks.text: Am I asking an early idea to pass a final quality test?
Core idea

Drafting and evaluation use different questions. Generate options before selecting among them, then apply standards relevant to the purpose. If every idea is rejected immediately, the search may become too narrow; if nothing is evaluated, the work never improves. Move deliberately between expansion and selection rather than treating them as one mood.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Imagination, critical thinking, and design are complementary stages of work, not rival personalities.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You sketch several ways to explain a concept, choose the clearest two, and test them with a reader.
Practice
Course note: Produce five possible approaches to a current problem without judging them during the first pass.
Course note: Apply two explicit criteria and select one to test.
Reflection
Course note: Which promising possibility did I discard before understanding it?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why separate generation and evaluation?
blocks.text: It allows a wider search before applying standards to choose and improve an option.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a repeatable work ritual
lessons.name: 23.03 Build a repeatable work ritual

blocks.text: What setup reduces the cost of returning to the project?
Core idea

Set a reliable time or cue, prepare materials, and define the next concrete action at the end of each session. Keep the ritual short enough that it does not become a substitute for creating. A routine can support work through low motivation, but it should adapt to changed responsibilities and energy rather than demand a perfect day.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Habits and deep focus supply the conditions; creative practice supplies the work itself.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You begin with yesterday's note about the next paragraph, work for a feasible period, and end by recording the next unresolved question.
Practice
Course note: Design a three-step start and a two-step close for one project.
Course note: Run it twice and remove any step that mainly delays the work.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of the ritual makes returning easier?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a useful creative ritual?
blocks.text: A brief repeatable setup that lowers friction and leads directly to substantive work.
Course note: Focus and recovery: [[06.05 Design a focused work session]] · [[06.08 Leave room for recovery and wandering]] · [[08.07 Treat recovery as part of training]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use constraints to create direction
lessons.name: 23.04 Use constraints to create direction

blocks.text: Which limitation could sharpen the work rather than merely obstruct it?
Core idea

A chosen constraint can reduce options and reveal a distinctive solution. A real constraint may instead require more resources or a smaller goal. Distinguish the two. Choose limits that serve the purpose, such as an audience, format, or duration, and revisit them if they prevent the central idea from being expressed.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Strategy and creativity meet where scarce resources require a deliberate choice of form.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A short presentation forces you to identify one claim and one example, improving clarity. A lack of accessible materials is a different constraint that may need support.
Practice
Course note: Name one chosen and one imposed constraint in your project.
Course note: Use the chosen constraint to make a specific design decision.
Reflection
Course note: Which limit helps focus, and which needs to be changed?
Recall check

blocks.question: When can a constraint help creative work?
blocks.text: When it narrows choices in service of the work's purpose without hiding a harmful or avoidable barrier.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Revise the work, not only your confidence
lessons.name: 23.05 Revise the work, not only your confidence

blocks.text: What specific feature would make this version more effective?
Core idea

Feedback about a draft should lead to a change in structure, evidence, rhythm, function, or fit for the audience. Global judgments about talent are poor revision instructions. Keep effective features and alter one problem at a time where possible. A new version should be compared with the previous version against the project's purpose.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Deliberate practice becomes creative revision when feedback is attached to a visible artifact.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Readers understand the opening but lose the thread in the middle. You reorder two sections and add a transition instead of rewriting everything.
Practice
Course note: Ask a reader one specific question about a draft's purpose.
Course note: Make one targeted revision and compare the two versions.
Reflection
Course note: What changed in the work itself?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes revision productive?
blocks.text: It changes a specific feature of an artifact based on feedback and a clear purpose.
Course note: Craft and experiment: [[24.03 Test demand before scaling]] · [[38.05 Use prototypes to answer a question]] · [[40.04 Design a reversible experiment]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use resistance as information
lessons.name: 23.06 Use resistance as information

blocks.text: What exactly am I avoiding when I avoid this project?
Core idea

Delay can arise from uncertainty, fear of judgment, missing skill, overload, or a goal you no longer endorse. Do not treat every hesitation as laziness or every difficulty as a sign to quit. Identify what happens immediately before you leave the task and choose a response: clarify the next action, learn a prerequisite, reduce scope, seek support, or reconsider the goal.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Emotional awareness and habit analysis give more useful detail than a simple command to defeat resistance.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You keep researching because you have not chosen the essay's claim. Writing a provisional claim changes the task more than another hour of browsing.
Practice
Course note: Record the moment you switch away from one project three times.
Course note: Address the most common uncertainty with a concrete change.
Reflection
Course note: Is the avoidance protecting me from discomfort or signaling a real mismatch?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why investigate resistance?
blocks.text: Different causes require different responses; a single label can hide the actionable obstacle.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Finish and release at the right standard
lessons.name: 23.07 Finish and release at the right standard

blocks.text: When is the work ready for its actual purpose?
Core idea

Define sufficient quality before the final stretch. Check accuracy, coherence, obligations to collaborators, and the needs of the audience. More polishing can help, but it has costs and diminishing returns. Release decisions should match stakes: a personal sketch and public health guidance need very different review. Preserve a path for correction after release where appropriate.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The concept of enough becomes concrete when you must stop revising and let the work meet the world.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A guide has been checked for factual errors and used by a test reader; decorative changes can wait until after its first release.
Practice
Course note: Write a release checklist tied to the artifact's real purpose and risk.
Course note: Identify the one remaining change that matters most, complete it, and choose a release date.
Reflection
Course note: Am I improving the work or avoiding its encounter with others?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should determine release readiness?
blocks.text: Fitness for purpose, factual and ethical stakes, obligations, and the marginal value of further revision.
Course note: Output and customer value: [[23.01 Choose a project small enough to finish]] · [[24.02 Define an offer with honest terms]] · [[38.07 Judge workmanship by use and context]].
Course note: Growth and enough: [[02.05 Define enough before chasing more]] · [[24.08 Review the business by value and harm]] · [[25.01 Define what money is for in your plan]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a portfolio of completed cycles
lessons.name: 23.08 Build a portfolio of completed cycles

blocks.text: What does a sequence of finished projects teach about my practice?
Core idea

Keep records of the brief, first version, feedback, revision, and final result. Compare projects for recurring strengths, bottlenecks, and changing interests. A portfolio is not just a display of polished outputs; it can preserve the learning that made them possible. Choose the next project based on that evidence rather than only on status or novelty.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Creative growth compounds through completed feedback cycles, not through an identity claim about being creative.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Three short articles show that your examples are strong but your conclusions remain vague. The next project includes a deliberate conclusion practice.
Practice
Course note: Create a record for one finished or nearly finished project.
Course note: Identify a recurring pattern across two projects and make it the next practice target.
Reflection
Course note: Which kind of work still matters after the novelty fades?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a useful portfolio record?
blocks.text: The choices, versions, feedback, and learning across completed projects.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make a draft that answers one question
lessons.name: 23.09 Make a draft that answers one question

blocks.text: What can the next version teach me that thinking alone cannot?
Core idea

A draft is an experiment in form. Choose one uncertainty about audience, structure, material, or meaning and make a version that exposes it. A rough draft should be complete enough to receive useful feedback; fragments can hide the difficulty of joining parts. Save discarded ideas without making the draft carry all of them. The goal is a visible object you can inspect, not a performance of natural talent.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] uses bounded tests. [[38 Craft, perception, and material practice]] uses prototypes to learn from materials.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A writer unsure about structure produces a full short essay with a beginning, argument, and ending before polishing sentences.
Practice
Course note: Name one creative uncertainty and make a small complete draft that tests it.
Course note: Ask one intended reader what they understood and where they lost the thread.
Reflection
Course note: Which question did making the draft answer?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a useful draft?
blocks.text: A complete-enough version that exposes a specific uncertainty to inspection and feedback.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Choose feedback for its job
lessons.name: 23.10 Choose feedback for its job

blocks.text: What kind of response will improve this stage of the work?
Core idea

Different feedback serves different decisions. An early draft may need a test of clarity and purpose; a near-final piece may need precision and defects. Specify the audience and the question before asking. Separate a reviewer's observation from their suggested fix: the observation may be accurate even when their proposed solution does not fit. Do not collect endless opinions that prevent you from choosing a direction.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] helps receive criticism without surrendering judgment. [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] sets review points while change is possible.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A designer asks intended users where they could not find a button, then tests alternative layouts instead of accepting the first requested color change.
Practice
Course note: Write a feedback request with the stage, intended audience, and two specific questions.
Course note: Sort one response into observation, interpretation, and suggested fix.
Reflection
Course note: Did I ask for reassurance when the work needed information?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why specify the job of feedback?
blocks.text: It directs attention to the decision the creator can still improve and reduces unhelpful opinion collection.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Protect a work rhythm without worshipping it
lessons.name: 23.11 Protect a work rhythm without worshipping it

blocks.text: How can regular creation fit a real life that changes?
Core idea

A ritual can lower the cost of starting by making time, place, and first action familiar. It is a support, not proof of virtue. Design a minimum version for disrupted days and a return path after absence. Notice whether the schedule produces work, recovery, and a life you still want. If the ritual becomes a way to avoid showing the work to others, it needs revision.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[05 Habits and behavior design]] explains cues and friction. [[06 Attention, time, and a workable day]] balances focus with other obligations.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An illustrator usually works for forty minutes after breakfast; on care-heavy days, ten minutes of sketching keeps contact with the project without pretending the day is ordinary.
Practice
Course note: Define a usual creative session and a feasible minimum session.
Course note: Plan the exact first action for returning after a missed week.
Reflection
Course note: Is my ritual helping me produce and revise, or merely helping me feel organized?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of a creative ritual?
blocks.text: To make starting and returning easier while serving the work and the rest of life.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Decide when a project is ready to share
lessons.name: 23.12 Decide when a project is ready to share

blocks.text: What standard of completeness fits the purpose and the stakes?
Core idea

Perfection is an impossible release criterion, but care still matters. Define the essential promise to the audience: what the work must do, what errors would cause harm, and what can be improved later. Test those essentials. If stakes are high, use stronger review before release. If stakes are low and revision remains possible, sharing a sound version can produce the feedback that private polishing cannot.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] uses acceptance checks. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] helps judge harms that cannot be dismissed as minor defects.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community event guide needs accurate accessibility and time information before sharing; its decorative layout can improve in a later edition.

steps.label: Share
steps.text: Release at a fitting standard and learn.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write three release criteria for a current project, including one non-negotiable accuracy or care check.
Course note: Decide what can be revised after people begin using it.
Reflection
Course note: Which unfinished detail really matters to the audience, and which only delays exposure?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should a creator choose a release standard?
blocks.text: By the work's purpose, audience, consequences of error, and ability to revise after release.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Start with a real customer problem
lessons.name: 24.01 Start with a real customer problem

blocks.text: Whose difficulty would the business address?
Core idea

A business idea needs a customer, a problem or desire, and a reason the proposed solution is useful. Describe the current alternative, including doing nothing. Avoid starting only with a product you want to sell or an identity you want to have. Customer interviews can reveal needs, but do not turn every conversation into a sales pitch.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Strategy asks for a diagnosis; value creation asks whether solving the diagnosed problem matters to someone willing and able to use the result.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A small firm notices that local groups struggle to track volunteer shifts. The first question is how they currently coordinate and where errors occur.
Practice
Course note: Describe one potential customer's task, current method, and costly friction.
Course note: Ask a potential user about recent actual behavior rather than a hypothetical willingness to buy.
Reflection
Course note: Am I solving their problem or displaying my idea?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should precede building an offer?
blocks.text: Evidence of a real customer need, current alternatives, and a plausible useful change.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define an offer with honest terms
lessons.name: 24.02 Define an offer with honest terms

blocks.text: What exactly will be delivered, to whom, and at what cost?
Core idea

An offer should specify the result, scope, price or exchange, timing, limits, and the customer's responsibilities. Clear terms protect both sides. Do not promise a transformation you cannot control or hide a material limitation behind persuasive language. A narrow reliable offer often teaches more than an ambitious vague one.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ethical persuasion becomes operational when the customer can evaluate and later verify the promise.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “We will organize your existing records into a searchable folder within two weeks; you provide the files and approve the categories” is a reviewable offer.
Practice
Course note: Write a one-paragraph offer with deliverable, scope, cost, timing, and limits.
Course note: Ask whether a reader can identify what is excluded.
Reflection
Course note: Which appealing phrase would become a dispute after purchase?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes an offer reliable?
blocks.text: Specific deliverables, terms, limits, and responsibilities that can be understood and checked.
Course note: Output and customer value: [[23.01 Choose a project small enough to finish]] · [[23.07 Finish and release at the right standard]] · [[38.07 Judge workmanship by use and context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Test demand before scaling
lessons.name: 24.03 Test demand before scaling

blocks.text: What would show that people value this enough to change behavior?
Core idea

Compliments and survey enthusiasm do not always translate into use or payment. Run a small legitimate test of the offer, observe repeat use, and ask why people do or do not return. Do not manufacture scarcity or use pressure to produce a misleading signal. A test can reveal that the problem is real but the proposed solution is wrong.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Evidence and business experimentation meet when interest is measured through actual behavior under transparent conditions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A service pilot attracts many sign-ups but few completed tasks. Interviews reveal that setup is too difficult, pointing to a design issue rather than a marketing shortage.
Practice
Course note: Define one behavior that would indicate meaningful interest.
Course note: Design a small, reversible test and a criterion for revising the offer.
Reflection
Course note: Am I counting praise when I need evidence of use?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is stronger than hypothetical interest?
blocks.text: Observed customer behavior under real, transparent conditions.
Course note: Habit and product design: [[05.01 Map the behavior loop]] · [[05.11 Evaluate a habit-forming product]] · [[06.02 Investigate internal triggers]].
Course note: Craft and experiment: [[23.05 Revise the work, not only your confidence]] · [[38.05 Use prototypes to answer a question]] · [[40.04 Design a reversible experiment]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand the economics of delivery
lessons.name: 24.04 Understand the economics of delivery

blocks.text: Does the value created support the cost of providing it?
Core idea

Estimate revenue, direct costs, recurring overhead, time, and cash timing. A sale can feel successful while delivery consumes more resources than expected. Record assumptions and compare them with actual transactions. Include fair compensation and obligations, not only the owner's hoped-for profit.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Accounting turns a value story into a resource test. Strategy may need to change when the economics do not fit the promise.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A custom service sells well but each project requires twice the estimated hours. The owner must change scope, process, or price rather than simply chase more sales.
Practice
Course note: Make a simple unit map for one offer: price, variable cost, delivery time, and fixed costs.
Course note: Identify the assumption most sensitive to error and how to measure it.
Reflection
Course note: What resource is being spent without appearing in the headline price?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why inspect unit economics?
blocks.text: A valued offer must also be delivered with sustainable use of time, money, and capacity.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Market through truthful relevance
lessons.name: 24.05 Market through truthful relevance

blocks.text: How will the right people recognize the offer's usefulness?
Core idea

Marketing connects a problem, a credible promise, and an audience that can evaluate it. Explain the use case in the audience's language, show evidence and limitations, and choose channels where the intended users already seek information. Attention is not the same as trust or fit.
