lessons.title: Understand spacing and support
lessons.name: 28.04 Understand spacing and support

blocks.text: How can teammates create useful options for one another?
Core idea

Passing options depend on distance, angle, timing, and the position of opposition. A triangle can create multiple connections, but its usefulness changes with movement and pressure. Communicate and adapt rather than standing in an ideal shape while play moves elsewhere. Respect roles and rule constraints in the chosen sport.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Systems thinking shows how individual movement can change the options available to everyone else.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A teammate moves into a visible support lane, allowing the player with the ball to avoid a forced risky pass.

steps.label: Move
steps.text: Create or protect a useful connection.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Draw a simple possession with three teammates and two defenders; mark available lanes.
Course note: Change one player's location and explain the new options and costs.
Reflection
Course note: Did my movement help the group even if I never touched the ball?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why does spacing matter?
blocks.text: It changes available connections, decisions, and pressure across the whole team.

Course note: Competition and cooperation: [[17.06 Generate options before dividing a fixed pie]] · [[20.05 Anticipate responses without pretending to predict people]] · [[20.06 Know when competition is the wrong frame]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare tactical formations by purpose
lessons.name: 28.05 Compare tactical formations by purpose

blocks.text: What does a formation make easier, and what does it expose?
Core idea

A formation is an initial organization of roles and spaces, not a guarantee of behavior. Compare how arrangements support possession, pressing, transition, and defensive cover under particular players and opponents. A number label alone says little about the movements that follow. Use match evidence and coaching feedback rather than treating one system as universally best.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Strategy and team leadership meet in the assignment of responsibilities and trade-offs.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A wider arrangement may create passing options on the flank while leaving a central gap if players do not coordinate transitions.
Practice
Course note: Compare two formations by one strength, one vulnerability, and one player demand.
Course note: Watch how the shape changes when possession is lost.
Reflection
Course note: Am I judging a formation by its diagram or its behavior?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a formation?
blocks.text: A starting organization whose value depends on roles, movement, opponents, and transitions.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Learn balance, coordination, and breath under supervision
lessons.name: 28.06 Learn balance, coordination, and breath under supervision

blocks.text: What supports controlled movement across a changing task?
Core idea

Balance depends on posture, base of support, movement, and the task at hand. Breath and pacing affect how a person manages effort. Study principles through low-risk exercises appropriate to your body and sport, then seek qualified supervision for contact or advanced techniques. Static diagrams cannot assess an individual's movement or injury risk.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Martial arts anatomy, core stability, and sport training share movement concepts, though their applications and hazards differ.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: In a coached non-contact drill, a learner moves slowly through a change of direction and notices whether they can regain stable posture.
Practice
Course note: Describe one safe movement's base, direction, and balance demands.
Course note: Ask a qualified coach for feedback on one observable feature.
Reflection
Course note: What does my body actually do that the book's illustration cannot show?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why use supervision for complex movement?
blocks.text: A qualified observer can adapt feedback and safety to the person and actual performance.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Respect the boundary between sport and harm
lessons.name: 28.07 Respect the boundary between sport and harm

blocks.text: Which material is appropriate for a course about better living?
Core idea

The collection includes competitive sport, historical martial traditions, weapon manuals, and harmful targeting instructions. These cannot all become unsupervised practice. Study cultural context, training ethics, safety, and conflict avoidance where relevant. Keep techniques involving weapons, incapacitation, or serious injury outside the course's how-to exercises. If a person faces real danger, qualified local guidance and immediate safety matter more than a book-derived maneuver.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Discipline and restraint are valuable themes across martial writing; operational harm is a different category with different risks.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A learner chooses an accredited, safety-conscious club and asks about protective rules, coaching, and injury procedures rather than practicing hazardous manual sequences alone.
Practice
Course note: Compare two training environments by supervision, rules, consent, and injury response.
Course note: Write the questions you would ask before joining a contact class.
Reflection
Course note: Is this practice building skill under rules or rehearsing avoidable harm?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why does training context matter?
blocks.text: Contact, weapons, and injury risk require rules, consent, qualified instruction, and appropriate safeguards.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Review team and individual learning together
lessons.name: 28.08 Review team and individual learning together

blocks.text: What did the session change for the learner and the group?
Core idea

Track a small number of skill and decision signals: technique under suitable challenge, quality of choices, communication, and recovery. Ask the athlete for their account and compare it with observation. Team outcomes can hide an individual's improvement; a personal success can still create a problem for teammates. Use the review to choose the next drill.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Feedback loops, leadership, and physical recovery combine in a good practice review.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Passing accuracy improves in an isolated exercise, but the player still hesitates under pressure. The next session varies the decision context rather than repeating only static passes.
Practice
Course note: Review a practice session using one individual and one team signal.
Course note: Choose the next drill because it addresses the observed limit.
Reflection
Course note: What did we measure because it was easy rather than because it mattered?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a sport practice review include?
blocks.text: Relevant individual and team signals, the learner's perspective, and a specific next practice target.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Learn to read the action before joining it
lessons.name: 28.09 Learn to read the action before joining it

blocks.text: What cues matter before I commit to a movement or pass?
Core idea

Skilled action begins with perception. Identify the positions, motion, rules, and opportunities relevant to the next choice. A cue has value only within the sport and level being practiced; noticing everything at once is neither possible nor useful. Start with a few reliable cues and ask a coach or teammate how they interpret them. Review missed cues without pretending that every later outcome was visible in advance.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] separates observed cues from inference. [[08 Practice, performance, and adaptation]] shows how feedback improves a specific skill.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A football player looks over a shoulder before receiving and notices an open teammate, changing the next pass.
Practice
Course note: Name three cues relevant to one safe, supervised sport situation.
Course note: Watch a short replay or demonstration and pause before the action to predict two possible choices.
Reflection
Course note: Which cue did I notice only after knowing the result?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is tactical perception?
blocks.text: Selecting cues relevant to a decision in the actual sport and using them before acting.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Design a drill with a clear transfer target
lessons.name: 28.10 Design a drill with a clear transfer target

blocks.text: Which part of real play should this drill improve?
Core idea

A drill is useful when it isolates a learnable component and later reconnects it to the conditions of performance. Specify the target decision or movement, the level of challenge, and the feedback available. If a drill removes all the pressure, timing, or choices that define the sport, success in the drill may transfer poorly. Progress from controlled practice to more representative play under qualified supervision and suitable safety rules.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07 Learning, memory, and understanding]] distinguishes recall from transfer. [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] asks what observation would show the drill helped.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A passing drill begins without defenders, then adds movement and a choice of receiver so the player practices looking before passing.
Practice
Course note: Describe one drill's target skill, simplified condition, and later real-play condition.
Course note: Choose one observation that would show transfer beyond the drill.
Reflection
Course note: Was I improving the drill score or the sport decision?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a drill transferable?
blocks.text: It connects an isolated skill to the cues, timing, and choices of actual performance.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use video and statistics without losing context
lessons.name: 28.11 Use video and statistics without losing context

blocks.text: What can a recorded clip or number show, and what might it hide?
Core idea

Video can reveal positioning and timing that memory misses, while a statistic can track patterns across attempts. Neither explains the whole action on its own. Note opponents, role, score, rule setting, and what the camera could not see. Choose a small number of measures connected to decisions; a highlight reel selects dramatic moments and may hide ordinary performance. Use review to identify a practice target, not to assign fixed labels to a player.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] warns about selected samples. [[26 Economics, incentives, and public choices]] shows that measures can change behavior.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A player's low pass completion may reflect attempts into difficult spaces rather than poor technique alone; video helps examine both choice and execution.
Practice
Course note: Pick a sport statistic and list two contextual facts needed to interpret it.
Course note: Review one clip and write one observation separately from an explanation.
Reflection
Course note: Which conclusion arrived before I had checked the role and context?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why pair sport statistics with context?
blocks.text: Numbers and clips show selected parts of performance and need role, conditions, and opportunity to be interpreted fairly.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make the training setting respectful and safe
lessons.name: 28.12 Make the training setting respectful and safe

blocks.text: What conditions let participants learn without unnecessary harm or humiliation?
Core idea

Good coaching matches challenge to experience, explains rules, and welcomes a stop or adjustment when a participant is uncomfortable or injured. Contact sports require qualified supervision, protective norms, and consent to the kind of practice being used. Feedback should describe a changeable action rather than shame a person's identity. A learner can be ambitious while still declining a drill that exceeds their current preparation or the agreed rules.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] supports useful feedback. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] treats consent and dignity as constraints on performance goals.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A martial arts class pairs beginners for a controlled drill, explains the stop signal, and changes intensity when someone reports a problem.

steps.label: Respond
steps.text: Adjust when safety or dignity requires it.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write three conditions for a safe learning environment in one sport.
Course note: Rewrite one shaming coaching comment as specific, actionable feedback.
Reflection
Course note: Did the culture of the setting make it easy for people to report a problem?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a safe sport learning setting provide?
blocks.text: Clear rules, appropriate supervision and progression, consent, specific feedback, and room to stop or adjust.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define safety by the situation
lessons.name: 29.01 Define safety by the situation

blocks.text: What specific risk exists, and what evidence supports that assessment?
Core idea

Safety planning begins with the actual environment, the behavior observed, and available exits or support. A feeling can alert you to pay attention, but it cannot by itself identify intent. Avoid profiling people by appearance or identity. If a concrete threat is present, prioritize distance and appropriate help over proving that your interpretation is right.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Intuition and observational caution both belong here, with the important limit that ambiguous cues are not a diagnosis of danger.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A stranger repeatedly blocks a doorway and ignores requests for space. The behavior, rather than clothing or expression, is relevant to the response.
Practice
Course note: Compare a vague uneasy feeling with a specific observable risk in two hypothetical scenes.
Course note: Identify an exit or support option for each.
Reflection
Course note: What am I inferring that I cannot actually observe?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should ground a safety assessment?
blocks.text: Concrete behavior, context, available options, and proportionate caution.
Course note: Safety and autonomy: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual]] · [[18.08 Build a defensive pause]] · [[29.03 Use distance and help before confrontation]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build everyday prevention into routines
lessons.name: 29.02 Build everyday prevention into routines

blocks.text: Which small preparation reduces a common risk?
Core idea

Familiar environments can still contain avoidable hazards. Check communication plans, lighting, reliable contacts, basic supplies, and routes appropriate to your setting. Avoid turning safety into constant vigilance. A good routine reduces repeated decisions while preserving ordinary freedom and attention for life.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Habit design and risk management meet in simple preparations that do not depend on heroic reactions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before a group trip, participants agree on meeting points and a way to contact one another if separated.
Practice
Course note: Choose one recurring activity and identify a likely, non-dramatic disruption.
Course note: Add one realistic preparation and test whether it is usable.
Reflection
Course note: Which preparation would help without making daily life narrower?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes prevention useful?
blocks.text: It addresses a plausible risk with a practical, low-burden preparation.
Course note: Defensive security and consent: [[18.08 Build a defensive pause]] · [[30.01 Begin with a threat model]] · [[30.08 Distinguish ethical security training from intrusion]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use distance and help before confrontation
lessons.name: 29.03 Use distance and help before confrontation

blocks.text: Can I leave, create space, or involve support?
Core idea

When an interaction begins to feel unsafe, identify ways to move toward safer people or places and contact appropriate help. Do not make verbal cleverness or physical technique the default answer. Context matters: some people cannot leave freely and may need an individualized support plan. Choose options that reduce exposure without escalating the other person's behavior.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: De-escalation, agency, and relationship boundaries share a priority: preserve safety and choice.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A heated dispute in a public venue leads you to step away toward staff and ask for help rather than continue arguing about who is right.

steps.label: Escalate
steps.text: Use appropriate emergency help if needed.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: For a hypothetical setting, list two exit and two help options.
Course note: Identify what would make each option unavailable and what alternative remains.
Reflection
Course note: Am I staying to win an argument after the situation has changed?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why prioritize distance?
blocks.text: It can reduce exposure to harm without requiring a confrontation or specialized physical skill.
Course note: Safety and autonomy: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual]] · [[18.08 Build a defensive pause]] · [[29.01 Define safety by the situation]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Speak to reduce escalation where possible
lessons.name: 29.04 Speak to reduce escalation where possible

blocks.text: What can I say that is clear, calm, and nonprovocative?
Core idea

Use short statements, avoid insults and threats, and name a practical next step. Listening can help when the other person is capable of dialogue, but it does not require remaining in danger. The goal is to lower intensity and preserve options, not to manipulate someone into compliance. If a person makes threats, use appropriate assistance rather than treating dialogue as a guaranteed solution.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Conflict communication applies to safety only within its limits; a course cannot promise control over another person's behavior.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “I am leaving now; I will speak with staff” gives a clear action without debating accusations.
Practice
Course note: Draft two short, nonprovocative exit statements for ordinary conflict.
Course note: Identify when you would stop talking and seek help.
Reflection
Course note: Am I trying to explain myself beyond the point where it helps?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the limit of de-escalation language?
blocks.text: It may reduce tension but cannot guarantee another person's response or replace leaving and help when danger persists.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make a support plan for repeated risk
lessons.name: 29.05 Make a support plan for repeated risk

blocks.text: What will I do if this concern occurs again?
Core idea

Repeated unwanted contact, threats, or coercion calls for a plan grounded in the person's circumstances. Document concrete incidents where safe, identify trusted contacts, and use relevant organizational or local protective channels. Avoid solitary tests of whether the situation is “really serious.” The right process depends on jurisdiction and safety; qualified local assistance can help shape it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Personal boundaries become more reliable when backed by institutional support and records.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After repeated unwanted visits, a person informs trusted contacts, preserves messages, and seeks appropriate local advice rather than trying to negotiate alone.
Practice
Course note: In a hypothetical repeated-risk case, list records, contacts, and available formal channels.
Course note: Identify one circumstance in which immediate help would be appropriate.
Reflection
Course note: What would make it easier to act early rather than wait for perfect certainty?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why plan for repeated risk?
blocks.text: A documented, supported response is more reliable than improvising alone under pressure.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read emergency advice by domain
lessons.name: 29.06 Read emergency advice by domain

blocks.text: Does this guide address the actual hazard I face?
Core idea

Fire, travel disruption, severe weather, injury, and violence require different expertise and local procedures. A general survival book can prompt preparedness questions, but old or region-specific instructions may be unsuitable. Use current official local guidance for actual emergencies. Do not mix hazardous weapon material into household safety planning.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The collection's survival and military texts are broad; responsible transfer requires matching hazard, context, and current authority.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A household asks local authorities about flood routes and alerts rather than relying on a general wilderness chapter.
Practice
Course note: Identify one relevant local hazard and the official information source for it.
Course note: Create a short list of unanswered preparedness questions.
Reflection
Course note: Which dramatic scenario is distracting me from the likely one?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why match emergency guidance to the hazard?
blocks.text: Different risks require different current local procedures and expertise.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Know the limits of physical defense manuals
lessons.name: 29.07 Know the limits of physical defense manuals

blocks.text: What can a book teach safely without hands-on supervision?
Core idea

A manual can describe history, terminology, rules, and some general concepts. It cannot assess a learner's body, control an opponent, supply protective equipment, or judge legal consequences. Techniques involving weapons, vulnerable targets, or incapacitation have serious risks and are unsuitable as unsupervised exercises. Seek reputable, rule-bound training for sport and appropriate local help for personal safety.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The source collection contains many combative systems with different purposes. The course treats them as context and supervised sport, not as a sequence of self-defense instructions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A reader uses a martial book to ask a club about safety rules and instructor qualifications, not to rehearse its most dangerous pages at home.
Practice
Course note: Identify what a manual can show and what only a qualified setting can assess.
Course note: Write criteria for a safe, consent-based training environment.
Reflection
Course note: What confidence am I gaining from reading that has never been tested safely?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why are physical defense manuals insufficient alone?
blocks.text: They cannot provide individualized feedback, safe resistance, protective controls, or context-specific judgment.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Review safety choices without blaming victims
lessons.name: 29.08 Review safety choices without blaming victims

blocks.text: What can improve the future response while respecting uncertainty and responsibility?
Core idea

After an incident, separate the actions of the person causing harm, the conditions that made it possible, and the options available to others at the time. Avoid hindsight claims that someone “should have known” from ambiguous signs. A useful review identifies changes to systems, support, or preparations without transferring blame away from wrongdoing.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Decision review and ethics prevent safety education from becoming a list of ways victims supposedly failed.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A venue improves staffing and reporting after repeated harassment rather than teaching patrons that they should have read a stranger's gestures better.
Practice
Course note: Review a hypothetical incident using perpetrator action, system conditions, and available protective options.
Course note: Propose one prevention change without assigning blame to the harmed person.
Reflection
Course note: What did hindsight make seem obvious that was not clear beforehand?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a safety review fair?
blocks.text: It keeps responsibility for harm clear while identifying feasible protective and system improvements.
Course note: Agency without blame: [[04.01 Sort control, influence, and concern]] · [[04.02 Separate responsibility from blame]] · [[14.06 Apologize with repair rather than performance]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Rehearse a safe exit before a tense moment
lessons.name: 29.09 Rehearse a safe exit before a tense moment

blocks.text: Where could I go and whom could I contact if a situation changed?
Core idea

A useful safety plan identifies practical options before stress narrows attention. In an unfamiliar setting, notice accessible exits, ordinary staff or support, and a way to contact help. This is preparation for choice, not a demand to scan every person for threat. Adapt to mobility, local conditions, and the actual risk. In an immediate emergency, use local emergency services and follow qualified responders rather than a memorized script from a book.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[06 Attention, time, and a workable day]] shows that preparation can reduce last-minute cognitive load. [[30 Digital security and privacy]] uses a similar idea for account recovery.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before a large event, friends agree where to meet if separated and identify staffed help points.

steps.label: Use
steps.text: Choose the safest available action if needed.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Make a short exit-and-contact plan for a hypothetical public event.
Course note: Check whether the plan works for a person with different access needs.
Reflection
Course note: Did my plan create options without making ordinary participation feel dangerous?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of a safety exit plan?
blocks.text: To preserve practical options and support contacts if a real situation becomes unsafe.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Respond to repeated unwanted contact
lessons.name: 29.10 Respond to repeated unwanted contact

blocks.text: When should an unwanted pattern move from private discomfort to documented support?
Core idea

Repeated boundary crossing deserves attention even when each incident is ambiguous alone. Record dates, behavior, and any messages without escalating contact to prove a point. Tell a trusted person or relevant service what is happening, and use workplace, school, platform, or local support channels as appropriate. The right response depends on context and current law; no course can classify a particular situation from a few details. The burden of another person's behavior belongs to the person doing it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[04 Agency, responsibility, and boundaries]] distinguishes a person's choices from blame for harm. [[18 Manipulation, propaganda, and independent judgment]] helps recognize pressure without assuming a diagnosis.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A colleague continues contacting someone after a clear request to stop. The recipient saves messages and asks a workplace contact about available options.
Practice
Course note: Write a hypothetical factual incident log entry without guessing the other person's motive.
Course note: List two appropriate support channels for the setting in the example.
Reflection
Course note: Did I minimize a pattern because no single event seemed decisive?
Recall check

blocks.question: What helps assess repeated unwanted contact?
blocks.text: A factual record of the pattern and timely support through appropriate people or services.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Help as a bystander without taking over
lessons.name: 29.11 Help as a bystander without taking over

blocks.text: What can a witness do that increases someone's options and safety?
Core idea

A bystander may be able to alert staff, create a chance to leave, call appropriate help, or check privately what the affected person wants. Choose an action that fits the risk and your capability; direct confrontation is not always safest. Do not make a public spectacle of the person receiving help or demand a detailed account on the spot. Afterward, let them decide what support they want where possible, while responding to immediate danger appropriately.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] starts with the other person's perspective. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] weighs care, consent, and likely consequences together.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: At a social event, a witness notices someone repeatedly being blocked from leaving a conversation and asks staff to assist while checking whether the person wants to move away.

steps.label: Follow
steps.text: Respect the person's choices where possible.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: List three bystander options for a hypothetical low-risk setting, ordered by likely safety.
Course note: Write one respectful question that offers help without taking control.
Reflection
Course note: Was my imagined intervention centered on the person's needs or on looking brave?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a bystander aim to increase?
blocks.text: The affected person's safety, practical options, and access to appropriate support.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Review a safety event without hindsight blame
lessons.name: 29.12 Review a safety event without hindsight blame

blocks.text: How can we learn from an event without pretending everyone had the later facts?
Core idea

After an incident, separate what was known at the time from what became clear afterward. Ask which supports, exits, rules, or communications worked and which failed. Do not turn a victim's ordinary action into the cause of another person's harmful choice. A useful review improves future options and institutional response; it does not require the affected person to retell details for others' education. Some events call for trauma-informed professional support rather than a group exercise.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] explains hindsight distortion. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] asks how institutional arrangements shape outcomes.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A venue reviews whether staff knew how to respond to a report and whether contact information was visible, without assigning fault to the person who sought help.

steps.label: Reconstruct
steps.text: Separate earlier knowledge from later facts.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write three system-focused review questions for a hypothetical event.
Course note: Separate contemporaneous facts from facts learned afterward.
Reflection
Course note: Did hindsight make an earlier uncertainty appear obvious?
Recall check

blocks.question: How can a safety review avoid victim blame?
blocks.text: It examines known information, available options, and system response while placing responsibility for harm on the harmful actor.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Begin with a threat model
lessons.name: 30.01 Begin with a threat model

blocks.text: What am I protecting, from what plausible risk, and at what cost?
Core idea

List important accounts, information, devices, and relationships. Consider who might seek access and how, using the actual context rather than every imaginable threat. Prioritize protections that reduce likely harm without making ordinary life unworkable. Review the model when your situation changes.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Safety planning and digital privacy share the need for proportionate preparation. The most dramatic scenario is not always the most relevant.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A student's main risks may be losing access to schoolwork and falling for a fake login message, not a sophisticated surveillance operation.
Practice
Course note: List three digital assets, plausible risks, and consequences.
Course note: Rank one protective action by likely benefit and effort.
Reflection
Course note: Which risk have I ignored because it is ordinary?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a threat model?
blocks.text: A context-specific account of what needs protection, from whom or what, and which safeguards are proportionate.
Course note: Defensive security and consent: [[18.08 Build a defensive pause]] · [[29.02 Build everyday prevention into routines]] · [[30.08 Distinguish ethical security training from intrusion]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Protect accounts with distinct credentials
lessons.name: 30.02 Protect accounts with distinct credentials

blocks.text: Would one compromised password expose several accounts?
Core idea

Reusing a password links otherwise separate accounts. Use unique strong credentials, a trustworthy manager where suitable, and additional authentication when available. Protect recovery methods too; a locked account can be as disruptive as an exposed one. Follow current service guidance because authentication options and threats change.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Habit design can make secure behavior less effortful by reducing the need to invent and remember many passwords.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A reused password appears in a breach. Unique credentials limit the damage to one service, while a prepared recovery method helps restore access.
Practice
Course note: Audit whether important accounts share credentials without writing passwords in this course.
Course note: Prioritize one account for stronger authentication and recovery review.
Reflection
Course note: Which recovery route would fail when I need it?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why use distinct credentials?
blocks.text: A breach of one service should not automatically unlock unrelated accounts.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Verify a message through a known channel
lessons.name: 30.03 Verify a message through a known channel

blocks.text: Is this request really from the person or service it claims to represent?
Core idea

Deceptive messages can imitate branding, urgency, authority, or a familiar contact. Avoid relying only on appearance. Use a known address, app, or phone number to verify requests for money, codes, credentials, or unusual files. A real sender should tolerate reasonable independent checking. Report suspicious messages through available channels.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Propaganda and persuasion literacy become practical defenses against phishing and impersonation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A message says your account will close unless you enter a code. You open the service through your saved route rather than the message's link.

steps.label: Report
steps.text: Use the service's channel if suspicious.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Compare the claims and requested action in two example messages.
Course note: Identify the independent channel you would use to verify each.
Reflection
Course note: Which emotion is the message trying to make urgent?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why verify independently?
blocks.text: The request's branding and apparent sender can be imitated, while a known channel reduces reliance on the suspicious message.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep software and backups usable
lessons.name: 30.04 Keep software and backups usable

blocks.text: Could I restore important work after a device or account problem?
Core idea

Updates can repair known weaknesses; backups reduce the damage from loss, failure, or malicious change. Prioritize important data and test whether a backup can actually be restored. Plan where recovery information is kept and who may need access. A backup that has never been checked may provide false confidence.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Recovery is part of risk management, not a sign that prevention has failed.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A writer keeps a separate copy of current drafts and periodically opens a restored file to confirm it is usable.
Practice
Course note: Identify your most important files and how they are currently backed up.
Course note: Test recovery of one non-sensitive file using your existing system.
Reflection
Course note: What would I discover only after losing the device?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why test a backup?
blocks.text: A stored copy is useful only if it can be found and restored when needed.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand privacy as a set of choices
lessons.name: 30.05 Understand privacy as a set of choices

blocks.text: Who can see, retain, and connect my data?
Core idea

Privacy varies by service, device, relationship, and setting. Examine what information is collected, how it is shared, and whether the default fits your purpose. Encryption and anonymity tools have different roles and limits. Avoid promising perfect invisibility from a single app or tactic; focus on actual risks and informed settings.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Digital privacy and autonomy meet when a person understands the trade-offs in sharing information.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A location feature is useful for a trip but need not remain available to every app afterward. You review its permissions when the trip ends.

steps.label: Choice
steps.text: Set access to fit the purpose.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Review permissions for one service or device feature you use.
Course note: Change one unnecessary sharing setting and check that the service still meets your needs.
Reflection
Course note: Which data flow did I agree to without noticing?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is privacy context-specific?
blocks.text: Different tools, audiences, data types, and purposes create different exposure and trade-offs.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Learn network and system basics defensively
lessons.name: 30.06 Learn network and system basics defensively

blocks.text: What path does information take when I use a service?
Core idea

Understand devices, networks, accounts, permissions, and the difference between public and private information at a conceptual level. This helps you ask better questions about protection and failure. Technical books include attack tools and outdated platform details; use them only in authorized training environments and update practice from current documentation. No general reading course grants permission to probe someone else's system.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Technical literacy makes security less mystical and improves collaboration with specialists.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Knowing that a shared account weakens individual accountability helps a team design separate access for staff.
Practice
Course note: Draw a simple map of your own authorized service: device, network, account, stored data.
Course note: Identify one access or permission question for its administrator or current documentation.
Reflection
Course note: What do I assume is “secure” because I cannot see the path?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the purpose of defensive technical literacy?
blocks.text: To understand systems and risks well enough to protect and ask informed questions within authorized boundaries.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Handle an incident without improvising secrecy
lessons.name: 30.07 Handle an incident without improvising secrecy

blocks.text: What would I do if an important account or device might be compromised?
Core idea

Identify what happened, preserve relevant evidence, use the service's official recovery process, and notify people who may be affected when appropriate. Avoid clicking further suspicious prompts or trying unverified fixes under pressure. Organizations need defined roles and current procedures for response and recovery. The exact steps depend on the incident and service.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: NIST's govern, identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover sequence expresses a full lifecycle; the course applies its broad logic without pretending to be an incident manual.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After noticing unauthorized account activity, a user goes through the service's official recovery channel and checks connected accounts rather than answering the suspicious sender.

steps.label: Respond
steps.text: Use official help and preserve facts.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: List the official recovery channels for one important account.
Course note: Write a short incident checklist covering evidence, access, affected people, and help.
Reflection
Course note: What information would I need to recover without making the incident worse?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why plan response before an incident?
blocks.text: A known recovery route and roles reduce confusion and delay under pressure.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish ethical security training from intrusion
lessons.name: 30.08 Distinguish ethical security training from intrusion

blocks.text: Do I have clear authority to test this system?
Core idea

Security learning can use owned devices, purpose-built labs, and written authorization with scope. Real accounts and third-party systems remain outside that scope without permission. Methods from offensive manuals can cause harm or violate rules even when a learner claims educational intent. Focus course practice on defensive understanding and consent-based labs.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This is an applied lesson in ethics and boundaries: capability does not establish authority.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A student uses a controlled training environment to understand a vulnerability class and documents protective lessons; they do not test the same idea on a public service.
Practice
Course note: Define owner, scope, allowed actions, and reporting path for a hypothetical training lab.
Course note: Identify what would make a planned test unauthorized.
Reflection
Course note: Am I treating curiosity as permission?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes security testing ethical?
blocks.text: Clear authorization, defined scope, controlled practice, and responsible reporting.
Course note: Defensive security and consent: [[18.08 Build a defensive pause]] · [[29.02 Build everyday prevention into routines]] · [[30.01 Begin with a threat model]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Reduce the data you leave behind
lessons.name: 30.09 Reduce the data you leave behind

blocks.text: Which information needs to be shared, stored, or kept at all?
Core idea

Privacy improves when fewer unnecessary copies of sensitive data exist. Review what an account or service asks for, how long you retain records, and who can access them. Keep what is needed for lawful obligations and useful recovery, and remove or restrict what has no clear purpose. Deletion is not always complete or immediate, so do not promise invisibility. A practical privacy choice balances function, safety, and the consequences of losing needed records.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[29 Safety, awareness, and de-escalation]] uses proportionate risk planning. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] asks about other people's information entrusted to you.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community organizer collects a contact method for event updates but avoids requesting unrelated personal details and limits who can open the list.

steps.label: Review
steps.text: Remove what no longer serves the purpose.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Review a hypothetical sign-up form and identify fields that lack a clear purpose.
Course note: Write a simple retention rule for the remaining information.
Reflection
Course note: What data did I keep because storage was easy rather than because it served a need?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is data minimization?
blocks.text: Collecting, sharing, and retaining only information needed for a defined purpose and obligation.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Prepare for account recovery before losing access
lessons.name: 30.10 Prepare for account recovery before losing access

blocks.text: Could I recover an important account or device without exposing it further?
Core idea

Strong account protection is incomplete if recovery depends on a lost device, forgotten code, or unavailable contact. Check recovery methods for essential accounts, keep backup codes or records in a protected place, and ensure trusted contacts have only the access they legitimately need. Test that recovery information is current without deliberately locking yourself out. Treat recovery messages as another place where impersonation can occur; verify through known channels.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] treats continuity as part of a handover. [[25 Money, records, and financial judgment]] benefits from reliable access to essential records.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Someone replaces a phone and discovers that a second factor was tied only to the old device. A prepared recovery method would have prevented a long lockout.
Practice
Course note: Make a private inventory of account recovery methods without recording secrets in the course notebook.
Course note: Identify one single point of failure and a safe backup approach.
Reflection
Course note: Which account would cause the most disruption if recovery failed today?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why plan account recovery?
blocks.text: It keeps legitimate access possible when a device or method fails without weakening ordinary protection.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Review app permissions as a privacy choice
lessons.name: 30.11 Review app permissions as a privacy choice

blocks.text: Does an app need the access it currently has to provide the function I use?
Core idea

Permissions can grant access to location, contacts, camera, files, or other data. Review them in the actual device settings and compare each with the feature you use. Some access may be needed only while a feature is active; other requests may be unnecessary. Changing a permission can break a feature, so test the result and choose knowingly. Do not infer that a permission alone proves malicious intent; examine the service and its behavior in context.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] cautions against overinterpreting a signal. [[30.05 Understand privacy as a set of choices]] connects privacy to trade-offs.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A weather app may use location for local forecasts, but a person can decide whether to give continuous access or enter a city manually.
Practice
Course note: In a hypothetical app list, label each requested permission by purpose, alternative, and concern.
Course note: Review one real app's permissions locally without sharing personal details in the notebook.
Reflection
Course note: Which permission did I grant once and never reconsider?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should an app permission be judged?
blocks.text: By the feature it enables, the access it grants, available alternatives, and the user's chosen trade-off.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Practice a calm response to a suspicious message
lessons.name: 30.12 Practice a calm response to a suspicious message

blocks.text: What steps preserve options when a message asks for urgent action?
Core idea

Urgency, secrecy, and requests for credentials or payment are reasons to pause and verify. Do not use a link or number supplied in the same suspicious message as your sole proof. Check through a known official channel, keep relevant evidence, and report through the service's established process if appropriate. If you already acted, change the relevant access and contact the affected provider through trusted means. A rehearsed response is more useful than trying to detect every trick by appearance alone.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[18 Manipulation, propaganda, and independent judgment]] examines pressure tactics. [[29 Safety, awareness, and de-escalation]] favors concrete options over speculation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A text claims a parcel requires immediate payment. The recipient opens the delivery service independently instead of following the text's link.

steps.label: Recover
steps.text: Report or secure access if needed.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write a three-step verification routine for a hypothetical urgent payment message.
Course note: Identify what evidence to preserve if the message is reported.
Reflection
Course note: Which element of urgency made the request feel more credible than it was?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the safest first response to an unexpected urgent account or payment request?
blocks.text: Pause and verify through a known independent channel before acting.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish behavior, experience, and explanation
lessons.name: 31.01 Distinguish behavior, experience, and explanation

blocks.text: What is observable, what is reported, and what is a theory about it?
Core idea

Psychology studies behavior and reported experience using many methods. A theory proposes mechanisms, while a person's own account describes what an experience is like. Do not collapse these levels. The same behavior can arise through different paths, and a person may know the feeling better than the cause. A useful explanation should make a checkable difference or clarify a specific case.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Older psychoanalytic theories, cognitive models, and neuroscience texts ask overlapping questions but use different evidence and concepts.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Someone avoids a meeting. You can observe the absence, hear their account of anxiety, and consider several causal explanations without treating one as established.
Practice
Course note: Sort three claims about one behavior into observation, report, and theory.
Course note: Ask what evidence would distinguish two proposed explanations.
Reflection
Course note: Which level have I treated as if it were another?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why separate levels of psychological explanation?
blocks.text: Behavior, subjective report, and causal theory provide different kinds of information.

Course note: Mind models and diagnosis: [[03.07 Recognize defensive explanations]] · [[16.03 Avoid diagnosing relatives from a checklist]] · [[31.05 Use psychological categories without self-diagnosis]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand emotion as information in decision-making
lessons.name: 31.02 Understand emotion as information in decision-making

blocks.text: What might feeling contribute to a judgment?
Core idea

Emotions can signal salience, bodily state, learned experience, and social meaning. They can also bias attention and intensify an unsupported story. Treat emotion as relevant information that needs interpretation rather than as either infallible truth or noise to suppress. A decision may require both feeling and explicit comparison of options.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Neuroscience accounts challenging a strict reason-emotion split meet the course's practical distinction between experience and inference.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Discomfort about a contract prompts you to inspect unclear terms. The feeling is useful as a cue to examine, not proof that the other party is deceptive.
Practice
Course note: Describe a recent feeling and the question it prompted.
Course note: Check the external evidence before acting on the feeling's first explanation.
Reflection
Course note: Have I dismissed a useful signal or granted it more certainty than it earned?
Recall check

blocks.question: How can emotion aid judgment?
blocks.text: It can direct attention to something important while still requiring interpretation and evidence.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Interpret the brain through careful models
lessons.name: 31.03 Interpret the brain through careful models

blocks.text: What does this brain explanation actually establish?
Core idea

Brain regions and neural processes contribute to perception, memory, emotion, and action, but a simple diagram rarely explains a whole personality or decision. Ask whether a claim comes from measurement, a model, or a metaphor. Avoid saying a brain scan proves a specific motive in one person. Neuroscience can constrain theories without replacing psychological and social context.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Popular brain-based self-help often makes broader claims than the underlying research. The philosophy of science module helps inspect that jump.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A book describes an “emotional brain” overriding a “rational brain.” The image may help discussion, but real decisions involve interacting systems and context.
Practice
Course note: Identify one brain metaphor and the specific finding it is meant to summarize.
Course note: Write what the metaphor omits or may mislead a reader to assume.
Reflection
Course note: Am I using technical vocabulary as proof without understanding the evidence?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a limit of simple brain diagrams?
blocks.text: They simplify interacting processes and do not by themselves identify an individual's motive or destiny.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Examine memory as reconstruction
lessons.name: 31.04 Examine memory as reconstruction

blocks.text: How reliable is my recollection of a meaningful event?
Core idea

Memory supports learning and identity but is affected by attention, later information, emotion, and retelling. A vivid memory can be sincerely held and still contain errors. Use contemporaneous records where accuracy matters, while respecting that a person's experience is not erased by uncertainty about details. Avoid using memory science as a blanket way to dismiss someone else's account.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Mnemonic techniques improve retrieval of chosen material, while autobiographical memory raises different questions about reconstruction and interpretation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two colleagues remember a meeting deadline differently. Checking the written agreement helps settle the practical issue without declaring either person dishonest.
Practice
Course note: Compare one recollection with a dated record if available.
Course note: Note what you know, what you infer, and what remains uncertain.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of my certainty comes from vividness rather than corroboration?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why can vivid memory still be uncertain?
blocks.text: Memory is reconstructed through attention and later interpretation rather than being a perfect recording.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use psychological categories without self-diagnosis
lessons.name: 31.05 Use psychological categories without self-diagnosis

blocks.text: Is this framework helping me understand a pattern or assigning an unsupported label?
Core idea

Concepts such as defense mechanisms, attachment, cognitive bias, and personality can prompt useful questions. Their definitions, evidence, and clinical use differ. Do not diagnose yourself or another person from a single chapter, quiz, or conflict. Focus on observed behavior and its effects, and use qualified care for persistent distress or serious concerns.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The collection includes scholarly psychology, popular typologies, and dramatic “dark psychology” books. Their claims require different scrutiny.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You notice a habit of explaining away feedback. You investigate when it happens instead of deciding that you have a permanent disorder.
Practice
Course note: Turn one psychological label into a specific, observable pattern.
Course note: Identify what the label does and does not explain.
Reflection
Course note: Does the category expand useful choices or narrow my view of the person?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a responsible use of a psychological category?
blocks.text: As a limited question or description supported by evidence, not a casual diagnosis.

Course note: Family history and current choice: [[16.01 Describe a family pattern without making it destiny]] · [[16.03 Avoid diagnosing relatives from a checklist]] · [[16.07 Set adult boundaries with family]].

Course note: Mind models and diagnosis: [[03.07 Recognize defensive explanations]] · [[16.03 Avoid diagnosing relatives from a checklist]] · [[31.01 Distinguish behavior, experience, and explanation]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare competing accounts of consciousness
lessons.name: 31.06 Compare competing accounts of consciousness

blocks.text: What is each theory trying to explain about experience?
Core idea

Consciousness discussions may address wakefulness, awareness of the world, self-awareness, felt experience, or the relation of mind and body. Specify the target before comparing theories. Neuroscience can examine correlates and mechanisms; philosophy asks what those findings imply and what remains unexplained. A speculative theory should be presented as such even when it uses scientific vocabulary.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Damasio, Freud, older speculative physics, and spiritual accounts cannot be collapsed into one proof. They disagree in method and claim.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A study of brain activity during perception informs how awareness works, but it does not settle every philosophical question about subjective experience.
Practice
Course note: Define two different meanings of consciousness and a question for each.
Course note: Compare one empirical and one philosophical claim by evidence and scope.
Reflection
Course note: Which problem did I assume was solved because the same word appeared in both texts?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why define the target of a consciousness theory?
blocks.text: Different accounts may explain different phenomena and require different kinds of evidence.

Course note: Spiritual meaning and empirical claims: [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence]] · [[34.01 Ask what kind of religious claim is being made]] · [[34.05 Study religious experience with interpretive humility]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Recognize stagecraft behind apparent mind reading
lessons.name: 31.07 Recognize stagecraft behind apparent mind reading

blocks.text: Could an impressive demonstration arise from information, suggestion, or selection?
Core idea

Mentalism and cold reading can be entertaining performances. They do not establish telepathy or access to private thoughts. Examine what the performer knew, how questions shaped responses, which misses were omitted, and whether a prediction was specific in advance. Enjoy the performance while preserving the distinction between stage effect and empirical ability.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The collection includes mentalism instructions and paranormal claims. Studying their mechanisms supports critical literacy without turning deception into a relationship technique.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A broad statement feels personal because the listener supplies the details. A controlled test would need predictions recorded before feedback and count failures too.
Practice
Course note: Analyze a harmless public demonstration for prior information, feedback, and selection.
Course note: Design a fair test of its claimed ability without performing deceptive readings on someone.
Reflection
Course note: Which detail made the effect feel impossible while the missing data stayed invisible?
Recall check

blocks.question: Does a convincing mind-reading performance prove telepathy?
blocks.text: No. Stagecraft, information, suggestion, and selective memory can produce convincing effects.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep a plural but disciplined mind model
lessons.name: 31.08 Keep a plural but disciplined mind model

blocks.text: Which explanation helps this problem without pretending to explain everything?
Core idea

Biological, psychological, social, and philosophical accounts can illuminate different levels of a person's life. Use the model matched to the question: a sleep problem, a communication conflict, and a metaphysical question require different methods. Models may interact, but they should not be blended into an unfalsifiable story. Preserve uncertainty and seek qualified help for serious symptoms.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This module widens the frame for ethics and philosophy, where facts about minds inform but do not alone determine what should be done.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person's concentration difficulty may involve workload, sleep, task design, and health. One dramatic label is unlikely to capture all relevant factors.
Practice
Course note: Map one difficulty at biological, personal, relational, and institutional levels.
Course note: Identify which level you can investigate next and which needs specialist input.
Reflection
Course note: Which favored explanation have I stretched beyond its evidence?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a plural mind model disciplined?
blocks.text: It matches each explanation to a specific question, evidence, and limit rather than claiming one lens explains all.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask which behavior a theory predicts
lessons.name: 31.09 Ask which behavior a theory predicts

blocks.text: How could I tell whether a psychological explanation is helping?
Core idea

A theory becomes more useful when it predicts a difference you could observe or when it organizes evidence better than alternatives. Name the behavior, the proposed mechanism, and a rival explanation. Avoid labeling a person from one action or using a theory to claim access to hidden motives. Context, self-report, and repeated observations matter. A model can be useful without explaining every case, and a failed prediction is an opportunity to narrow its scope.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] asks for discriminating evidence. [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] protects the person's account from being overwritten by a favored theory.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Someone misses a meeting. Competing explanations include fear, scheduling conflict, and simple oversight; a respectful check is more informative than a diagnosis.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Seek relevant evidence and the person's account.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write two explanations for a hypothetical behavior and one different prediction from each.
Course note: Draft a question that checks the person's account without implying a diagnosis.
Reflection
Course note: What did my preferred theory make too easy to assume?
Recall check

blocks.question: What improves a psychological explanation?
blocks.text: Clear scope, competing alternatives, and observations that could distinguish the explanations.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Notice how body state can shape judgment
lessons.name: 31.10 Notice how body state can shape judgment

blocks.text: Which bodily and emotional conditions may affect a decision without determining it?
Core idea

Fatigue, arousal, pain, and emotion can influence what feels urgent or possible. They are part of the decision context, not evidence that a thought is automatically false. Pause before a high-stakes choice when conditions are unusually intense, and record what matters about the situation. If symptoms persist or impair functioning, consider qualified care. A book about brain and emotion offers models, not a way to diagnose yourself from one day.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[03 Emotions, acceptance, and a steadier response]] makes room to notice feelings. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] adds decision stakes and timing.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After a sleepless night, a manager drafts a difficult reply but waits to send it until they can review its facts and tone.
Practice
Course note: Identify two conditions that affect your decision quality and one low-cost response for each.
Course note: Create a pause rule for a consequential decision when one of those conditions is present.
Reflection
Course note: Did I treat a body state as irrelevant or as a complete explanation?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should body state enter judgment?
blocks.text: As relevant context that may justify a pause or support, without automatically invalidating or determining the decision.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate a memory from an inference about it
lessons.name: 31.11 Separate a memory from an inference about it

blocks.text: What part of this recollection do I remember, and what part have I concluded later?
Core idea

Remembering reconstructs an event using cues and later knowledge. Confidence and vividness do not always show accuracy. For a consequential event, write the earliest account available, mark direct observations, and note later interpretations separately. Seek independent records when appropriate, while respecting privacy and the limits of those records. Do not use uncertainty about memory to dismiss a person's experience; use it to be precise about what a claim can establish.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07 Learning, memory, and understanding]] studies retrieval. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] asks how records and later narratives interact.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team member remembers that everyone agreed to a deadline, but meeting notes show the date was proposed and never confirmed.
Practice
Course note: Rewrite a hypothetical recollection into observed detail, later interpretation, and missing information.
Course note: Name one independent record that could help without claiming it captures the whole experience.
Reflection
Course note: Which later conclusion had merged with my memory of the event?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why separate recollection from later inference?
blocks.text: Memory can incorporate later meaning, so the distinction makes a consequential account clearer and more checkable.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use a mental model without turning it into an identity
lessons.name: 31.12 Use a mental model without turning it into an identity

blocks.text: When is a label helping me act, and when is it narrowing a person?
Core idea

Categories can help organize patterns and ask for relevant support. They can also make changeable behavior appear permanent, hide context, or invite amateur diagnosis. State what the model explains, what it does not, and whose expertise is needed for a clinical claim. Address the specific situation and person in front of you rather than treating a category as a full biography. Let a model earn its usefulness through better questions and outcomes.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[16 Family, development, and relational patterns]] avoids turning early patterns into destiny. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] treats dignity as a constraint on judgment.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A teacher notices a student struggles to start tasks and changes the support offered; they do not infer a diagnosis from one classroom pattern.

steps.label: Limit
steps.text: Name what the label cannot show.

steps.label: Support
steps.text: Choose an appropriate next question or resource.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Take a broad behavior label and rewrite it as a specific observation with context.
Course note: List two alternative explanations or support questions the label might obscure.
Reflection
Course note: Did the category help me respond or only make me feel certain?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a safe use of a psychological category?
blocks.text: Use it as a limited question or organizing tool, while preserving context, individual variation, and clinical boundaries.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask what a belief does without claiming why it is true
lessons.name: 31.13 Ask what a belief does without claiming why it is true

blocks.text: How can I study a belief's psychological role while respecting the question of its truth?
Core idea

A belief can organize identity, community, memory, or action. Studying those roles does not settle whether the belief's central claim is true or false. Likewise, a person's sincerity does not prove the claim. Separate descriptive questions about how belief forms and functions from philosophical, historical, or empirical questions about what it asserts. Avoid reducing believers to one psychological cause or treating all beliefs as interchangeable.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[34 Religion, spiritual traditions, and belief]] examines traditions on their own terms. [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] matches evidence to the kind of claim.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Researchers may ask how a shared ritual supports belonging; participants may also ask whether the ritual expresses a real spiritual truth. The questions are related but distinct.
Practice
Course note: Write one descriptive and one truth-oriented question about a hypothetical belief.
Course note: Identify the evidence or conversation each question would require.
Reflection
Course note: Did I use an explanation of belief formation as if it had decided belief's truth?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a psychological account of belief establish?
blocks.text: It may explain aspects of formation or function, but it does not by itself settle the belief's truth.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate what is from what ought to be
lessons.name: 32.01 Separate what is from what ought to be

blocks.text: Which part of this argument describes a fact, and which part recommends a value?
Core idea

A description of common behavior does not by itself establish that the behavior is right. An ethical conclusion needs a value, principle, or account of what matters. State both the facts and the normative premise. People can agree on the facts and disagree about the value, or agree on the value and disagree about facts.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Science informs consequences; ethics judges which consequences and duties matter. Neither can silently replace the other.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: “Most teams work late” does not establish that late work is fair. The missing question concerns obligations, consent, and costs.
Practice
Course note: Identify the factual and value premises in one everyday moral claim.
Course note: Ask which premise a reasonable dissenter might reject.
Reflection
Course note: Where have I hidden a value judgment inside a statement of fact?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why cannot a descriptive claim settle an ethical question alone?
blocks.text: A conclusion about what ought to be done requires a normative premise or value.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare consequences, duties, and character
lessons.name: 32.02 Compare consequences, duties, and character

blocks.text: Which ethical lens reveals what another might miss?
Core idea

Consequence-focused reasoning asks what effects an action has. Duty-focused reasoning asks what obligations and limits apply. Virtue-focused reasoning asks what kind of conduct expresses good character. Each can identify a different issue; none is an automatic calculator. Compare their questions and where they conflict in a concrete case.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ethical theory becomes useful when it improves the questions you ask of a real decision.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Sharing a colleague's private story might produce short-term support for a project, violate confidentiality, and express disloyalty. All three lenses matter.
Practice
Course note: Analyze one modest decision through outcomes, duties, and character.
Course note: Identify a case where the lenses pull in different directions.
Reflection
Course note: Which lens do I use to avoid an uncomfortable consideration?
Recall check

blocks.question: What do three major ethical lenses emphasize?
blocks.text: Consequences, obligations, and qualities of action or character.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use reciprocity without erasing differences
lessons.name: 32.03 Use reciprocity without erasing differences

blocks.text: Would I accept the treatment I am giving, after considering the other person's actual needs?
Core idea

Reciprocity encourages consistency and perspective-taking, but people differ in needs, power, and preferences. “I would be fine with it” cannot replace asking the affected person. Use the principle to catch double standards, then check context and consent. A fair rule should be one you can explain to everyone it affects.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Golden-rule traditions and modern care ethics overlap but differ on how much attention to individual circumstances is required.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You would welcome public praise; a colleague strongly prefers private acknowledgment. Reciprocity prompts care, while listening determines the form.
Practice
Course note: Test one planned action from the other person's position.
Course note: Ask what they actually prefer rather than projecting your own preference.
Reflection
Course note: Where does my imagined perspective fail to represent theirs?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a limit of simple reciprocity?
blocks.text: Others may have different needs and preferences, so perspective-taking should be checked with them.
Course note: Empathy and disagreement: [[10.08 Disagree with the strongest version]] · [[14.02 Reflect back without performing agreement]] · [[17.05 Use empathy without pretending to agree]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Treat consent and dignity as real constraints
lessons.name: 32.04 Treat consent and dignity as real constraints

blocks.text: Does this action use another person merely as a means to my goal?
Core idea

A desirable outcome does not automatically justify deception, coercion, or disregard of a person's agency. Explain relevant information, allow meaningful refusal, and account for vulnerability and power. Duties of care and confidentiality may remain even when a shortcut would improve a metric. In complex cases, legal and professional obligations may require current qualified guidance.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Kantian and rights-based arguments put limits on the instrumental tactics found in some persuasion and strategic texts.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A manager cannot justify secretly using employee private data by saying it might improve productivity.
Practice
Course note: Identify whose consent or dignity a proposed action affects.
Course note: Redesign the action so those people can participate knowingly or decline.
Reflection
Course note: Whose choice disappears in my plan?
Recall check

blocks.question: What ethical limit does dignity place on a plan?
blocks.text: People must not be treated only as tools whose informed choice can be bypassed for an outcome.
Course note: Consent and persuasion: [[15.05 Treat consent as ongoing communication]] · [[17.01 Define ethical influence]] · [[18.01 Distinguish influence from manipulation]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Consider distribution, not only totals
lessons.name: 32.05 Consider distribution, not only totals

blocks.text: Who bears the cost of the outcome I call good?
Core idea

An action can improve an average while concentrating harm on a smaller group. Examine gains and losses separately, including people absent from the decision. Consider whether burdens fall on those with less power or fewer alternatives. Aggregate benefit matters, but it does not erase a question about fairness, rights, or repair.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Systems thinking and political philosophy make ethical review more complete than a single efficiency number.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A service change speeds most requests but leaves people with limited internet access unable to participate. The distribution changes the evaluation.
Practice
Course note: Make a stakeholder map for one proposed improvement.
Course note: Identify a mitigation or redesign for the group bearing the largest cost.
Reflection
Course note: Which person disappears in the average?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why examine distribution?
blocks.text: A good total can conceal serious unequal burdens or exclusion.
Course note: Ethics and institutions: [[32.07 Learn from ethical failure in history]] · [[39.04 Detect how authority can normalize harm]] · [[39.08 Practice public reasoning]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Face a duty conflict honestly
lessons.name: 32.06 Face a duty conflict honestly

blocks.text: Which obligations collide, and what can be preserved?
Core idea

Some dilemmas involve genuine competing duties: loyalty and truthfulness, safety and privacy, individual need and group fairness. Name each obligation in its strongest form and examine available options. Avoid resolving the conflict by pretending one duty never existed. A choice may still involve regret and a responsibility to explain or repair.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
