blocks.text: Epic and philosophical texts often dramatize duty conflicts. Their value lies in sharpening judgment, not handing down an effortless rule for every setting.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A colleague asks you to conceal an error that affects others. Loyalty matters, but so does preventing harm; the response should protect both as far as possible.
Practice
Course note: Write two conflicting duties in one case without caricaturing either.
Course note: Generate an option that preserves part of each, then state what it cannot preserve.
Reflection
Course note: What cost will remain even after the best available choice?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a duty conflict genuine?
blocks.text: Two legitimate obligations cannot both be fully satisfied under the available conditions.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Learn from ethical failure in history
lessons.name: 32.07 Learn from ethical failure in history

blocks.text: How did a respectable idea or institution become harmful?
Core idea

Historical harms can be enabled by prestigious authorities, group incentives, exclusion, and claims that a policy serves a greater good. Examine the actual evidence, who lacked power to object, and how dissent was handled. Avoid reducing the lesson to “bad people in the past”; identify mechanisms that could recur. Historical context explains how a view arose but does not excuse the harm.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Texts on eugenics, race, state violence, and public management show why ethical review needs evidence and accountable power.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A movement dresses coercive policy in scientific language while excluding affected people from decision-making. The legitimacy of the institution does not validate the policy.
Practice
Course note: Analyze a historical case by claim, authority, evidence, affected people, and dissent.
Course note: Identify a present-day safeguard that addresses one mechanism, without claiming the situations are identical.
Reflection
Course note: Which authority cue would have made the claim feel safe to me?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why study ethical failure historically?
blocks.text: It reveals mechanisms by which authority, incentives, and exclusion can normalize harm.
Course note: Ethics and institutions: [[32.05 Consider distribution, not only totals]] · [[39.04 Detect how authority can normalize harm]] · [[39.08 Practice public reasoning]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Write an ethical decision record
lessons.name: 32.08 Write an ethical decision record

blocks.text: How can I explain a difficult choice to those affected?
Core idea

State the facts, uncertainty, values, duties, likely consequences, affected people, rejected options, and plan for review. A record will not make the choice painless or universally accepted. It makes the reasoning visible and revisable. Include how you will listen to those bearing costs and what repair would be owed if assumptions prove wrong.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This joins decision quality to moral accountability before moving into broader philosophical worldviews.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team records why a resource decision was made, the groups it may burden, and when the outcome will be reviewed.
Practice
Course note: Create a one-page ethical decision record for a modest real or hypothetical choice.
Course note: Ask who would reasonably challenge the record and on what grounds.
Reflection
Course note: What would I rather leave unsaid because it weakens my preferred conclusion?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in an ethical decision record?
blocks.text: Facts, values, duties, consequences, affected people, alternatives, uncertainty, and review.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Test a principle on the hard case
lessons.name: 32.09 Test a principle on the hard case

blocks.text: Would I accept this rule when it burdens someone I care about or benefits someone I oppose?
Core idea

A principle is easier to endorse in a case where it favors us. Test it on cases with reversed identities and inconvenient consequences. Then ask whether differences between the cases are morally relevant rather than merely emotionally salient. Consistency does not mean treating unlike situations as identical; it means explaining the difference openly. A hard case can refine a rule without proving that all rules are empty.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[10 Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement]] examines consistency in reasoning. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] shows why public standards need to survive changes in who holds power.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A group supports a right to challenge decisions when its own members are affected. It then asks whether the same right applies to a rival group.
Practice
Course note: Write a principle behind a real judgment and reverse the roles in a hypothetical case.
Course note: Name any difference that still justifies treating the two cases differently.
Reflection
Course note: Did my principle change because the facts changed or because my loyalty did?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a hard-case test reveal?
blocks.text: Whether a proposed principle survives role reversal or needs a clearly relevant exception.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Include absent people in a decision
lessons.name: 32.10 Include absent people in a decision

blocks.text: Who will experience the effects but cannot speak in the room?
Core idea

Decisions often favor the people present, powerful, or easy to count. List those who will bear costs later, including dependents, future users, and people excluded by access barriers. You cannot speak for them with certainty, but you can seek representative input, relevant evidence, and safeguards. Record which interests remain uncertain. A fair process makes this uncertainty visible rather than assuming silence means consent.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[26 Economics, incentives, and public choices]] examines distribution. [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] assigns responsibility for affected people beyond the immediate decision makers.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A school changes a digital process after consulting staff, then discovers that some families have limited device access. Their interests needed attention before rollout.
Practice
Course note: List three absent groups in a hypothetical institutional decision.
Course note: Propose one feasible way to learn about each group's likely experience.
Reflection
Course note: Which people were absent because reaching them would slow the decision?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why identify absent stakeholders?
blocks.text: A decision can shift costs onto people who are not represented in the discussion.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish a good intention from a justified action
lessons.name: 32.11 Distinguish a good intention from a justified action

blocks.text: What else must be examined when someone meant well?
Core idea

Intention matters for understanding a choice, but it does not erase foreseeable harm, ignored warnings, or a duty to repair. Examine what the person knew, what alternatives were available, how the action affected others, and how they respond after learning more. Avoid reducing an entire person to one outcome while still taking that outcome seriously. An ethical review should support learning and accountability together.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] looks for side effects and displaced costs. [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] shows how acknowledgment and repair can follow a mistake.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An organizer changes a meeting time to help most participants but overlooks those with care duties. The intention explains the choice; it does not remove the need to address the exclusion.
Practice
Course note: Analyze a hypothetical well-meant action under intention, foreseeable effects, and available alternatives.
Course note: Write one repair action that responds to the actual burden.
Reflection
Course note: Did I use intention to understand the choice or to excuse its effect?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why are good intentions ethically insufficient?
blocks.text: They do not by themselves settle consequences, ignored information, alternatives, or duties of repair.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Give a moral disagreement a useful shape
lessons.name: 32.12 Give a moral disagreement a useful shape

blocks.text: Are we disputing facts, values, priorities, or what a principle means here?
Core idea

A disagreement becomes more tractable when its source is named. Participants may share a value but disagree about evidence, or accept the same facts while weighing duties differently. Ask each side to state its strongest reason and what would change its view. Some conflicts remain after clarification; a fair process can still decide action while recording dissent. Avoid using forced agreement as a measure of respect.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[10 Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement]] separates argument structure from rhetoric. [[17 Influence, persuasion, and negotiation]] seeks workable decisions without pretending all interests match.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two volunteers agree that an event should be accessible but disagree whether a proposed venue meets that standard. They need evidence about access before debating priorities.
Practice
Course note: Sort one hypothetical disagreement into facts, meanings, values, and priorities.
Course note: Write a fair version of each side's strongest reason.
Reflection
Course note: Was I arguing about a value when the missing issue was a fact, or the reverse?
Recall check

blocks.question: How can a moral disagreement be clarified?
blocks.text: Identify whether the dispute concerns facts, meanings, values, or priorities, then examine the strongest reasons on each side.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask what kind of question you are asking
lessons.name: 33.01 Ask what kind of question you are asking

blocks.text: Is this question empirical, conceptual, ethical, or existential?
Core idea

Questions about measurement, the meaning of a term, what is right, and how to live require different kinds of reasoning. They can interact, but a result in one category may not settle another. State the question precisely and identify what would count as a relevant answer. This prevents a scientific finding from being treated as a complete moral argument or a personal conviction from being presented as a measurement.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course has used these distinctions throughout; philosophy makes the underlying method explicit.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Whether a practice lowers stress is empirical; whether a life should be organized around calm is a value question.
Practice
Course note: Classify four questions from your own life by kind and explain your choice.
Course note: Identify one question that contains two kinds and separate them.
Reflection
Course note: Which method have I used on a question it cannot answer alone?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why classify a question's kind?
blocks.text: Different questions need different evidence, concepts, and standards of argument.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Examine how knowledge is possible
lessons.name: 33.02 Examine how knowledge is possible

blocks.text: What must I assume in order to claim I know this?
Core idea

Knowledge involves more than confidence. Ask how the belief was formed, what justifies it, whether the source is reliable, and what could correct it. Philosophers disagree on the exact account. For practical purposes, make your reasons visible and separate direct experience from inference and testimony. Radical doubt can reveal assumptions, but it cannot be the only activity of a life that requires action.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Kantian questions about the conditions of experience and scientific questions about evidence are related without being identical.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You know a meeting happened from direct participation; you know a distant event through reports whose sources and methods need examination.
Practice
Course note: Trace one belief to direct observation, inference, or testimony.
Course note: Identify a condition under which you would revise it.
Reflection
Course note: Where have I mistaken certainty of feeling for strength of justification?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a knowledge claim make visible?
blocks.text: Its source, supporting reasons, limits, and possible correction.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing
lessons.name: 33.03 Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing

blocks.text: Am I treating my way of organizing experience as the whole of reality?
Core idea

Perception gives a perspective shaped by attention and concepts. We classify what we encounter, and classifications help while leaving features out. This does not imply that nothing is real or that every interpretation is equally good. Compare perspectives, test consequences, and ask which categories serve the question. Difficult philosophical accounts of experience should be studied as arguments, not reduced to slogans.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ontology and epistemology meet where a useful category is mistaken for a complete description of an individual or event.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Calling someone “unreliable” may summarize several missed promises, but it can hide the differing conditions and possible changes.
Practice
Course note: Choose one category you use often and list what it captures and omits.
Course note: Describe the same case from another relevant perspective.
Reflection
Course note: What have I treated as the thing itself because my label feels precise?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a limit of a concept?
blocks.text: It selects features for a purpose and may omit other relevant aspects of the thing described.
Course note: Model and reality: [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality]] · [[35.02 Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration]] · [[35.06 Understand specialist reference books]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare freedom and social obligation
lessons.name: 33.04 Compare freedom and social obligation

blocks.text: What kind of freedom is at stake, and whose obligations support it?
Core idea

Freedom can mean lack of interference, capacity to act, participation in collective decisions, or self-direction. These meanings can conflict. A rule may limit one choice while protecting another person's security; a formal right may be unusable without resources. State the conception of freedom and the affected people before debating whether a policy increases it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Aristotle, Rousseau, modern political thought, and self-help speak of agency in different contexts. Their differences matter.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A workplace gives flexible hours but no childcare support. Formal flexibility may not create equal practical freedom for every worker.
Practice
Course note: Describe one policy through two meanings of freedom.
Course note: Identify the obligation or resource each meaning requires.
Reflection
Course note: Which person's freedom is absent from my first account?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why define freedom in an argument?
blocks.text: Different meanings can support different judgments about the same rule or institution.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Study a philosophical tradition in context
lessons.name: 33.05 Study a philosophical tradition in context

blocks.text: What problem was this tradition responding to?
Core idea

Philosophical traditions emerge in particular histories and use concepts with meanings that change in translation. Read a claim with its question, opponents, and intended practice. Avoid extracting a line from Stoicism, Buddhism, or samurai ethics and making it a universal productivity rule. Compare how a tradition explains a problem and the costs of adopting its view.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Historical context preserves real disagreements across the collection instead of smoothing them into a motivational blend.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A Stoic distinction about judgment may help a modern decision, but it does not automatically settle a debate about unjust institutions.
Practice
Course note: Choose one tradition and identify its central question, proposed answer, and historical setting.
Course note: Explain one useful transfer and one limit of that transfer.
Reflection
Course note: Which appealing phrase have I detached from the argument it belonged to?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why read traditions in context?
blocks.text: Their claims address specific questions and assumptions that may differ from present concerns.

Course note: Classical rules and exceptions: [[20.07 Compare strategic traditions in context]] · [[21.05 Compare fixes against the same criteria]] · [[22.07 Handle a change request without losing the plan]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use thought experiments to expose commitments
lessons.name: 33.06 Use thought experiments to expose commitments

blocks.text: What does this imagined case reveal about my principle?
Core idea

A thought experiment simplifies a situation so a principle can be tested. Specify which feature the case isolates and which real-world details it removes. Your reaction can reveal an intuition, but an intuition is not the final argument. Change one feature at a time and see whether your judgment shifts for a reason you can explain.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ethical reasoning, logic, and philosophy of mind use imagined cases to clarify concepts before confronting more complicated evidence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A promise-keeping case becomes harder when keeping the promise would cause serious harm. The change reveals whether you think the duty is absolute.
Practice
Course note: Create a simple case testing one principle you hold.
Course note: Change one relevant feature and explain any change in your judgment.
Reflection
Course note: Which detail did I leave out that real decisions would require?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a thought experiment for?
blocks.text: To isolate and test a concept or principle, while recognizing the simplification's limits.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare pessimism, hope, and meaning
lessons.name: 33.07 Compare pessimism, hope, and meaning

blocks.text: What picture of human life does this worldview offer?
Core idea

Some texts emphasize suffering, alienation, or the instability of achievement. Others emphasize purpose, progress, faith, or creative action. Ask what evidence and values underlie each picture, what it sees clearly, and what it neglects. A worldview should not be accepted merely because it is comforting or rejected because it is difficult. It also should not be used to diagnose another person's life from afar.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Literature, existential memoir, religious traditions, and social critique offer different ways to understand a good life.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A critique of consumer status helps you question a purchase, while a story about meaningful work may help you choose what to build instead.
Practice
Course note: Compare two worldviews by human problem, proposed response, and neglected condition.
Course note: Identify a lived case that complicates each.
Reflection
Course note: Which worldview gives me clarity, and which gives me an excuse?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should worldviews be compared?
blocks.text: By their questions, reasons, explanatory strengths, omissions, and practical consequences.
Course note: Meaning after loss: [[02.04 Find meaning without romanticizing suffering]] · [[02.07 Distinguish hope from a guarantee]] · [[36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Form a provisional philosophy of practice
lessons.name: 33.08 Form a provisional philosophy of practice

blocks.text: Which principles will guide action while remaining open to challenge?
Core idea

Choose a small set of principles you can explain and test: how you seek truth, treat others, use effort, and respond to uncertainty. Identify tensions among them rather than pretending they are perfectly consistent. A practical philosophy should shape actual commitments and allow revision when it harms people or fails to explain experience.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The next modules on religion, science, and literature will widen the material from which this provisional account can learn.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: You commit to intellectual honesty and care, then notice a case where blunt disclosure would cause avoidable harm. The tension calls for judgment about timing and form, not abandonment of either principle.
Practice
Course note: Write four provisional principles and one action each would change.
Course note: Identify one conflict between two principles and how you would deliberate.
Reflection
Course note: What would make me revise a principle rather than defend it for identity's sake?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a practical philosophy provisional?
blocks.text: It guides action through explicit reasons while remaining open to evidence, conflict, and revision.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build an argument from premises to conclusion
lessons.name: 33.09 Build an argument from premises to conclusion

blocks.text: What must be true for this philosophical conclusion to follow?
Core idea

A philosophical claim is clearer when its supporting steps are visible. Write the conclusion, list the premises, and ask whether the inference is valid and whether the premises are defensible. A valid argument can begin from a disputed premise; a true-sounding conclusion can rest on weak reasoning. Identify hidden assumptions and the best objection. The aim is to understand a position well enough to test it, not to win by terminology.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[10 Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement]] provides argument structure. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] uses explicit premises when values conflict.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An argument that every free choice must be unconstrained depends on a particular definition of freedom; naming it lets others examine the claim.
Practice
Course note: Turn one philosophical statement into a conclusion and two or three premises.
Course note: Write the strongest objection to a premise rather than to the person's character.
Reflection
Course note: Which assumption was carrying the most weight invisibly?
Recall check

blocks.question: What are the two main checks on a philosophical argument?
blocks.text: Whether the conclusion follows from its premises and whether those premises are justified.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare accounts of the self without flattening them
lessons.name: 33.10 Compare accounts of the self without flattening them

blocks.text: What does each account mean by a person continuing over time?
Core idea

Philosophical and psychological traditions can emphasize memory, body, social role, consciousness, or practical commitments. They may answer different questions under the same word 'self.' Define the question before comparing answers: legal responsibility, lived identity, moral development, and metaphysical persistence need not have one test. Use an example to show where accounts diverge. Do not turn a complex tradition into a slogan for personal improvement.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[31 Mind, behavior, and consciousness]] examines experience and explanation. [[34 Religion, spiritual traditions, and belief]] shows that traditions attach different meanings to personhood.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person changes values over decades. One account emphasizes continuity of memory, another the body's life, and another their relations and commitments.

steps.label: Probe
steps.text: Find a case that separates them.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose one identity question and compare two accounts in their own terms.
Course note: Find a case where the accounts would give different answers.
Reflection
Course note: Was I asking one question while comparing answers to another?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why define a question before comparing accounts of self?
blocks.text: Different accounts may address different kinds of continuity, responsibility, or experience.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask what would count as a good life
lessons.name: 33.11 Ask what would count as a good life

blocks.text: Which goods are ends, and which are tools for living well?
Core idea

Pleasure, achievement, belonging, virtue, freedom, and meaning can support one another and sometimes compete. Ask what a proposed life ideal includes, what it neglects, and whose circumstances it assumes. Money and status can be useful instruments without defining the entire goal. A personal answer should remain revisable through experience and honest conversation with people affected by it. A tradition can illuminate a choice without settling it for everyone.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[02 Values, meaning, and a direction worth choosing]] turns priorities into choices. [[25 Money, records, and financial judgment]] asks what resources are for.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Someone accepts a promotion for higher income, then weighs the loss of care time and creative work against what that income enables.

steps.label: Live
steps.text: Test priorities through choices and review.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: List five goods you want in a life and distinguish ends from means.
Course note: Describe a real trade-off between two of those goods without claiming one is always superior.
Reflection
Course note: Which good had I pursued as a measure while forgetting its purpose?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a good-life question practical?
blocks.text: It clarifies which goods matter, how they conflict, and what choices express them under real constraints.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Practice charitable disagreement with a tradition
lessons.name: 33.12 Practice charitable disagreement with a tradition

blocks.text: Can I state a view fairly before rejecting or adapting it?
Core idea

Read a position in its historical and conceptual setting. Identify the problem its author was trying to solve, the strongest reason for the view, and the terms that carry special meaning. Then state the objection. Agreement is not required; charity prevents an easy caricature from substituting for understanding. Also examine harms or exclusions a tradition may contain. A serious reading can preserve what is useful while refusing what is unsupported or unjust.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[36 Literature, story, and human possibility]] reads works in context. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] asks how ideas interact with power.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A reader examines an older account of duty, finds its concern with loyalty understandable, and still challenges whom the account excluded.
Practice
Course note: Write a fair three-sentence version of a philosophical view you disagree with.
Course note: Add one historically grounded objection and one idea worth retaining.
Reflection
Course note: Did my criticism address the strongest version of the view?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does charitable disagreement require?
blocks.text: Representing a view's problem and strongest reasons accurately before offering a serious objection.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask what kind of religious claim is being made
lessons.name: 34.01 Ask what kind of religious claim is being made

blocks.text: Is this a doctrine, practice, experience, history, or testable statement?
Core idea

Religious language can express a community's teaching, a personal experience, a moral practice, an interpretation of history, or a claim about physical events. These require different forms of understanding and evaluation. Respectful study begins by accurately stating the claim in its tradition, then asking the appropriate questions. Respect does not require treating every claim as empirically established.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Earlier lessons separated kinds of questions; this distinction prevents both dismissive caricature and unearned scientific certainty.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A statement that prayer gives meaning differs from a claim that a specific ritual reliably cures a disease. The second requires health evidence and care.
Practice
Course note: Classify three spiritual statements by claim type.
Course note: State what would count as understanding and what would count as evidence for each.
Reflection
Course note: Have I changed the kind of claim while responding to it?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why classify religious claims?
blocks.text: Doctrine, experience, history, ethics, and empirical prediction have different meanings and standards.

Course note: Spiritual meaning and empirical claims: [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence]] · [[31.06 Compare competing accounts of consciousness]] · [[34.05 Study religious experience with interpretive humility]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read a sacred text with translation and commentary in view
lessons.name: 34.02 Read a sacred text with translation and commentary in view

blocks.text: How is this passage being interpreted, and by whom?
Core idea

A text can have several translations and commentarial traditions. Note speaker, setting, genre, key terms, and the interpretive choices made. Avoid assuming one English rendering is the only original meaning. A commentary can illuminate a tradition while also advancing its own doctrinal commitments. Compare interpretations before extracting a universal life rule.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Multiple Bhagavad Gita editions in the collection are a chance to preserve interpretive differences rather than merge them silently.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two commentaries emphasize different implications of duty and action in the same scene. You record both and their reasons.
Practice
Course note: Choose a short passage and compare two available interpretations by key term and practical implication.
Course note: Identify what context you need before applying it to your life.
Reflection
Course note: Whose interpretation have I mistaken for the only text?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why compare commentary?
blocks.text: Translation and interpretation can shape a passage's practical meaning.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare traditions without flattening them
lessons.name: 34.03 Compare traditions without flattening them

blocks.text: Where do these traditions genuinely agree and disagree?
Core idea

Traditions may share practices such as reflection, restraint, or service while differing about God, self, salvation, liberation, authority, and the purpose of practice. State a similarity narrowly enough to be true and preserve substantial differences. Avoid treating every tradition as an interchangeable source of motivational quotations.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The source collection includes Christian, Hindu, Buddhist, Taoist, Catholic, Satanist, and other perspectives. Their disagreements are part of what a thoughtful course should show.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two traditions value disciplined conduct but explain its ultimate purpose in incompatible metaphysical terms. Both claims remain visible.
Practice
Course note: Compare two traditions by central aim, account of the person, and source of authority.
Course note: Name one similarity and one irreducible difference.
Reflection
Course note: Which difference did I erase to make a pleasant synthesis?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should traditions be compared?
blocks.text: Through specific shared practices and real differences in aims, doctrines, and authority.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand faith without making it a medical guarantee
lessons.name: 34.04 Understand faith without making it a medical guarantee

blocks.text: What does this tradition mean by faith, and what is being promised?
Core idea

Faith may mean trust, commitment, assent, or a practiced relationship with the sacred. Different authors use it differently. Claims that strong belief guarantees healing, wealth, or safety can burden people when outcomes differ and can delay necessary care. Study the doctrinal meaning while keeping empirical and clinical questions separate.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Religious growth texts and modern health evidence may address different questions; when a spiritual claim predicts bodily outcomes, evidence and patient safety become relevant.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person draws comfort from prayer while also following a qualified care plan. They need not interpret an illness as proof of insufficient belief.
Practice
Course note: Define how one source uses faith and the outcome it associates with it.
Course note: Separate spiritual meaning from any testable guarantee in the passage.
Reflection
Course note: Who could be harmed if the promise is taken as certain?
Recall check

blocks.question: Does faith alone establish a medical outcome?
blocks.text: No. A spiritual commitment and an empirical treatment claim are different matters.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Study religious experience with interpretive humility
lessons.name: 34.05 Study religious experience with interpretive humility

blocks.text: What does the person report, and what explains it?
Core idea

A religious or extraordinary experience can be deeply meaningful to the person who reports it. The report and its interpretation are distinct. Psychological, cultural, neurological, and theological accounts may offer different explanations, and available evidence may not settle the metaphysical question. Avoid mocking the experience or presenting one favored explanation as established without support.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Consciousness, near-death reports, and anthropology show how subjective meaning and causal inquiry can coexist without being collapsed.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A near-death account may change a person's life. That effect does not by itself prove a particular account of the afterlife.
Practice
Course note: Write one report as experience and then list possible interpretations separately.
Course note: Identify which claims could be checked and which remain philosophical or theological.
Reflection
Course note: Am I dismissing meaning or inflating it into proof?
Recall check

blocks.question: What distinction helps study religious experience?
blocks.text: The person's reported experience is different from a claim about its ultimate cause.

Course note: Spiritual meaning and empirical claims: [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence]] · [[31.06 Compare competing accounts of consciousness]] · [[34.01 Ask what kind of religious claim is being made]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Examine belief formation and group life
lessons.name: 34.06 Examine belief formation and group life

blocks.text: How do family, community, ritual, and evidence shape belief?
Core idea

Beliefs develop through relationships, stories, practices, argument, and social identity. Recognizing these influences does not automatically make a belief false. Ask what reasons people give, what role belonging plays, and how doubt or change is treated. Preserve the freedom to explore without using “indoctrination” as a blanket description of every religious upbringing.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Social psychology and religion studies connect around belief formation while retaining a distinction between explaining a belief and judging its truth.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person inherits a practice from family and later examines its reasons. Both the inheritance and the examination matter to the story.
Practice
Course note: Map three influences on one belief without deciding its truth from origin alone.
Course note: Write the strongest reason a thoughtful adherent might offer.
Reflection
Course note: Am I using an origin story as a substitute for examining the claim?
Recall check

blocks.question: Does knowing why a belief formed settle its truth?
blocks.text: No. Formation and justification are related but distinct questions.
Course note: Romance and manipulation: [[15.01 Approach another person as a chooser]] · [[15.08 Notice manipulation disguised as romance]] · [[18.04 Check emotional dependency and isolation]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Respect pluralism in shared life
lessons.name: 34.07 Respect pluralism in shared life

blocks.text: How can people with different convictions cooperate fairly?
Core idea

Shared institutions need rules that allow participation across deep differences. Distinguish freedom of belief and expression from a right to impose a contested doctrine on everyone. Discuss public reasons, rights, and practical accommodations where possible. Conflict will remain in some areas; the aim is a fair process that protects people and makes reasons visible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Political philosophy and interfaith dialogue meet where disagreement must be lived with rather than erased.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A workplace accommodates several religious observances through a transparent scheduling process that also respects people with no religious affiliation.
Practice
Course note: Design a fair process for one hypothetical shared-space conflict.
Course note: Identify whose needs and freedoms it protects and where it remains imperfect.
Reflection
Course note: Which conviction am I expecting others to accept without a shared reason?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is religious pluralism in practice?
blocks.text: Fair cooperation and protection of rights among people who retain different convictions.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep spiritual practice and critical inquiry together
lessons.name: 34.08 Keep spiritual practice and critical inquiry together

blocks.text: What can I practice sincerely while continuing to ask questions?
Core idea

Reflection, prayer, meditation, ritual, and service may have meaning within a tradition. Practice need not end inquiry, and inquiry need not strip practice of personal significance. Be honest about what you know, believe, hope, and cannot establish. When a practice involves health, money, or another person's autonomy, apply the relevant evidence and ethical standards too.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This course treats traditions as sources of questions and lived practices, while preserving real doctrinal and empirical disagreements.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person keeps a gratitude ritual because it helps them attend to valued relationships, while remaining skeptical of claims that the ritual controls external events.
Practice
Course note: Describe one spiritual or reflective practice by its meaning, claimed effects, and limits.
Course note: State an open question you can live with while practicing or studying it.
Reflection
Course note: What would intellectual honesty look like in this area of my life?
Recall check

blocks.question: Can spiritual practice coexist with inquiry?
blocks.text: Yes, when meaning, belief, empirical claims, and ethical consequences are stated honestly.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare interpretations within a tradition
lessons.name: 34.09 Compare interpretations within a tradition

blocks.text: Who is speaking for a tradition, and what do others within it say?
Core idea

A tradition is rarely a single voice. Communities differ by history, authority, translation, practice, and the question being asked. When someone describes what a religion teaches, identify the text, interpreter, and community involved. Compare positions on a specific issue before making a broad statement. Respecting diversity does not mean denying real doctrines or disagreements; it means describing them accurately.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[33 Philosophy, knowledge, and the good life]] practices fair representation. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] examines how institutions preserve and contest interpretations.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two readers of the same sacred passage may agree on its importance while differing about how literally it applies to modern social duties.

steps.label: Describe
steps.text: State the scope of the claim.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a hypothetical claim about a tradition and list what source and community information would clarify it.
Course note: Write a comparison question that does not assume one member speaks for all.
Reflection
Course note: Which easy generalization disappeared when I asked who was interpreting?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why compare views within a religious tradition?
blocks.text: Texts and practices can be interpreted differently by communities and authorities within the same tradition.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish spiritual counsel from a factual guarantee
lessons.name: 34.10 Distinguish spiritual counsel from a factual guarantee

blocks.text: Is this advice offering meaning, a practice, or a promised outcome in the world?
Core idea

Prayer, meditation, ritual, and moral teaching can be important to people. A claim that a practice guarantees a medical, financial, or physical outcome is a different kind of claim and needs different evidence. Ask what is promised, to whom, and under what conditions. Avoid turning lack of the promised result into blame for someone's faith or character. For consequential health or financial decisions, keep qualified care and current facts in view.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] evaluates empirical predictions. [[37 Health literacy and responsible care]] protects choices where inaccurate promises can cause harm.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community offers prayer and practical support to an ill member without claiming prayer replaces diagnosis or guarantees recovery.
Practice
Course note: Classify three hypothetical statements as spiritual meaning, practice guidance, or testable prediction.
Course note: Rewrite one overconfident guarantee as an honest statement of what the practice can and cannot promise.
Reflection
Course note: Did a meaningful tradition become a factual claim without evidence?
Recall check

blocks.question: What changes when spiritual advice promises a physical outcome?
blocks.text: It becomes an empirical claim with consequences that require evidence and should not replace appropriate care.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read a practice in its lived setting
lessons.name: 34.11 Read a practice in its lived setting

blocks.text: How do people actually use this belief or ritual in ordinary life?
Core idea

A text alone cannot show every way a community lives. Ask how a practice is taught, adapted, and connected to family, service, grief, celebration, or discipline. Listen to participants while recognizing that one person's experience is not the whole tradition. Avoid collecting practices as isolated techniques for self-improvement without understanding their meaning and limits. Participation should respect the community's norms and people's consent.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[16 Family, development, and relational patterns]] examines practices across generations. [[36 Literature, story, and human possibility]] attends to voice and context.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A daily reading is also a family conversation and a way of remembering relatives; its significance exceeds the words on a page.
Practice
Course note: Form three respectful questions about the social setting of a practice.
Course note: Compare a textual description with a first-person account without treating either as exhaustive.
Reflection
Course note: What did I miss by treating a living practice as a portable productivity method?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why study a religious practice in context?
blocks.text: Its meaning and use depend partly on the people, relationships, history, and norms around it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Discuss belief across disagreement respectfully
lessons.name: 34.12 Discuss belief across disagreement respectfully

blocks.text: How can people with different convictions share a decision without requiring conversion?
Core idea

Shared life often requires agreement about action while beliefs remain different. Clarify the practical decision, each person's non-negotiable constraints, and any common reasons for cooperation. Do not demand that someone translate every conviction into your vocabulary before it counts, but make public effects and rights discussable. Distinguish respect for a person's freedom of conscience from agreement with every claim they make. Record what remains disputed.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] helps maintain contact through disagreement. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] gives a structure for shared obligations.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Neighbors with different beliefs coordinate a food program by agreeing on access, safety, and volunteer roles while leaving theology unsettled.
Practice
Course note: Write a shared action statement for a hypothetical mixed-belief group.
Course note: Identify one unresolved conviction and one practical rule all can understand.
Reflection
Course note: Was I seeking cooperation or hidden agreement on every premise?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can make cooperation possible across belief differences?
blocks.text: A clear shared action, respected constraints, discussable public effects, and room for unresolved conviction.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Hold an outside explanation beside an inside account
lessons.name: 34.13 Hold an outside explanation beside an inside account

blocks.text: How can I compare a research explanation with what practitioners say a practice means?
Core idea

An outside account may examine cognition, social effects, or history. An inside account may describe worship, obligation, transcendence, or community. Neither should be silently substituted for the other. State what each explains, how it was obtained, and what it does not address. Ask whether disagreement is about evidence, meaning, or the very question being asked. This permits critical study without treating participants as unaware of their own practice or treating testimony as proof of every external claim.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[31 Mind, behavior, and consciousness]] separates reported experience from theory. [[33 Philosophy, knowledge, and the good life]] clarifies kinds of questions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A participant describes a daily prayer as devotion; a researcher studies its effect on attention. Both accounts may be informative without being equivalent.
Practice
Course note: Write two short accounts of a hypothetical practice, one first-person and one analytical, labeling their questions.
Course note: Identify one claim neither account can establish alone.
Reflection
Course note: Which account had I treated as a replacement for the other?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why compare inside and outside accounts?
blocks.text: They can answer different questions about meaning, experience, function, and evidence.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Move from a question to a measurable model
lessons.name: 35.01 Move from a question to a measurable model

blocks.text: What quantity or relationship would help answer this question?
Core idea

A technical model begins by specifying the system, variables, assumptions, and desired output. Measurements need units, definitions, and a method of collection. A model can be mathematically neat and still describe the wrong system. Ask what would be observed if the model were useful and what it leaves out.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Causal reasoning and systems thinking supply general tools, while each scientific discipline adds specialized methods.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A project asks whether a room's temperature changes after ventilation. It records time, temperature, and conditions rather than relying on a vague feeling that the air is better.
Practice
Course note: Turn one ordinary question into variables, units, and a comparison.
Course note: Identify one unmeasured factor that could change the result.
Reflection
Course note: What have I called a measurement without defining it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What must a useful technical model specify?
blocks.text: The system, variables, units or definitions, assumptions, and the question it aims to answer.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration
lessons.name: 35.02 Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration

blocks.text: What does each line, arrow, scale, or label assert?
Core idea

Diagrams compress relationships and can make an explanation easier to inspect. Read axes, units, direction, and omitted features before interpreting the visual. A causal arrow is stronger than a line showing association; a schematic may not be drawn to scale. If a diagram is image-only or poorly scanned, do not invent its meaning from a caption alone.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course's own diagrams are authored study aids. They should be tested against the written lesson rather than treated as new evidence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A chart appears to show a dramatic increase until you notice that its vertical axis begins close to the first value.
Practice
Course note: Analyze one technical figure by labels, scale, and what it leaves out.
Course note: Redraw its claim in words and compare the strength of the two versions.
Reflection
Course note: Which visual choice changed my impression before I read the data?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should be checked first in a technical diagram?
blocks.text: Labels, units, scale, direction, and whether the depicted relationship is descriptive or causal.
Course note: Model and reality: [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality]] · [[33.03 Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing]] · [[35.06 Understand specialist reference books]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish classification from explanation
lessons.name: 35.03 Distinguish classification from explanation

blocks.text: Does this category tell me why something happens?
Core idea

A classification groups cases by shared features. An explanation proposes why those features occur. Ontologies, taxonomies, and diagnostic systems help organize information but may change as knowledge advances. Ask how a category is defined, whether cases can overlap, and what the category permits you to infer. Do not treat a label as a mechanism.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ontology and psychology both rely on categories; scientific rigor requires checking what those categories actually support.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Calling a material “corrosive” identifies a safety property, but explaining its behavior requires the conditions and relevant chemistry.
Practice
Course note: Choose one technical category and state its defining features.
Course note: Identify a claim about cause that the category alone does not establish.
Reflection
Course note: Where have I substituted naming for explaining?
Recall check

blocks.question: Does classification establish cause?
blocks.text: No. It organizes observations; causal explanation requires further evidence and mechanism.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Think across scale in astronomy and physics
lessons.name: 35.04 Think across scale in astronomy and physics

blocks.text: How do observation and model connect when the object cannot be manipulated directly?
Core idea

Astronomy and parts of physics rely on observation, mathematical prediction, and comparison across scales rather than direct intervention on every object. Instruments extend what can be measured, while models explain patterns and generate new predictions. Distinguish established physical relationships from metaphysical interpretations appended to them.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The source collection pairs astronomy and relativity with spiritual speculation. Shared words such as energy or time do not make the claims equivalent.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A telescope records light from a distant object; a model interprets its spectrum and motion. The observation does not prove a theological meaning of the event.
Practice
Course note: Trace one astronomical claim through observation, instrument, model, and uncertainty.
Course note: Identify where an interpretation goes beyond the measured result.
Reflection
Course note: Which poetic analogy have I mistaken for a physical mechanism?
Recall check

blocks.question: How can distant phenomena be studied scientifically?
blocks.text: Through repeatable observations, instruments, models, and predictions checked against evidence.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read engineering as constrained design
lessons.name: 35.05 Read engineering as constrained design

blocks.text: What must a design achieve, and what limits it?
Core idea

Engineering selects and tests a system under constraints such as performance, cost, materials, safety, and maintenance. A reactor example may involve balances and kinetics; a public service may involve flow and reliability. The underlying lesson is to make assumptions and trade-offs explicit. Detailed professional calculations require training, current standards, and review.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Strategy and systems thinking meet engineering when a model must work under real conditions rather than only on paper.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A design that maximizes one output may create a heat or maintenance problem. The full system changes the preferred option.
Practice
Course note: For a nonhazardous design, state the objective, three constraints, and two failure modes.
Course note: Identify what data you would need before choosing among designs.
Reflection
Course note: Which constraint did the attractive first solution ignore?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes engineering design more than choosing a clever mechanism?
blocks.text: It must meet a purpose under multiple real constraints and be checked for failure.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand specialist reference books
lessons.name: 35.06 Understand specialist reference books

blocks.text: What does a reference entry provide, and what does it require me to know already?
Core idea

A technical reference can provide definitions, measurements, methods, and cross-references. It may assume professional training and include procedures with serious risks. Use it to understand what specialists measure and how they organize knowledge, not as a shortcut to clinical, chemical, or forensic practice. Check edition, scope, and current standards before relying on details.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The collection includes professional radiology, toxicology, engineering, and psychology references. Their presence broadens literacy but does not turn the course into those professions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A drug-analysis monograph explains that identification uses multiple measurements; a lay reader cannot use the entry to identify or treat a poisoning safely.
Practice
Course note: Inspect a reference entry for scope, units, assumptions, and intended user.
Course note: State one question it answers and one question needing a qualified specialist.
Reflection
Course note: What expertise is the entry silently assuming?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a limit of a specialist reference?
blocks.text: It often presumes professional context, training, current standards, and safe procedures beyond general reading.
Course note: Model and reality: [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality]] · [[33.03 Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing]] · [[35.02 Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Examine formal proof and its assumptions
lessons.name: 35.07 Examine formal proof and its assumptions

blocks.text: Does the conclusion follow within the stated system?
Core idea

Formal reasoning makes rules and premises explicit. A proof establishes a result within a system when the steps follow accepted rules; it does not automatically establish that the assumptions describe a physical case. Different logical frameworks may accept different principles or emphasize constructive methods. Learn the role of assumptions before treating formal certainty as worldly certainty.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Advanced logic and philosophy of mathematics extend the earlier validity lesson. The transfer to science requires a model that fits observation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An equation is derived correctly for an idealized system but fails as a real prediction when an ignored friction effect matters.
Practice
Course note: Identify premises and inference steps in a short formal argument.
Course note: Name an assumption that would need checking before applying it to a real case.
Reflection
Course note: Where have I mistaken internal rigor for external fit?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does formal proof establish?
blocks.text: A conclusion follows from specified premises and rules; empirical fit is a separate question.
Course note: Claim and proof: [[10.01 Find the claim and its support]] · [[10.02 Distinguish validity from truth]] · [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a technical learning route
lessons.name: 35.08 Build a technical learning route

blocks.text: What prerequisite should I master before the specialist chapter?
Core idea

A broad collection invites jumping into impressive advanced topics. Map prerequisite concepts, symbols, and safe practical skills first. Use worked examples and recall checks before moving to a dense reference. When the topic has health, chemical, or security consequences, use authorized education and supervision. A good route makes the limits of independent study visible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The entire integrated course is a prerequisite map across fields; specialist depth still requires domain-specific study.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before reading reactor design equations, a learner studies units, material balances, and basic kinetics in a formal course.
Practice
Course note: Choose one advanced topic and draw a three-step prerequisite chain.
Course note: Test the earliest step with a simple worked example.
Reflection
Course note: Am I skipping a prerequisite because the advanced topic sounds more exciting?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why map technical prerequisites?
blocks.text: Advanced material assumes concepts and methods that need to be learned and checked in sequence.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish a model's fit from its truth everywhere
lessons.name: 35.09 Distinguish a model's fit from its truth everywhere

blocks.text: Under which conditions does this scientific model work well?
Core idea

A model selects features of the world to explain or predict. Its success in one range does not grant unlimited scope. Ask what was measured, what assumptions simplified the situation, and where predictions have been tested. A model can be highly useful while incomplete. When moving between astronomy, psychology, engineering, and everyday life, check whether the relevant variables and scales still match.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] evaluates evidence for a claim. [[20 Strategy, competition, and cooperation]] warns against transferring an analogy as a recipe.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A simple orbit diagram can teach the relation between bodies while leaving out perturbations needed for precise navigation.

steps.label: Apply
steps.text: Use it only where fit is justified.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a familiar model and list one useful prediction and two omitted factors.
Course note: Name a setting where the omissions would matter more.
Reflection
Course note: Did I mistake a model's clarity for unlimited reach?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the scope of a model?
blocks.text: The conditions and questions for which its assumptions and tests make it useful.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read a technical result through its uncertainty
lessons.name: 35.10 Read a technical result through its uncertainty

blocks.text: How precise is the result, and what kind of uncertainty remains?
Core idea

Measurements and estimates can vary because of instruments, sampling, model assumptions, or natural variation. Read a reported number with its unit, method, range, and context. A small numerical difference may be meaningless; a broad interval may still inform a decision. Distinguish uncertainty that more data could reduce from uncertainty caused by a poor model or missing variable. Do not turn an error range into a claim that nothing can be known.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] asks for calibrated confidence. [[26 Economics, incentives, and public choices]] shows why public numbers need interpretation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two estimates of attendance differ by a few people. If both use rough counts, the difference may not justify a claim that one program outperformed the other.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: Ask whether precision is enough for the purpose.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Annotate a hypothetical statistic with unit, method, range, and missing context.
Course note: State which uncertainty would matter for the decision at hand.
Reflection
Course note: Did I use an exact-looking number to avoid discussing how it was produced?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should accompany a technical number?
blocks.text: Its unit, method, relevant uncertainty, and the decision context in which it is used.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Separate a mechanism from an observed association
lessons.name: 35.11 Separate a mechanism from an observed association

blocks.text: Does the evidence show how a change produces an effect?
Core idea

An association can suggest a question but may reflect a confounder, reverse direction, or selection. A proposed mechanism describes intermediate steps and should lead to additional checks. Even a plausible mechanism does not by itself prove the effect occurs at a meaningful size in real settings. Compare alternatives and, where ethically possible, look for evidence from interventions or natural contrasts. Keep causal language proportionate to the method.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] introduces confounding. [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] uses a small test to distinguish explanations.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: People using a study app score higher. They may have started more motivated; observing how the app changes practice and comparing similar learners would strengthen the causal case.
Practice
Course note: Turn an association claim into two competing causal explanations.
Course note: Name one observation or safe test that would distinguish them.
Reflection
Course note: Was the mechanism evidence, an explanation, or only a plausible story?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is a plausible mechanism insufficient to establish causation?
blocks.text: The effect and its size still need evidence that addresses confounding and alternative explanations.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Approach a specialist field through prerequisite questions
lessons.name: 35.12 Approach a specialist field through prerequisite questions

blocks.text: What must I understand before a dense reference becomes useful?
Core idea

Specialist books assume language, mathematics, methods, and professional context. Identify the question you need to answer, then work backward to the prerequisites and a suitable introductory source. Separate conceptual understanding from permission to perform a procedure. Use diagrams, worked examples, and a glossary to check comprehension, but confirm any consequential application with a qualified expert and current standards. Difficulty is a signal to sequence learning, not proof that the field is impossible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[07 Learning, memory, and understanding]] builds from prior knowledge. [[37 Health literacy and responsible care]] keeps specialist interpretation tied to qualified care.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before reading a chemical reactor reference, a learner studies conservation, units, and simple rate concepts, then asks a qualified instructor about real equipment.

steps.label: Consult
steps.text: Use expert guidance for consequential application.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a difficult topic and list five prerequisites in a plausible order.
Course note: Write a question that distinguishes understanding a concept from carrying out a professional procedure.
Reflection
Course note: Which missing prerequisite made the original text seem more mysterious than it was?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should a reader enter a specialist field?
blocks.text: Start with a precise question and its prerequisites, while respecting the boundary between literacy and professional practice.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a small vocabulary for a complex topic
lessons.name: 35.13 Build a small vocabulary for a complex topic

blocks.text: Which things, types, and relationships need clear names before we can reason together?
Core idea

A useful classification scheme defines its domain, categories, relationships, and examples. Start small: list the things people discuss, distinguish a type from an individual item, and name relationships such as 'part of' or 'causes.' Test edge cases with other readers. A tidy diagram can still encode a disputed assumption, so record who chose the terms and where the scheme fails. The goal is clearer shared work, not a claim that the vocabulary perfectly mirrors reality.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] defines terms doing the work. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] uses maps whose boundaries affect conclusions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A library team distinguishes a 'book edition' from a 'physical copy' so its catalogue does not treat every copy as a different work.
Practice
Course note: Choose a small domain and define four categories, three relationships, and one example of each.
Course note: Ask another person to classify an edge case and note any disagreement.
Reflection
Course note: Which assumption became visible only when I tried to define the categories?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in a small ontology?
blocks.text: A defined domain, categories, relationships, examples, and explicit limits or disputed cases.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Trace a technical claim to its origin
lessons.name: 35.14 Trace a technical claim to its origin

blocks.text: Which step in the chain turned a finding into this headline or diagram?
Core idea

A claim may pass from study to summary to presentation to a popular example. At each step, scope and uncertainty can change. Find the original question and method when the claim matters, then compare the later version with its actual result. Record the date because technical knowledge and standards can change. A source trail supports accurate interpretation without requiring a general reader to become a specialist in every field.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] examines method and inference. [[18 Manipulation, propaganda, and independent judgment]] notices selective framing.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A slide calls a pattern a proven cause; the underlying study only compared two groups at one time. The reader marks the stronger causal word as a later addition.
Practice
Course note: Draw a three-step source trail for a hypothetical technical headline.
Course note: Identify one word or number that changed meaning along the chain.
Reflection
Course note: Was I trusting the polished presentation more than the original question and method?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why trace a technical claim's provenance?
blocks.text: To see where scope, certainty, or wording changed between the original finding and a later presentation.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Enter a story through its point of view
lessons.name: 36.01 Enter a story through its point of view

blocks.text: Who tells this story, and what can they know?
Core idea

A narrator selects events, language, and order. First-person confidence does not guarantee accuracy, and third-person narration may still follow a limited perspective. Ask what the narrator knows, what other characters might say, and which details are withheld. This enriches the reading without requiring every narrator to be labeled unreliable.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Observation and bias skills apply to literature as interpretive tools, while a novel's aim may be artistic rather than evidentiary.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A character explains a conflict in flattering terms, while later actions complicate the account. The gap becomes part of the story's meaning.
Practice
Course note: Describe one scene from a second character's likely perspective.
Course note: Identify a fact the narrator could not directly know.
Reflection
Course note: Which judgment did the storytelling voice invite me to accept too quickly?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why examine point of view?
blocks.text: It reveals how selection and limited knowledge shape the reader's understanding.
Course note: Story and evidence: [[36.03 Use fables and maxims as provocations]] · [[36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history]] · [[39.03 Read a historical claim through sources and context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read unreliable structure as an invitation to investigate
lessons.name: 36.02 Read unreliable structure as an invitation to investigate

blocks.text: What does the form make difficult to settle?
Core idea

Some works use nested accounts, missing documents, disrupted chronology, or conflicting narrators. Track what each layer claims and what remains uncertain. Do not rush to flatten the work into a single secret message. Ambiguity can be deliberate and productive, requiring the reader to hold multiple interpretations and justify them with the text.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course's habit of preserving contradictions finds an artistic analogue in works such as layered fiction and collaborative mysteries.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A commentator claims to explain a poem, but their notes reveal more about their own obsessions than the poem's meaning.
Practice
Course note: Draw the narrative layers of one complex story.
Course note: Support two plausible interpretations with different details.
Reflection
Course note: What did I erase to make the story tidy?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can narrative ambiguity do?
blocks.text: It makes interpretation an active, evidence-based process rather than a single answer to extract.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use fables and maxims as provocations
lessons.name: 36.03 Use fables and maxims as provocations

blocks.text: What human tendency does this short form isolate?
Core idea

A fable or maxim compresses a pattern into a memorable scene or sentence. Identify its claim, then test where it helps and where it overgeneralizes. Satire and wit often depend on exaggeration. A sharp observation about pride, status, or self-interest is not a universal law of psychology.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Brief literary forms can sharpen self-reflection when paired with counterexamples and context.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A fable about flattery helps you notice a sales tactic, but it does not prove that every compliment is manipulation.
Practice
Course note: Turn one maxim into a testable, qualified claim.
Course note: Find a case where it illuminates behavior and one where it misleads.
Reflection
Course note: Did I enjoy the sentence so much that I stopped checking it?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should a maxim be used?
blocks.text: As a compressed insight to interpret and test, not as an exceptionless law.

Course note: Story and evidence: [[36.01 Enter a story through its point of view]] · [[36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history]] · [[39.03 Read a historical claim through sources and context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Examine moral choice through character
lessons.name: 36.04 Examine moral choice through character

blocks.text: What reasons does the character give, and what consequences follow?
Core idea

Fiction can place readers near motives, rationalizations, and conflicting loyalties. Track the character's stated reasons, actions, effects on others, and later reinterpretations. Do not reduce a complex novel to a single “lesson.” Its value can lie in making a simple moral slogan feel inadequate while still allowing judgment about harm.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Ethical theory becomes more demanding when characters must act with incomplete information and bear consequences.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A character justifies a harmful act through an abstract theory, but their relationships and guilt complicate the theory's claim to moral clarity.
Practice
Course note: Map a character's claim, action, affected people, and later response.
Course note: Analyze the choice with two ethical lenses from the previous module.
Reflection
Course note: Which person in the story disappears from the character's justification?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can fiction contribute to ethics?
blocks.text: It stages motives, consequences, and perspective in ways that test simplified moral claims.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish memoir, witness, and history
lessons.name: 36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history

blocks.text: What can this personal account show, and what broader claim needs corroboration?
Core idea

Memoir provides situated testimony and meaning. Historical analysis asks about a wider pattern using documents, comparisons, and context. A witness may be indispensable while still having limited access to the whole system. Respect both the testimony and the need to check broader claims. Do not treat trauma as an inspirational device for unrelated everyday goals.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Accounts of imprisonment, war, and survival in the collection deserve context and care, not extraction into generic productivity slogans.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A prisoner's account conveys conditions they lived through. Claims about the entire system require additional records and other accounts.
Practice
Course note: Separate one memoir passage's direct experience from its historical generalization.
Course note: Identify what other evidence would help investigate the wider claim.
Reflection
Course note: Am I learning from the testimony or using its suffering as a metaphor for my inconvenience?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a memoir's evidential strength?
blocks.text: Situated testimony of lived experience, with broader generalizations requiring additional corroboration.
Course note: Meaning after loss: [[02.04 Find meaning without romanticizing suffering]] · [[02.07 Distinguish hope from a guarantee]] · [[33.07 Compare pessimism, hope, and meaning]].
Course note: Anecdote and selection: [[09.03 Notice selection and survivorship]] · [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence]] · [[13.06 Tell an example without claiming it proves everything]].
Course note: Story and evidence: [[36.01 Enter a story through its point of view]] · [[36.03 Use fables and maxims as provocations]] · [[39.03 Read a historical claim through sources and context]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read historical language in its setting
lessons.name: 36.06 Read historical language in its setting

blocks.text: Which meanings and assumptions differ from those of today?
Core idea

Older texts may use categories of race, gender, class, nation, or virtue that carry historical assumptions and sometimes clear harms. Identify the author's context and audience, then evaluate the claim and its consequences. Context helps understanding but does not require endorsement. Translation and edition history can also change how a passage reads.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Intellectual history, political writing, and literary interpretation meet in careful attention to language and power.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An early twentieth-century political text treats a racial hierarchy as natural. You examine its context and evidence while recognizing the harm of the claim.
Practice
Course note: Identify one historically situated term and how its use differs from a current one.
