Course note: Compare the author's assumption with relevant evidence or perspectives absent from the text.
Reflection
Course note: Am I excusing a claim as “of its time” or condemning it without understanding how it worked?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does historical context provide?
blocks.text: An explanation of how a claim arose and operated, without automatically justifying it.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare fictional worlds with lived systems
lessons.name: 36.07 Compare fictional worlds with lived systems

blocks.text: Which social rule or institution is the story making visible?
Core idea

Fiction can exaggerate or estrange familiar arrangements so their costs become easier to see. Identify the rule the story alters and how characters respond. Then ask what real evidence would be needed before applying the analogy to present society. A compelling fictional world can sharpen a question without establishing a sociological conclusion.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Social critique, systems thinking, and literature collaborate when metaphor opens investigation rather than closing it.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A story about alienation raises questions about work and family obligation. Those questions can guide observation without proving one causal account of modern life.
Practice
Course note: State one social assumption a story challenges.
Course note: Design a real-world question that would test part of the analogy.
Reflection
Course note: Where does the story's power come from its art rather than its literal accuracy?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a responsible transfer from fiction to society?
blocks.text: Use the story to form questions, then seek independent evidence for real-world claims.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep a reading journal of changes in interpretation
lessons.name: 36.08 Keep a reading journal of changes in interpretation

blocks.text: How did this work change my first judgment?
Core idea

Record an early impression, the passage or event that challenged it, and the revised interpretation. Include uncertainty and another plausible reading. This makes reading an active practice rather than a hunt for a quotable line. It can also reveal your own recurring assumptions about status, motive, and responsibility.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The same review cycle used for decisions and practice becomes a way to learn from art without demanding one final moral.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A character first appears selfish; later context reveals a protective motive, while the harm of their action remains. Your account becomes more precise.
Practice
Course note: Write an early and later interpretation of one work with textual evidence for each.
Course note: Name one question the work leaves genuinely open.
Reflection
Course note: Which judgment of mine changed because I kept reading?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a reading journal preserve?
blocks.text: The evolution of an interpretation, its evidence, and unresolved alternatives.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Track who controls what the reader knows
lessons.name: 36.09 Track who controls what the reader knows

blocks.text: Which facts are shown, withheld, or filtered through a narrator?
Core idea

A story can create meaning by controlling perspective. Note who speaks, when they speak, what they could know, and what another character might report differently. A narrator's confident explanation may be part of the story rather than the author's verdict. Keep a small record of clues and revise an interpretation when later details change it. This practice strengthens attention to language without treating every narrator as deceptive.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] separates report from inference. [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] examines how wording guides attention.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A novel's narrator describes a rival as selfish, but scenes show the narrator repeatedly omitting the rival's reasons.

steps.label: Revise
steps.text: Update the reading when new evidence appears.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Annotate one short fictional scene with what is observed and what the narrator concludes.
Course note: Rewrite a two-sentence event summary from another character's limited view.
Reflection
Course note: Which detail changed meaning when I asked who was telling the story?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why track a narrator's knowledge?
blocks.text: A story's claims are filtered through a speaker with a particular position, information, and interests.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read a maxim against a counterexample
lessons.name: 36.10 Read a maxim against a counterexample

blocks.text: Where might a memorable line be useful, and where would it mislead?
Core idea

A maxim compresses experience into a striking sentence. Its force can make a conditional insight sound universal. State the situation in which it helps, then construct a plausible counterexample and an exception. Compare competing maxims when they recommend opposite actions. The result is not that every short lesson is useless, but that its usefulness depends on judgment about context.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[10 Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement]] tests general claims. [[20 Strategy, competition, and cooperation]] treats compact strategic rules as prompts, not scripts.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: 'Act quickly' may help in a reversible opportunity but mislead in a costly medical or contractual choice.

steps.label: Use
steps.text: Apply it only where conditions fit.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a short moral or practical maxim and write its likely scope.
Course note: Create one counterexample and revise the maxim into a conditional statement in your own words.
Reflection
Course note: What did the memorable wording make me forget about conditions?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should a maxim be used?
blocks.text: As a compact prompt whose scope and exceptions must be tested against the actual situation.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare a character's choices with their explanations
lessons.name: 36.11 Compare a character's choices with their explanations

blocks.text: What does a character do when their stated values are tested?
Core idea

Literature lets us observe the gap between a person's self-description and their actions across time. Track the decision, available alternatives, pressure, and later explanation. Avoid turning a complex character into a diagnosis or a single moral lesson. Ask how the setting and other people's responses shape the choice. This can deepen moral imagination without treating fiction as direct evidence about all real people.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] examines intentions and effects. [[31 Mind, behavior, and consciousness]] warns against overclaiming hidden motives.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A character insists they value honesty but conceals a harmful act. The reader examines fear, advantage, and consequence rather than assigning one permanent label.
Practice
Course note: Make a two-column record of one character's stated belief and consequential actions.
Course note: Identify a scene that complicates your first judgment.
Reflection
Course note: Did I use the story to examine a tension or to confirm a simple theory of people?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can a character's choices reveal?
blocks.text: How stated values, pressures, alternatives, and consequences interact in a particular story.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep witness, fiction, and history distinct
lessons.name: 36.12 Keep witness, fiction, and history distinct

blocks.text: What kind of claim can this narrative support?
Core idea

A novel can illuminate possibilities; a memoir offers situated testimony; a historical study makes claims supported by records and methods. Each can be powerful, but their authority differs. Ask whose voice is missing, what was remembered later, and what can be checked independently. Do not dismiss a witness because one detail is uncertain, and do not generalize one witness's experience to everyone in the setting. Let each genre contribute what it can.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] asks what evidence supports a generalization. [[39 History, citizenship, and public institutions]] reads public claims through records and context.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A prison memoir conveys lived experience; a historian may compare archives and many accounts to evaluate an institutional pattern.
Practice
Course note: Label three claims from a hypothetical novel, memoir, and history by the evidence each offers.
Course note: Name one independent record that could test a broad historical claim.
Reflection
Course note: Which narrative's emotional force made me overlook its evidential limits?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why distinguish narrative genres?
blocks.text: Fiction, testimony, and historical research offer different kinds of insight and support different kinds of claims.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Give one clue more than one plausible reading
lessons.name: 36.13 Give one clue more than one plausible reading

blocks.text: What else could this action mean if my first story is wrong?
Core idea

A narrative clue is an observed detail plus an interpretation. In a collaborative mystery, later writers can make an earlier detail support a different coherent account. Readers can use that structure to practice generating alternatives without denying the detail. Keep alternatives constrained by what the story actually shows and update them when new information arrives. The exercise also reminds us that real people's motives are not directly visible from one action.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] separates observation from inference. [[14 Listening, conflict, and repair]] asks rather than assuming another person's motive.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A character avoids a meeting. Fear, a secret task, or an ordinary scheduling conflict could fit until later scenes narrow the possibilities.

steps.label: Update
steps.text: Use later evidence to narrow them.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a clue in a story and write two interpretations that fit the facts so far.
Course note: Identify one later detail that would distinguish the interpretations.
Reflection
Course note: Which story felt inevitable only because I had stopped considering alternatives?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why give a clue multiple readings?
blocks.text: It keeps the observed detail separate from a favored interpretation until evidence narrows the possibilities.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Turn a symptom into a care question
lessons.name: 37.01 Turn a symptom into a care question

blocks.text: What am I experiencing, and what information would a clinician need?
Core idea

Record the concern, onset, frequency, severity, relevant conditions, medicines, and effect on daily life as accurately as you can. Avoid deciding the diagnosis from a list of possible causes. A professional can combine your account with examination and appropriate tests. Seek timely help when symptoms are severe, persistent, changing, or concerning in context.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Observation and uncertainty skills support safer conversations about health when they are used to prepare for care rather than replace it.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Instead of “I have a circulation disease,” you record when a symptom began, what accompanies it, and what changed before seeking assessment.
Practice
Course note: Create a neutral symptom record for a hypothetical case.
Course note: Write three clear questions a clinician could answer.
Reflection
Course note: Which conclusion have I reached before gathering the basic facts?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why record symptoms without self-diagnosis?
blocks.text: The record improves professional assessment while leaving causal interpretation open.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Evaluate a treatment promise
lessons.name: 37.02 Evaluate a treatment promise

blocks.text: Who was studied, what changed, and what harms or alternatives were considered?
Core idea

A confident title or testimonial does not establish that a method cures everyone. Identify the exact outcome, comparison, duration, adverse effects, and whether evidence applies to the person's circumstances. Consider existing treatment and the risk of delay. Do not stop prescribed care because an older book or advertisement promises a permanent solution.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Causal reasoning, persuasion literacy, and ethics converge when a claim affects health decisions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A book claims to eliminate a common sexual-health problem forever. You examine the causes it addresses and seek qualified assessment instead of assuming one method fits all.
Practice
Course note: Write the PICO-like elements of one health claim: population, intervention, comparison, outcome.
Course note: Identify a possible harm or delayed-care cost omitted from the pitch.
Reflection
Course note: What makes the promise feel certain beyond its evidence?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a treatment claim specify?
blocks.text: The relevant people, intervention, comparison, outcomes, harms, and limits of the evidence.

Course note: Health decisions under uncertainty: [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes]] · [[27.07 Understand food claims through adequacy and context]] · [[37.07 Ask about benefits, harms, and alternatives together]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand sexual health as wellbeing and choice
lessons.name: 37.03 Understand sexual health as wellbeing and choice

blocks.text: Does this advice respect health, comfort, consent, and the people involved?
Core idea

Sexual wellbeing includes physical, emotional, relational, and social aspects. People vary in bodies, preferences, and circumstances. Discuss concerns and boundaries openly, respect ongoing consent, and use current qualified information for contraception, infection prevention, or persistent difficulties. Avoid gender stereotypes and products that convert embarrassment into a guaranteed-cure sale.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Relationship skills and medical literacy both matter; neither replaces the other.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Partners discuss comfort and a recurring concern, then seek appropriate clinical advice rather than interpreting the issue as proof of lost attraction.
Practice
Course note: Draft three respectful questions for a hypothetical sexual-health conversation.
Course note: Separate a relational expectation from a medical question that needs qualified input.
Reflection
Course note: Which assumption comes from a stereotype rather than the people involved?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in sexual health literacy?
blocks.text: Respect, consent, accurate information, and appropriate care for physical and relational concerns.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Distinguish wellness practice from clinical care
lessons.name: 37.04 Distinguish wellness practice from clinical care

blocks.text: Is this a general habit or a response to a health condition?
Core idea

Sleep routines, movement, and reflective practices may support wellbeing, but an individual condition can require diagnosis and treatment. Avoid treating ordinary advice as a cure for persistent symptoms. A clinical workbook may contain useful language but also assume a practitioner, assessment, and safeguards. Use the text for understanding and questions while seeking fitting care when needed.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Mental performance and mental health share some vocabulary while differing in stakes and support requirements.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person practices a calming routine and also seeks professional help when anxiety repeatedly disrupts work and relationships.
Practice
Course note: Classify three pieces of advice as general habit, clinical method, or uncertain.
Course note: Identify what assessment or support would be needed before applying a clinical method.
Reflection
Course note: Am I calling a condition a mindset problem because that feels easier to solve?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why distinguish wellness from clinical care?
blocks.text: General habits cannot diagnose or replace individualized treatment for a condition.

Course note: Physical challenge and care: [[08.02 Work at a useful level of challenge]] · [[27.02 Understand load, adaptation, and progression]] · [[28.02 Progress from isolated technique to live decisions]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read imaging and test results with a professional
lessons.name: 37.05 Read imaging and test results with a professional

blocks.text: What does this result show, and what does it not establish by itself?
Core idea

A scan, lab value, or report must be interpreted with symptoms, history, test quality, and clinical context. A professional reference can teach that normal variation and incidental findings exist; it cannot turn a general reader into a diagnostician. Ask the clinician what the finding means, how certain it is, and what follow-up is appropriate.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Technical literacy and uncertainty help patients ask better questions without self-interpreting complex medical data.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A scan report mentions an incidental feature. The clinician explains whether it is relevant to the presenting concern and whether follow-up is needed.
Practice
Course note: Write questions about meaning, uncertainty, alternatives, and follow-up for a hypothetical report.
Course note: Identify what context a specialist would require to interpret it.
Reflection
Course note: Have I treated one image or number as the whole diagnosis?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why is a medical result not self-interpreting?
blocks.text: Its significance depends on clinical context, test limits, and professional interpretation.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read drug and poison information by role
lessons.name: 37.06 Read drug and poison information by role

blocks.text: Is this reference intended for a patient, clinician, analyst, or emergency responder?
Core idea

Drug and toxicology references contain specialized measurements and procedures. Their use depends on training, setting, and current protocols. A lay reader should not infer dosing, identification, treatment, or safety from a technical entry. For a suspected exposure or adverse reaction, use appropriate local medical or emergency services promptly.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Specialist references can reveal how experts structure evidence while still being unsuitable as a personal instruction manual.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A monograph lists laboratory tests for a compound. This does not permit home identification or treatment of an exposure.

steps.label: Help
steps.text: Use appropriate services for actual exposure.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify the intended user and limits of one technical reference entry.
Course note: Write the information an emergency professional would need from a caller, without inventing a treatment.
Reflection
Course note: Which technical detail gives me confidence I have not earned?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why does a toxicology reference require context?
blocks.text: Its data and methods assume professional training, equipment, and current protocols.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask about benefits, harms, and alternatives together
lessons.name: 37.07 Ask about benefits, harms, and alternatives together

blocks.text: What are all reasonable options, including doing nothing for now?
Core idea

A care decision should consider expected benefit, possible harm, uncertainty, personal circumstances, and alternatives. The right balance depends on the situation and the person's preferences. Ask what happens with observation, a different approach, or no immediate intervention. A dramatic “natural versus conventional” frame can hide useful options on both sides.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Decision records and informed consent become practical through shared questions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A patient asks about the likely benefit, common harms, and other options for a proposed treatment, then decides with their clinician.
Practice
Course note: Make a question list for a hypothetical choice covering benefits, harms, alternatives, and timing.
Course note: Identify which answer depends on individual medical history.
Reflection
Course note: Which option have I overlooked because the discussion was framed as a two-way contest?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in an informed care choice?
blocks.text: Benefits, harms, uncertainty, alternatives, timing, and the person's circumstances and preferences.
Course note: Health decisions under uncertainty: [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes]] · [[27.07 Understand food claims through adequacy and context]] · [[37.02 Evaluate a treatment promise]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep a personal health-information boundary
lessons.name: 37.08 Keep a personal health-information boundary

blocks.text: Which information should I record, share, or keep private?
Core idea

Health information can be sensitive. Record enough for useful care and continuity, but consider who can access notes, apps, and shared devices. Ask how information will be used when enrolling in a service or study. Privacy should not become a reason to withhold critical facts from qualified care; choose appropriate channels and permissions.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Digital privacy and health literacy meet in the practical management of sensitive information.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person brings a concise symptom history to an appointment while avoiding unnecessary posting of test results in a public forum.
Practice
Course note: Review where your health records and self-tracking data are stored.
Course note: Identify one sharing choice to change or clarify.
Reflection
Course note: Am I sharing to obtain useful help or because a platform makes sharing easy?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should guide health-data sharing?
blocks.text: The purpose of care, sensitivity of the information, who can access it, and the person's informed choice.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Prepare a useful appointment question
lessons.name: 37.09 Prepare a useful appointment question

blocks.text: What information would help a professional understand my concern and my goals?
Core idea

A care conversation improves when the concern is described concretely: onset, pattern, severity, relevant changes, medicines or exposures when appropriate, and what you want help deciding. Bring a concise record rather than a self-diagnosis assembled from search results. Ask what possibilities are being considered and what follow-up would change the plan. Emergency symptoms require local urgent care rather than waiting for a routine appointment or a course exercise.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] turns a vague concern into a useful question. [[31 Mind, behavior, and consciousness]] keeps reported experience distinct from theory.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person notes when pain occurs, what changes it, and how it affects work, then asks which signs would call for follow-up.
Practice
Course note: Draft a hypothetical one-minute description of a health concern without naming a diagnosis.
Course note: Add two questions about next steps and uncertainty.
Reflection
Course note: Did I prepare information that helps care or a conclusion I want confirmed?
Recall check

blocks.question: What belongs in a useful care question?
blocks.text: A concrete description of the concern, its pattern and impact, relevant context, and the decision needing help.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Ask what a test result changes
lessons.name: 37.10 Ask what a test result changes

blocks.text: Will this test help choose a different action, or only produce another number?
Core idea

Tests have purposes, limits, and possible harms. Ask what question a test addresses, how reliable the result is in your situation, what a positive or negative result would mean, and what happens next. A normal result may not explain every symptom; an unusual result may need confirmation or context. Interpret specialist imaging, laboratory, or drug information with qualified professionals and current guidance, not from an isolated page of a technical book.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[35 Science, models, and technical literacy]] explains uncertainty and specialist context. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] asks whether information changes a decision.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A clinician and patient discuss whether imaging would change treatment now or whether another first step is more appropriate.

steps.label: Act
steps.text: Agree on the next step for each result.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Write four questions to ask before a hypothetical non-urgent test.
Course note: For positive and negative outcomes, state what decision would follow in the hypothetical case.
Reflection
Course note: Was I seeking a decision aid or the feeling that every uncertainty had a number?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a health test useful?
blocks.text: It addresses a defined question and has results that can be interpreted and used in a care decision.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare health advice by population and outcome
lessons.name: 37.11 Compare health advice by population and outcome

blocks.text: Was this advice tested for people and outcomes like mine?
Core idea

A study or book may concern a particular age group, condition, training level, or measure. Before applying its conclusion, check who was studied, what was compared, how long follow-up lasted, and which harms were observed. A personal story can suggest a question but cannot establish an average effect. When advice conflicts with an existing condition or care plan, discuss it with a qualified professional. Avoid universal promises from a narrow result.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] examines study design. [[27 Physical training, recovery, and nutrition literacy]] applies the same question to exercise and food claims.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A supplement claim based on trained athletes does not automatically describe benefit for an older person with a medical condition.

steps.label: Fit
steps.text: Discuss personal relevance with qualified care.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Create a population, comparison, outcome, and time checklist for a hypothetical health claim.
Course note: Identify one way an effect could differ for another group.
Reflection
Course note: Which similarity between me and the study participants had I assumed rather than checked?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why examine population in health advice?
blocks.text: Effects and risks may differ across people, conditions, and settings from those originally studied.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Make a follow-up plan understandable
lessons.name: 37.12 Make a follow-up plan understandable

blocks.text: What should I do after receiving care, and when should I seek help again?
Core idea

A care plan is easier to use when it states the intended action, expected course, possible concerns, and review point in plain language. Ask who to contact if the plan cannot be followed or symptoms change. Record the instructions accurately and check them with the professional; do not improvise medication changes from a general course. Include practical constraints such as cost, transport, or care duties so the plan can be adjusted responsibly.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] treats handover and ownership as part of completion. [[25 Money, records, and financial judgment]] recognizes resource constraints in real decisions.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: After an appointment, a patient confirms when a follow-up is due and what change would require earlier contact.

steps.label: Review
steps.text: Know when and how to follow up.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Rewrite a hypothetical vague care instruction into actions, timing, and a contact question.
Course note: Identify one practical barrier to following it and a question to raise with the care team.
Reflection
Course note: What part of the plan would I struggle to explain to someone helping me?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a follow-up plan usable?
blocks.text: Clear actions, timing, warning conditions, contact route, and accommodation of practical constraints.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Begin a craft with observation
lessons.name: 38.01 Begin a craft with observation

blocks.text: What does the material or object actually do?
Core idea

Craft begins with looking closely at shape, texture, behavior, and change under ordinary conditions. Record what you see before imposing a favored style or explanation. Different crafts use different senses and standards, but each benefits from precise attention. A description can become more useful when tied to a comparison and a purpose.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Observation skills move from arguments into hands-on practice without losing the need to distinguish fact and interpretation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A drawing student observes how a cup's rim changes shape from their viewpoint before applying a memorized oval.
Practice
Course note: Describe one ordinary object through shape, texture, and one surprising detail.
Course note: Compare it with a second object and state what changed in your description.
Reflection
Course note: Which feature did I draw or name from memory instead of seeing?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why begin craft with observation?
blocks.text: Material and viewpoint can challenge assumptions that a generic template hides.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Learn perspective as a constructed view
lessons.name: 38.02 Learn perspective as a constructed view

blocks.text: From where is the scene being seen?
Core idea

Perspective systems map three-dimensional relationships onto a surface. A change in viewpoint alters apparent size and direction. Curvilinear, isometric, and other systems make different choices about distortion and use. Learn the rule and its intended effect, then test it against a real scene. An unusual projection is not an error if it serves the design knowingly.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The earlier model lesson applies visually: a representation selects relationships rather than copying reality without interpretation.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An isometric drawing keeps parallel edges parallel for clarity, while a fisheye view emphasizes a wide field with visible distortion.
Practice
Course note: Sketch one simple room from two viewpoints or projection conventions.
Course note: State what each drawing preserves and distorts.
Reflection
Course note: Which visual rule am I using without knowing its purpose?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does a perspective system do?
blocks.text: It defines how spatial relationships are represented on a surface, preserving some features and distorting others.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build sensory vocabulary through comparison
lessons.name: 38.03 Build sensory vocabulary through comparison

blocks.text: What difference can I describe without pretending everyone experiences it identically?
Core idea

Taste, smell, texture, and visual character are often described through analogy. Compare samples under similar conditions and use specific words for differences in intensity, duration, and association. Sensory judgments include individual variation and cultural learning. A rich description helps another person imagine an experience but cannot guarantee they will perceive it the same way.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Writing and observation meet in sensory criticism. The aim is communicable attention, not false objectivity.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Two fragrances both seem floral, but one becomes powdery and soft while the other remains sharp and brief. The comparison gives the words meaning.
Practice
Course note: Compare two harmless everyday sensory experiences using at least three precise differences.
Course note: Ask another person what they noticed and keep both accounts.
Reflection
Course note: Which adjective describes the object, and which describes my memory or preference?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why compare sensory samples?
blocks.text: Comparison makes descriptive differences clearer while allowing for individual perception.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand tools and material constraints
lessons.name: 38.04 Understand tools and material constraints

blocks.text: What can this tool or material do safely and reliably?
Core idea

A craft method depends on material properties, tool limits, protective practices, and the maker's skill. Read safety information before attempting a new process. Some technical books include heat, blades, chemicals, or other hazards that require qualified training and proper facilities. The course can teach planning and material literacy without turning hazardous procedures into casual home projects.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Engineering and safety modules become concrete when a physical process has consequences beyond a diagram.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A learner examines the properties of different materials and chooses a supervised introductory workshop before using unfamiliar powered tools.
Practice
Course note: For one harmless craft, list material behavior, tool function, and likely failure modes.
Course note: Identify what training or safety setup would be needed for an advanced version.
Reflection
Course note: Am I choosing a tool because I understand it or because the finished object looks appealing?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should precede unfamiliar material practice?
blocks.text: Understanding material and tool limits, relevant safety requirements, and the level of supervision needed.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Use prototypes to answer a question
lessons.name: 38.05 Use prototypes to answer a question

blocks.text: What uncertainty could a small version resolve?
Core idea

A prototype is an intentionally incomplete version used to test a specific assumption. It may reveal fit, shape, comfort, comprehension, or production difficulty. Choose the cheapest safe form that can answer the question. Do not confuse a polished sample with a useful test if it never exposes the uncertain part.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Business experiments and craft prototypes share a logic, though physical materials add different constraints.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Before building an entire object, a maker creates a cardboard size model to test whether the dimensions fit its intended space.
Practice
Course note: Name one design uncertainty and a safe prototype that could resolve it.
Course note: Define what observation would lead you to change the design.
Reflection
Course note: Which expensive step am I taking before testing the central assumption?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is a prototype for?
blocks.text: To answer a specific design question before committing to a full version.
Course note: Craft and experiment: [[23.05 Revise the work, not only your confidence]] · [[24.03 Test demand before scaling]] · [[40.04 Design a reversible experiment]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Practice one technical component at a time
lessons.name: 38.06 Practice one technical component at a time

blocks.text: Which movement or judgment is limiting the finished result?
Core idea

A whole craft can overwhelm a beginner. Isolate one component, practice it under manageable conditions, and return it to the full work. Seek feedback from someone who can observe the process, not only the finished artifact. Repetition may build control, but change the drill when it no longer teaches.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Sport and creative practice use the same cycle of isolate, vary, and integrate while retaining domain-specific safety.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A drawing learner practices a series of ellipses from observation, then uses that control in a still-life study.

steps.label: Integrate
steps.text: Apply it to the full work.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Identify one component skill in a craft you want to learn.
Course note: Design five safe repetitions with one feedback criterion and a full-task application.
Reflection
Course note: Did the isolated drill improve the real artifact?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why return an isolated skill to a whole task?
blocks.text: A drill can improve one component without guaranteeing it works in context.
Course note: Repetition and improvement: [[05.09 Distinguish repetition from deliberate improvement]] · [[07.08 Ask for feedback that identifies an error]] · [[08.03 Build a feedback loop]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Judge workmanship by use and context
lessons.name: 38.07 Judge workmanship by use and context

blocks.text: What does a well-made result need to do for its user or viewer?
Core idea

Quality can include function, durability, clarity, beauty, accessibility, and fit for context. The criteria differ by object and audience. Ask what matters before applying a fashionable style or one maker's preferred standard. A beautiful result can fail its use; a plain result can be carefully made for a demanding purpose.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Values and business service help determine craft standards without reducing art to efficiency.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A field guide prioritizes legible diagrams and durable pages, while an exhibition piece may explore ambiguity deliberately.
Practice
Course note: Write three quality criteria for one artifact and rank them by purpose.
Course note: Ask an intended user or viewer which criterion you missed.
Reflection
Course note: Which standard comes from status rather than the work's actual use?
Recall check

blocks.question: What determines craft quality?
blocks.text: The artifact's purpose, context, and relevant standards of function, experience, and care.
Course note: Output and customer value: [[23.01 Choose a project small enough to finish]] · [[23.07 Finish and release at the right standard]] · [[24.02 Define an offer with honest terms]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Preserve a maker's learning record
lessons.name: 38.08 Preserve a maker's learning record

blocks.text: What should I carry from this attempt into the next one?
Core idea

Keep sketches, prototypes, measurements, choices, and a short account of what changed. Record mistakes without hiding successful details. Over time, the record reveals both technique and taste: what you can execute and what you choose to make. A craft practice grows through a sequence of informed attempts rather than a single finished object.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course's capstone uses this same principle across life projects: show the process, evidence, and revision.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A maker documents why a material failed, what replacement was tried, and how the final object performed in use.
Practice
Course note: Create a one-page record for a recent making attempt.
Course note: Choose the next test based on the record's most important unresolved question.
Reflection
Course note: What did the material teach me that planning alone did not?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a maker's record preserve?
blocks.text: Process choices, observations, failures, successful features, and the next test.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a sample before committing material
lessons.name: 38.09 Build a sample before committing material

blocks.text: What can a small model reveal before the full piece is made?
Core idea

A sample lets a maker test proportion, appearance, feel, or process at lower cost. Choose the uncertainty first and make a sample that represents the relevant condition. A sketch may answer a composition question but not a durability question; a material swatch may show finish but not final scale. Record what changed in your plan. Use appropriate instruction and protective procedures for tools, heat, chemicals, or sharp materials rather than treating a book diagram as a safety course.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] designs bounded tests. [[23 Creative work and sustained projects]] uses drafts to expose uncertainty.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An artist makes three perspective thumbnails before beginning a large drawing; a maker tests a finish on scrap before applying it to a finished object.

steps.label: Revise
steps.text: Change the plan using its limits and findings.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Name one uncertainty in a making project and a low-cost sample that tests it.
Course note: State one important property the sample cannot test.
Reflection
Course note: Was I buying or cutting material before answering a cheaper design question?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a craft sample useful?
blocks.text: It represents the specific property under question while limiting cost and revealing what remains untested.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Train observation with paired comparisons
lessons.name: 38.10 Train observation with paired comparisons

blocks.text: What difference can I describe without calling one version better too soon?
Core idea

Perception improves when two examples are compared under similar conditions. Name features such as proportion, contrast, texture, timing, or scent without reducing them immediately to like and dislike. Then ask what the difference does for the intended use or experience. Language helps memory and communication, but a term is useful only when it points to something observable or reliably felt. Respect sensory differences between people.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] separates description from judgment. [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] supplies precise words without pretending they settle taste.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A student compares two drawings of the same room and describes horizon placement and distortion before choosing the one that serves a dramatic scene.
Practice
Course note: Compare two safe examples in a craft you know and list five descriptive differences.
Course note: Explain which difference matters to the intended purpose and why.
Reflection
Course note: Did my first preference prevent me from observing the actual differences?
Recall check

blocks.question: How do paired comparisons train craft perception?
blocks.text: They make specific differences easier to notice, name, and connect to an intended effect.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Keep a process record that can teach the next attempt
lessons.name: 38.11 Keep a process record that can teach the next attempt

blocks.text: What should I write down before memory turns a trial into a story?
Core idea

A maker's record captures materials, settings, sequence, conditions, result, and changes considered. Include failures and unexpected successes. A short photograph or sketch may preserve a detail better than prose; explain what the image shows. Avoid recording only the final polished object, since the decisions that produced it are what future work can use. Protect private client or collaborator information where relevant.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[08 Practice, performance, and adaptation]] learns from feedback. [[40 Integration and the life-practice capstone]] uses records to compare cycles.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A maker notes which paper, tool angle, and lighting were used in a drawing study, then compares the resulting lines a week later.

steps.label: Iterate
steps.text: Change one relevant factor next time.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Create a one-page process log for a hypothetical craft attempt.
Course note: Add one observation that would help you repeat a successful detail.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of a past result can I no longer explain because I did not record it?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why keep a craft process record?
blocks.text: It preserves conditions and choices so later attempts can reproduce, revise, or learn from the result.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Judge a made object in its real setting
lessons.name: 38.12 Judge a made object in its real setting

blocks.text: Does the work serve the person, place, and use it was made for?
Core idea

Workmanship includes fit to purpose, not just visible complexity. Test how an object or artifact is handled, read, maintained, and experienced in the setting where it belongs. Ask intended users for specific observations while retaining responsibility for safety and technical limits. A display photograph can flatter features that fail in use; a plain object may excel at its task. Consider repairability and the cost of upkeep where they matter.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[24 Business, customers, and useful value]] measures value in use. [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] includes acceptance and handover.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A hand-drawn sign looks elegant up close but cannot be read from the path where visitors must choose a direction.
Practice
Course note: Write three real-use checks for a hypothetical made object.
Course note: Ask how a person would clean, update, or repair it after delivery.
Reflection
Course note: Was I judging the work where it would be used or where it looked best?
Recall check

blocks.question: What does fit to purpose add to craft judgment?
blocks.text: It asks whether the made thing works for its intended user, setting, maintenance, and consequences.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare scent before reading the label
lessons.name: 38.13 Compare scent before reading the label

blocks.text: How does a name or expectation change the words I use for a sensation?
Core idea

Sensory judgment can be shaped by labels, memory, and changing perception over time. In a safe setting, compare familiar, non-irritating scents without reading their names first; describe what you notice, then read the labels and revisit your description. Do not use unknown chemicals or treat scent as a medical test. The aim is to separate the first experience from the story a name invites, while accepting that sensory vocabulary and sensitivity differ between people.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] separates description from expectation. [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] shows how words help and limit perception.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person smells two familiar teas before seeing their names and finds that the labels change which notes they notice on a second pass.
Practice
Course note: With safe familiar materials, write three descriptive words for two scents before checking their names.
Course note: Revisit later and note which description stayed stable and which changed.
Reflection
Course note: Did the label help me notice a feature or make me invent one?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why compare a scent before reading its label?
blocks.text: It helps reveal how expectation and naming can influence a sensory description.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: See the institution behind an individual outcome
lessons.name: 39.01 See the institution behind an individual outcome

blocks.text: Which rules and structures shape the choices people can make?
Core idea

Individual action occurs within law, organizations, markets, families, and public services. Map the rules, resources, and incentives before explaining an outcome only by character. An institution is maintained by people and can change, but change requires understanding its decision points and power. Avoid treating every structural explanation as proof that personal action is irrelevant.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Agency and systems thinking meet political theory when the scale expands beyond one person's routine.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A student repeatedly misses a service appointment because transport and office hours conflict. The solution may involve scheduling policy as well as individual planning.
Practice
Course note: Map one public or organizational outcome through rules, resources, and individual choices.
Course note: Identify a decision point where the arrangement could be changed.
Reflection
Course note: Which constraint have I mistaken for a personal trait?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why study institutions?
blocks.text: Rules and resources shape available choices and recurring outcomes beyond individual intention.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Define citizenship beyond a label
lessons.name: 39.02 Define citizenship beyond a label

blocks.text: Who belongs, who participates, and who is excluded?
Core idea

Citizenship can describe legal status, political participation, recognition, and access to rights. Historical systems often distribute these unevenly. Ask whose voice counts in a decision and whether formal membership gives practical power. Do not assume one national history explains another; compare institutions and experiences carefully.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Political philosophy and studies of race show that a universal-sounding category can hide unequal treatment.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A community consultation is formally open to everyone but held at a time and place that exclude many workers. Participation is narrower than the invitation suggests.
Practice
Course note: Examine a public process by formal eligibility and practical ability to participate.
Course note: Identify one change that would make participation more meaningful.
Reflection
Course note: Who is described as included while remaining unheard?
Recall check

blocks.question: What can citizenship include beyond status?
blocks.text: Meaningful participation, recognition, and access to rights and institutions.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Read a historical claim through sources and context
lessons.name: 39.03 Read a historical claim through sources and context

blocks.text: What evidence supports this account of what happened?
Core idea

Historical writing uses documents, testimony, chronology, and interpretation. Distinguish primary records from later argument and check whose records survived. A dramatic narrative may omit contrary cases or the perspective of people with less power. Context helps explain choices while leaving room for moral judgment about them.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The earlier memoir lesson becomes a broader historical method when accounts must be compared across sources.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A policy is described as an inevitable response to a crisis. Reviewing contemporary debates shows that alternatives were proposed at the time.
Practice
Course note: Take one historical claim and identify the evidence types supporting it.
Course note: Look for an absent perspective or alternative decision documented in the period.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of the story became “inevitable” only after I knew the ending?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a historical interpretation stronger?
blocks.text: Clear sourcing, chronology, context, comparison, and attention to absent or conflicting evidence.
Course note: Story and evidence: [[36.01 Enter a story through its point of view]] · [[36.03 Use fables and maxims as provocations]] · [[36.05 Distinguish memoir, witness, and history]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Detect how authority can normalize harm
lessons.name: 39.04 Detect how authority can normalize harm

blocks.text: When did a harmful practice become respectable, and who challenged it?
Core idea

Harmful policies may be presented through professional language, religious endorsement, administrative routine, or appeals to national progress. Trace how authority was claimed and how dissent was handled. Do not assume current institutions are immune, but also do not use a historical analogy without comparing facts and scale. The goal is to recognize mechanisms that warrant scrutiny.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Historical eugenics and institutional violence illustrate why evidence, dignity, and accountability must be joined.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A group calls coercion a public benefit and excludes affected people from deliberation. The absence of their voice is part of the mechanism.
Practice
Course note: Analyze one historical case by claim, endorsing authority, affected people, and dissent.
Course note: Identify a present safeguard that addresses one mechanism specifically.
Reflection
Course note: Which respected messenger might have made the practice seem unquestionable?
Recall check

blocks.question: How can authority normalize harm?
blocks.text: Prestige and routine can make weak evidence and unequal power appear legitimate unless challenged.
Course note: Ethics and institutions: [[32.05 Consider distribution, not only totals]] · [[32.07 Learn from ethical failure in history]] · [[39.08 Practice public reasoning]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Understand propaganda as a public system
lessons.name: 39.05 Understand propaganda as a public system

blocks.text: Who is shaping the message, through which channels, for what purpose?
Core idea

Public persuasion may combine framing, repetition, trusted intermediaries, and selective evidence. Trace a message's sponsor, audience, claim, and omissions. Do not assume coordination from similarity alone; institutions can repeat a frame through shared incentives. Evaluate the underlying policy or event independently where possible.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The manipulation module addressed personal judgment; public communication adds scale, media systems, and collective consequence.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Several campaigns describe a regulation as protecting freedom, but they use the word differently. Reading the rule and the sponsors' interests clarifies the dispute.
Practice
Course note: Map one public message by sponsor, audience, channel, evidence, and desired action.
Course note: Compare it with a primary document or a differently framed account.
Reflection
Course note: What information would the audience need to disagree intelligently?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should a propaganda analysis inspect?
blocks.text: Sponsor, audience, channels, framing, evidence, omissions, and desired behavior.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Examine state capacity and accountability
lessons.name: 39.06 Examine state capacity and accountability

blocks.text: Can an institution do what it promises, and how can it be corrected?
Core idea

A public institution needs authority, information, staff, resources, coordination, and a way to learn from failure. Good intentions cannot replace these conditions. Review incentives and oversight, especially when decisions affect people who cannot easily leave or opt out. Transparency should make correction possible, not only produce more reports.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Organizational behavior and political theory meet where the cost of failure is borne by the public.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: An emergency plan lists responsibilities but supplies no communication path between agencies. A simulation reveals the gap before a crisis.
Practice
Course note: Map the capabilities one public promise would require.
Course note: Identify an independent correction or appeal channel for affected people.
Reflection
Course note: Which promise sounds clear while its means are missing?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a public promise credible?
blocks.text: Sufficient capacity, coordination, review, and accountability to those affected.
Course note: Authority and accountability: [[19.02 Match authority with accountability]] · [[19.04 Invite dissent before a decision]] · [[19.08 Review power and responsibility]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare nations without turning them into stereotypes
lessons.name: 39.07 Compare nations without turning them into stereotypes

blocks.text: What can one country's case teach, and what cannot transfer?
Core idea

National histories involve interacting policies, demographics, culture, external pressures, and chance. Avoid treating a country as one personality or a policy as the sole cause of a long trend. Use comparisons to generate questions and identify conditions that differ. Respect the people behind aggregate labels and the date of the analysis.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Economic narratives and political history need the same causal caution used in personal decisions, at a much larger scale.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A reform credited with an economic recovery may coincide with demographic or global changes. Comparing timelines and other cases narrows the claim.
Practice
Course note: List three contextual factors in a country comparison.
Course note: State one lesson that may transfer and one reason it might not.
Reflection
Course note: Which national label is doing the work of an explanation?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why be cautious with country analogies?
blocks.text: Many interacting conditions differ, so a single story rarely transfers unchanged.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Practice public reasoning
lessons.name: 39.08 Practice public reasoning

blocks.text: How can I make a civic claim that others can examine?
Core idea

State the proposal, problem, evidence, values, affected groups, trade-offs, and a review method. Address a strong objection and make uncertainty visible. The aim is not to remove conviction but to make the reasoning accountable in a shared space. Avoid using a person's identity to dismiss their evidence or using a statistic to erase their lived effect.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: This module brings logic, ethics, systems, and communication into public life before the final capstone returns them to a chosen project.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A neighborhood proposal for safer crossings includes incident data, accessibility concerns, costs, alternatives, and a way to test the change.
Practice
Course note: Write a one-page public argument with claim, reasons, values, costs, and objection.
Course note: Ask someone with a different stake which issue it misses.
Reflection
Course note: Can people affected by my proposal see and challenge its reasons?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes public reasoning accountable?
blocks.text: Visible evidence, values, affected people, trade-offs, strong objections, and a path for review.
Course note: Ethics and institutions: [[32.05 Consider distribution, not only totals]] · [[32.07 Learn from ethical failure in history]] · [[39.04 Detect how authority can normalize harm]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Trace a public decision to its authority
lessons.name: 39.09 Trace a public decision to its authority

blocks.text: Who had the power to decide, and how could the decision be challenged?
Core idea

Institutions act through roles, procedures, and legal powers that differ by place and time. When evaluating a public decision, identify the body responsible, the rule it claims to use, the record of its reasoning, and available review routes. Do not assume that a persuasive official statement proves authority or that every unpopular outcome is unlawful. Current local rules require direct verification. Understanding process helps citizens ask better questions and makes accountability more concrete.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[19 Leadership, teams, and institutions]] studies decision rights. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] asks whether a valid process also treats people fairly.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Residents question a park closure by finding the responsible council body, meeting record, stated reason, and public comment route.
Practice
Course note: Map the decision path in a hypothetical municipal choice: proposal, authority, record, review.
Course note: Write one factual question a citizen could ask at each stage.
Reflection
Course note: Was I criticizing a person while the relevant decision sat elsewhere in the process?
Recall check

blocks.question: What helps assess a public decision's accountability?
blocks.text: Its authority, procedure, reasons, records, and available routes for review or correction.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Look for missing records in a historical story
lessons.name: 39.10 Look for missing records in a historical story

blocks.text: Whose account survived, and whose experience is harder to see?
Core idea

Historical claims depend on sources that were created and preserved unevenly. Officials, publishers, and powerful groups often leave more records than people with less access. Identify the source type, purpose, date, and missing perspectives. An absence is not proof that a specific event occurred, but it can limit confidence in a broad claim. Compare multiple kinds of evidence and state what remains uncertain.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[36 Literature, story, and human possibility]] distinguishes witness from historical synthesis. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] asks how selection affects an apparent pattern.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A policy archive shows officials praising a program, while letters and later interviews may reveal how recipients experienced it.
Practice
Course note: Analyze a hypothetical historical claim with source, creator, purpose, and missing voice.
Course note: Propose one additional type of record that could change the account.
Reflection
Course note: Which absence had I mistakenly treated as evidence of consent?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why inspect missing voices in history?
blocks.text: The surviving record may reflect unequal power and preserve some experiences more readily than others.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Analyze a campaign's message and channel
lessons.name: 39.11 Analyze a campaign's message and channel

blocks.text: How does a public message shape what people notice and whom they trust?
Core idea

Public communication can inform, persuade, mobilize, or manipulate. Examine the claim, evidence, emotional frame, audience, sponsor, repetition, and channel. Ask what alternative information is omitted and whether the source invites checking. A message's emotional effect does not make it false, and technical accuracy does not remove selective framing. The goal is an independent judgment about both content and distribution.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[18 Manipulation, propaganda, and independent judgment]] identifies pressure tactics. [[13 Language, questions, and clear expression]] shows how wording can set the question.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A campaign posts a striking photograph and a single statistic. A reader checks the time period, denominator, sponsor, and what policy the message asks them to support.
Practice
Course note: Deconstruct a hypothetical public message into claim, frame, sponsor, audience, and omission.
Course note: Write one question that would test the central statistic or image context.
Reflection
Course note: Which part of the delivery made the claim feel trustworthy before I examined it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What should be examined in public persuasion?
blocks.text: The claim, evidence, framing, sponsor, audience, channel, and omitted alternatives.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Compare institutional performance with lived access
lessons.name: 39.12 Compare institutional performance with lived access

blocks.text: Does a service's reported success match people's ability to use it?
Core idea

Institutions may report total output, cost, speed, or compliance while users experience delays, exclusion, or poor quality. Match each headline measure to the purpose of the service and the groups it serves. Investigate who appears in the data and who never reaches the counting point. Use both records and affected people's accounts, recognizing the limits of each. A fair review asks what action the institution will take when measures and experience diverge.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[26 Economics, incentives, and public choices]] reads averages and distribution. [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] watches for displaced costs.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A clinic reports shorter appointments, while some patients cannot explain the agreed next step; speed alone is an incomplete measure.

steps.label: Purpose
steps.text: Define what the service should achieve.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Choose a hypothetical public service and list one output, one quality, and one access measure.
Course note: Identify a group that may be absent from the institution's data.
Reflection
Course note: Was the public number measuring the institution's activity or the user's result?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should institutional performance be assessed?
blocks.text: By connecting outputs to quality, access, distribution, and the service's real purpose.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Choose a problem worthy of integration
lessons.name: 40.01 Choose a problem worthy of integration

blocks.text: What real situation would benefit from several of the course's skills?
Core idea

Select a project with a specific stake, a feasible first action, and enough complexity to require more than one lens. It might concern learning, work, relationships, community, or health literacy. Avoid choosing a crisis that needs immediate specialist care as a course exercise. Define who is affected and what success would look like without promising total transformation.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course is one sequence because self-knowledge, evidence, action, and ethics meet in actual situations rather than staying in separate book chapters.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A person wants a sustainable study practice that fits caregiving duties and improves a specific work skill.
Practice
Course note: State the project, people affected, baseline, and one bounded outcome.
Course note: Check that the first trial is feasible and its stakes appropriate for self-directed work.
Reflection
Course note: Why is this project meaningful beyond completing the course?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a good capstone project?
blocks.text: A meaningful, bounded situation where several skills can be tested safely and reviewed.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a cross-module explanation
lessons.name: 40.02 Build a cross-module explanation

blocks.text: Which ideas have different jobs in this project?
Core idea

Choose several lessons that contribute distinct functions: one clarifies the aim, one explains the current pattern, one guides action, one checks evidence, and one protects ethics or wellbeing. Do not select ideas merely because they sound compatible. State a real tension or limit between them and how the project will handle it.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The knowledge map supports integration when each link has a reason, not when every concept is connected to everything.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Values set a study goal; habit design creates a cue; attention planning protects time; decision review measures learning; family commitments limit the schedule.
Practice
Course note: Link at least four lessons from different modules with a sentence explaining each job.
Course note: Add one disagreement or limit and how it affects the plan.
Reflection
Course note: Which concept am I using as decoration rather than as a decision aid?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes integration more than collecting ideas?
blocks.text: Each idea has a defined role, a reason for connection, and a stated limit or tension.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Create a baseline and decision record
lessons.name: 40.03 Create a baseline and decision record

blocks.text: What do I know before acting, and what am I choosing under uncertainty?
Core idea

Record present behavior, constraints, resources, affected people, alternatives, and reasons for the chosen trial. Include what would count as improvement and what could go wrong. This record prevents a later result from rewriting the original reasoning. Keep the measurement proportionate to the project rather than collecting data for its own sake.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The first module's starting brief becomes stronger after evidence, systems, and ethics have been studied.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A study project records actual weekly sessions, interruptions, and learning checks before changing the schedule.
Practice
Course note: Write a one-page baseline and decision record for your capstone.
Course note: Ask a trusted person whether one important constraint or stakeholder is missing.
Reflection
Course note: Which assumption would I most like to leave unmeasured?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why record the baseline before acting?
blocks.text: It gives later review an honest comparison and preserves the reasons available at the time.

lessons.title: Design a reversible experiment
lessons.name: 40.04 Design a reversible experiment

blocks.text: What small action can teach me whether this approach helps?
Core idea

Choose an action, a period, a relevant signal, and a condition for stopping or changing it. Keep obligations and consent clear. Change few variables at once so the result is interpretable. A trial can produce useful learning even if it does not meet the hoped-for outcome, provided the evidence is recorded honestly.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Habits, strategy, and causal reasoning converge in the design of a practical experiment.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: For two weeks, a team tests a shorter meeting with written prework and compares decision quality and staff burden, not only meeting length.
Practice
Course note: Specify action, duration, signal, review date, and stop condition.
Course note: Explain why the trial is safe and reversible enough for this setting.
Reflection
Course note: What would I learn if the trial fails?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a useful experiment?
blocks.text: A specific action, relevant observation, clear review, and a feasible way to change course.
Course note: Craft and experiment: [[23.05 Revise the work, not only your confidence]] · [[24.03 Test demand before scaling]] · [[38.05 Use prototypes to answer a question]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Run the trial and record what happened
lessons.name: 40.05 Run the trial and record what happened

blocks.text: What actions and results occurred, including unexpected ones?
Core idea

Carry out the plan as agreed and record deviations, context, feedback, and consequences for other people. Do not hide misses or change the success criterion after seeing the outcome. If safety or ethics change, stop or revise appropriately and record why. A small honest record is more valuable than an impressive but selective story.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Practice logs, financial records, and scientific notebooks share an ethic of preserving actual events for later judgment.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A routine works on two days and fails on a third because caregiving changes the schedule. The record reveals a need for a fallback window.
Practice
Course note: Keep a dated log of each capstone attempt and relevant conditions.
Course note: Note one unplanned effect on a person or responsibility outside the main metric.
Reflection
Course note: What would my memory omit if I had not written it down?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why record deviations?
blocks.text: They help explain the outcome and reveal whether the plan fits real conditions.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Review outcome and decision quality separately
lessons.name: 40.06 Review outcome and decision quality separately

blocks.text: What worked, what did not, and what remains uncertain?
Core idea

Compare results with the baseline, then evaluate the process used to choose the trial. A good decision may have an unlucky result; a favorable result may hide a weak method or shifted cost. Ask what alternative explanations fit and whose experience is missing. Preserve strengths and name one targeted change rather than judging the whole person or project.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The course's core distinction between event, inference, and judgment returns at a higher level of complexity.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: The new schedule increases study time but reduces sleep. The outcome is mixed, and the next cycle needs a different allocation.
Practice
Course note: Write separate paragraphs for observed outcome and quality of the original decision.
Course note: Identify one alternative explanation and one unseen cost.
Reflection
Course note: Which result am I tempted to call a total success or failure?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why separate result from decision process?
blocks.text: Chance, context, and unintended effects can make an outcome a poor verdict on the original reasoning.

Course note: Good decision, mixed outcome: [[12.03 Separate decision quality from outcome quality]] · [[21.08 Decide whether to continue, change, or stop]] · [[25.07 Notice behavioral traps around money]].
