lessons.title: Make a field guide for the next cycle
lessons.name: 40.07 Make a field guide for the next cycle

blocks.text: What should I keep, change, stop, or investigate next?
Core idea

A field guide is a concise account another person, or your future self, can use: the situation, useful distinctions, tested actions, evidence, limits, and next decision. Do not write universal advice from one personal trial. State the conditions under which the result may transfer and the questions it leaves open.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Learning becomes contribution when the result is communicated honestly without pretending a single experience solves everyone's life.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A learner writes that a short morning session worked when materials were ready and caregiving was covered; the guide includes the failure conditions too.
Practice
Course note: Create a two-page field guide with evidence, limits, and next action.
Course note: Ask a reader which statement sounds more certain than the record permits.
Reflection
Course note: What is genuinely useful to carry forward?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a field guide responsible?
blocks.text: It shares tested insight with context, uncertainty, and limits instead of a universal guarantee.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Build a continuing review practice
lessons.name: 40.08 Build a continuing review practice

blocks.text: How will I keep learning after the course's final lesson?
Core idea

Choose a realistic rhythm for reviewing values, commitments, evidence, and changing conditions. Keep the practice light enough to maintain and useful enough to affect a decision. Return to lessons when a real problem makes them relevant; do not treat completion as proof of mastery. Invite feedback and retain the right to revise a framework that no longer serves the people involved.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: The final outcome is a way of living with attention, care, and correction, assembled from the course rather than any single book.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A monthly review checks one goal, one relationship commitment, one evidence question, and one change for the next period.
Practice
Course note: Set a review rhythm and a short list of questions you will actually use.
Course note: Schedule the first post-course review and identify one person or record that can challenge your view.
Reflection
Course note: What will make my practice more honest and more humane over time?
Recall check

blocks.question: What continues after course completion?
blocks.text: A repeatable cycle of action, observation, feedback, and revision guided by values and limits.
Course note: The continuing practice: [[01.16 Write your personal starting brief]] · [[02.10 Make a values agreement with your future self]] · [[40.03 Create a baseline and decision record]].
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Choose a project with an honest boundary
lessons.name: 40.09 Choose a project with an honest boundary

blocks.text: What can this course help me test without claiming to solve my whole life?
Core idea

A capstone should be large enough to connect several abilities and small enough to review with evidence. Define the situation, people affected, what is within your control, and what requires consent or specialist help. Name the outcome and a time boundary. Do not convert every relationship or health issue into an experiment. A bounded project makes a result interpretable and leaves room for dignity, uncertainty, and ordinary life.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[01 Self-knowledge and your starting point]] begins from an actual baseline. [[21 Practical problem solving and experiments]] turns a gap into a testable question.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A student improves a weekly study process over six weeks, rather than promising to become an entirely different person by the end of term.
Practice
Course note: Draft a capstone brief with scope, people, outcome, time, and limits.
Course note: Remove one aim that cannot be evaluated within the chosen period.
Reflection
Course note: Was I choosing a project I could learn from or a grand identity promise?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes a capstone project bounded?
blocks.text: A defined situation, outcome, time period, affected people, and clear limits on control and risk.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Connect lessons by the jobs they perform
lessons.name: 40.10 Connect lessons by the jobs they perform

blocks.text: Why does each selected idea belong in this project?
Core idea

A list of favorite lessons is not integration. Assign each idea a task: diagnose the problem, design a habit, gather evidence, protect a boundary, communicate with others, or review the outcome. State where two ideas support each other and where they pull in different directions. If an idea has no clear role, leave it out. Integration should make the action and its limits clearer rather than produce an impressive diagram.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] joins diagnosis and action. [[32 Ethics, fairness, and difficult choices]] checks the cost of the plan to others.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A team project uses a baseline lesson to define the issue, a time-planning lesson to fit the work, a listening lesson to gather feedback, and an evidence lesson to review the change.
Practice
Course note: Select four lessons from different modules and write one job for each.
Course note: Name one tension between two selected ideas and how it will be monitored.
Reflection
Course note: Which idea was present only because I admired it, not because the project needed it?
Recall check

blocks.question: What makes course ideas integrated?
blocks.text: Each has a specific job in the same project, with interactions and tensions made explicit.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Show evidence without overstating the result
lessons.name: 40.11 Show evidence without overstating the result

blocks.text: What can I conclude from the trial I actually ran?
Core idea

Compare the observed result with the baseline and intended outcome. Describe what changed in your action, what else changed in the setting, who was affected, and how certain the observation is. A single successful week may justify continuing a practice, not claiming a universal method. A disappointing result can reveal a weak hypothesis, a poor implementation, or an unsuitable measure. Keep the original decision record visible so hindsight does not improve your earlier reasoning on paper.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[11 Evidence, science, and causal claims]] limits causal inference. [[09 Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment]] protects against a confident story after the fact.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A new planning routine coincides with more finished work for three weeks, but the learner also had fewer obligations; the report names both changes.
Practice
Course note: Write a three-paragraph trial report: action, observation, alternative explanations.
Course note: State one claim the evidence supports and one stronger claim it does not yet support.
Reflection
Course note: Was I reporting what happened or selling the plan to myself?
Recall check

blocks.question: How should a capstone result be reported?
blocks.text: With baseline, observed change, implementation, alternative explanations, uncertainty, and a limited conclusion.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Design the next cycle from what was learned
lessons.name: 40.12 Design the next cycle from what was learned

blocks.text: What should continue, change, stop, or be investigated next?
Core idea

The capstone ends with a decision, not a final judgment on the person. Keep actions that served the chosen aim at an acceptable cost. Change parts that failed for a plausible reason, stop parts that caused harm or added little value, and investigate uncertainties that could alter the next plan. Choose a future review date and a way to notice drift. Share the field guide in terms another person can understand, while protecting private information and context.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[05 Habits and behavior design]] supports continuation. [[22 Planning, collaboration, and delivery]] turns learning into a usable handover.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: A learner keeps a weekly review, shortens a daily checklist nobody used, and tests whether a different meeting time improves participation.

steps.label: Return
steps.text: Set evidence and date for review.

blocks.text: Practice
Course note: Make a keep, change, stop, and investigate table for a hypothetical capstone.
Course note: Schedule a next review and name the evidence to bring to it.
Reflection
Course note: Did I let the result shape the next cycle, or did I return to the original plan by habit?
Recall check

blocks.question: What is the capstone's final product?
blocks.text: A defensible next cycle grounded in the trial's result, costs, uncertainties, and a future review.
Course note: Return to [[Course Index]].

lessons.title: Set a return point beyond the first success
lessons.name: 40.13 Set a return point beyond the first success

blocks.text: How will I know whether this change remains useful after the course ends?
Core idea

A successful trial can fade when ordinary demands return, and a disappointing trial may improve after revision. Choose a future date, a small set of observations, and a person or record that will help you review honestly. State what would count as continued value and what would prompt change. Do not turn the review into permanent self-surveillance. The course's final product is a practice you can revisit, including the freedom to stop a method that no longer serves its purpose.

blocks.title: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: [[05 Habits and behavior design]] builds reset points. [[12 Decisions, strategy, and systems]] keeps a plan reviewable when assumptions change.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.text: Three months after a study experiment, a learner checks whether the new routine still supports understanding and leaves room for rest, then adjusts it for a changed timetable.
Practice
Course note: Add a future review date and three observations to your capstone plan.
Course note: Write one condition for continuing, adjusting, and stopping the method.
Reflection
Course note: What would make me keep a method because it once worked, even after its purpose changed?
Recall check

blocks.question: Why set a return point after the capstone?
blocks.text: A later review tests whether the change still serves its purpose under ordinary, changing conditions.

Course note: This is one integrated course built around abilities and prerequisites. Ideas from the collection meet inside shared lessons; the path is not divided into separate book courses. All explanations, examples, questions, and diagrams here are authored Course notes. WhiteEye’s original course remains separate.
Choose a sustainable pace

Course note: Begin with the starting-point module. Work through two or three lessons in a study session, then use one idea in a real situation. A module per week is a starting suggestion, not a deadline. Technical and reflective modules may need more time. Reading every page quickly is not the objective.
Read, connect, practice, reflect

Course note: Each lesson has a learning question, a developed idea, a connection or distinction, an example, a visual sequence, two practices, and a recall check. Try answering the recall question before revealing its answer. Use Previous and Next to follow the sequence; the chapter menu and knowledge map let you revisit connected ideas.
Keep a record

Course note: Your lesson position, completion, practice checkboxes, and saved reflections persist for this browser. Course 1 and Course 2 have separate records. Save reflections with the notebook control; use [[Daily Practice Log]] and [[Weekly Review Template]] for longer records. This browser identity is not an account shared across devices.
Read critically

Course note: The collection mixes practical methods, philosophy, memoir, fiction, older technical references, religious claims, and disputed ideas. The course distinguishes their roles. A compelling story is not proof; a diagram is not a clinical diagnosis; a general framework is not specialist certification. Use [[Connections and Tensions]] and [[Gaps and Questions]] when approaches disagree.

Course note: Use the questions to find the skill you want to practice. Follow the full order when the prerequisites are unfamiliar.
Self-knowledge and your starting point
Course note: [[01.01 Start with a baseline, not an ideal self|What is actually happening in my life before I try to improve it?]]
Course note: [[01.02 Separate facts, interpretations, and judgments|Which parts of my story are observations, and which parts have I added?]]
Course note: [[01.03 Examine your life across several domains|Am I asking success in one area to compensate for everything else?]]
Course note: [[01.04 Look for patterns across a year|What recurs when I examine more than my most recent experience?]]
Course note: [[01.05 Identify the roles that carry real commitments|Which responsibilities have I chosen, inherited, or merely assumed?]]
Course note: [[01.06 Describe strengths with evidence|What can I already do reliably, and under what conditions?]]
Course note: [[01.07 Use the Johari window without treating it as a diagnosis|What might others notice about me that I do not notice myself?]]
Course note: [[01.08 Turn feedback into a decision|What will I do with a compliment or criticism after I hear it?]]
Course note: [[01.09 Distinguish approval from self-direction|Am I choosing this action because it matters, or because I need a reaction?]]
Course note: [[01.10 Make comparison answer a specific question|What exactly am I trying to learn by comparing myself with someone else?]]
Course note: [[01.11 Examine where a desire came from|Do I want the experience itself, the result, or the identity attached to it?]]
Course note: [[01.12 Map constraints and usable resources|What can I work with now, and what genuinely limits the next step?]]
Course note: [[01.13 Notice the short-term payoff of a repeated behavior|What does this behavior accomplish immediately, even if I dislike its later effects?]]
Course note: [[01.14 Test a personal story with a counterexample|What evidence would complicate the story I tell about myself?]]
Course note: [[01.15 Turn a complaint into a learning question|What question would make this difficulty easier to investigate?]]
Course note: [[01.16 Write your personal starting brief|What have I learned well enough to choose the first improvement experiment?]]
Course note: [[01.17 Review rituals as evidence of priorities|What do my ordinary routines reveal that my stated priorities miss?]]
Course note: [[01.18 Ask whose standard is being applied|When I say I am behind, whose timetable am I using?]]
Course note: [[01.19 Ask another person for a concrete outside view|How can I learn from someone else's view without handing them authority over my identity?]]
Course note: [[01.20 Notice when belonging becomes a performance|Where am I changing myself to earn a place, and what does it cost?]]
Course note: [[01.21 Map identity claims to current evidence|Which descriptions of me are still useful, and which belong to an older chapter?]]
Values, meaning, and a direction worth choosing
Course note: [[02.01 Turn a value into a way of acting|How can a value guide an ordinary decision?]]
Course note: [[02.02 Choose the difficulty attached to the ambition|Am I willing to do the ordinary work behind the outcome I admire?]]
Course note: [[02.03 Write a mission that can change a decision|What would a useful personal mission actually help me choose?]]
Course note: [[02.04 Find meaning without romanticizing suffering|How can I seek meaning in difficulty without pretending the difficulty was necessary?]]
Course note: [[02.05 Define enough before chasing more|What would sufficient success look like in this area of life?]]
Course note: [[02.06 Use mortality to clarify priorities|What deserves attention when I remember that time is finite?]]
Course note: [[02.07 Distinguish hope from a guarantee|Can I act with hope while admitting that the outcome is uncertain?]]
Course note: [[02.08 Choose contribution without erasing yourself|How can I help others in a way I can sustain?]]
Course note: [[02.09 Keep purpose larger than one role|What remains meaningful if a job, relationship, or status changes?]]
Course note: [[02.10 Make a values agreement with your future self|Which principles will guide the next month of choices?]]
Course note: [[02.11 Separate a value from a status symbol|Am I pursuing the activity I value or the image associated with it?]]
Course note: [[02.12 Test a value when it becomes inconvenient|How can I tell whether a stated principle really guides my choices?]]
Course note: [[02.13 Build hope that can survive revision|How can I remain hopeful without making a prediction I cannot support?]]
Course note: [[02.14 Let gratitude and dissatisfaction coexist|Can I appreciate what is present while still asking for change?]]
Course note: [[02.15 Define success in the life it should serve|What would an achievement enable, and what might it displace?]]
Emotions, acceptance, and a steadier response
Course note: [[03.01 Name the experience before explaining it|What am I feeling, noticing, and wanting to do right now?]]
Course note: [[03.02 Allow a feeling without endorsing its story|Can I acknowledge an emotion without treating every thought beside it as true?]]
Course note: [[03.03 Put a little distance between you and a thought|How can I examine a thought without becoming absorbed in it?]]
Course note: [[03.04 Give worry a concrete question|Is this concern asking for action, information, or repeated reassurance?]]
Course note: [[03.05 Respond to anger without surrendering the issue|How can I address a real problem without acting on every angry impulse?]]
Course note: [[03.06 Distinguish guilt, shame, and repair|Am I evaluating an action or condemning my whole self?]]
Course note: [[03.07 Recognize defensive explanations|What might I be avoiding when I insist on my first explanation?]]
Course note: [[03.08 Avoid all-or-nothing pictures of people|Can I recognize a person's strengths and limitations at the same time?]]
Course note: [[03.09 Practice self-compassion with an action attached|What would a fair and supportive response to my own difficulty sound like?]]
Course note: [[03.10 Make room for ordinary enjoyment|Have I made improvement so demanding that I no longer participate in life?]]
Course note: [[03.11 Separate discomfort, danger, and the need for support|What kind of response does this difficult experience call for?]]
Course note: [[03.12 Build a personal response sequence|What sequence can help me respond more deliberately to an ordinary emotional trigger?]]
Course note: [[03.13 Turn worry into a bounded planning task|When does thinking about a problem help, and when does it only repeat alarm?]]
Course note: [[03.14 Choose an emotion response for its purpose|Which way of responding to a feeling helps this situation?]]
Course note: [[03.15 Separate pain from the story about pain|How can I take pain seriously without assuming I know its full cause?]]
Course note: [[03.16 Distinguish restoration from numbing|Does this activity help me return to life, or postpone what matters until the cost grows?]]
Course note: [[03.17 Use a quiet pause to hear the real concern|What becomes clearer when I stop adding input for a moment?]]
Agency, responsibility, and boundaries
Course note: [[04.01 Sort control, influence, and concern|Which part of this situation can I actually act on?]]
Course note: [[04.02 Separate responsibility from blame|What response is available even when I did not cause the problem?]]
Course note: [[04.03 State a boundary as your action|How do I make a limit clear without pretending to control someone else?]]
Course note: [[04.04 Say no without inventing a defense|How can I decline a request honestly and clearly?]]
Course note: [[04.05 Make promises small enough to keep|What exactly am I committing to deliver?]]
Course note: [[04.06 Distinguish solitude from isolation|Is time alone helping me return to life or helping me avoid it indefinitely?]]
Course note: [[04.07 Hold standards without demanding universal approval|Can I tolerate disagreement while remaining open to correction?]]
Course note: [[04.08 Build an agency plan for one recurring difficulty|How will I combine action, boundaries, and support in a real situation?]]
Course note: [[04.09 Decide when to disengage|When is leaving a situation the responsible action?]]
Course note: [[04.10 Repair your part without owning the whole conflict|How can I apologize for my action without accepting responsibility for everything that happened?]]
Course note: [[04.11 Negotiate a commitment before capacity breaks|How can I change an obligation honestly when my capacity changes?]]
Course note: [[04.12 Ask for help while retaining a decision|What can another person contribute without becoming responsible for my whole choice?]]
Course note: [[04.13 Honor support with a clear next step|What should I do after someone has given useful help?]]
Habits and behavior design
Course note: [[05.01 Map the behavior loop|What sets this action in motion and keeps it repeating?]]
Course note: [[05.02 Make the first action unambiguous|What is the smallest clear action that genuinely begins the work?]]
Course note: [[05.03 Attach a behavior to a reliable cue|When and where will I remember to act?]]
Course note: [[05.04 Design the environment around the choice|What in my surroundings makes the desired action easier or harder?]]
Course note: [[05.05 Use rewards without losing the purpose|What consequence makes the behavior worth repeating now?]]

Course note: [[05.08 Recover after a missed repetition|What will I do when the plan inevitably meets a difficult day?]]
Course note: [[05.09 Distinguish repetition from deliberate improvement|Am I getting better or becoming more automatic at the same level?]]
Course note: [[05.10 Understand compounding without magical arithmetic|How can small actions accumulate, and where do they stop helping?]]
Course note: [[05.11 Evaluate a habit-forming product|Is this product helping me do what I chose or repeatedly pulling me elsewhere?]]
Course note: [[05.12 Run a habit experiment|What will I test rather than merely promise?]]
Course note: [[05.13 Replace a behavior without losing its function|What need does an unwanted habit serve, and what else could serve it?]]
Course note: [[05.14 Change friction before relying on resolve|Which small obstacle or convenience determines what I usually do?]]
Course note: [[05.15 Use accountability without making shame the mechanism|How can a commitment to another person help without turning a missed day into concealment?]]
Course note: [[05.16 Build a reset point into a habit|What happens after a week that does not fit the usual routine?]]
Course note: [[05.17 Audit whether a habit still serves its purpose|Is this routine helping the value that created it?]]
Attention, time, and a workable day
Course note: [[06.01 Distinguish traction from distraction|What did I intend to do with this period of time?]]
Course note: [[06.02 Investigate internal triggers|What experience am I trying to leave when I switch tasks?]]
Course note: [[06.03 Schedule values, not just incoming demands|Where does my calendar make room for what I say matters?]]
Course note: [[06.04 Separate urgent from important|Does this demand need immediate attention, and does it serve a significant purpose?]]
Course note: [[06.05 Design a focused work session|What conditions would make one period of demanding work easier to begin and sustain?]]
Course note: [[06.06 Coordinate availability instead of silently disappearing|How can I protect focus while remaining reliable to others?]]
Course note: [[06.07 Choose a practical policy for digital inputs|Which messages, feeds, and alerts deserve automatic access to my attention?]]
Course note: [[06.08 Leave room for recovery and wandering|Does my attention plan include periods when I am not forcing output?]]
Course note: [[06.09 Close the day with a next action|What can I leave clear enough that tomorrow does not begin with rediscovery?]]
Course note: [[06.10 Review time through evidence|What did the week reveal about my plan's assumptions?]]
Course note: [[06.11 Make a daily list fit the actual day|How can a task list help without pretending the day has unlimited capacity?]]
Course note: [[06.12 Recognize busywork as avoidance of uncertainty|Am I doing easy visible tasks to postpone a harder important one?]]
Course note: [[06.13 Give interruptions an agreed route|How can I protect focus while remaining reachable for real needs?]]
Course note: [[06.14 Leave a buffer for work that does not announce itself|Why does a tightly filled calendar fail even when my estimates look reasonable?]]
Course note: [[06.15 Limit inputs to fit the work in front of you|Which incoming information is useful for this task, and which only creates activity?]]
Course note: [[06.16 Count the cost of switching tasks|What happens when I repeatedly leave a difficult task and return?]]
Learning, memory, and understanding
Course note: [[07.01 Begin with a question you can answer|What exactly am I trying to learn from this material?]]
Course note: [[07.02 Explain before rereading|Can I reconstruct the idea without seeing the page?]]

Course note: [[07.16 Test a remembered lesson against the page|Did I learn the author's claim, or a simpler version I made up?]]
Practice, performance, and adaptation
Course note: [[08.01 Define the skill you are practicing|What component of performance needs attention today?]]
Course note: [[08.02 Work at a useful level of challenge|Is the task difficult enough to teach me and manageable enough to attempt?]]
Course note: [[08.03 Build a feedback loop|What signal will tell me whether my attempt improved?]]

Course note: [[08.05 Train under varied conditions|Will this skill still work outside the exact conditions in which I learned it?]]
Course note: [[08.06 Respond to pressure with a process cue|What should I attend to when the stakes feel high?]]
Course note: [[08.07 Treat recovery as part of training|What allows repeated practice without accumulating avoidable harm?]]
Course note: [[08.08 Study failure without worshipping it|What did the unsuccessful attempt actually teach?]]
Course note: [[08.09 Build a practice cycle|What will I repeatedly do, inspect, and change?]]
Course note: [[08.10 Separate practice from performance|Why should training look different from the moment I must deliver?]]
Course note: [[08.11 Use a brief pre-performance routine|How can I prepare for a demanding attempt without making preparation an endless ritual?]]
Course note: [[08.12 Train the weak link without making it your identity|How do I improve a limiting component of a skill?]]
Course note: [[08.13 Set a challenge limit before motivation takes over|What conditions would make continuing practice unwise today?]]
Course note: [[08.14 Select feedback near the decision it should improve|When and from whom will feedback be specific enough to use?]]
Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment
Course note: [[09.01 Describe before interpreting|What did I actually see or hear?]]
Course note: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual|Compared with what is this behavior unusual?]]
Course note: [[09.03 Notice selection and survivorship|Who or what is missing from the examples I can see?]]
Course note: [[09.04 Use base rates before vivid details|How common is this outcome before I consider the special story?]]
Course note: [[09.05 Look for confirmation and disconfirmation|What evidence would challenge my preferred explanation?]]
Course note: [[09.06 Interpret body language with humility|What can a nonverbal cue tell me, and what remains uncertain?]]
Course note: [[09.07 Recognize framing and anchoring|How is the presentation of a choice influencing my judgment?]]
Course note: [[09.08 Separate intuition from expertise|When is a fast judgment likely to be informative?]]
Course note: [[09.09 Keep uncertainty visible|How sure am I, and why?]]
Course note: [[09.10 Run an observation audit|Which of my judgments deserves another look?]]
Course note: [[09.11 Stop sunk costs from making the next choice|What should I do when I have already spent time or money on a poor route?]]
Course note: [[09.12 Check availability before judging frequency|Am I treating a memorable example as a common event?]]
Course note: [[09.13 Keep hindsight from rewriting the decision|How can I judge an earlier choice after I know how it turned out?]]
Course note: [[09.14 Calibrate confidence with a track record|How can I know whether my certainty is earned?]]
Course note: [[09.15 Notice regression after an extreme result|Did my intervention cause a return to normal, or might the extreme result have changed anyway?]]
Course note: [[09.16 Notice the evidence that is missing|If my explanation were right, what else would I expect to see?]]
Course note: [[09.17 Audit a first impression with a short record|How accurate are my quick judgments when I can check them later?]]
Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement
Course note: [[10.01 Find the claim and its support|What is this person asking me to believe, and why?]]
Course note: [[10.02 Distinguish validity from truth|Would the conclusion follow if the premises were true?]]
Course note: [[10.03 Work carefully with if and only if|Does this condition guarantee the result, or is it merely required?]]
Course note: [[10.04 Interpret and, or, not, and all|What exactly does the statement include or exclude?]]
Course note: [[10.05 Test an argument with a counterexample|Can the reasons be true while the conclusion fails?]]
Course note: [[10.06 Identify a reasoning error without name-calling|What step of the reasoning fails?]]
Course note: [[10.07 Ask questions that open the reasoning|Which question would clarify an assumption or reveal a consequence?]]
Course note: [[10.08 Disagree with the strongest version|What would make the opposing view reasonable to someone informed?]]
Course note: [[10.09 Use logic in an everyday decision|What conclusion am I drawing, and what would make it warranted?]]
Course note: [[10.10 Keep the scope of a negative clear|What exactly is being denied in this statement?]]
Course note: [[10.11 Test all, some, and none with small cases|How do quantity words change what follows from a claim?]]
Course note: [[10.12 Map premises before debating a conclusion|Which reasons are doing the work in this argument?]]
Course note: [[10.13 Use contradiction as a test, not a trick|How can an impossible consequence show that an assumption needs revision?]]
Course note: [[10.14 Separate a confident speaker from a supported claim|What reasons remain if I set aside the speaker's status and delivery?]]
Course note: [[10.15 Ask whether a reason reaches the conclusion|Even if this fact is true, does it support the proposed action?]]
Evidence, science, and causal claims
Course note: [[11.01 Ask what a claim would predict|If this explanation is useful, what should we expect to observe?]]
Course note: [[11.02 Distinguish correlation from intervention|Would changing this factor change the outcome?]]
Course note: [[11.03 Look for confounding variables|What third factor might influence both the presumed cause and result?]]
Course note: [[11.04 Understand comparison groups and selection|Who was included, excluded, or assigned differently?]]
Course note: [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality|What does this model illuminate, and what does it leave out?]]
Course note: [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence|What can one vivid story establish?]]
Course note: [[11.07 Consider replication, uncertainty, and revision|Has a result held up under repeated and independent checks?]]
Course note: [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes|How much confidence does this decision require?]]
Course note: [[11.09 Distinguish observation, intervention, and counterfactual|What kind of causal question am I asking?]]
Course note: [[11.10 Draw a causal path before adjusting for variables|Which variables might explain a relationship, and which might lie on the path I want to study?]]
Course note: [[11.11 Separate prediction from explanation|Can a model be useful for forecasting while still giving a poor account of why something happens?]]
Course note: [[11.12 Treat surprising data as a question for the model|What should I do when evidence conflicts with my preferred explanation?]]
Course note: [[11.13 Check whether a measure is only a proxy|What real outcome am I hoping this number represents?]]
Course note: [[11.14 Treat a null result as information|What did a test rule out, and what remains possible when it shows little change?]]
Decisions, strategy, and systems
Course note: [[12.01 Define the decision before using a model|What choice is actually before me?]]
Course note: [[12.02 Use opportunity cost and reversibility|What do I give up by choosing this option, and can I change course?]]
Course note: [[12.03 Separate decision quality from outcome quality|Was the process sound given what was known at the time?]]
Course note: [[12.04 Build a strategy kernel|What obstacle does my plan address, and how do its actions fit together?]]
Course note: [[12.05 Use feedback loops to see change over time|What effect might this action create that later feeds back into the situation?]]
Course note: [[12.06 Beware local optimization|Could improving one measure make the whole situation worse?]]
Course note: [[12.07 Use scenarios rather than one confident forecast|What would I do if different plausible futures occur?]]
Course note: [[12.08 Make a decision reviewable|How will I know whether to continue, adjust, or stop?]]
Course note: [[12.09 See stocks, flows, and delays in a changing system|Why can a sensible action take time to change the result I care about?]]
Course note: [[12.10 Find a proximate objective|What useful target can I reach when the final ambition is still distant?]]
Course note: [[12.11 Check for a chain-link bottleneck|Does the whole result depend on several parts working together?]]
Course note: [[12.12 Use a decision threshold before results arrive|What evidence would make me continue, revise, or stop a plan?]]
Course note: [[12.13 Plan for a surprise without pretending to predict it|What would I do if an important assumption changed suddenly?]]
Course note: [[12.14 Keep a reserve for the constraint that matters|Which capacity must remain available when the plan meets reality?]]
Language, questions, and clear expression
Course note: [[13.01 State the point before decorating it|What do I want the listener or reader to understand?]]
Course note: [[13.02 Define the term doing the work|Which word might we be using in different senses?]]

Course note: [[13.04 Use a sequence of questions to explore a problem|What should I ask first, and what can wait?]]

Course note: [[13.07 Adapt tone without losing honesty|How can I make a difficult message receivable and still clear?]]
Course note: [[13.08 Check what the other person understood|How will I know my meaning arrived intact?]]
Course note: [[13.09 Use silence to make room for an answer|What happens when I stop filling every pause after a question?]]
Course note: [[13.10 Ask one question at a time|Why do several questions in one sentence often produce a partial answer?]]
Course note: [[13.11 Move between abstract claims and concrete cases|How do I clarify a big word without getting trapped in a single anecdote?]]
Course note: [[13.12 Use humor without making a person the cost|Does this joke invite connection, or require someone else to absorb embarrassment?]]
Course note: [[13.13 Use the other person's stated criteria|What does the person say matters to them about this choice?]]
Listening, conflict, and repair

Course note: [[14.02 Reflect back without performing agreement|Can I show understanding before offering my view?]]
Course note: [[14.03 Slow a heated exchange|What would reduce harm and improve the chance of a useful conversation?]]
Course note: [[14.04 Use requests instead of character verdicts|What specific behavior needs to change?]]
Course note: [[14.05 Recognize recurring interaction patterns|Are we repeating a familiar exchange that never solves the issue?]]
Course note: [[14.06 Apologize with repair rather than performance|What does the harmed person need from my response?]]
Course note: [[14.07 Know when conversation is insufficient|Does this situation need a boundary, decision, or outside support?]]
Course note: [[14.08 Close a difficult conversation clearly|What has actually been agreed, and what remains unresolved?]]
Course note: [[14.09 Validate an experience without endorsing every conclusion|How can I show that I heard someone while still examining the facts?]]
Course note: [[14.10 Interrupt only to improve the conversation|When is an interruption useful, and how can I make it respectful?]]
Course note: [[14.11 Break a repeated conflict cycle|How can two people change a conflict pattern that keeps recreating itself?]]
Course note: [[14.12 Separate the factual correction from the hurt|Can I correct a detail while still attending to the person's experience?]]
Course note: [[14.13 Prepare a difficult conversation around a request|What do I need the other person to understand and decide?]]
Relationships, consent, and mutual choice
Course note: [[15.01 Approach another person as a chooser|What would respectful interest look like when both people can say yes or no?]]
Course note: [[15.02 Build conversation through curiosity|What would help us learn whether we enjoy talking with each other?]]
Course note: [[15.03 Read messages by their pattern, not one delay|What can I reasonably infer from this communication pattern?]]
Course note: [[15.04 Discuss expectations before resentment accumulates|What do we each think this relationship involves?]]

Course note: [[15.06 Recognize reciprocity without scorekeeping|Are care and effort moving in both directions over time?]]
Course note: [[15.07 Distinguish attachment patterns from fixed types|What happens between us when security feels uncertain?]]
Course note: [[15.08 Notice manipulation disguised as romance|Is this behavior building mutual trust or reducing someone's freedom to choose?]]
Course note: [[15.09 Decide whether compatibility is present|Do our values, behavior, and expectations fit well enough to continue?]]
Course note: [[15.10 Agree on availability instead of testing it|How can people discuss contact and reassurance without turning them into loyalty tests?]]

Course note: [[15.13 Give attention without performing charm|Am I interested in the person, or in being seen as interesting?]]
Course note: [[15.14 Build friendship through ordinary reliability|What repeated actions show that this relationship is safe and mutual?]]
Family, development, and relational patterns
Course note: [[16.01 Describe a family pattern without making it destiny|Which early expectation might still affect my choices?]]

Course note: Answer before opening each card. These answers are Course notes, not quotations or claims of perfect certainty. Return to the full lesson when the distinction is unclear.
Self-knowledge and your starting point

blocks.question: What makes a useful baseline?
blocks.text: A dated description of observable events and conditions, including what already works, against which a later change can be compared.

blocks.question: Does separating interpretation from observation mean ignoring feelings?
blocks.text: No. Feelings are part of your experience; the explanation attached to them still needs to be examined.

blocks.question: Does a domain review require perfect balance?
blocks.text: No. It makes unequal priorities visible so that you can choose and revisit them deliberately.

blocks.question: What is the difference between a pattern and a destiny?
blocks.text: A pattern describes repeated observations under particular conditions; it does not prove that future events must repeat them.

blocks.question: Why separate a role from its specific commitments?
blocks.text: A broad identity can conceal incompatible or unspoken expectations; specific commitments can be clarified, prioritized, and renegotiated.

blocks.question: What is an evidence-based strength statement?
blocks.text: A description of a demonstrated behavior, its result, and the conditions that made it reliable.

blocks.question: What does the blind area represent?
blocks.text: Information others notice about you that you have not recognized; their reports still need context and examination.

blocks.question: What should happen between receiving feedback and changing behavior?
blocks.text: Examine the evidence and relevant standard, then choose a specific response you can justify and review.

blocks.question: What makes feedback different from dependence on approval?
blocks.text: Feedback informs a standard you can examine; dependence makes another person's reaction the sole standard of worth.

blocks.question: When does comparison become a learning tool?
blocks.text: When it identifies a relevant, observable difference that suggests a practice or a question, rather than a total ranking of people.

blocks.question: Does a socially influenced desire have to be rejected?
blocks.text: No. Its origin is information; the decision depends on whether you endorse its aims, costs, and ordinary practice.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of a resource-and-constraint map?
blocks.text: To choose a feasible next action and identify which conditions require change, support, or further information.

blocks.question: Why examine immediate consequences as well as later costs?
blocks.text: The immediate payoff can help explain why a behavior repeats even when its long-term effects are unwanted.

blocks.question: What is the goal of finding a counterexample to a self-story?
blocks.text: To improve the accuracy and scope of the claim, so that it can guide investigation instead of acting as a fixed identity.

blocks.question: What distinguishes a learning question from a disguised accusation?
blocks.text: A learning question allows multiple possible answers and identifies evidence; a disguised accusation already assumes the verdict.

blocks.question: What is the essential difference between a starting brief and a declaration of identity?
blocks.text: A starting brief links observations to a testable next step and can change when the evidence changes.

blocks.question: Why inspect a routine before changing it?
blocks.text: Its actual conditions, effects, and trade-offs may differ from the story you tell about it.

blocks.question: What should be checked before adopting a comparison as a verdict?
blocks.text: Who set the standard, what it measures, and which differences in circumstances it ignores.

blocks.question: Why request an example instead of a personality verdict?
blocks.text: An example ties feedback to observable behavior and a specific context that you can examine or change.

blocks.question: What distinguishes chosen adaptation from costly performance?
blocks.text: Whether it helps participation while preserving important needs and values, or repeatedly hides them to secure approval.

blocks.question: Why revisit a self-label?
blocks.text: A label may persist after its evidence or context changes and can narrow future choices.
Values, meaning, and a direction worth choosing

blocks.question: How does a value differ from a goal?
blocks.text: A value is a continuing quality of action; a goal is a particular outcome that can be completed or revised.

blocks.question: Does difficulty make a goal valuable?
blocks.text: No. Difficulty is a cost to evaluate against the goal's meaning, consequences, and feasibility.

blocks.question: What tests whether a mission is useful?
blocks.text: It helps make a concrete choice and can be revised in response to experience.

blocks.question: Does finding meaning justify what happened?
blocks.text: No. A meaningful response and a judgment that an event was harmful can both be true.

blocks.question: What is an enough threshold?
blocks.text: A revisable standard of sufficiency tied to a purpose, rather than an automatic demand for more.

blocks.question: What makes reflection on limited time practical?
blocks.text: It changes a present priority or commitment without turning every moment into a performance demand.

blocks.question: How can hope remain realistic?
blocks.text: By supporting worthwhile action while acknowledging uncertainty, constraints, and the need to revise a plan.

blocks.question: What makes contribution sustainable?
blocks.text: A useful, agreed commitment that respects the recipient's agency and the giver's real capacity.

blocks.question: Why describe purpose with verbs?
blocks.text: Activities and contributions can reveal meaningful possibilities beyond a single title or role.

blocks.question: What keeps a values agreement useful?
blocks.text: Specific actions, visible trade-offs, protected limits, and a date to review what actually happened.

blocks.question: What is the difference between a value and its symbol?
blocks.text: A value guides action across situations; a symbol is one possible public marker that may or may not serve it.

blocks.question: Why do inconvenient cases clarify a value?
blocks.text: They show the action you choose when the principle competes with comfort, approval, or another duty.

blocks.question: What distinguishes workable hope from a guarantee?
blocks.text: Workable hope commits to a valued possibility and revisable action while acknowledging that the outcome is uncertain.

blocks.question: How can gratitude and change work together?
blocks.text: Appreciation can describe what is good while dissatisfaction identifies a real need for action.

blocks.question: What should a success measure be tied to?
blocks.text: The capability or life purpose it serves, along with the costs of the path to it.
Emotions, acceptance, and a steadier response

blocks.question: Why separate feeling from action urge?
blocks.text: An urge is information about a possible response, not an instruction you must follow.

blocks.question: Does acceptance mean agreement or resignation?
blocks.text: No. It acknowledges present experience while leaving room for judgment, support, and constructive change.

blocks.question: Does noticing a thought establish whether it is true?
blocks.text: No. It creates distance; evaluating its truth requires evidence and reasoning.

blocks.question: What distinguishes problem-solving from repetitive worry?
blocks.text: Problem-solving changes information, options, or actions; repetitive worry can circle the same uncertainty without doing so.

blocks.question: Does managing anger require abandoning a valid complaint?
blocks.text: No. It helps choose a response that addresses the complaint without unnecessary escalation.

blocks.question: What makes responsibility different from self-condemnation?
blocks.text: Responsibility identifies actions, consequences, repair, and future change rather than reducing a person to a global label.

blocks.question: Why use defense-mechanism language cautiously?
blocks.text: It is interpretive and can become an unfalsifiable accusation if every denial is treated as confirmation.

blocks.question: Does a nuanced view weaken boundaries?
blocks.text: No. Boundaries can be based on specific unacceptable behavior without declaring a person wholly good or bad.

blocks.question: How can self-compassion support accountability?
blocks.text: It acknowledges difficulty while preserving the ability to examine consequences and take corrective action.

blocks.question: What is the aim of unmeasured enjoyment?
blocks.text: To participate in a valued experience without making external performance its sole justification.

blocks.question: Why distinguish discomfort from danger?
blocks.text: Because persistence, investigation, care, and protection are different responses to different conditions.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of a response sequence?
blocks.text: To create a repeatable pause between an experience and a chosen action, with room to learn from imperfect attempts.

blocks.question: What makes planning different from rumination?
blocks.text: Planning produces a bounded question, action, or contingency; rumination repeats possibilities without adding usable information.

blocks.question: How should an emotion response be judged?
blocks.text: By its fit with the situation and the action it supports, not only by immediate relief.

blocks.question: Why is a pain record more useful than a confident label?
blocks.text: It preserves timing, conditions, and effects that can inform assessment without pretending to establish the cause.

blocks.question: What helps distinguish restoration from numbing?
blocks.text: Its function and repeated effect on recovery, important needs, and the ability to return to chosen action.

blocks.question: What is a useful purpose of a quiet pause?
blocks.text: To notice a concern or assumption clearly enough to choose an appropriate next step.
Agency, responsibility, and boundaries

blocks.question: What distinguishes influence from control?
blocks.text: Influence can affect an outcome without determining it.

blocks.question: Does taking action imply accepting blame?
blocks.text: No. A useful response, the cause of a problem, and moral accountability are separate questions.

blocks.question: How does a boundary differ from a demand?
blocks.text: It specifies your participation and actions rather than assuming authority over another person's choices.

blocks.question: What makes a refusal reliable?
blocks.text: A clear decision, truthful explanation where useful, and no promise beyond your capacity.

blocks.question: What belongs in a clear commitment?
blocks.text: A defined action, timing, dependencies, and a plan for communicating changes.

blocks.question: What helps distinguish solitude from harmful withdrawal?
blocks.text: Its degree of choice, its effects, and whether access to support and valued participation remains available.

blocks.question: What keeps independence from becoming rigidity?
blocks.text: A clear standard and a genuine account of what could change the decision.

blocks.question: What belongs in an agency plan?
blocks.text: Chosen actions, requests, boundaries, support, and a review of real outcomes.

blocks.question: What makes disengagement responsible rather than avoidant?
blocks.text: It protects a legitimate limit and includes an appropriate later action when the underlying obligation remains.

blocks.question: What belongs in a precise repair?
blocks.text: Your specific action, its effect, and the change you will make, without claiming control over another person's choices.

blocks.question: What should a renegotiated commitment include?
blocks.text: The original promise, the changed constraint, specific alternatives, and a clear new agreement.

blocks.question: How can asking for help preserve agency?
blocks.text: By defining the needed contribution while keeping decision rights and next actions clear.

blocks.question: What is a clear response to useful help?
blocks.text: State what you understood, what you will do, and any relevant follow-up without surrendering your own choice.
Habits and behavior design

blocks.question: Why inspect the whole loop?
blocks.text: The setting and immediate consequence can explain repetition better than a global label about willpower.

blocks.question: What makes a small start useful?
blocks.text: It reduces a real barrier and begins the intended activity rather than replacing it with unrelated preparation.

blocks.question: What should a useful cue provide?
blocks.text: A recognizable moment and setting in which the intended behavior is feasible.

blocks.question: Why change the environment?
blocks.text: To make the intended behavior more available and reduce repeated reliance on effortful remembering or restraint.

blocks.question: What should a habit reward support?
blocks.text: Repetition of a worthwhile behavior without undermining its purpose or your ability to choose.

blocks.question: How can identity remain flexible?
blocks.text: By tying it to observable, revisable patterns of action rather than treating it as a permanent verdict.

blocks.question: What is the main purpose of a habit record?
blocks.text: To reveal behavior and conditions that help you learn, not to turn a streak into a measure of personal worth.

blocks.question: What makes recovery effective?
blocks.text: A feasible return plus an examination of the conditions that caused the miss.

blocks.question: Why is repetition alone insufficient for improvement?
blocks.text: It can reinforce existing performance, including errors, unless feedback and an appropriate challenge change the practice.

blocks.question: What limits a compounding metaphor?
blocks.text: Real behavior is affected by quality, feedback, constraints, interruptions, and changing conditions rather than a guaranteed growth rate.

blocks.question: Does higher engagement prove a product helps the user?
blocks.text: No. Engagement must be evaluated against the user's aims, outcomes, and ability to choose.

blocks.question: What makes a habit experiment informative?
blocks.text: A specific behavior, visible conditions, a simple record, and a planned review that can change the design.

blocks.question: Why should a replacement address the function of a habit?
blocks.text: The cue and need remain after the old action is removed, so an unrelated substitute may not be usable when the moment arrives.

blocks.question: What is friction in behavior design?
blocks.text: The effort or delay between a cue and an action, which can be changed to support a chosen behavior.

blocks.question: What makes accountability useful for learning?
blocks.text: Specific actions, honest reporting, and a plan for revision after a miss rather than pressure to hide it.

blocks.question: Why include a reset point in a habit?
blocks.text: It gives a feasible return after disruption and a way to redesign a pattern that no longer fits.

blocks.question: When should a habit be reviewed?
blocks.text: When its purpose, effects, or costs may have changed enough to alter the right action.
Attention, time, and a workable day

blocks.question: Is an activity inherently a distraction?
blocks.text: Its relation to your chosen purpose and commitments matters; the same activity can serve or interrupt them.

blocks.question: Why inspect internal triggers?
blocks.text: Because changing external prompts alone may leave the discomfort or ambiguity driving the diversion untouched.

blocks.question: What is a values-based schedule?
blocks.text: A realistic allocation of time that includes chosen priorities as well as obligations and can be revised openly.

blocks.question: What is the difference between urgent and important?
blocks.text: Urgency concerns when action is needed; importance concerns its consequences and relation to worthwhile aims.

blocks.question: What should a focus ritual accomplish?
blocks.text: Reduce setup decisions and support attention to a clearly defined task.

blocks.question: Why coordinate focus time?
blocks.text: Other people's work may depend on your availability, so clear agreements protect both concentration and reliability.

blocks.question: What makes an input policy useful?
blocks.text: It preserves necessary communication while reducing prompts that do not serve a chosen purpose.

blocks.question: Why include recovery in an attention plan?
blocks.text: Attention is used across a whole day, and sustainable work requires more than repeatedly demanding maximum concentration.

blocks.question: What belongs in a useful closing note?
blocks.text: Completed work, unresolved questions, and a specific next action with enough context to resume.

blocks.question: What should a weekly time review produce?
blocks.text: A concrete adjustment based on observed patterns, while preserving effective parts of the plan.

blocks.question: What turns a task list into a realistic plan?
blocks.text: Comparing estimated effort with available time and making explicit choices about what will not fit.

blocks.question: How can busywork differ from useful administration?
blocks.text: It may create visible activity while repeatedly displacing a more important task whose uncertainty has not been addressed.

blocks.question: What must an interruption policy include?
blocks.text: A focus period, a route for genuine urgency, a time for ordinary requests, and agreement with affected people.

blocks.question: What does a buffer represent?
blocks.text: Capacity for ordinary uncertainty, transitions, and follow-up that a task-only estimate leaves out.

blocks.question: What is a task-specific input limit?
blocks.text: A temporary choice to admit information needed for the current question while routing other inputs to a later review.

blocks.question: Why record a restart cue before switching?
blocks.text: It preserves the next step and unresolved context so returning requires less reconstruction.
Learning, memory, and understanding

blocks.question: What makes a learning goal testable?
blocks.text: It specifies a performance or explanation that can be attempted and checked.

blocks.question: Why test recall before rereading?
blocks.text: Retrieval exposes gaps that familiarity with the page can conceal.

blocks.question: Why classify the knowledge type?
blocks.text: Different kinds of knowledge require different practice and evidence of understanding.

blocks.question: What is a memory cue for?
blocks.text: It aids retrieval; understanding and appropriate use still need separate checks.

blocks.question: What does a memory palace provide?
blocks.text: Spatial retrieval cues for ordered information, not automatic understanding or proof.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of spaced retrieval?
blocks.text: To check and strengthen recall over time while directing more practice to unstable knowledge.

blocks.question: Why use near misses in learning?
blocks.text: They reveal which features actually distinguish a concept from similar cases.

blocks.question: What makes feedback actionable?
blocks.text: It identifies a specific feature of performance against a standard that can guide another attempt.

blocks.question: What makes transfer responsible?
blocks.text: It identifies a shared mechanism while checking differences, limits, and consequences in the new setting.

blocks.question: What makes a knowledge link useful?
blocks.text: An explicit relationship that can be explained, applied, and revised.

blocks.question: Why use self-written questions during reading?
blocks.text: They make the intended understanding explicit and create a retrieval test beyond recognition.

blocks.question: How do you know a memory cue works?
blocks.text: It reliably retrieves the intended information after a delay without confusing it with similar items.

blocks.question: What should be diagnosed when a memory palace fails?
blocks.text: The order and distinctness of locations and images, plus whether the underlying material is understood.

blocks.question: What does teaching back reveal about a procedure?
blocks.text: Whether you understand its conditions and decision points rather than only remembering step names.

blocks.question: What makes a field note useful?
blocks.text: It preserves dated observations and uncertainty separately from later interpretation.

blocks.question: Why compare retrieval with the source?
blocks.text: Recall can expose learning and also reveal missing qualifications or mistaken claims.
Practice, performance, and adaptation

blocks.question: Why isolate a component?
blocks.text: It makes practice and feedback specific enough to change performance.

blocks.question: What makes challenge useful?
blocks.text: It reveals a correctable limitation while remaining feasible and appropriately safe.

blocks.question: What belongs in a feedback loop?
blocks.text: Attempt, observation, explanation, and a targeted change for the next attempt.

blocks.question: What can mental rehearsal reasonably support?
blocks.text: Preparation of attention and sequence when paired with real practice and feedback.

blocks.question: Why vary practice conditions?
blocks.text: To test whether a skill transfers beyond the exact drill or example used to learn it.

blocks.question: What makes a process cue useful?
blocks.text: It directs attention to a task-relevant action that has been practiced.

blocks.question: Why is recovery part of practice?
blocks.text: Repeated learning and performance depend on conditions that allow adaptation and reduce avoidable harm.

blocks.question: Does failure automatically produce growth?
blocks.text: No. Learning requires examining causes, limits, and a testable change.

blocks.question: What makes a practice cycle adaptive?
blocks.text: Specific attempts, relevant feedback, recovery, and a planned decision about the next cycle.

blocks.question: What is the practical difference between practice and performance?
blocks.text: Practice can isolate and repair components; performance uses the current skill in a whole task under real constraints.

blocks.question: What makes a useful pre-performance routine?
blocks.text: It is brief, repeatable, and directs attention to the task without requiring a particular feeling or guaranteeing an outcome.

blocks.question: Why retest a weak-link drill in the whole task?
blocks.text: Improvement in an isolated component matters only if it transfers to performance in context.

blocks.question: Why set a challenge limit in advance?
blocks.text: It preserves judgment about safety and recovery when effort and identity make stopping harder to consider.

blocks.question: What makes performance feedback actionable?
blocks.text: It describes a specific attempt and a change that can be tested in the relevant setting.
Observation, bias, and calibrated judgment

blocks.question: Why separate observation from interpretation?
blocks.text: It makes the inference visible, testable, and open to other explanations.

blocks.question: What is needed to interpret an anomaly?
blocks.text: A relevant baseline, context, and more evidence than a single ambiguous cue.

blocks.question: What is survivorship bias?
blocks.text: A distorted conclusion caused by examining visible survivors while missing relevant failures or excluded cases.

blocks.question: Why consider base rates?
blocks.text: They provide a starting context for interpreting case-specific clues rather than letting vividness set the whole estimate.

blocks.question: What makes a hypothesis useful?
blocks.text: It leads to observations that could distinguish it from other explanations.

blocks.question: What is a responsible use of nonverbal cues?
blocks.text: As context-sensitive prompts for clarification, not as unique proof of a hidden mental state.

blocks.question: What is anchoring?
blocks.text: An initial reference point influences later judgment, sometimes beyond its evidential value.

blocks.question: What conditions strengthen intuition?
blocks.text: Repeated experience in a sufficiently regular environment with useful feedback.

blocks.question: What does calibrated judgment require?
blocks.text: Stating evidence, alternatives, and confidence at a level the evidence can support.

blocks.question: What is an observation audit for?
blocks.text: To inspect how a conclusion arose and choose a check that could improve it.

blocks.question: What is the sunk-cost mistake?
blocks.text: Allowing an irrecoverable past investment to decide a future choice when it does not change the options' future value.

blocks.question: Why is recall ease a weak frequency measure?
blocks.text: Vividness and recency affect memory, while frequency requires information about the wider set of cases.

blocks.question: How does a decision record limit hindsight bias?
blocks.text: It preserves the information and reasons available before the outcome was known.

blocks.question: What is calibration?
blocks.text: The match between expressed confidence and how often comparable judgments prove correct over time.

blocks.question: What is regression toward the mean?
blocks.text: Extreme observations in a variable process tend to be followed by less extreme observations, which can mislead simple before-and-after judgments.

blocks.question: When is missing evidence informative?
blocks.text: When a hypothesis predicts observable evidence that should have appeared under the actual conditions.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of an impression audit?
blocks.text: To compare recorded predictions with outcomes and calibrate which cues are reliable in which settings.
Logic, arguments, and fair disagreement

blocks.question: What must happen before evaluating an argument?
blocks.text: Its conclusion and supporting reasons should be reconstructed fairly.

blocks.question: What does validity test?
blocks.text: Whether the conclusion follows from the premises if those premises are assumed true.

blocks.question: Does “if A then B” imply “if B then A”?
blocks.text: No. B may have other sufficient causes.

blocks.question: What does “not all” mean?
blocks.text: At least one member of the group does not have the stated property.

blocks.question: What does a counterexample show?
blocks.text: That a universal claim or inference needs revision when a relevant case satisfies its conditions but defeats its conclusion.

blocks.question: What makes a fallacy diagnosis useful?
blocks.text: It identifies the exact inferential problem and explains how it affects the conclusion.

blocks.question: What distinguishes inquiry from rhetorical questioning?
blocks.text: A genuine question allows the answer to affect the conversation and is applied fairly to both sides.

blocks.question: Why steelman an opposing view?
blocks.text: It directs disagreement toward the strongest real reasons instead of an easily defeated substitute.

blocks.question: What can logic contribute to a decision?
blocks.text: It clarifies implications and assumptions while leaving factual and value judgments visible.

blocks.question: What is the scope of a negative?
blocks.text: The part of a statement that the negative applies to, which can change the statement's meaning.

blocks.question: Why does one example not prove an 'all' claim?
blocks.text: A universal claim covers every member of the group; one example checks only one member.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of an argument map?
blocks.text: To show how premises and assumptions support a conclusion so each part can be tested fairly.

blocks.question: What does a contradiction establish?
blocks.text: That the set of premises and steps cannot all be correct as stated, not necessarily which single premise failed.

blocks.question: How should authority affect an argument?
blocks.text: It can guide where to investigate, but the claim still needs relevant scope and support.

blocks.question: What is a relevance check?
blocks.text: Testing whether a stated reason actually supports the conclusion through a defensible premise or mechanism.
Evidence, science, and causal claims

blocks.question: What makes an empirical claim examinable?
blocks.text: It specifies observable implications and conditions under which evidence could require revision.

blocks.question: Why does association alone not establish causation?
blocks.text: Several causal structures and selection effects can produce the same observed pattern.

blocks.question: What is a confounder?
blocks.text: A factor that affects both the proposed cause and outcome, distorting the observed association.

blocks.question: Why inspect selection?
blocks.text: Who enters and remains in a comparison can change the apparent effect and its applicability.

blocks.question: What is a model's proper role?
blocks.text: To simplify selected features for explanation or prediction while keeping assumptions and omissions visible.

blocks.question: What can an anecdote establish most directly?
blocks.text: That a reported experience occurred for someone, while broader frequency and causal claims need further evidence.

blocks.question: Why does independent replication matter?
blocks.text: It checks whether a result survives new samples, methods, and investigators.

blocks.question: What should set the evidence threshold?
blocks.text: The decision's stakes, reversibility, alternatives, and potential harms.

blocks.question: Why is observing an association different from intervening?
blocks.text: The groups may differ in other ways, so changing a factor may not reproduce the observed association.

blocks.question: What is the role of a causal diagram?
blocks.text: It makes assumed relationships and variable roles visible for testing; it does not prove that the arrows are correct.

blocks.question: Why can prediction and explanation diverge?
blocks.text: A pattern can forecast outcomes without revealing the causal mechanism, and a plausible mechanism may still predict poorly.

blocks.question: How should an anomaly be handled?
blocks.text: Check the observation, examine assumptions, and derive tests that could refine the explanation.

blocks.question: What is the main risk of a proxy measure?
blocks.text: The proxy can improve while the underlying outcome stays the same or gets worse.

blocks.question: Why is a null result not a final verdict?
blocks.text: Its meaning depends on whether the change occurred, the measure and duration could detect an effect, and alternative explanations.
Decisions, strategy, and systems

blocks.question: What should be clear before choosing a decision model?
blocks.text: The actual choice, available options, stakes, owner, and timing.

blocks.question: What is opportunity cost?
blocks.text: The value of the best realistic alternative forgone when a choice uses a limited resource.

blocks.question: Why separate decision quality from outcome?
blocks.text: Uncertainty can produce success from a poor process or failure from a sound one.

blocks.question: What are the three parts of a strategy kernel?
blocks.text: A diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding approach, and coordinated actions that implement it.

blocks.question: Why include feedback and delays?
blocks.text: Actions can change later conditions and responses, so immediate effects may not represent the full result.

blocks.question: What is local optimization?
blocks.text: Improving a part or metric in a way that may worsen the wider system or purpose.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of scenario planning?
blocks.text: To expose assumptions and prepare adaptable choices across plausible futures.

blocks.question: What makes a decision reviewable?
blocks.text: A recorded rationale, relevant signals, a review point, and conditions for revising the choice.

blocks.question: What is the difference between a stock and a flow?
blocks.text: A stock is an accumulated quantity; flows are the rates or events that add to or remove from it.

blocks.question: What makes an objective proximate?
blocks.text: It is close enough to act on and verify while resolving a meaningful part of the larger challenge.

blocks.question: What is a chain-link system?
blocks.text: A system whose overall performance depends on several complementary parts, so a weak part can limit the value of improvements elsewhere.

blocks.question: Why set a decision threshold in advance?
blocks.text: It makes the response to evidence less vulnerable to wishful revision after the result is known.

blocks.question: What makes a scenario plan actionable?
blocks.text: A plausible changed condition, an observable trigger, preserved options, and a feasible first response.

blocks.question: When is a reserve strategically useful?
blocks.text: When a shortage in a critical resource would stop the whole plan or impose a large cost.
Language, questions, and clear expression

blocks.question: What should precede stylistic polish?
blocks.text: A clear point, relevant support, and an understanding of the audience's needs.

blocks.question: When should a term be defined?
blocks.text: When differing meanings could change the claim, obligation, or decision.

blocks.question: What makes an open question genuine?
blocks.text: It leaves room for more than one answer and the answer can affect the conversation.

blocks.question: Why sequence questions?
blocks.text: Early context can change which later questions and solutions are relevant.

blocks.question: What is the practical purpose of grammatical precision?
blocks.text: To make actors, conditions, and relationships clear enough for the intended action or understanding.

blocks.question: What can one example establish?
blocks.text: It can illustrate a case or possibility; broader frequency and causal claims require more evidence.

blocks.question: What makes considerate communication honest?
blocks.text: It respects the recipient while keeping the facts, decision, and next step clear.

blocks.question: How can shared understanding be checked?
blocks.text: By confirming the intended meaning, responsibilities, and next action rather than inferring agreement from silence.

blocks.question: What is a useful role for silence after a question?
blocks.text: It gives the other person space to think and answer, while leaving room to clarify if needed.

blocks.question: Why ask one question at a time?
blocks.text: It lets the other person understand and answer the current question and lets the next question follow the evidence.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of moving between abstract and concrete language?
blocks.text: To clarify a principle's meaning and limits through cases without treating one case as proof of everything.

blocks.question: What makes conversational humor considerate?
blocks.text: It fits context, respects power and dignity, and responds to how the other person actually receives it.

blocks.question: How should someone's criteria guide language?
blocks.text: Ask for the criteria, check understanding, and address them honestly without pretending to know a hidden type.
Listening, conflict, and repair

blocks.question: Why ask about an interest beneath a position?
blocks.text: It may reveal the actual need and additional workable options.

blocks.question: What makes reflection authentic?
blocks.text: It accurately checks understanding while leaving room for correction and does not pretend agreement.

blocks.question: What makes a conflict pause responsible?
blocks.text: It reduces escalation, protects safety, and includes a genuine plan to return when appropriate.

blocks.question: Why avoid a character verdict?
blocks.text: It can obscure the specific behavior and change that the situation requires.

blocks.question: How should an interaction pattern be used?
blocks.text: As a revisable description of recurring moves that can suggest a different response.

blocks.question: What belongs in a useful apology?
blocks.text: Specific acknowledgment, attention to the effect, appropriate repair, and a credible change.

blocks.question: When is conversation not enough?
blocks.text: When safety, power, repeated harm, or structural obligations require protective action or formal support.

blocks.question: What should a conversation close make visible?
blocks.text: Agreements, owners, timing, unresolved issues, and the next process.

blocks.question: What can validation acknowledge without establishing?
blocks.text: A person's real experience and concern, while leaving the cause and interpretation open to inquiry.

blocks.question: What makes an interruption constructive?
blocks.text: It serves a clear conversational need and preserves the other person's chance to continue.

blocks.question: What is the useful unit of analysis in a repeated conflict?
blocks.text: The sequence of actions and interpretations that both people can examine, with safety limits kept clear.

blocks.question: Why separate correction and hurt in conflict?
blocks.text: A factual error can be corrected while the person's experienced impact still deserves attention.

blocks.question: What belongs in a difficult conversation opening?
blocks.text: A clear topic, concrete observation, effect, and workable request with room for the other person's account.
Relationships, consent, and mutual choice

blocks.question: What makes interest respectful?
blocks.text: A clear invitation that preserves both people's freedom to choose and decline.

blocks.question: What makes conversation reciprocal?
blocks.text: Both people have room to answer, ask, share, and change direction.

blocks.question: Why judge a pattern rather than one delay?
blocks.text: One response can have many causes; repeated behavior and explicit conversation give more relevant information.

blocks.question: Why discuss relationship expectations?
blocks.text: Important terms may differ between people, and explicit conversation supports informed mutual choice.

blocks.question: What makes consent ongoing?
blocks.text: A person's choice can change as the interaction changes, and each new choice must be respected.

blocks.question: What is reciprocity in a relationship?
blocks.text: A sustainable pattern of mutual concern and responsive contribution, not a perfect tally of identical acts.

blocks.question: How should attachment language be used?
blocks.text: As a tentative lens for patterns and needs, not a fixed diagnosis from limited information.

blocks.question: What distinguishes connection from coercive attachment?
blocks.text: Connection preserves informed mutual choice; coercive tactics reduce it through pressure or hidden control.

blocks.question: What should compatibility assessment consider?
blocks.text: Observed behavior, shared and conflicting expectations, negotiable differences, and each person's free choice.

blocks.question: What makes an availability agreement mutual?
blocks.text: Both people state needs and constraints and choose a workable pattern they can revisit.

blocks.question: What is a fair response to relationship ambiguity?
blocks.text: Check the pattern, ask clearly, respect the answer, and choose your own limit under remaining uncertainty.

blocks.question: Why is a book's intimacy advice insufficient for a particular partner?
blocks.text: It cannot determine that person's current preferences, boundaries, health, or consent.

blocks.question: What distinguishes attention from charm performance?
blocks.text: Attention responds to the other person's actual words and choices instead of using them mainly to display oneself.

blocks.question: What builds ordinary friendship reliability?
blocks.text: Repeated follow-through, respect for limits, honest expectations, and repair after mistakes.
Family, development, and relational patterns

blocks.question: How should an early pattern be used?
blocks.text: As a tentative explanation to examine, not a permanent identity or complete causal story.

blocks.question: What is a concrete way to examine availability?
blocks.text: Look at repeated responses to needs and distress rather than relying solely on a global label.
