Course note: Use these distinctions as working definitions in this course. Each entry links to the lesson where the idea is explained and applied.

Course note: [[01.01 Start with a baseline, not an ideal self|Start with a baseline, not an ideal self]] — A dated description of observable events and conditions, including what already works, against which a later change can be compared.

Course note: [[01.02 Separate facts, interpretations, and judgments|Separate facts, interpretations, and judgments]] — No. Feelings are part of your experience; the explanation attached to them still needs to be examined.

Course note: [[01.03 Examine your life across several domains|Examine your life across several domains]] — No. It makes unequal priorities visible so that you can choose and revisit them deliberately.

Course note: [[01.04 Look for patterns across a year|Look for patterns across a year]] — A pattern describes repeated observations under particular conditions; it does not prove that future events must repeat them.

Course note: [[01.05 Identify the roles that carry real commitments|Identify the roles that carry real commitments]] — A broad identity can conceal incompatible or unspoken expectations; specific commitments can be clarified, prioritized, and renegotiated.
Course note: [[01.06 Describe strengths with evidence|Describe strengths with evidence]] — A description of a demonstrated behavior, its result, and the conditions that made it reliable.

Course note: [[01.07 Use the Johari window without treating it as a diagnosis|Use the Johari window without treating it as a diagnosis]] — Information others notice about you that you have not recognized; their reports still need context and examination.
Course note: [[01.08 Turn feedback into a decision|Turn feedback into a decision]] — Examine the evidence and relevant standard, then choose a specific response you can justify and review.

Course note: [[01.09 Distinguish approval from self-direction|Distinguish approval from self-direction]] — Feedback informs a standard you can examine; dependence makes another person's reaction the sole standard of worth.

Course note: [[01.10 Make comparison answer a specific question|Make comparison answer a specific question]] — When it identifies a relevant, observable difference that suggests a practice or a question, rather than a total ranking of people.

Course note: [[01.11 Examine where a desire came from|Examine where a desire came from]] — No. Its origin is information; the decision depends on whether you endorse its aims, costs, and ordinary practice.

Course note: [[01.12 Map constraints and usable resources|Map constraints and usable resources]] — To choose a feasible next action and identify which conditions require change, support, or further information.

Course note: [[01.13 Notice the short-term payoff of a repeated behavior|Notice the short-term payoff of a repeated behavior]] — The immediate payoff can help explain why a behavior repeats even when its long-term effects are unwanted.

Course note: [[01.14 Test a personal story with a counterexample|Test a personal story with a counterexample]] — To improve the accuracy and scope of the claim, so that it can guide investigation instead of acting as a fixed identity.

Course note: [[01.15 Turn a complaint into a learning question|Turn a complaint into a learning question]] — A learning question allows multiple possible answers and identifies evidence; a disguised accusation already assumes the verdict.
Course note: [[01.16 Write your personal starting brief|Write your personal starting brief]] — A starting brief links observations to a testable next step and can change when the evidence changes.
Course note: [[01.17 Review rituals as evidence of priorities|Review rituals as evidence of priorities]] — Its actual conditions, effects, and trade-offs may differ from the story you tell about it.
Course note: [[01.18 Ask whose standard is being applied|Ask whose standard is being applied]] — Who set the standard, what it measures, and which differences in circumstances it ignores.

Course note: [[01.19 Ask another person for a concrete outside view|Ask another person for a concrete outside view]] — An example ties feedback to observable behavior and a specific context that you can examine or change.

Course note: [[01.20 Notice when belonging becomes a performance|Notice when belonging becomes a performance]] — Whether it helps participation while preserving important needs and values, or repeatedly hides them to secure approval.
Course note: [[01.21 Map identity claims to current evidence|Map identity claims to current evidence]] — A label may persist after its evidence or context changes and can narrow future choices.

Course note: [[02.01 Turn a value into a way of acting|Turn a value into a way of acting]] — A value is a continuing quality of action; a goal is a particular outcome that can be completed or revised.

Course note: [[02.02 Choose the difficulty attached to the ambition|Choose the difficulty attached to the ambition]] — No. Difficulty is a cost to evaluate against the goal's meaning, consequences, and feasibility.
Course note: [[02.03 Write a mission that can change a decision|Write a mission that can change a decision]] — It helps make a concrete choice and can be revised in response to experience.
Course note: [[02.04 Find meaning without romanticizing suffering|Find meaning without romanticizing suffering]] — No. A meaningful response and a judgment that an event was harmful can both be true.
Course note: [[02.05 Define enough before chasing more|Define enough before chasing more]] — A revisable standard of sufficiency tied to a purpose, rather than an automatic demand for more.
Course note: [[02.06 Use mortality to clarify priorities|Use mortality to clarify priorities]] — It changes a present priority or commitment without turning every moment into a performance demand.

Course note: [[02.07 Distinguish hope from a guarantee|Distinguish hope from a guarantee]] — By supporting worthwhile action while acknowledging uncertainty, constraints, and the need to revise a plan.

Course note: [[02.08 Choose contribution without erasing yourself|Choose contribution without erasing yourself]] — A useful, agreed commitment that respects the recipient's agency and the giver's real capacity.
Course note: [[02.09 Keep purpose larger than one role|Keep purpose larger than one role]] — Activities and contributions can reveal meaningful possibilities beyond a single title or role.

Course note: [[02.10 Make a values agreement with your future self|Make a values agreement with your future self]] — Specific actions, visible trade-offs, protected limits, and a date to review what actually happened.

Course note: [[02.11 Separate a value from a status symbol|Separate a value from a status symbol]] — A value guides action across situations; a symbol is one possible public marker that may or may not serve it.

Course note: [[02.12 Test a value when it becomes inconvenient|Test a value when it becomes inconvenient]] — They show the action you choose when the principle competes with comfort, approval, or another duty.

Course note: [[02.13 Build hope that can survive revision|Build hope that can survive revision]] — Workable hope commits to a valued possibility and revisable action while acknowledging that the outcome is uncertain.

Course note: [[02.14 Let gratitude and dissatisfaction coexist|Let gratitude and dissatisfaction coexist]] — Appreciation can describe what is good while dissatisfaction identifies a real need for action.
Course note: [[02.15 Define success in the life it should serve|Define success in the life it should serve]] — The capability or life purpose it serves, along with the costs of the path to it.
Course note: [[04.01 Sort control, influence, and concern|Sort control, influence, and concern]] — Influence can affect an outcome without determining it.
Course note: [[04.02 Separate responsibility from blame|Separate responsibility from blame]] — No. A useful response, the cause of a problem, and moral accountability are separate questions.
Course note: [[04.03 State a boundary as your action|State a boundary as your action]] — It specifies your participation and actions rather than assuming authority over another person's choices.
Course note: [[04.04 Say no without inventing a defense|Say no without inventing a defense]] — A clear decision, truthful explanation where useful, and no promise beyond your capacity.
Course note: [[04.05 Make promises small enough to keep|Make promises small enough to keep]] — A defined action, timing, dependencies, and a plan for communicating changes.

Course note: [[04.06 Distinguish solitude from isolation|Distinguish solitude from isolation]] — Its degree of choice, its effects, and whether access to support and valued participation remains available.

Course note: [[04.07 Hold standards without demanding universal approval|Hold standards without demanding universal approval]] — A clear standard and a genuine account of what could change the decision.

Course note: [[04.08 Build an agency plan for one recurring difficulty|Build an agency plan for one recurring difficulty]] — Chosen actions, requests, boundaries, support, and a review of real outcomes.
Course note: [[04.09 Decide when to disengage|Decide when to disengage]] — It protects a legitimate limit and includes an appropriate later action when the underlying obligation remains.

Course note: [[04.10 Repair your part without owning the whole conflict|Repair your part without owning the whole conflict]] — Your specific action, its effect, and the change you will make, without claiming control over another person's choices.

Course note: [[04.11 Negotiate a commitment before capacity breaks|Negotiate a commitment before capacity breaks]] — The original promise, the changed constraint, specific alternatives, and a clear new agreement.
Course note: [[04.12 Ask for help while retaining a decision|Ask for help while retaining a decision]] — By defining the needed contribution while keeping decision rights and next actions clear.

Course note: [[04.13 Honor support with a clear next step|Honor support with a clear next step]] — State what you understood, what you will do, and any relevant follow-up without surrendering your own choice.
Course note: [[05.01 Map the behavior loop|Map the behavior loop]] — The setting and immediate consequence can explain repetition better than a global label about willpower.

Course note: [[05.02 Make the first action unambiguous|Make the first action unambiguous]] — It reduces a real barrier and begins the intended activity rather than replacing it with unrelated preparation.
Course note: [[05.03 Attach a behavior to a reliable cue|Attach a behavior to a reliable cue]] — A recognizable moment and setting in which the intended behavior is feasible.

Course note: [[05.04 Design the environment around the choice|Design the environment around the choice]] — To make the intended behavior more available and reduce repeated reliance on effortful remembering or restraint.
Course note: [[05.05 Use rewards without losing the purpose|Use rewards without losing the purpose]] — Repetition of a worthwhile behavior without undermining its purpose or your ability to choose.
Course note: [[05.06 Let identity follow evidence|Let identity follow evidence]] — By tying it to observable, revisable patterns of action rather than treating it as a permanent verdict.
Course note: [[05.07 Track enough to learn|Track enough to learn]] — To reveal behavior and conditions that help you learn, not to turn a streak into a measure of personal worth.
Course note: [[05.08 Recover after a missed repetition|Recover after a missed repetition]] — A feasible return plus an examination of the conditions that caused the miss.

Course note: [[05.09 Distinguish repetition from deliberate improvement|Distinguish repetition from deliberate improvement]] — It can reinforce existing performance, including errors, unless feedback and an appropriate challenge change the practice.

Course note: [[05.10 Understand compounding without magical arithmetic|Understand compounding without magical arithmetic]] — Real behavior is affected by quality, feedback, constraints, interruptions, and changing conditions rather than a guaranteed growth rate.
Course note: [[05.11 Evaluate a habit-forming product|Evaluate a habit-forming product]] — No. Engagement must be evaluated against the user's aims, outcomes, and ability to choose.
Course note: [[05.12 Run a habit experiment|Run a habit experiment]] — A specific behavior, visible conditions, a simple record, and a planned review that can change the design.

Course note: [[05.13 Replace a behavior without losing its function|Replace a behavior without losing its function]] — The cue and need remain after the old action is removed, so an unrelated substitute may not be usable when the moment arrives.

Course note: [[05.14 Change friction before relying on resolve|Change friction before relying on resolve]] — The effort or delay between a cue and an action, which can be changed to support a chosen behavior.

Course note: [[05.15 Use accountability without making shame the mechanism|Use accountability without making shame the mechanism]] — Specific actions, honest reporting, and a plan for revision after a miss rather than pressure to hide it.
Course note: [[05.16 Build a reset point into a habit|Build a reset point into a habit]] — It gives a feasible return after disruption and a way to redesign a pattern that no longer fits.

Course note: [[05.17 Audit whether a habit still serves its purpose|Audit whether a habit still serves its purpose]] — When its purpose, effects, or costs may have changed enough to alter the right action.
Course note: [[09.01 Describe before interpreting|Describe before interpreting]] — It makes the inference visible, testable, and open to other explanations.

Course note: [[09.02 Establish a baseline before calling something unusual|Establish a baseline before calling something unusual]] — A relevant baseline, context, and more evidence than a single ambiguous cue.

Course note: [[09.03 Notice selection and survivorship|Notice selection and survivorship]] — A distorted conclusion caused by examining visible survivors while missing relevant failures or excluded cases.

Course note: [[09.04 Use base rates before vivid details|Use base rates before vivid details]] — They provide a starting context for interpreting case-specific clues rather than letting vividness set the whole estimate.
Course note: [[09.05 Look for confirmation and disconfirmation|Look for confirmation and disconfirmation]] — It leads to observations that could distinguish it from other explanations.
Course note: [[09.06 Interpret body language with humility|Interpret body language with humility]] — As context-sensitive prompts for clarification, not as unique proof of a hidden mental state.
Course note: [[09.07 Recognize framing and anchoring|Recognize framing and anchoring]] — An initial reference point influences later judgment, sometimes beyond its evidential value.
Course note: [[09.08 Separate intuition from expertise|Separate intuition from expertise]] — Repeated experience in a sufficiently regular environment with useful feedback.
Course note: [[09.09 Keep uncertainty visible|Keep uncertainty visible]] — Stating evidence, alternatives, and confidence at a level the evidence can support.
Course note: [[09.10 Run an observation audit|Run an observation audit]] — To inspect how a conclusion arose and choose a check that could improve it.

Course note: [[09.11 Stop sunk costs from making the next choice|Stop sunk costs from making the next choice]] — Allowing an irrecoverable past investment to decide a future choice when it does not change the options' future value.

Course note: [[09.12 Check availability before judging frequency|Check availability before judging frequency]] — Vividness and recency affect memory, while frequency requires information about the wider set of cases.
Course note: [[09.13 Keep hindsight from rewriting the decision|Keep hindsight from rewriting the decision]] — It preserves the information and reasons available before the outcome was known.

Course note: [[09.14 Calibrate confidence with a track record|Calibrate confidence with a track record]] — The match between expressed confidence and how often comparable judgments prove correct over time.

Course note: [[09.15 Notice regression after an extreme result|Notice regression after an extreme result]] — Extreme observations in a variable process tend to be followed by less extreme observations, which can mislead simple before-and-after judgments.
Course note: [[09.16 Notice the evidence that is missing|Notice the evidence that is missing]] — When a hypothesis predicts observable evidence that should have appeared under the actual conditions.

Course note: [[09.17 Audit a first impression with a short record|Audit a first impression with a short record]] — To compare recorded predictions with outcomes and calibrate which cues are reliable in which settings.
Course note: [[10.01 Find the claim and its support|Find the claim and its support]] — Its conclusion and supporting reasons should be reconstructed fairly.
Course note: [[10.02 Distinguish validity from truth|Distinguish validity from truth]] — Whether the conclusion follows from the premises if those premises are assumed true.
Course note: [[10.03 Work carefully with if and only if|Work carefully with if and only if]] — No. B may have other sufficient causes.
Course note: [[10.04 Interpret and, or, not, and all|Interpret and, or, not, and all]] — At least one member of the group does not have the stated property.

Course note: [[10.05 Test an argument with a counterexample|Test an argument with a counterexample]] — That a universal claim or inference needs revision when a relevant case satisfies its conditions but defeats its conclusion.

Course note: [[10.06 Identify a reasoning error without name-calling|Identify a reasoning error without name-calling]] — It identifies the exact inferential problem and explains how it affects the conclusion.

Course note: [[10.07 Ask questions that open the reasoning|Ask questions that open the reasoning]] — A genuine question allows the answer to affect the conversation and is applied fairly to both sides.
Course note: [[10.08 Disagree with the strongest version|Disagree with the strongest version]] — It directs disagreement toward the strongest real reasons instead of an easily defeated substitute.
Course note: [[10.09 Use logic in an everyday decision|Use logic in an everyday decision]] — It clarifies implications and assumptions while leaving factual and value judgments visible.
Course note: [[10.10 Keep the scope of a negative clear|Keep the scope of a negative clear]] — The part of a statement that the negative applies to, which can change the statement's meaning.
Course note: [[10.11 Test all, some, and none with small cases|Test all, some, and none with small cases]] — A universal claim covers every member of the group; one example checks only one member.

Course note: [[10.12 Map premises before debating a conclusion|Map premises before debating a conclusion]] — To show how premises and assumptions support a conclusion so each part can be tested fairly.

Course note: [[10.13 Use contradiction as a test, not a trick|Use contradiction as a test, not a trick]] — That the set of premises and steps cannot all be correct as stated, not necessarily which single premise failed.

Course note: [[10.14 Separate a confident speaker from a supported claim|Separate a confident speaker from a supported claim]] — It can guide where to investigate, but the claim still needs relevant scope and support.

Course note: [[10.15 Ask whether a reason reaches the conclusion|Ask whether a reason reaches the conclusion]] — Testing whether a stated reason actually supports the conclusion through a defensible premise or mechanism.
Course note: [[11.01 Ask what a claim would predict|Ask what a claim would predict]] — It specifies observable implications and conditions under which evidence could require revision.
Course note: [[11.02 Distinguish correlation from intervention|Distinguish correlation from intervention]] — Several causal structures and selection effects can produce the same observed pattern.
Course note: [[11.03 Look for confounding variables|Look for confounding variables]] — A factor that affects both the proposed cause and outcome, distorting the observed association.

Course note: [[11.04 Understand comparison groups and selection|Understand comparison groups and selection]] — Who enters and remains in a comparison can change the apparent effect and its applicability.

Course note: [[11.05 Separate model, mechanism, and reality|Separate model, mechanism, and reality]] — To simplify selected features for explanation or prediction while keeping assumptions and omissions visible.

Course note: [[11.06 Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence|Weigh anecdotes and systematic evidence]] — That a reported experience occurred for someone, while broader frequency and causal claims need further evidence.
Course note: [[11.07 Consider replication, uncertainty, and revision|Consider replication, uncertainty, and revision]] — It checks whether a result survives new samples, methods, and investigators.
Course note: [[11.08 Match evidence to the stakes|Match evidence to the stakes]] — The decision's stakes, reversibility, alternatives, and potential harms.

Course note: [[11.09 Distinguish observation, intervention, and counterfactual|Distinguish observation, intervention, and counterfactual]] — The groups may differ in other ways, so changing a factor may not reproduce the observed association.

Course note: [[11.10 Draw a causal path before adjusting for variables|Draw a causal path before adjusting for variables]] — It makes assumed relationships and variable roles visible for testing; it does not prove that the arrows are correct.

Course note: [[11.11 Separate prediction from explanation|Separate prediction from explanation]] — A pattern can forecast outcomes without revealing the causal mechanism, and a plausible mechanism may still predict poorly.

Course note: [[11.12 Treat surprising data as a question for the model|Treat surprising data as a question for the model]] — Check the observation, examine assumptions, and derive tests that could refine the explanation.
Course note: [[11.13 Check whether a measure is only a proxy|Check whether a measure is only a proxy]] — The proxy can improve while the underlying outcome stays the same or gets worse.

Course note: [[11.14 Treat a null result as information|Treat a null result as information]] — Its meaning depends on whether the change occurred, the measure and duration could detect an effect, and alternative explanations.
Course note: [[12.01 Define the decision before using a model|Define the decision before using a model]] — The actual choice, available options, stakes, owner, and timing.
Course note: [[12.02 Use opportunity cost and reversibility|Use opportunity cost and reversibility]] — The value of the best realistic alternative forgone when a choice uses a limited resource.
Course note: [[12.03 Separate decision quality from outcome quality|Separate decision quality from outcome quality]] — Uncertainty can produce success from a poor process or failure from a sound one.
Course note: [[12.04 Build a strategy kernel|Build a strategy kernel]] — A diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding approach, and coordinated actions that implement it.

Course note: [[12.05 Use feedback loops to see change over time|Use feedback loops to see change over time]] — Actions can change later conditions and responses, so immediate effects may not represent the full result.
Course note: [[12.06 Beware local optimization|Beware local optimization]] — Improving a part or metric in a way that may worsen the wider system or purpose.

Course note: [[12.07 Use scenarios rather than one confident forecast|Use scenarios rather than one confident forecast]] — To expose assumptions and prepare adaptable choices across plausible futures.
Course note: [[12.08 Make a decision reviewable|Make a decision reviewable]] — A recorded rationale, relevant signals, a review point, and conditions for revising the choice.

Course note: [[12.09 See stocks, flows, and delays in a changing system|See stocks, flows, and delays in a changing system]] — A stock is an accumulated quantity; flows are the rates or events that add to or remove from it.
Course note: [[12.10 Find a proximate objective|Find a proximate objective]] — It is close enough to act on and verify while resolving a meaningful part of the larger challenge.

Course note: [[12.11 Check for a chain-link bottleneck|Check for a chain-link bottleneck]] — A system whose overall performance depends on several complementary parts, so a weak part can limit the value of improvements elsewhere.

Course note: [[12.12 Use a decision threshold before results arrive|Use a decision threshold before results arrive]] — It makes the response to evidence less vulnerable to wishful revision after the result is known.

Course note: [[12.13 Plan for a surprise without pretending to predict it|Plan for a surprise without pretending to predict it]] — A plausible changed condition, an observable trigger, preserved options, and a feasible first response.

Course note: [[12.14 Keep a reserve for the constraint that matters|Keep a reserve for the constraint that matters]] — When a shortage in a critical resource would stop the whole plan or impose a large cost.
Course note: [[17.01 Define ethical influence|Define ethical influence]] — Truthful information, room for informed choice, and attention to consequences for the affected people.
Course note: [[17.02 Prepare interests and alternatives|Prepare interests and alternatives]] — It provides a realistic comparison for evaluating offers and limits.
Course note: [[17.03 Listen before proposing a solution|Listen before proposing a solution]] — The proposed solution should address the person's actual aim and constraints.
Course note: [[17.04 Make value concrete|Make value concrete]] — It specifies who benefits, what changes, under which conditions, and at what cost.
Course note: [[17.05 Use empathy without pretending to agree|Use empathy without pretending to agree]] — Understanding of a concern, not automatic agreement with every requested outcome.

Course note: [[17.06 Generate options before dividing a fixed pie|Generate options before dividing a fixed pie]] — When different priorities allow changes in scope, timing, risk, or other terms that improve the fit for both sides.
Course note: [[17.07 Handle an objection as information|Handle an objection as information]] — Information about facts, costs, priorities, trust, or a choice that needs to be respected.
Course note: [[17.08 Close with terms that can be delivered|Close with terms that can be delivered]] — Defined actions, owners, timing, conditions, and a way to review or change it.

Course note: [[17.09 Separate information exchange from bargaining|Separate information exchange from bargaining]] — Understanding interests and constraints first can reveal options that an immediate concession fight would hide.

Course note: [[17.10 Compare concessions by value, not symmetry|Compare concessions by value, not symmetry]] — Parties may value the same term differently, so a clear exchange can improve both options without equal sacrifice.

Course note: [[17.11 Use a calibrated question to reveal constraints|Use a calibrated question to reveal constraints]] — To reveal interests and constraints so both parties can examine workable options, not to force agreement.
Course note: [[17.12 Confirm who will do what after agreement|Confirm who will do what after agreement]] — Clear deliverables, owners, timing, dependencies, and a shared record of the terms.

Course note: [[17.13 Build a professional connection by usefulness|Build a professional connection by usefulness]] — Specific interest, relevant contribution, respect for the person's time and choice, and no hidden demand for immediate return.
Course note: [[17.14 Make appreciation specific and fair|Make appreciation specific and fair]] — It truthfully names a specific action and effect without exaggeration or a hidden demand.
Course note: [[20.01 Distinguish goal, plan, tactic, and strategy|Distinguish goal, plan, tactic, and strategy]] — A diagnosis of the challenge and a coherent approach to overcoming it.
Course note: [[20.02 Find the decisive constraint|Find the decisive constraint]] — A limiting step or condition that constrains the performance of the larger process.
Course note: [[20.03 Allocate effort where it matters|Allocate effort where it matters]] — A clear connection between the main challenge, expected effect, resource cost, and excluded alternatives.
Course note: [[20.04 Use position and timing|Use position and timing]] — The usefulness of a move depends on current resources, constraints, timing, and likely responses.

Course note: [[20.05 Anticipate responses without pretending to predict people|Anticipate responses without pretending to predict people]] — Several plausible responses, incentives, uncertainty, and opportunities to gather information.
Course note: [[20.06 Know when competition is the wrong frame|Know when competition is the wrong frame]] — When shared interests, repeat relationships, or joint value are ignored.
Course note: [[20.07 Compare strategic traditions in context|Compare strategic traditions in context]] — Their aims, assumptions, and moral limits differ, so transfer needs justification.
Course note: [[20.08 Write a strategic brief|Write a strategic brief]] — It links diagnosis, coordinated action, ethical limits, and evidence that can revise the plan.

Course note: [[20.09 Choose a setting that suits the real goal|Choose a setting that suits the real goal]] — It can alter constraints and opportunities so a legitimate goal becomes more reachable without merely increasing effort.

Course note: [[20.10 Use information without pretending it is complete|Use information without pretending it is complete]] — It targets unknowns that could change the action and weighs the cost and ethics of obtaining them.

Course note: [[20.11 Distinguish a strategic analogy from a recipe|Distinguish a strategic analogy from a recipe]] — Borrow a specific structural insight while naming differences in rules, stakes, and ethics before applying it.

Course note: [[20.12 Ask when a clever tactic damages the relationship|Ask when a clever tactic damages the relationship]] — The full goal, including future cooperation, trust, costs, and ethical limits.

Course note: [[20.13 Use a warning signal without becoming alarmist|Use a warning signal without becoming alarmist]] — To prompt timely review of a consequential assumption, not to prove a prediction automatically.

Course note: [[21.01 Describe the gap before naming a solution|Describe the gap before naming a solution]] — The current and desired conditions, affected people, context, and evidence of the gap, without assuming one fix.
Course note: [[21.02 Set the boundary of the problem|Set the boundary of the problem]] — It defines a feasible investigation while exposing connected factors and costs that the chosen scope may omit.
Course note: [[21.03 Separate symptoms from candidate causes|Separate symptoms from candidate causes]] — It proposes a mechanism that should predict additional observations or responses to change.

Course note: [[21.04 Break a complex problem into linked parts|Break a complex problem into linked parts]] — A part can improve while the whole problem remains or worsens if important connections are ignored.
Course note: [[21.05 Compare fixes against the same criteria|Compare fixes against the same criteria]] — It reduces the chance of changing the standard to favor the first solution you liked.

Course note: [[21.06 Design a small test that could fail informatively|Design a small test that could fail informatively]] — A defined change, relevant observation, comparison where possible, time boundary, and result that could challenge the hypothesis.

Course note: [[21.07 Watch for side effects and displaced costs|Watch for side effects and displaced costs]] — A burden moved to another person, stage, or time while the chosen measure appears to improve.

Course note: [[21.08 Decide whether to continue, change, or stop|Decide whether to continue, change, or stop]] — Whether the change was implemented as intended and whether it improved the relevant outcome without unacceptable side effects.

Course note: [[21.09 Define evidence before a proposed change|Define evidence before a proposed change]] — It makes the comparison clearer and reduces the temptation to redefine success after seeing the outcome.
Course note: [[21.10 Choose a reversible first step|Choose a reversible first step]] — Its likely costs, including trust and disruption, can be contained or repaired if the idea fails.
Course note: [[21.11 Ask whether a fix works beyond the pilot|Ask whether a fix works beyond the pilot]] — Its conditions, attention, or capacity may change when the approach becomes routine.

Course note: [[21.12 Keep a decision record others can challenge|Keep a decision record others can challenge]] — It preserves the original reasons, alternatives, uncertainties, and review conditions for later comparison.
Course note: [[25.01 Define what money is for in your plan|Define what money is for in your plan]] — It guides trade-offs and keeps financial measures tied to actual needs and values.

Course note: [[25.02 Track cash flow without moralizing it|Track cash flow without moralizing it]] — Cash shortages can occur when obligations arrive before income even if monthly totals seem adequate.
Course note: [[25.03 Build a budget as a revisable plan|Build a budget as a revisable plan]] — A future income-and-expense plan that should be compared with actual results and revised.
Course note: [[25.04 Understand assets, liabilities, and net position|Understand assets, liabilities, and net position]] — Resources with value and obligations owed at a point in time.
Course note: [[25.05 Compare borrowing by full cost and purpose|Compare borrowing by full cost and purpose]] — Purpose, full repayment cost, timing, terms, and the ability to meet future obligations.

Course note: [[25.06 Treat investing as risk management, not a prediction contest|Treat investing as risk management, not a prediction contest]] — No. It can reduce concentration, while broad market and other risks remain.
Course note: [[25.07 Notice behavioral traps around money|Notice behavioral traps around money]] — A past irrecoverable payment cannot be changed by continuing an unsuitable choice.
Course note: [[25.08 Know the limits of general money advice|Know the limits of general money advice]] — Rules, products, risks, and personal circumstances can change materially.
Course note: [[25.09 Reconcile the record with reality|Reconcile the record with reality]] — It compares a personal or business record with independent transactions and investigates differences.

Course note: [[25.10 Keep uncertainty visible in a money forecast|Keep uncertainty visible in a money forecast]] — They show how choices hold up under different plausible conditions without claiming to know the future.

Course note: [[25.11 Compare fees and incentives before choosing help|Compare fees and incentives before choosing help]] — Compensation and total fees can affect recommendations and the net result for the person using the service.

Course note: [[25.12 Build a money review around decisions|Build a money review around decisions]] — A clear decision grounded in actual records, changed assumptions, and the purpose the money serves.

Course note: [[25.13 Separate near-term resilience from distant wealth goals|Separate near-term resilience from distant wealth goals]] — Near-term obligations require availability and stability that distant goals may not require in the same way.
Course note: [[26.01 Begin with scarcity and trade-offs|Begin with scarcity and trade-offs]] — Limited resources have alternative uses, each with costs and benefits.
Course note: [[26.02 Compare marginal changes|Compare marginal changes]] — The added benefit and added cost of a small change from the current position.

Course note: [[26.03 Understand incentives without reducing people to them|Understand incentives without reducing people to them]] — Rules can change actual choices, including unintended responses and shifted costs.
Course note: [[26.04 See how exchange can create value|See how exchange can create value]] — When parties value alternatives differently and can choose on informed, acceptable terms.
Course note: [[26.05 Read prices as signals with limits|Read prices as signals with limits]] — It reflects some market conditions but does not reveal every cause or external cost by itself.

Course note: [[26.06 Use simple accounting for public and business claims|Use simple accounting for public and business claims]] — A clearer view of resource flows and obligations, while leaving value judgments explicit.
Course note: [[26.07 Interpret averages, risk, and distribution|Interpret averages, risk, and distribution]] — An average can hide who experiences gains, losses, or exceptional outcomes.

Course note: [[26.08 Read national economic stories as hypotheses|Read national economic stories as hypotheses]] — Outcomes arise from interacting conditions, and an explanation may not transfer unchanged to another setting.

Course note: [[26.09 Follow a policy through incentives and response|Follow a policy through incentives and response]] — People can adjust to changed rules, creating indirect benefits, burdens, or side effects beyond the intended effect.
Course note: [[26.10 Separate growth from living standards|Separate growth from living standards]] — It can hide price changes, uneven gains, unpaid work, and other conditions people experience.

Course note: [[26.11 Examine a trade barrier from several positions|Examine a trade barrier from several positions]] — The goal, mechanism, affected groups, transition costs, alternatives, and likely responses.

Course note: [[26.12 Ask what a historical economic analogy leaves out|Ask what a historical economic analogy leaves out]] — As a hypothesis about a mechanism whose relevant similarities, differences, and evidence must be examined.
Course note: [[26.13 Add institutions to an economic model|Add institutions to an economic model]] — Rules and organizations shape how incentives translate into actual choices and outcomes.

Course note: [[31.01 Distinguish behavior, experience, and explanation|Distinguish behavior, experience, and explanation]] — Behavior, subjective report, and causal theory provide different kinds of information.

Course note: [[31.02 Understand emotion as information in decision-making|Understand emotion as information in decision-making]] — It can direct attention to something important while still requiring interpretation and evidence.

Course note: [[31.03 Interpret the brain through careful models|Interpret the brain through careful models]] — They simplify interacting processes and do not by themselves identify an individual's motive or destiny.
Course note: [[31.04 Examine memory as reconstruction|Examine memory as reconstruction]] — Memory is reconstructed through attention and later interpretation rather than being a perfect recording.

Course note: [[31.05 Use psychological categories without self-diagnosis|Use psychological categories without self-diagnosis]] — As a limited question or description supported by evidence, not a casual diagnosis.

Course note: [[31.06 Compare competing accounts of consciousness|Compare competing accounts of consciousness]] — Different accounts may explain different phenomena and require different kinds of evidence.

Course note: [[31.07 Recognize stagecraft behind apparent mind reading|Recognize stagecraft behind apparent mind reading]] — No. Stagecraft, information, suggestion, and selective memory can produce convincing effects.

Course note: [[31.08 Keep a plural but disciplined mind model|Keep a plural but disciplined mind model]] — It matches each explanation to a specific question, evidence, and limit rather than claiming one lens explains all.
Course note: [[31.09 Ask which behavior a theory predicts|Ask which behavior a theory predicts]] — Clear scope, competing alternatives, and observations that could distinguish the explanations.

Course note: [[31.10 Notice how body state can shape judgment|Notice how body state can shape judgment]] — As relevant context that may justify a pause or support, without automatically invalidating or determining the decision.

Course note: [[31.11 Separate a memory from an inference about it|Separate a memory from an inference about it]] — Memory can incorporate later meaning, so the distinction makes a consequential account clearer and more checkable.

Course note: [[31.12 Use a mental model without turning it into an identity|Use a mental model without turning it into an identity]] — Use it as a limited question or organizing tool, while preserving context, individual variation, and clinical boundaries.

Course note: [[31.13 Ask what a belief does without claiming why it is true|Ask what a belief does without claiming why it is true]] — It may explain aspects of formation or function, but it does not by itself settle the belief's truth.
Course note: [[32.01 Separate what is from what ought to be|Separate what is from what ought to be]] — A conclusion about what ought to be done requires a normative premise or value.
Course note: [[32.02 Compare consequences, duties, and character|Compare consequences, duties, and character]] — Consequences, obligations, and qualities of action or character.

Course note: [[32.03 Use reciprocity without erasing differences|Use reciprocity without erasing differences]] — Others may have different needs and preferences, so perspective-taking should be checked with them.

Course note: [[32.04 Treat consent and dignity as real constraints|Treat consent and dignity as real constraints]] — People must not be treated only as tools whose informed choice can be bypassed for an outcome.
Course note: [[32.05 Consider distribution, not only totals|Consider distribution, not only totals]] — A good total can conceal serious unequal burdens or exclusion.
Course note: [[32.06 Face a duty conflict honestly|Face a duty conflict honestly]] — Two legitimate obligations cannot both be fully satisfied under the available conditions.
Course note: [[32.07 Learn from ethical failure in history|Learn from ethical failure in history]] — It reveals mechanisms by which authority, incentives, and exclusion can normalize harm.
Course note: [[32.08 Write an ethical decision record|Write an ethical decision record]] — Facts, values, duties, consequences, affected people, alternatives, uncertainty, and review.
Course note: [[32.09 Test a principle on the hard case|Test a principle on the hard case]] — Whether a proposed principle survives role reversal or needs a clearly relevant exception.
Course note: [[32.10 Include absent people in a decision|Include absent people in a decision]] — A decision can shift costs onto people who are not represented in the discussion.

Course note: [[32.11 Distinguish a good intention from a justified action|Distinguish a good intention from a justified action]] — They do not by themselves settle consequences, ignored information, alternatives, or duties of repair.

Course note: [[32.12 Give a moral disagreement a useful shape|Give a moral disagreement a useful shape]] — Identify whether the dispute concerns facts, meanings, values, or priorities, then examine the strongest reasons on each side.
Course note: [[33.01 Ask what kind of question you are asking|Ask what kind of question you are asking]] — Different questions need different evidence, concepts, and standards of argument.
Course note: [[33.02 Examine how knowledge is possible|Examine how knowledge is possible]] — Its source, supporting reasons, limits, and possible correction.

Course note: [[33.03 Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing|Distinguish appearance, concept, and thing]] — It selects features for a purpose and may omit other relevant aspects of the thing described.
Course note: [[33.04 Compare freedom and social obligation|Compare freedom and social obligation]] — Different meanings can support different judgments about the same rule or institution.

Course note: [[33.05 Study a philosophical tradition in context|Study a philosophical tradition in context]] — Their claims address specific questions and assumptions that may differ from present concerns.

Course note: [[33.06 Use thought experiments to expose commitments|Use thought experiments to expose commitments]] — To isolate and test a concept or principle, while recognizing the simplification's limits.
Course note: [[33.07 Compare pessimism, hope, and meaning|Compare pessimism, hope, and meaning]] — By their questions, reasons, explanatory strengths, omissions, and practical consequences.

Course note: [[33.08 Form a provisional philosophy of practice|Form a provisional philosophy of practice]] — It guides action through explicit reasons while remaining open to evidence, conflict, and revision.

Course note: [[33.09 Build an argument from premises to conclusion|Build an argument from premises to conclusion]] — Whether the conclusion follows from its premises and whether those premises are justified.

Course note: [[33.10 Compare accounts of the self without flattening them|Compare accounts of the self without flattening them]] — Different accounts may address different kinds of continuity, responsibility, or experience.

Course note: [[33.11 Ask what would count as a good life|Ask what would count as a good life]] — It clarifies which goods matter, how they conflict, and what choices express them under real constraints.

Course note: [[33.12 Practice charitable disagreement with a tradition|Practice charitable disagreement with a tradition]] — Representing a view's problem and strongest reasons accurately before offering a serious objection.

Course note: [[35.01 Move from a question to a measurable model|Move from a question to a measurable model]] — The system, variables, units or definitions, assumptions, and the question it aims to answer.

Course note: [[35.02 Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration|Read a diagram as a claim, not decoration]] — Labels, units, scale, direction, and whether the depicted relationship is descriptive or causal.

Course note: [[35.03 Distinguish classification from explanation|Distinguish classification from explanation]] — No. It organizes observations; causal explanation requires further evidence and mechanism.

Course note: [[35.04 Think across scale in astronomy and physics|Think across scale in astronomy and physics]] — Through repeatable observations, instruments, models, and predictions checked against evidence.
Course note: [[35.05 Read engineering as constrained design|Read engineering as constrained design]] — It must meet a purpose under multiple real constraints and be checked for failure.

Course note: [[35.06 Understand specialist reference books|Understand specialist reference books]] — It often presumes professional context, training, current standards, and safe procedures beyond general reading.

Course note: [[35.07 Examine formal proof and its assumptions|Examine formal proof and its assumptions]] — A conclusion follows from specified premises and rules; empirical fit is a separate question.
Course note: [[35.08 Build a technical learning route|Build a technical learning route]] — Advanced material assumes concepts and methods that need to be learned and checked in sequence.

Course note: [[35.09 Distinguish a model's fit from its truth everywhere|Distinguish a model's fit from its truth everywhere]] — The conditions and questions for which its assumptions and tests make it useful.

Course note: [[35.10 Read a technical result through its uncertainty|Read a technical result through its uncertainty]] — Its unit, method, relevant uncertainty, and the decision context in which it is used.

Course note: The collection is broad but uneven. A filename is not proof that a complete edition is present, and repeated editions do not add independent evidence. Some scans contain difficult text or image-only diagrams. This course integrates the collection’s teachable themes; it does not reproduce every page, catalog entry, game variation, drill, recipe, or professional procedure.
Questions to keep open

Course note: Which advice transfers to your circumstances? Which claims rest on anecdotes or older evidence? Which accounts disagree about agency, competition, faith, intimacy, and success? What would change your judgment?
Where the course has limits

Course note: Specialist medical interpretation, individualized treatment, current legal and tax rules, investment selection, unsupervised combat techniques, and unauthorized access to computer systems are not established by completing a reading course. Technical material is used for literacy, critical evaluation, supervised learning, and defensive understanding. Religious and paranormal claims are examined as claims and traditions rather than converted into scientific facts.
Your unanswered questions

Course note: Record the question, why it matters, what the supplied material actually supports, what remains missing, and the kind of evidence or qualified help that would resolve it. Do not fill a gap with certainty merely to make the course feel complete.

Course note: Build a personal practice portfolio around one worthwhile, bounded improvement project. Use ideas from several modules in the same project and show what happened.
The brief
Course note: Define the situation, baseline, value, desired outcome, constraints, stakeholders, and review date. Explain why the project matters.
The design
Course note: Connect at least four lessons from different modules. Give each a specific job in the plan. Include one tension or limit rather than claiming every method agrees.
The experiment
Course note: Run a feasible trial. Record actions, observations, unintended effects, and changes. Protect consent, commitments, and appropriate limits.
The review
Course note: Compare the result with the baseline. Distinguish outcome quality from decision quality, name uncertainty, and revise your explanation.
The next cycle
Course note: Present a concise field guide: what to keep, what to stop, what to test next, and when to review again. Include evidence from your own attempts.
Course note: A strong capstone is specific, honest about limits, and useful for the next decision. It is not a performance of having perfected your life.
